chapters.title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
chapters.summary: In this chapter: chemical reactions in daily life; chemical equations and balancing; combination and exothermic reactions; decomposition and endothermic reactions.

lessons.title: Chemical Reactions in Daily Life

activities.prompt: Why does milk left out on a summer day smell different by evening?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: When Things Change Around Us
activities.body: Look around you. Milk left out in summer changes. An iron pan in damp air changes. Food you eat gets digested. In all these, the starting substance changes its nature and identity a little. When such a chemical change happens, we say a chemical reaction has taken place.
keyPoints: Milk left in summer heat changes.
Iron left in humid air changes.
A chemical change means a chemical reaction has happened.
activities.explanation: Chemical reactions are happening all around you, every day.

activities.prompt: Priya forgot a glass of milk on the table all summer afternoon. By evening the milk smelled strange and looked different. Did a chemical reaction happen in the glass?
steps: The milk stayed at room temperature on a hot day, so it changed.
The changed milk now smells and looks different from fresh milk.
This means the nature and identity of the milk changed somewhat.
Whenever a chemical change occurs, a chemical reaction has taken place, so yes, a reaction happened in the milk.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: You leave a bowl of milk on the table on a hot summer day. What happens to it?
options: It stays exactly the same
It changes
It turns into ice
It becomes heavier
activities.explanation: Milk left at room temperature in summer changes. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: When a magnesium ribbon burns, it shines with a dazzling ______ flame.
activities.hint: Think of the brightest colour you know.
activities.explanation: Magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame. It is hard to miss!

activities.prompt: Magnesium burns in air and a white powder is left behind. What is this powder?
options: Magnesium oxide
Potassium iodide
Lead nitrate
Zinc granules
activities.explanation: Magnesium joins with oxygen in the air to form magnesium oxide.

activities.prompt: Match each thing from your book to what happens with it.
pairs: burns with a dazzling white flame
activities.explanation: Each of these is a chemical reaction from your book. Great matching!

activities.prompt: Put the burning of magnesium in the right order.
items: Take a magnesium ribbon
Burn it in air
It burns with a dazzling white flame
A white powder, magnesium oxide, is formed
activities.explanation: Magnesium meets oxygen in the air and burns brightly, leaving magnesium oxide. You ordered it perfectly!

activities.prompt: Which of these can show that a chemical reaction has taken place?
options: A change in colour
A gas is given off
A change in temperature
All of these
activities.explanation: A chemical reaction may show a change in state or colour, a gas given off, or a change in temperature. Any of these can be a clue!

activities.prompt: Ravi leaves an iron nail on the wet bathroom window. After some days the nail looks different. Why did the nail change?
options: The humid air slowly changed the iron into something new
The nail only got dirty, so washing will make it new
The nail melted a little in the warm bathroom air
The nail lost its shine because water washed its surface

why.The nail only got dirty, so washing will: Thinks change is only surface dirt that can be cleaned off
why.The nail melted a little in the warm bat: Thinks heat melted the nail, but melting is not the change here
why.The nail lost its shine because water wa: Thinks it is only loss of shine, not a change in identity

activities.explanation: Correct: iron in humid air changes, so its nature changed and a reaction happened

activities.prompt: Meera eats a banana. Inside her body the banana changes into new substances. What has happened inside her body?
options: A chemical reaction, because the banana's identity changed
No reaction, because the banana only got softer
No reaction, because nothing was burned or heated
A reaction only if the banana changed colour first

why.No reaction, because the banana only got: Thinks softening is the only change and identity stayed the same
why.No reaction, because nothing was burned: Thinks burning or heating is needed for every chemical reaction
why.A reaction only if the banana changed co: Thinks colour change is compulsory for every chemical reaction

activities.explanation: Correct: digestion changes the starting substance, so a chemical reaction took place

activities.prompt: Two clear liquids are mixed in a beaker. A yellow solid appears and the liquid changes colour. A student says, 'Nothing happened, both liquids were clear before.' What is the flaw in this claim?
options: A change in colour shows a chemical reaction happened
The student is right, because clear liquids cannot react
The solid appeared by magic, so no reaction happened
Only a change in temperature can show a reaction

why.The student is right, because clear liqu: Thinks clear liquids can never react with each other
why.The solid appeared by magic, so no react: Thinks a new solid appearing is not a real change
why.Only a change in temperature can show a: Thinks temperature change is the only sign of a reaction

activities.explanation: Correct: a chemical reaction may show a change in colour or state

activities.prompt: Zinc granules are dropped into dilute hydrochloric acid. Bubbles of gas rise fast and the tube feels warmer. Which signs show a chemical reaction happened?
options: Evolution of a gas and change in temperature
Only the bubbles, because warmth is not a sign
Only the warmth, because gases never show reactions
Neither sign, because the zinc just sank in the acid

why.Only the bubbles, because warmth is not: Thinks gas bubbles count but warmth does not count
why.Only the warmth, because gases never sho: Thinks temperature change counts but gas does not count
why.Neither sign, because the zinc just sank: Thinks sinking means nothing changed, ignoring gas and heat

activities.explanation: Correct: a reaction may show evolution of a gas and change in temperature

activities.prompt: A student wants to test if mixing two solutions gives a chemical reaction. Which is the fair test to do?
options: Mix them and watch for state, colour, gas or temperature change
Mix them and shake hard, because shaking makes reactions
Mix them and taste a little, because taste shows reactions
Mix them and wait one second, because reactions are instant

why.Mix them and shake hard, because shaking: Thinks shaking itself causes a chemical reaction
why.Mix them and taste a little, because tas: Thinks tasting is a safe and fair way to test reactions
why.Mix them and wait one second, because re: Thinks every reaction finishes instantly, so waiting is useless

activities.explanation: Correct: changes in state, colour, gas or temperature show a reaction

lessons.title: Chemical Equations and Balancing

activities.prompt: Why can't atoms ever disappear when chemicals react?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Describing a Reaction in Words
activities.body: A chemical reaction can be described in a sentence. A shorter way is a word-equation. In a word-equation, the substances that change are called reactants. The new substance formed is called the product. An arrow shows the reactants changing into the product. For example, when magnesium burns: Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide.
keyPoints: A word-equation is a short way to describe a reaction.
Reactants are the substances that undergo change.
The product is the new substance formed.
The arrow shows reactants changing to products.
activities.explanation: Word-equations help you see what changes into what.

activities.prompt: A teacher burns a shiny magnesium ribbon in air. It turns into a soft white powder. The student wonders: where did this powder come from, and did any mass appear from nowhere?
steps: The magnesium joined with oxygen from the air, so both of them changed, which makes them the reactants.
A new substance appeared, the white powder, so that powder must be the product of the change.
The word-equation Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide shows exactly this change happening.
Since mass can neither be created nor destroyed, the powder's mass came from the magnesium and oxygen, so the total mass stays the same.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Why Do We Balance Equations?
activities.body: A chemical equation represents a chemical reaction. An unbalanced equation has unequal mass on both sides. But mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a reaction. So we balance the equation. Balancing uses the smallest whole number coefficient. That way, atoms of each element match on both sides.
keyPoints: An unbalanced equation has unequal mass on both sides.
Mass can neither be created nor destroyed.
Balancing uses the smallest whole number coefficient.
activities.explanation: Balancing keeps the mass the same before and after the reaction.

activities.prompt: Which word-equation shows magnesium burning in air?
options: Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide
Magnesium oxide → Magnesium + Oxygen
Magnesium + Magnesium oxide → Oxygen
activities.explanation: Magnesium and oxygen are the reactants, and magnesium oxide is the product. Well done!

activities.prompt: In a reaction, the new substance that is formed is called the ______. Which word fits?
options: reactant
product
arrow
activities.explanation: The new substance formed during the reaction is the product. The substances that change are the reactants.

activities.prompt: An equation with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides is called an ______ equation.
activities.hint: Think of a see-saw with equal weight on both sides.
activities.explanation: In a balanced equation, each element has the same number of atoms on both sides.

activities.prompt: Match each symbol to what it tells you about a substance's physical state.
activities.explanation: These symbols show the physical state of each substance in an equation. Aqueous means dissolved in water.

activities.prompt: Why must a chemical equation be balanced?
options: Because mass can neither be created nor destroyed
Because equations look tidier when balanced
Because products are always heavier than reactants
activities.explanation: Mass is never created or destroyed in a reaction, so both sides must have equal mass. Great thinking!

activities.prompt: Put the steps for writing a balanced equation in the correct order.
items: Write the reaction as a word-equation
Write the chemical equation for the reaction
Count the atoms of each element on both sides
Balance using the smallest whole number coefficient
activities.explanation: First describe the reaction in words, then in symbols, then count atoms, and finally balance. You are becoming a chemistry expert!

activities.prompt: Magnesium burns in air. It joins with oxygen. A white powder forms. Nothing escapes into the air. What happens to the total mass of everything?
options: It stays the same.
It becomes less, because burning destroys some mass.
It becomes more, because fire adds extra weight.
It changes, but we cannot say how.

why.It becomes less, because burning destroy: Wrong: thinks burning makes matter disappear, but mass is never destroyed in a reaction.
why.It becomes more, because fire adds extra: Wrong: thinks fire adds mass from nowhere, but mass is never created in a reaction.
Wrong: thinks mass is unpredictable, but the law of conservation of mass lets us predict it.

activities.explanation: Right: mass can neither be created nor destroyed, so the total mass stays the same.

activities.prompt: A friend writes: Hydrogen + Oxygen → Water. She counts the atoms. The left side has more oxygen atoms than the right side. Why must she fix her equation?
options: Because both sides must have the same atoms, since mass stays equal.
Because the arrow must be drawn longer to show a big change.
Because word-equations must always have more words on the left.
Because water always needs extra oxygen added to it.

why.Because the arrow must be drawn longer t: Wrong: thinks the arrow's size matters, but only the atom counts on each side matter.
why.Because word-equations must always have: Wrong: thinks balancing is about words, but it is about atoms of each element.
why.Because water always needs extra oxygen: Wrong: thinks you can add atoms to one side, but atoms cannot be created in a reaction.

activities.explanation: Right: an unbalanced equation has unequal mass, so atom counts must match on both sides.

activities.prompt: A student writes (aq) after magnesium in an equation. But the magnesium is a solid strip. It is not mixed into water. What is the flaw in his writing?
options: Magnesium is a solid, so it should be marked (s).
Magnesium is a gas, so it should be marked (g).
Magnesium is a liquid, so it should be marked (l).
Magnesium should have no symbol at all after it.

why.Magnesium is a gas, so it should be mark: Wrong: thinks magnesium is a gas, but a magnesium strip is clearly a solid.
why.Magnesium is a liquid, so it should be m: Wrong: thinks magnesium is a liquid, but a magnesium strip is clearly a solid.
why.Magnesium should have no symbol at all a: Wrong: thinks solids get no symbol, but every physical state has its own symbol.

activities.explanation: Right: (aq) means dissolved in water, but solid magnesium should be marked (s).

activities.prompt: Zinc is heated with oxygen. The zinc and oxygen get used up. A new substance, zinc oxide, forms. In the word-equation for this, where does zinc oxide go?
options: On the right side, after the arrow.
On the left side, before the arrow.
Above the arrow, written in small letters.
Below the arrow, written in small letters.

Wrong: thinks new substances go on the left, but the left side holds the reactants.
why.Above the arrow, written in small letter: Wrong: thinks products sit above the arrow, but the arrow only shows the change.
why.Below the arrow, written in small letter: Wrong: thinks products sit below the arrow, but the arrow only shows the change.

activities.explanation: Right: zinc oxide is the product, and products are written after the arrow.

lessons.sceneCaption: Ignited magnesium burning brightly in air, the reaction that forms magnesium oxide.

lessons.title: Combination and Exothermic Reactions

activities.prompt: Why does mixing quicklime with water make things so hot?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two reactions join the party
activities.body: When two or more substances join to make one single product, that is a combination reaction. Some reactions also give out heat. These are called exothermic reactions. Calcium oxide and water combine to form slaked lime, and this reaction gives out a lot of heat.
keyPoints: A combination reaction makes one product from two or more reactants.
An exothermic reaction releases heat along with its products.
Calcium oxide and water combine to form slaked lime and release much heat.
activities.explanation: Joining substances into one product, with heat given out, is the heart of this lesson.

activities.prompt: A new wall looks dull. After some days it shines on its own. Why does this happen?
steps: The wall was painted with slaked lime, which comes from calcium oxide and water.
Slaked lime slowly reacts with carbon dioxide present in the air around the wall.
This slow reaction makes calcium carbonate, which forms a shiny layer on the wall.
So the wall shines because slaked lime slowly changes into calcium carbonate in air.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Why do walls shine?
activities.body: Slaked lime is calcium hydroxide. It reacts slowly with carbon dioxide in the air. This forms calcium carbonate, which gives a shiny finish to the walls. So the shine you see after whitewashing comes from calcium carbonate.
keyPoints: Slaked lime is calcium hydroxide.
It reacts slowly with carbon dioxide in the air.
Calcium carbonate gives walls a shiny finish.
activities.explanation: The slow reaction with carbon dioxide in air brings the shine to your walls.

activities.title: Spot the combination
activities.prompt: What is a combination reaction?
options: One product formed from two or more reactants
Two products formed from one reactant
A reaction that absorbs heat from surroundings
activities.explanation: Well done! In a combination reaction, substances join to form a single product.

activities.title: A fresh coat for the walls
activities.prompt: A solution of slaked lime is used for ______ of walls.
activities.hint: Think of what people do to walls before a festival.
activities.explanation: Right! Slaked lime dissolved in water is used for whitewashing walls.

activities.title: The secret of the shine
activities.prompt: A freshly whitewashed wall shines after a few days. Why?
options: Calcium carbonate forms on it
Water evaporates from the wall
Slaked lime melts in sunlight
activities.explanation: Great thinking! Calcium carbonate formed on the wall gives the shiny finish.

activities.title: Match the pairs
activities.prompt: Match each item with what it forms or does.
activities.explanation: All matched! Each pair shows a combination or an exothermic example from the lesson.

activities.title: The whitewash story
activities.prompt: Put the whitewashing story in the correct order.
items: Calcium oxide reacts vigorously with water
Slaked lime is formed with much heat
The slaked lime solution is used for whitewashing
It reacts slowly with carbon dioxide in air
Calcium carbonate gives the walls a shiny finish
activities.explanation: Perfect order! From quicklime to shiny walls, you traced the whole journey.

activities.prompt: A builder mixes calcium oxide with water in a bucket. The bucket becomes very hot. The builder touches the outside of the bucket. What will he feel?
options: The bucket feels cold because water always cools things down.
The bucket feels hot because the reaction gives out a lot of heat.
The bucket feels normal because mixing powders never changes temperature.
The bucket feels hot only if he mixes it with his hands.

why.The bucket feels cold because water alwa: Wrong: water does not always cool things; here the reaction itself gives out heat.
why.The bucket feels normal because mixing p: Wrong: mixing can change temperature; this reaction releases a large amount of heat.
why.The bucket feels hot only if he mixes it: Wrong: the heat comes from the reaction itself, not from how he mixes it.

activities.explanation: Right: calcium oxide and water react vigorously and release a large amount of heat.

activities.prompt: A student says: 'When calcium oxide and water mix, two new things must form because two things were mixed.' Is she right?
options: Yes, two reactants always make two products.
No, two or more reactants can combine to form one single product.
Yes, more reactants always mean more products.
No, calcium oxide and water cannot react at all.

why.Yes, two reactants always make two produ: Wrong: the number of products does not have to match the number of reactants.
why.Yes, more reactants always mean more pro: Wrong: reactants can join together, so one product can form from many reactants.
why.No, calcium oxide and water cannot react: Wrong: calcium oxide reacts vigorously with water to form slaked lime.

activities.explanation: Right: a combination reaction forms one product from two or more reactants.

activities.prompt: Two students whitewash walls. One uses slaked lime solution. The other uses plain water. After some days, one wall shines. Why?
options: The shiny wall got slaked lime, which slowly turns into shiny calcium carbonate in air.
The shiny wall got more water, and water makes walls shiny when it dries.
Both walls will shine the same, because air shines any wall slowly.
The shiny wall dried faster, and fast drying always makes walls shiny.

why.The shiny wall got more water, and water: Wrong: water alone cannot form the shiny layer; slaked lime is needed.
why.Both walls will shine the same, because: Wrong: plain water has no slaked lime, so no calcium carbonate can form on it.
why.The shiny wall dried faster, and fast dr: Wrong: drying speed does not matter; the shiny finish comes from calcium carbonate.

activities.explanation: Right: slaked lime reacts slowly with carbon dioxide in air, forming calcium carbonate that shines.

activities.prompt: A gas stove burns natural gas and the flame heats a pot of water. Where does the heat of the flame come from?
options: From the pot, because hot pots always give heat to burning gas.
From the air, because air pushes heat into the burning gas.
From the burning of natural gas, which releases heat along with products.
From the flame's colour, because bright colours always make heat.

why.From the pot, because hot pots always gi: Wrong: the pot receives heat; it does not give heat to the burning gas.
why.From the air, because air pushes heat in: Wrong: air helps burning but does not push heat into the flame.
why.From the flame's colour, because bright: Wrong: the colour of a flame does not create the heat released.

activities.explanation: Right: burning of natural gas is exothermic, so it releases heat along with products.

activities.prompt: A student claims: 'Respiration must be endothermic because it happens inside the body, and the body stays warm only from outside heat.' What is the flaw in her claim?
options: She is right, because the body cannot make any heat by itself.
She is wrong, because respiration is an exothermic process that releases heat inside the body.
She is right, because only food can warm the body, never reactions.
She is wrong, because respiration absorbs heat and cools the body down.

why.She is right, because the body cannot ma: Wrong: the body does make heat by itself through reactions like respiration.
why.She is right, because only food can warm: Wrong: reactions inside the body, like respiration, release heat themselves.
why.She is wrong, because respiration absorb: Wrong: respiration releases heat; it does not absorb heat and cool the body.

activities.explanation: Right: respiration is an exothermic process, so it releases heat inside the body.

activities.prompt: Hydrogen and oxygen are combined in a closed jar. A single new substance forms and the jar feels warm. What kind of reaction is this, and why?
options: A combination reaction, because two substances joined to form one product, and it released heat.
Only an exothermic reaction, because two substances always stay separate in a jar.
A combination reaction, because the jar being warm proves two products formed.
Not a real reaction, because gases cannot combine to form anything new.

why.Only an exothermic reaction, because two: Wrong: gases can combine; hydrogen and oxygen form water in one product.
why.A combination reaction, because the jar: Wrong: warmth shows heat is released, not that two products formed.
why.Not a real reaction, because gases canno: Wrong: gases can react; water can be formed from hydrogen and oxygen.

activities.explanation: Right: hydrogen and oxygen combine to form one product, water, and heat is released.

lessons.title: Decomposition and Endothermic Reactions

activities.prompt: Why do some crystals change colour and give off fumes when heated?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: One substance splits into many
activities.body: In a decomposition reaction, one reactant breaks into simpler products. Think of a parcel unwrapping itself into several small gifts. To make this happen, the reaction needs energy. The energy can come as heat, light or electricity. Reactions that absorb energy are called endothermic.
keyPoints: A decomposition reaction has one reactant breaking into simpler products.
Decomposition needs energy as heat, light or electricity.
Reactions that absorb energy are endothermic.
activities.explanation: One substance splits apart, and energy must be put in to make it happen.

activities.prompt: A student heats green ferrous sulphate crystals in a dry boiling tube. The green colour fades and a sharp smell fills the room. What is happening inside the tube?
steps: The crystals are green, but heating makes the colour change, so heat is doing something inside the tube.
One substance is breaking into new things like ferric oxide and gases, because the smell of burning sulphur appears.
Heat gave the energy for this breaking, so this is thermal decomposition, not a normal mixing.
So the green crystals did not just melt; they split into simpler products using heat energy.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Reactions that take energy in
activities.body: Some reactions are like a plant drinking water: they take energy in. Decomposition reactions need energy as heat, light or electricity. That is why we heat ferrous sulphate, or leave silver chloride in sunlight. Any reaction that absorbs energy is called endothermic.
keyPoints: Decomposition needs energy as heat, light or electricity.
Reactions that absorb energy are endothermic.
Heating is one way to give the energy needed.
activities.explanation: Endothermic reactions soak up energy, just like a sponge soaks up water.

activities.prompt: What happens in a decomposition reaction?
options: Two reactants join into one product
One reactant breaks into simpler products
One product swaps places with another
Nothing changes at all
activities.explanation: In decomposition, a single reactant breaks into simpler products, like a parcel splitting into smaller gifts.

activities.prompt: You heat ferrous sulphate crystals in a dry boiling tube. What can you smell?
options: The smell of burning paper
The smell of burning sulphur
The smell of burning wood
No smell at all
activities.explanation: On heating, the characteristic odour of burning sulphur can be smelt.

activities.prompt: When ferrous sulphate crystals are heated, their green colour changes.
activities.explanation: The crystals are green at first, and heating makes the colour change. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: Calcium oxide is also called lime or ______ lime.
activities.hint: It is a word that means fast.
activities.explanation: Calcium oxide has two common names: lime and quick lime.

activities.prompt: Match each substance or word with what happens to it.
pairs: Gives calcium oxide and carbon dioxide
activities.explanation: Each substance has its own special change when heated or left in sunlight.

activities.prompt: Put these steps of the ferrous sulphate experiment in the right order.
items: Ferrous sulphate crystals are placed in a dry boiling tube
The crystals are heated
The green colour of the crystals changes
The smell of burning sulphur can be smelt
Ferric oxide, sulphur dioxide and sulphur trioxide form
activities.explanation: First heat the crystals, then watch the colour change, smell the sulphur, and finally the new products appear.

activities.prompt: Green ferrous sulphate crystals are heated in a dry boiling tube. A sharp smell like burning sulphur comes out. What does this smell tell us?
options: New gas products have formed inside the tube
The crystals have only melted into a liquid
The green colour has simply washed away
The tube has become too hot to hold

why.The crystals have only melted into a liq: This confuses melting with breaking into new substances.
why.The green colour has simply washed away: This thinks colour change alone explains everything, ignoring the new smell.
why.The tube has become too hot to hold: This focuses on the heat, not on what the smell proves.

activities.explanation: Right: gases like sulphur dioxide are new products, so their smell shows decomposition happened.

activities.prompt: A student says: heating ferrous sulphate is a combination reaction because two things join. Another student disagrees. Who is right and why?
options: The first student, because heat joins the crystals together
The second student, because one substance splits into simpler products
The first student, because the smell proves joining happened
Neither student, because heating never changes a substance

why.The first student, because heat joins th: This mistakes heating for joining substances together.
why.The first student, because the smell pro: This reads the smell as a sign of joining, which is backwards.
why.Neither student, because heating never c: This wrongly believes heating can never change a substance.

activities.explanation: Right: ferrous sulphate alone breaks into ferric oxide and gases, so it is decomposition.

activities.prompt: Calcium carbonate breaks into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide when heated. Lime is made this way. Why must heat be supplied for this?
options: Heat gives the energy the breaking needs
Heat makes the carbon dioxide smell stronger
Heat keeps the calcium oxide white and clean
Heat stops the calcium carbonate from melting

why.Heat makes the carbon dioxide smell stro: This invents a role for heat that the facts do not support.
why.Heat keeps the calcium oxide white and c: This confuses colour with the energy needed for breaking.
why.Heat stops the calcium carbonate from me: This thinks heat prevents melting, which is not the reason here.

activities.explanation: Right: decomposition needs energy, and heat supplies it in thermal decomposition.

activities.prompt: White silver chloride is left on a table in bright sunlight. It slowly turns grey. What kind of change is this most like?
options: Decomposition using light as the energy
Combination using light to join substances
Melting caused by the warmth of the room
Burning caused by oxygen in the air

why.Combination using light to join substanc: This forgets that decomposition splits, it does not join.
why.Melting caused by the warmth of the room: This blames gentle warmth instead of the light doing the work.
why.Burning caused by oxygen in the air: This adds burning, which is not part of this change.

activities.explanation: Right: light supplies energy, and the colour change shows a new substance formed.

activities.prompt: Lead nitrate is heated and brown fumes come out. A friend claims the fumes prove two substances combined. What is the flaw in this claim?
options: Fumes can come from one substance breaking down
Fumes only appear when two substances combine
Brown fumes always mean the substance melted
Heating can never produce fumes from solids

why.Fumes only appear when two substances co: This accepts the claim without checking how decomposition works.
why.Brown fumes always mean the substance me: This confuses fumes with simple melting.
why.Heating can never produce fumes from sol: This wrongly denies that heating solids can give fumes.

activities.explanation: Right: decomposition of one substance can release fumes, so fumes do not prove combining.

activities.prompt: A student heats calcium carbonate in one tube and ferrous sulphate in another. Both tubes are heated the same way. What do the two experiments share?
options: Both use heat to break one substance down
Both produce a gas with a burning sulphur smell
Both turn the contents grey in the tube
Both need electricity instead of heat to work

why.Both produce a gas with a burning sulphu: Only ferrous sulphate gives the burning sulphur smell.
why.Both turn the contents grey in the tube: Grey colour belongs to silver chloride in sunlight, not these tubes.
why.Both need electricity instead of heat to: Both experiments use heat, not electricity.

activities.explanation: Right: both are thermal decompositions, using heat to split one reactant.

lessons.sceneCaption: Holding a test tube while heating, as done when ferrous sulphate crystals are heated.

lessons.title: Displacement and Double Displacement Reactions

activities.prompt: Why does a shiny nail turn blue water clear?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Pushing Out and Swapping Partners
activities.body: In a displacement reaction, one element pushes another out of its compound. Iron pushes copper out of copper sulphate solution, so the blue colour fades. Zinc and lead are more reactive than copper, so they can push copper out too. In a double displacement reaction, two compounds swap their ions. Sometimes this makes an insoluble solid called a precipitate.
keyPoints: A more reactive element displaces a less reactive one from its compound.
Iron, zinc and lead can displace copper.
Double displacement reactions exchange ions between reactants.
An insoluble solid formed in a reaction is called a precipitate.
activities.explanation: More reactive elements push out less reactive ones, and some reactions swap ions to form a precipitate.

activities.prompt: Riya dips an iron nail into blue copper sulphate solution. Next day the blue colour has faded. What happened to the copper in the solution?
steps: The solution was blue because copper was in it, so a fading colour means copper is leaving the solution.
Iron is touching the solution, so iron must be doing something to the copper compound.
Iron takes the copper's place in the compound, because iron can push copper out.
So the copper moved out of the solution, and iron took its place there.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What happens in a displacement reaction?
options: An element displaces another from its compound
Two compounds exchange ions
A white solid dissolves in water
Two elements join to form a mixture
activities.explanation: In displacement, one element pushes another out of its compound. The other options describe different things.

activities.prompt: When iron reacts with copper sulphate solution, the blue colour of the solution ______.
activities.hint: The colour slowly becomes weaker.
activities.explanation: As iron takes copper out of the solution, the blue colour fades away.

activities.prompt: Why do we rub iron nails with sand paper before the experiment?
options: To clean the nails
To make the nails blue
To heat the nails up
To make the nails heavier
activities.explanation: Rubbing with sand paper cleans the nails so the reaction works well.

activities.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.
pairs: An element pushes another out of its compound
An insoluble solid formed in a reaction
Reactants exchange ions with each other
A reaction that produces a precipitate
activities.explanation: These four words describe the reactions you have met in this lesson.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of the iron nail experiment in order.
items: Clean the iron nails by rubbing with sand paper
Put the nails in copper sulphate solution
The iron reacts with the copper sulphate solution
The blue colour of the solution fades
Iron displaces copper from the solution
activities.explanation: First clean the nails, then dip them in the solution. The reaction makes the blue colour fade as iron displaces copper.

activities.prompt: A student takes two iron nails. She rubs one nail with sand paper. She puts both nails into copper sulphate solution. The rubbed nail reacts faster. Why did she rub one nail first?
options: To make the nail heavier so it sinks faster
To clean the nail surface so iron touches the solution
To make the nail look shiny for the photo
To warm the nail up so it reacts faster

why.To make the nail heavier so it sinks fas: Wrong: weight does not change much, and sinking speed is not the reason for reacting.
why.To make the nail look shiny for the phot: Wrong: shine is only how it looks, not why the reaction happens.
why.To warm the nail up so it reacts faster: Wrong: rubbing does not make the nail warm enough to change the reaction.

activities.explanation: Right: rubbing cleans the surface, so iron can really touch the solution and react.

activities.prompt: A student puts a zinc piece into copper sulphate solution. The blue colour fades like it did with iron. She says zinc did the same job as iron. Is she right?
options: No, only iron can ever take copper out of a solution
No, the colour faded for a different reason this time
Yes, zinc also pushed copper out of its compound
Yes, but zinc worked only because iron was also present

why.No, only iron can ever take copper out o: Wrong: iron is not the only element that can push copper out.
why.No, the colour faded for a different rea: Wrong: the fading has the same reason, copper leaving the solution.
why.Yes, but zinc worked only because iron w: Wrong: zinc works on its own; iron is not needed at all.

activities.explanation: Right: zinc is more reactive than copper, so zinc pushes copper out too.

activities.prompt: A student puts a copper piece into a solution of a zinc compound. Nothing seems to happen. She says copper is lazy. What is the real reason nothing happened?
options: Copper is less reactive, so it cannot push zinc out
The solution was too blue for any change to show
Copper pieces are always too big to react with solutions
Zinc compounds never react with any metal piece at all

why.The solution was too blue for any change: Wrong: colour of the solution does not stop a reaction from happening.
why.Copper pieces are always too big to reac: Wrong: size of the piece is not the reason here.
why.Zinc compounds never react with any meta: Wrong: zinc compounds do react, but only with more reactive metals.

activities.explanation: Right: copper is less reactive than zinc, so copper cannot displace zinc.

activities.prompt: A student mixes sodium sulphate solution with barium chloride solution. A white solid appears and sinks down. Her friend says the solid is just sand that fell in. Why is the friend wrong?
options: Sand is white too, so the friend could still be right
The solid formed from the two solutions mixing, not sand
The solid is sand because barium chloride always contains sand
The solid is sand because sodium sulphate always contains sand

why.Sand is white too, so the friend could s: Wrong: both being white does not prove the solid is sand.
why.The solid is sand because barium chlorid: Wrong: barium chloride solution does not contain sand.
why.The solid is sand because sodium sulphat: Wrong: sodium sulphate solution does not contain sand.

activities.explanation: Right: the white solid formed when the two solutions mixed and exchanged ions.

activities.prompt: Two students each mix sodium sulphate with barium chloride. Student A uses a clean dry test tube. Student B uses a test tube with old sand dust in it. Both see a white solid. Whose test tube shows the real reaction best?
options: Student B, because the extra sand makes more white solid
Student A, because only her white solid came from the mixing
Both are equal, because sand and precipitate look the same
Neither, because white solids always mean the test failed

why.Student B, because the extra sand makes: Wrong: extra sand adds white dust, but that dust is not the reaction product.
why.Both are equal, because sand and precipi: Wrong: they are not equal; one result is spoiled by sand.
why.Neither, because white solids always mea: Wrong: a white precipitate here means the reaction worked, not failed.

activities.explanation: Right: her tube was clean, so the white precipitate truly came from the two solutions.

lessons.sceneAlt: Copper metal produced by reacting a copper sulphate solution with metallic zinc, photographed at a university.
lessons.sceneCaption: Copper prepared by cementation of a copper sulphate solution with metallic zinc, showing zinc displacing copper.

lessons.title: Oxidation, Reduction, Corrosion and Rancidity

activities.prompt: Why does a shiny spoon slowly lose its shine over time?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Gaining and Losing Oxygen
activities.body: Heat some copper powder and it grows a black coat. This is copper(II) oxide. Oxygen from the air joined the copper, so we say copper was oxidised. Now pass hydrogen over the hot black powder. The coat turns brown again because the copper oxide loses its oxygen. Losing oxygen is called reduction. In many reactions, one thing is oxidised while the other is reduced.
keyPoints: Heated copper gets a black coat of copper(II) oxide.
A substance that gains oxygen is oxidised.
A substance that loses oxygen is reduced.
Hydrogen turns the black coat brown again.
activities.explanation: Oxygen moving from one substance to another changes both of them.

activities.prompt: A child heats copper powder on a old metal spoon. The shiny brown powder slowly turns black. The child asks: why did the shiny copper change colour?
steps: The hot copper is touching the oxygen in the air around it.
Oxygen gets added to the copper, so a new substance forms on top.
This new substance is copper oxide, and it looks black.
So the copper was oxidised, because it gained oxygen, and that is why it turned black.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Corrosion and Rancidity
activities.body: Metals around us do not stay bright forever. Substances around a metal can attack it. This is called corrosion. Iron gets a reddish brown powder on it. Silver grows a black coating and copper grows a green coating. Food can change too. When fats and oils in food are oxidised, their smell and taste turn bad. We say they have become rancid.
keyPoints: Corrosion happens when substances around a metal attack it.
Iron gets a reddish brown coating.
Silver turns black and copper turns green.
Oxidised fats and oils become rancid.
activities.explanation: Both corrosion and rancidity happen because substances react with things around them.

activities.prompt: You heat some copper powder in a dish. What do you see on it?
options: A green shiny coat
A black coat of copper(II) oxide
A reddish brown powder
It stays bright and unchanged
activities.explanation: Oxygen joins the hot copper and forms black copper(II) oxide. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: When hydrogen is passed over hot copper(II) oxide, the oxide ______ oxygen and turns brown.
activities.hint: Think of the opposite of gaining.
activities.explanation: Losing oxygen is reduction, so the copper oxide is reduced and turns brown.

activities.prompt: A substance that gains oxygen during a reaction is said to be oxidised.
activities.explanation: That is exactly what oxidised means. The copper gained oxygen and was oxidised.

activities.prompt: In one reaction, substance A gains oxygen while substance B loses oxygen. What do we call this reaction?
options: A melting reaction
A redox reaction
A freezing reaction
A mixing reaction
activities.explanation: One substance is oxidised and the other is reduced at the same time. That is why we call it a redox reaction.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of the copper experiment in the right order.
items: Copper powder is heated strongly
A black coating of copper(II) oxide forms
Hydrogen gas is passed over the hot black powder
The copper oxide loses oxygen and is reduced
The black coating turns brown again
activities.explanation: First copper gains oxygen and is oxidised. Then hydrogen takes that oxygen away, so the oxide is reduced and turns brown.

activities.prompt: Some copper powder is heated in a dish. Oxygen from the air touches the hot powder. Oxygen gets added to the copper. What will the powder look like after some time?
options: It will have a black coating on it
It will stay shiny brown like before
It will get a green coating on it
It will turn into a reddish-brown powder

why.It will stay shiny brown like before: This child thinks heating alone cannot change how a metal looks.
why.It will get a green coating on it: This child mixes up copper's coating with silver's black or copper's green corrosion coating.
why.It will turn into a reddish-brown powder: This child mixes up copper oxide with the reddish-brown coating that iron gets.

activities.explanation: Right: copper gains oxygen and becomes copper oxide, which is black.

activities.prompt: Black copper oxide is heated in a tube. Hydrogen gas is passed over it. The black coating slowly turns brown again. The copper oxide gave away its oxygen. What happened to the copper oxide?
options: It was reduced, because it lost its oxygen
It was oxidised, because it got heated strongly
It corroded, because substances around it attacked it
It became rancid, because it stayed hot for long

why.It was oxidised, because it got heated s: This child thinks heating a substance always means it is oxidised.
why.It corroded, because substances around i: This child mixes up redox changes with corrosion, which attacks metals slowly.
why.It became rancid, because it stayed hot: This child mixes up redox changes with rancidity, which happens to fats and oils.

activities.explanation: Right: a substance that loses oxygen during a reaction is reduced.

activities.prompt: Hydrogen gas is passed over hot black copper oxide. The hydrogen takes away the oxygen from the copper oxide. So the hydrogen gains oxygen in this reaction. What happened to the hydrogen?
options: It was oxidised, because it gained oxygen
It was reduced, because it took oxygen away
It corroded, because it touched a metal surface
It stayed the same, because gases cannot change

why.It was reduced, because it took oxygen a: This child thinks the gas that removes oxygen must itself be reduced.
why.It corroded, because it touched a metal: This child thinks touching a metal always causes corrosion on the other substance.
why.It stayed the same, because gases cannot: This child thinks only solids and liquids can be oxidised or reduced.

activities.explanation: Right: a substance that gains oxygen during a reaction is oxidised.

activities.prompt: In the copper oxide and hydrogen reaction, the copper oxide loses oxygen. At the same time, the hydrogen gains that oxygen. One substance lost oxygen and the other gained it. What can we call this whole reaction?
options: A redox reaction, because one change happened with the other
Only an oxidation, because oxygen moved to a new place
Only a reduction, because the black colour went away
A corrosion reaction, because a metal surface was involved

why.Only an oxidation, because oxygen moved: This child notices only the gain of oxygen and forgets the loss happening too.
why.Only a reduction, because the black colo: This child notices only the loss of oxygen and forgets the gain happening too.
why.A corrosion reaction, because a metal su: This child thinks any reaction with a metal must be corrosion.

activities.explanation: Right: when one reactant is oxidised and the other is reduced, it is a redox reaction.

activities.prompt: A silver spoon in a drawer turns black. A copper pot in the kitchen turns green. Both metals are attacked by substances around them. Ravi says only iron articles can get corroded. What is wrong with his claim?
options: Silver and copper also get corroded, shown by their coatings
Only iron gets attacked, so the other metals changed some other way
Black and green coatings mean the metals are getting cleaner
Corrosion can happen only when a metal is heated first

why.Only iron gets attacked, so the other me: This child thinks corrosion is something only iron can ever show.
why.Black and green coatings mean the metals: This child thinks any new colour on a metal means it is cleaner, not attacked.
why.Corrosion can happen only when a metal i: This child thinks heating is needed first, but corrosion needs no heating.

activities.explanation: Right: black coating on silver and green on copper are examples of corrosion.

activities.prompt: A packet of fried snacks is left open on the table. Air keeps touching the fats and oils in it. After many days the smell and taste become unpleasant. Why did this happen?
options: The fats and oils were oxidised and became rancid
The fats and oils were reduced and became rancid
The fats and oils corroded like an iron article does
The fats and oils lost oxygen and became rancid

why.The fats and oils were reduced and becam: This child remembers the word rancid but mixes up oxidation with reduction.
why.The fats and oils corroded like an iron: This child mixes up the change in food with corrosion, which attacks metals.
why.The fats and oils lost oxygen and became: This child thinks losing oxygen causes rancidity, but gaining oxygen does.

activities.explanation: Right: when fats and oils are oxidised, they become rancid.

lessons.sceneAlt: A magnesium ribbon burning with a bright white flame.
lessons.sceneCaption: A burning magnesium ribbon photographed with very short exposure to show oxidation detail.

activities.context: During the summer holidays, Ravi notices three things at home. A bowl of milk left on the table overnight smells and tastes different in the morning. An old iron nail kept in the humid store room no longer looks the same. Meanwhile, his little sister's stomach is busy breaking down her dinner after she eats. Ravi wonders whether all three happenings are of the same kind.
activities.prompt: Ravi argues that digestion in his sister's body should not be grouped with the milk and the nail. Is he right?
options: No, because digestion is also a situation where the nature and identity of the starting substance change
Yes, because digestion happens inside the body while the other two happen outside
Yes, because digestion does not involve any starting substance at all
No, because digestion is faster than the change in milk and the nail

why.Yes, because digestion happens inside th: Wrong: inside versus outside the body is not the deciding point; the kind of change is.
why.Yes, because digestion does not involve: Wrong: digestion clearly starts with food, so saying there is no starting substance is false.
why.No, because digestion is faster than the: Wrong: speed of the change is not the criterion used to group these situations.

activities.explanation: Correct: food getting digested is listed alongside milk changing and iron changing, since the starting substance's nature and identity change in each.

activities.context: During the summer holidays, Ravi notices three things at home. A bowl of milk left on the table overnight smells and tastes different in the morning. An old iron nail kept in the humid store room no longer looks the same. Meanwhile, his little sister's stomach is busy breaking down her dinner after she eats. Ravi wonders whether all three happenings are of the same kind.
activities.prompt: If Ravi wants to tell his teacher that a chemical reaction has taken place in each of the three situations, what should he say is the common reason?
options: A chemical change has occurred in each situation
A new container was used in each situation
Each situation happened during the summer holidays
Each situation was first noticed by Ravi himself

why.A new container was used in each situati: Wrong: the container has nothing to do with whether a reaction occurred.
why.Each situation happened during the summe: Wrong: the season is not what makes a reaction happen.
why.Each situation was first noticed by Ravi: Wrong: who noticed the change is irrelevant to whether a reaction took place.

activities.explanation: Correct: whenever a chemical change occurs, a chemical reaction has taken place, so this is the right justification.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): When magnesium ribbon burns, the white powder formed can be identified as magnesium oxide.
Reason (R): Magnesium oxide forms from magnesium and oxygen present in air.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true and the formation from magnesium and oxygen in air explains why the white powder is magnesium oxide.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Adding zinc granules to dilute hydrochloric acid shows that a chemical reaction has taken place.
Reason (R): Every chemical reaction must show a change in temperature, and only a temperature change counts as evidence.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true because a reaction may show gas evolution or temperature change, but the reason is false since a temperature change is not the only possible evidence.

activities.prompt: Explain why a lead nitrate solution and a potassium iodide solution, when mixed, are said to have undergone a chemical reaction.
activities.answer: When lead nitrate solution is mixed with potassium iodide solution, the mixture shows a change in colour, which is one of the signs that a chemical reaction may show. Since the nature and identity of the starting substances change somewhat, a chemical change has occurred, and whenever a chemical change occurs, a chemical reaction has taken place. So the mixing of these two solutions is a chemical reaction.
points: Names both solutions being mixed
Points to the change observed as a sign a reaction may show
States that the nature and identity of the starting substances change
Links chemical change to a chemical reaction having taken place
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a science activity, Riya burns a ribbon of magnesium in air. Her teacher first writes the reaction as a sentence, then shortens it to: Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide. Riya asks why an arrow is used instead of an equal sign. The teacher replies that the arrow shows the direction of change, and that the shiny ribbon and the air are the substances that undergo the chemical change.
activities.prompt: In Riya's activity, magnesium and oxygen are best described as:
options: Products, because they are written on the left of the arrow
Reactants, because they undergo the chemical change
Products, because magnesium oxide forms from them
Reactants, because they are present as a solution in water

why.Products, because they are written on th: Wrong: substances on the left of the arrow are not products; products form after the change.
why.Products, because magnesium oxide forms: Wrong: magnesium oxide is the product; magnesium and oxygen are what change into it.
why.Reactants, because they are present as a: Wrong: being reactants has nothing to do with being dissolved in water; nothing here is a solution in water.

activities.explanation: Correct: the substances that undergo chemical change are called reactants, and magnesium and oxygen do that here.

activities.context: During a science activity, Riya burns a ribbon of magnesium in air. Her teacher first writes the reaction as a sentence, then shortens it to: Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide. Riya asks why an arrow is used instead of an equal sign. The teacher replies that the arrow shows the direction of change, and that the shiny ribbon and the air are the substances that undergo the chemical change.
activities.prompt: If Riya's teacher had written 'Magnesium + Oxygen = Magnesium oxide' instead of using an arrow, the main problem would be that:
options: The equal sign wrongly suggests both sides are the same substance rather than a change
The word-equation would become too long compared to the sentence form
Magnesium oxide could no longer be called the product of the reaction
The substances would no longer undergo any chemical change

why.The word-equation would become too long: Wrong: replacing one symbol with another does not make the word-equation longer than the sentence.
why.Magnesium oxide could no longer be calle: Wrong: magnesium oxide would still be the substance formed; only the symbol for change is wrong.
why.The substances would no longer undergo a: Wrong: the chemical change still happens in reality; only the way it is written is affected.

activities.explanation: Correct: the arrow shows reactants changing into products; an equal sign loses this idea of change.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): In the word-equation Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide, magnesium oxide is written on the right of the arrow.
Reason (R): The new substance formed during a reaction is called the product, and products are written on the right of the arrow.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Magnesium oxide is the new substance formed, so it is the product and appears on the right of the arrow.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): In a chemical reaction, the total mass can increase because new substance is formed.
Reason (R): Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because mass is conserved, while the reason correctly states the law of conservation of mass.

activities.prompt: Explain why an equation must be balanced, referring to what happens to mass in a chemical reaction.
activities.answer: An equation must be balanced because mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. An unbalanced equation has unequal mass on both sides, which would mean atoms have appeared or disappeared, and this cannot happen. A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, so the total mass is equal on both sides. While balancing, the smallest whole number coefficient is used, so the equation stays in its simplest correct form.
points: States the law: mass can neither be created nor destroyed.
Links unbalanced equation to unequal mass on the two sides.
States that a balanced equation has equal atoms of each element on both sides.
Mentions using the smallest whole number coefficient.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Ravi's family is renovating their old house. The painter mixes a white powder, calcium oxide, with water in a large bucket to prepare slaked lime for whitewashing the walls. As soon as the water is added, the bucket becomes very hot and steam rises. Two days after the whitewashing is done, the walls look bright and shiny. Ravi wonders why the bucket heated up and why the walls changed their look after a few days.
activities.prompt: A new painter suggests pouring all the water into the bucket of calcium oxide in one go, very quickly. What is he likely to notice, and what should he do?
options: The mixing will be vigorous and release a large amount of heat, so he should add the water carefully
Nothing will happen, so he can pour the water as fast as he likes
The mixture will become cold, so he should pour quickly before it cools further
The mixture will turn shiny immediately, so he should pour quickly to see the effect

why.Nothing will happen, so he can pour the: Wrong: the reaction is vigorous and heats up, so it cannot be ignored
why.The mixture will become cold, so he shou: Wrong: the reaction releases heat rather than making the mixture cold
why.The mixture will turn shiny immediately,: Wrong: the shine on walls comes much later from reaction with carbon dioxide in air, not at the mixing stage

activities.explanation: Correct: calcium oxide reacts vigorously with water and releases a large amount of heat, so care is needed

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The reaction between calcium oxide and water is a combination reaction.
Reason (R): Calcium oxide and water combine to form a single product.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and forming a single product from two reactants is exactly what makes it a combination reaction.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Whitewashed walls turn dull over time because calcium carbonate is a dull substance.
Reason (R): Calcium carbonate gives a shiny finish to walls.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because calcium carbonate actually gives a shiny finish, which makes the reason true.

activities.prompt: Explain why the container becomes hot when calcium oxide is mixed with water, and name the type of reaction involved.
activities.answer: When calcium oxide is mixed with water, it reacts vigorously with the water to produce slaked lime. During this reaction, a large amount of heat is released along with the product. Reactions that release heat along with the products are called exothermic reactions, so the container becomes hot. At the same time, calcium oxide and water combine to form a single product, so this is also a combination reaction.
points: Calcium oxide reacts vigorously with water to form slaked lime
A large amount of heat is released in this reaction
Reactions releasing heat along with products are exothermic
It is also a combination reaction since one product is formed from two reactants
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a science activity, Riya heats some green ferrous sulphate crystals in a dry boiling tube. After some time, she notices the colour of the crystals has changed, and a smell resembling burning sulphur comes from the tube. Her teacher says the crystals have broken down into simpler substances, and that the heat from the burner supplied the energy needed for this change to happen.
activities.prompt: If Riya had heated calcium carbonate instead of ferrous sulphate, what would she most likely observe?
options: A colour change with a smell of burning sulphur
A gas being given off, with no sulphur smell
The crystals turning grey in sunlight
No change at all, since calcium carbonate cannot be heated

why.A colour change with a smell of burning: The sulphur smell is specific to ferrous sulphate breaking down, not to calcium carbonate.
why.The crystals turning grey in sunlight: Grey colour appears when silver chloride is left in sunlight, not when calcium carbonate is heated.
why.No change at all, since calcium carbonat: Calcium carbonate does decompose on heating, so 'no change' is wrong.

activities.explanation: Correct: calcium carbonate decomposes on heating into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide, a gas.

activities.context: During a science activity, Riya heats some green ferrous sulphate crystals in a dry boiling tube. After some time, she notices the colour of the crystals has changed, and a smell resembling burning sulphur comes from the tube. Her teacher says the crystals have broken down into simpler substances, and that the heat from the burner supplied the energy needed for this change to happen.
activities.prompt: Riya's friend says the change in the boiling tube is not decomposition because two different smells and colours appeared. What is the best response?
options: He is right, because decomposition can only give one product
He is wrong, because one reactant can break into more than one simpler product
He is right, because two observations mean two separate reactions occurred
He is wrong, because the colour change alone proves it is endothermic

why.He is right, because decomposition can o: Decomposition gives simpler products, not necessarily a single one.
why.He is right, because two observations me: Multiple observations can come from one reactant breaking into several products; two reactions are not needed.
why.He is wrong, because the colour change a: A colour change alone does not prove a reaction is endothermic; the energy input does.

activities.explanation: Correct: one reactant (ferrous sulphate) breaks into several simpler products, so multiple observations fit decomposition.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): White silver chloride kept in sunlight turns grey.
Reason (R): Decomposition reactions can be driven by light energy.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the ability of light to drive decomposition explains the greying of silver chloride.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Chemical Reactions and Equations

activities.prompt: Which of these shows a chemical reaction has taken place?
options: Milk left out on a hot day changes
Water is poured from one jug to another
A pencil is sharpened into two pieces
Ice is kept in a warm glass
activities.explanation: When milk changes, its nature and identity change a little. That means a chemical reaction has happened. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: In a chemical reaction, mass can be created and destroyed freely.
activities.explanation: Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. That is why we balance equations!

activities.prompt: In a word-equation, the substances that undergo the chemical change are called ______.
activities.hint: They are the starters of the reaction, on the left of the arrow.
activities.explanation: Reactants undergo the change, and the new substance formed is the product. You are getting this!

activities.prompt: Match each reaction type with what happens in it.
pairs: Two or more reactants form one product
One reactant breaks into simpler products
An element pushes another out of its compound
activities.explanation: Each reaction type has its own special move. Matching them helps you spot them in real life.

activities.prompt: Put the whitewashing story in the right order.
items: Calcium oxide reacts vigorously with water to make slaked lime
A large amount of heat is released
The slaked lime solution is used for whitewashing walls
Calcium hydroxide reacts slowly with carbon dioxide in the air
Calcium carbonate gives the walls a shiny finish
activities.explanation: First quicklime meets water, then the walls are painted, and slowly the shiny calcium carbonate forms. Lovely ordering!

activities.prompt: Decomposition reactions need energy as heat, light or electricity. What kind of reactions are they?
options: Endothermic reactions
Exothermic reactions
Displacement reactions
Precipitation reactions
activities.explanation: Reactions that absorb energy are endothermic. Decomposition needs energy, so it fits perfectly.

activities.prompt: Zinc is less reactive than copper, so zinc cannot displace copper from copper sulphate.
activities.explanation: Zinc is actually more reactive than copper, so it does displace copper from copper sulphate. Good careful thinking!

activities.prompt: When sodium sulphate and barium chloride solutions mix, a white insoluble substance called a ______ forms.
activities.hint: It is the solid that settles out of the solution.
activities.explanation: The insoluble substance formed is a precipitate, and this is a precipitation reaction. Superb recall!

activities.prompt: Copper powder gains oxygen when heated and becomes copper(II) oxide. What has happened to the copper?
options: It has been oxidised
It has been reduced
It has been dissolved
It has been precipitated
activities.explanation: A substance that gains oxygen during a reaction is oxidised. Copper gained oxygen, so it was oxidised. Brilliant!

activities.prompt: Match each experiment with what you would observe.
pairs: Silver chloride is kept in sunlight
Iron nail in copper sulphate solution
activities.explanation: Colour, fumes and flames are clues that a chemical reaction is happening. You have learned to read them like a detective!

boss.sceneCaption: A burning magnesium ribbon photographed with very short exposure to show oxidation detail.
