chapters.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
chapters.summary: In this chapter: lesson 1: indicators and acids and bases in the laboratory; lesson 2: reactions of acids and bases; lesson 3: common acids and bases in water; lesson 4: strength, ph and everyday importance.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Indicators and acids and bases in the laboratory

activities.prompt: Why does a curry stain turn red when you scrub it with soap?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is an indicator?
activities.body: Some substances are acids and some are bases. Acids taste sour. Bases taste bitter. But you must never taste things in a lab! So we use indicators. An indicator changes colour to tell us if a substance is acidic or basic. Litmus and turmeric are natural indicators. Methyl orange and phenolphthalein are synthetic indicators made in factories.
keyPoints: Indicators show acid or base by a colour change.
Litmus and turmeric are natural indicators.
Methyl orange and phenolphthalein are synthetic indicators.
activities.explanation: Indicators are our safe colour helpers for testing acids and bases.

activities.title: Mix acid and base

tasks.then: More base than acid: litmus turns blue.

activities.takeaway: Equal amounts of acid and base cancel out and make a neutral solution.
activities.explanation: Equal amounts of acid and base cancel out and make a neutral solution.

activities.prompt: Meera scrubs soap on a curry stain on her white cloth. The stain turns reddish-brown. She washes the cloth with lots of water. Why does the stain turn yellow again?
steps: The curry stain has turmeric, which is a natural indicator.
Soap makes the stain change colour, so soap acts like a base on the indicator.
Washing with plenty of water removes the soap from the cloth.
Without the soap, the stain goes back to yellow, so the colour change was because of the soap.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which of these is a natural indicator?
options: Methyl orange
Litmus
Phenolphthalein
activities.explanation: Litmus comes from lichen, a natural source. The other two are synthetic indicators.

activities.prompt: You dip a red litmus paper into a liquid. It turns blue. What is the liquid?
options: A base
An acid
Pure water
activities.explanation: Bases change red litmus to blue. Acids do the opposite with blue litmus.

activities.prompt: Litmus solution is a purple dye extracted from ______.
activities.hint: It is a plant-like growth that grows on rocks and trees.
activities.explanation: Litmus is a purple dye taken from lichen. That is why it is a natural indicator.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what it does or shows.
activities.explanation: Acids are sour and turn blue litmus red. Bases are bitter and turn red litmus blue.

activities.prompt: Some indicators are special because their smell changes in acids and bases. What are they called?
options: Olfactory indicators
Synthetic indicators
Natural indicators
activities.explanation: Olfactory indicators are substances whose odour changes in acidic or basic media.

activities.prompt: Put the curry stain experiment in the correct order.
items: There is a curry stain on white cloth.
Soap is scrubbed on the stain.
The stain becomes reddish-brown.
The cloth is washed with plenty of water.
The stain turns yellow again.
activities.explanation: Soap makes the turmeric in curry change colour. Plenty of water washes it back to yellow.

activities.prompt: A curry stain turned reddish-brown after soap was scrubbed on it. Then the cloth was washed with plenty of water. Why did the stain turn yellow again?
options: The water washed the soap away from the cloth.
The water made the stain stronger and darker.
The water turned the soap into a new stain.
The water changed the cloth into a new colour.

why.The water made the stain stronger and da: Wrong. He thinks water adds colour, but water only washes the soap off.
why.The water turned the soap into a new sta: Wrong. He thinks water makes new stains, but water cleans the cloth.
why.The water changed the cloth into a new c: Wrong. He thinks water dyes the cloth, but water only removes the soap.

activities.explanation: Right. Plenty of water removes the soap, so the stain goes back to yellow.

activities.prompt: Sara puts a drop of sour lemon juice on blue litmus paper. What will she see?
options: The paper turns red.
The paper turns blue.
The paper turns yellow.
The paper stays the same.

Wrong. He thinks blue stays blue, but acids change blue litmus to red.
Wrong. He mixes up turmeric colours with litmus colours.
Wrong. He thinks sour things do nothing, but acids change blue litmus.

activities.explanation: Right. Lemon juice is sour, and acids turn blue litmus red.

activities.prompt: A liquid tastes bitter. Amit puts a drop of it on red litmus paper. What will happen?
options: The paper turns blue.
The paper turns red.
The paper turns purple.
The paper loses its colour.

Wrong. He thinks all liquids turn litmus red, but only acids do that.
Wrong. He thinks litmus always turns purple, but bases turn it blue.
Wrong. He thinks litmus fades, but bases change red litmus to blue.

activities.explanation: Right. Bitter things are bases, and bases turn red litmus blue.

activities.prompt: A soap stain on cloth turned reddish-brown. Priya says, 'The stain changed colour, so the soap must be sour like an acid.' What is wrong with her claim?
options: Sour acids turn blue litmus red, not cloth stains red-brown.
Sour acids turn red litmus blue, so soap is not sour.
Sour acids make stains yellow, so soap is not sour.
Sour acids never change the colour of anything at all.

why.Sour acids turn red litmus blue, so soap: Wrong. She mixes up what acids do to red litmus with what bases do.
why.Sour acids make stains yellow, so soap i: Wrong. She thinks acids make stains yellow, but water washing makes it yellow.
why.Sour acids never change the colour of an: Wrong. She thinks acids change nothing, but acids do change blue litmus to red.

activities.explanation: Right. Acids are known by blue litmus turning red, not by this stain change.

lessons.sceneAlt: Blue and red litmus paper strips showing how they change colour when placed in acid or base solutions.
lessons.sceneCaption: Blue and red litmus paper showing colour changes when placed in acids and bases.

sceneCredit.text: Litmus paper by Chemicalinterest, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Chemicalinterest

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Reactions of acids and bases

activities.prompt: What happens when you mix a metal with an acid?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What acids and bases do
activities.body: Acids and bases love to react! When an acid meets a metal, it gives a salt and hydrogen gas. When an acid meets a base, we get a salt and water. This is called neutralisation. Acids also react with carbonates to make carbon dioxide. Watch the bubbles and colour changes!
keyPoints: Acid plus metal gives salt and hydrogen gas.
Acid plus base gives salt and water. This is neutralisation.
Acid plus carbonate gives salt, carbon dioxide and water.
activities.explanation: Acids and bases take part in many exciting reactions that make new things.

activities.title: Mix acid and base

tasks.then: More base than acid: litmus turns blue.

activities.takeaway: Equal amounts of acid and base cancel out and make a neutral solution.
activities.explanation: Equal amounts of acid and base cancel out and make a neutral solution.

activities.prompt: Riya cleans a tarnished metal spoon with a lemon. She sees tiny bubbles rising. What is making the bubbles?
steps: The spoon is metal and lemon juice is an acid, so they can react together.
When an acid touches a metal, the metal pushes the hydrogen out of the acid.
That pushed-out hydrogen escapes as hydrogen gas, which we see as bubbles.
So the bubbles are hydrogen gas made by the acid and metal reacting.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Zinc metal is dropped into an acid. What are the products?
options: Salt and hydrogen gas
Salt and oxygen gas
Water and salt only
Carbon dioxide and water
activities.explanation: An acid plus a metal always gives a salt and hydrogen gas. Well done!

activities.prompt: Acid plus base gives salt and water. What is this reaction called?
options: Neutralisation
Displacement
Burning
Freezing
activities.explanation: The acid and base cancel each other out to make salt and water. This is neutralisation.

activities.prompt: When a metal reacts with an acid, the metal pushes hydrogen atoms out of the acid as hydrogen gas.
activities.explanation: Yes! The metal displaces hydrogen atoms from the acid, and the gas escapes.

activities.prompt: When sodium hydroxide reacts with zinc, we get hydrogen gas and sodium ______.
activities.hint: Think of the salt made from zinc and sodium together.
activities.explanation: Sodium hydroxide with zinc gives sodium zincate and hydrogen gas. Great spotting!

activities.prompt: Copper oxide is stirred into hydrochloric acid. What happens to the solution?
options: It turns blue-green
It turns bright red
It turns black
It stays colourless
activities.explanation: Copper oxide dissolves in the acid and the solution becomes blue-green. Lovely colour change!

activities.prompt: Match each reaction with what it makes.
activities.explanation: Each pair of chemicals makes its own special products. You matched them like a scientist!

activities.prompt: Priya drops a small piece of metal into an acid in a test tube. Bubbles start coming out. She holds her ear near the tube. What is the gas in the bubbles most likely doing?
options: It is hydrogen coming out of the acid
It is air that was hiding inside the metal
It is the acid turning into a gas and escaping
It is water vapour made by the warm tube

why.It is air that was hiding inside the met: Wrong: this thinks the metal was full of trapped air, but the gas comes from the reaction.
why.It is the acid turning into a gas and es: Wrong: this thinks the acid itself becomes a gas, but the acid turns into a salt instead.
why.It is water vapour made by the warm tube: Wrong: this blames warmth, but the bubbles come from the reaction, not from heating.

activities.explanation: Right: the metal pushes hydrogen out of the acid, so the bubbles are hydrogen gas.

activities.prompt: A student says: 'When a metal reacts with an acid, the metal disappears and nothing is left.' You do the reaction and look at the tube afterwards. What will you find that proves the student wrong?
options: A new salt is left behind in the tube
The acid has turned into plain water
The metal has changed into hydrogen gas
Nothing is left, the student is correct

why.The acid has turned into plain water: Wrong: this confuses the acid-metal reaction with neutralisation, which makes water.
why.The metal has changed into hydrogen gas: Wrong: the hydrogen comes from the acid, not from the metal turning into gas.
why.Nothing is left, the student is correct: Wrong: something new is always formed, so the tube is not empty.

activities.explanation: Right: acid plus metal gives a salt and hydrogen gas, so a salt stays in the tube.

activities.prompt: Two tubes are set up. Tube A has zinc with sodium hydroxide. Tube B has zinc with an acid. Both tubes show bubbles. What is the same about both tubes?
options: Both tubes give off hydrogen gas
Both tubes make a salt and water
Both tubes give off carbon dioxide gas
Both tubes turn a blue-green colour

why.Both tubes make a salt and water: Wrong: water forms in neutralisation, not when a metal reacts with an acid or a base.
why.Both tubes give off carbon dioxide gas: Wrong: carbon dioxide comes from carbonates, not from metals with acids or bases.
why.Both tubes turn a blue-green colour: Wrong: the blue-green colour happens with copper oxide in acid, not with zinc.

activities.explanation: Right: zinc with a base gives hydrogen, and zinc with an acid also gives hydrogen.

activities.prompt: Meena mixes baking soda, which is sodium hydrogencarbonate, with some acid in a glass. The mixture fizzes strongly. Her brother says the fizz is hydrogen gas. What should Meena tell him?
options: The fizz is carbon dioxide, not hydrogen
The fizz is hydrogen, her brother is right
The fizz is air pushed out by the soda
The fizz is water turning into a gas

why.The fizz is hydrogen, her brother is rig: Wrong: he is mixing up the metal reaction, which gives hydrogen, with the carbonate reaction.
why.The fizz is air pushed out by the soda: Wrong: the gas is made by the reaction, it was not already hiding in the soda.
why.The fizz is water turning into a gas: Wrong: water is a product here, but it stays as liquid, not as a gas.

activities.explanation: Right: sodium hydrogencarbonate with an acid gives carbon dioxide, which makes the fizz.

activities.prompt: A student adds some copper oxide powder to acid and stirs. The powder slowly disappears and the liquid turns blue-green. Another student says: 'The powder just melted like ice.' What is the better explanation?
options: The copper oxide reacted with the acid and dissolved
The copper oxide melted because the acid was warm
The copper oxide dissolved in water made by the acid
The copper oxide sank and became invisible at the bottom

why.The copper oxide melted because the acid: Wrong: melting needs heat, but here a chemical reaction with the acid is happening.
why.The copper oxide dissolved in water made: Wrong: the colour change shows a reaction with the acid, not simple dissolving in water.
why.The copper oxide sank and became invisib: Wrong: something at the bottom would still be seen, but the powder has truly gone.

activities.explanation: Right: copper oxide really reacts with acid and dissolves, giving the blue-green colour.

lessons.sceneAlt: A student in a laboratory holds a test tube where magnesium metal reacts with hydrochloric acid to release hydrogen gas.
lessons.sceneCaption: Magnesium reacting with hydrochloric acid releases hydrogen gas, which burns in air to form water.

sceneCredit.text: Получение водорода при помощи металла и соляной кислоты by Голубева Наталья, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Common acids and bases in water

activities.prompt: Why does pouring acid into water need so much care?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Acids and bases meet water
activities.body: Acids make hydrogen ions, H+(aq), when they mix with water. Bases make hydroxide ions, OH–, in water. Bases that dissolve in water are called alkalis. These ions carry electric current through the solution. Mixing an acid or a base with water gives out a lot of heat, so we must be careful.
keyPoints: Acids produce hydrogen ions, H+(aq), in water.
Bases produce hydroxide ions, OH–, in water.
Bases soluble in water are called alkalis.
Dissolving an acid or base in water is highly exothermic.
activities.explanation: Water helps acids and bases split into ions that can carry current.

activities.prompt: Riya adds water to a bottle of strong acid. Her friend says to pour the acid into the water instead. Why is her friend right?
steps: Dissolving acid in water gives out a lot of heat, so the mixture gets very hot.
If water is poured into acid, only a little water touches lots of acid at once.
The small amount of water heats up very fast and can splash out.
So the acid must be added slowly to water with stirring, because water can absorb the heat safely.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Water is the helper
activities.body: The hydrogen ions in an acid like HCl are made only when water is present. H+ joins with H2O to form H3O+. Adding more water to an acid or base lowers the ion concentration per unit volume. This is why we always add acid slowly to water while stirring.
keyPoints: H+ ions in HCl are produced only in the presence of water.
H+ combines with H2O to form H3O+.
Adding water decreases ion concentration per unit volume.
Always add acid slowly to water with constant stirring.
activities.explanation: Water lets ions form, and stirring keeps the mixing safe.

activities.prompt: Electric current flows through an acidic solution. What carries the current?
options: Tiny metal pieces
Ions in the solution
Bubbles of air
Heat from the wire
activities.explanation: Ions moving in the acidic solution carry the electric current. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: Bases that are soluble in water are called ______.
activities.hint: Think of the special name for bases that dissolve in water.
activities.explanation: Soluble bases get a special name: alkalis. You remembered it!

activities.prompt: All acids give hydrogen gas when they react with metals.
activities.explanation: Yes! Reacting with metals is how all acids make hydrogen gas.

activities.prompt: Match each ion or molecule with what it is.
pairs: formed when H+ and OH– combine
activities.explanation: H+ and OH– are the key ions, and they join to make water again.

activities.prompt: You add more water to a solution of a base. What happens to the ions?
options: Ion concentration per unit volume decreases
Ion concentration per unit volume increases
The ions all turn into metal
The ions stop the current forever
activities.explanation: Adding water spreads the ions out, so there are fewer ions in each unit of volume. Great thinking!

activities.prompt: Put the steps for diluting an acid in the right order.
items: Take some water in a container
Add the acid slowly to the water
Keep stirring constantly
activities.explanation: Acid goes into water slowly, with constant stirring, because so much heat is given out.

activities.prompt: Zinc metal is dropped into an acid solution. Bubbles start coming out. The bubbles are of a gas. Which gas is coming out?
options: Oxygen gas
Hydrogen gas
Water vapour
Carbon dioxide gas

why.Oxygen gas: Thinks bubbles must always be oxygen, which is a common guess.
why.Water vapour: Thinks the bubbles are just the water boiling away.
why.Carbon dioxide gas: Mixes up acids with carbonated drinks, which give carbon dioxide.

activities.explanation: Right: all acids give hydrogen gas when they react with metals.

activities.prompt: A dry acid powder has no water near it. It is touched with a dry tester and no current flows. Water is then mixed in and the tester works. Why did the current flow after adding water?
options: Water made the powder softer to touch
Water helped the acid form ions that carry current
Water cooled the acid down slowly
Water made the acid stronger than before

why.Water made the powder softer to touch: Thinks softness helps electricity, but softness is not the reason.
why.Water cooled the acid down slowly: Thinks temperature is the key idea here, which it is not.
why.Water made the acid stronger than before: Thinks water makes acids stronger, but water only lets ions form.

activities.explanation: Right: hydrogen ions form in the presence of water, and ions carry the current.

activities.prompt: A student says an acid solution has only one kind of charged particle in it. Is the student correct?
options: No, an acid has a positive ion and also a negative ion
Yes, an acid has only positive ions in it
Yes, an acid has only negative ions in it
No, an acid has no charged particles at all

why.Yes, an acid has only positive ions in i: Thinks only the H+ ion exists and forgets the other ion.
why.Yes, an acid has only negative ions in i: Thinks only the negative ion exists and forgets H+.
why.No, an acid has no charged particles at: Thinks solutions have no ions, but ions carry the current.

activities.explanation: Right: an acid has H+ as the cation and an anion with it.

activities.prompt: A student pours a strong base quickly into a small cup of water without stirring. The cup gets very hot fast. What should the student have done?
options: Added the base slowly to water while stirring it
Added more base at once to finish faster
Used a closed lid to keep the heat inside
Poured the water into the base instead

why.Added more base at once to finish faster: Thinks speed is good, but more base at once makes more heat.
why.Used a closed lid to keep the heat insid: Thinks trapping heat helps, but trapped heat is more dangerous.
why.Poured the water into the base instead: Reverses the safe rule; water must not be poured into the base.

activities.explanation: Right: dissolving a base is very hot, so slow adding with stirring keeps it safe.

activities.prompt: Cup A has a strong acid with many ions in a little water. Cup B has the same acid mixed with much more water. A tester glows in both cups. In which cup does the bulb glow less, and why?
options: Cup A, because it has more water per ion
Cup B, because water lowers the ions in each unit volume
Cup A, because water lowers the ions in each unit volume
Cup B, because it has more ions in each unit volume

why.Cup A, because it has more water per ion: Says Cup A but gives the reason for Cup B, so it is mixed up.
why.Cup A, because water lowers the ions in: Gives the right reason but points to the wrong cup.
why.Cup B, because it has more ions in each: Thinks more water means more ions per volume, which is backwards.

activities.explanation: Right: adding water spreads the ions out, so fewer ions sit in each unit volume.

lessons.sceneAlt: Red litmus paper changing colour when dipped in sodium hydroxide solution.
lessons.sceneCaption: Red litmus paper reacts with sodium hydroxide, a base.

sceneCredit.text: The result of red litmus paper reaction with a base by Kanesskong, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Kanesskong

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Strength, pH and everyday importance

activities.prompt: Why does a bee sting hurt, and how can pH help?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How strong is an acid?
activities.body: Some acids are strong and some are weak. A universal indicator is a mixture of several indicators. It shows different colours at different amounts of hydrogen ions. The pH scale measures hydrogen ions in a solution. pH 7 is neutral. Below 7 is acidic. Acids that give more H+ ions are strong acids.
keyPoints: A universal indicator is a mixture of several indicators.
The pH scale measures hydrogen ion concentration in a solution.
pH 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic, and strong acids give more H+ ions.
activities.explanation: pH is a simple number that tells you how acidic a solution is.

activities.prompt: Riya drinks lemon juice. Her mouth starts to feel strange. She wonders if her mouth pH has changed and if her teeth could be in danger.
steps: Lemon juice is acidic, so it adds hydrogen ions to her mouth.
More hydrogen ions mean a lower pH, so her mouth pH drops.
Tooth decay starts when mouth pH goes below 5.5.
So if the pH drops low enough, her teeth could be at risk, and rinsing with water helps.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is a universal indicator?
options: A single indicator used in every lab
A mixture of several indicators
A special kind of base
A machine that heats solutions
activities.explanation: Well done! A universal indicator is made by mixing several indicators together.

activities.prompt: A solution has a pH of 4. What kind of solution is it?
options: A neutral solution
A basic solution
An acidic solution
It has no pH
activities.explanation: Values less than 7 on the pH scale mean an acidic solution. You got it!

activities.prompt: A neutral solution has a pH of 7.
activities.explanation: Yes! pH 7 sits right in the middle, neither acidic nor basic.

activities.prompt: Acid rain is rain water with a pH less than ______.
activities.hint: It is just below six.
activities.explanation: Rain with pH below 5.6 is called acid rain. Great remembering!

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what the lesson says about it.
activities.explanation: Each pair comes straight from the lesson. Super matching!

activities.prompt: Put these pH values in order, starting with the most acidic.
activities.explanation: Lower pH means more acidic, so 5.5 comes first and 7.8 last. Brilliant ordering!

activities.prompt: Two acids are tested. Acid A gives many H+ ions in water. Acid B gives only a few H+ ions. Which acid is the strong acid, and why?
options: Acid B, because weak acids taste stronger.
Acid A, because more H+ ions make an acid strong.
Acid B, because fewer ions always mean more strength.
Acid A, because strong acids are always safe to touch.

why.Acid B, because weak acids taste stronge: This confuses strength with taste; strength depends on H+ ions given.
why.Acid B, because fewer ions always mean m: This reverses the rule; fewer ions mean a weaker acid.
why.Acid A, because strong acids are always: The conclusion is right but the reason is wrong; safety is not the rule here.

activities.explanation: Correct. Acids that give more H+ ions are strong acids.

activities.prompt: A student says: 'A solution with pH 6 is neutral because 6 is close to 7.' What is the flaw in this claim?
options: Only pH 7 is neutral; pH 6 is acidic.
pH 6 is neutral, but only in warm water.
pH 6 is neutral because it is an even number.
pH 6 is basic because it is below 7.

This adds a wrong idea; temperature does not change the neutral value.
why.pH 6 is neutral because it is an even nu: This confuses maths with chemistry; even numbers do not matter here.
This reverses the rule; below 7 means acidic, not basic.

activities.explanation: Correct. Only pH 7 is neutral; values less than 7 are acidic.

activities.prompt: After a bee sting, a friend says: 'Rub a base like an antacid cream on it. It will make the pain worse.' Is the friend right?
options: Yes, bases always increase pain from stings.
No, the base can neutralise the acid from the sting.
Yes, because bee stings leave a base on the skin.
No, but only because bee stings contain no acid at all.

why.Yes, bases always increase pain from sti: This is a fear-based guess; bases can actually cancel the acid.
why.Yes, because bee stings leave a base on: This mixes up the facts; a bee sting leaves an acid, not a base.
why.No, but only because bee stings contain: The action is right but the reason is wrong; the sting does leave an acid.

activities.explanation: Correct. The sting leaves an acid, and a base can cancel it, easing the pain.

lessons.sceneAlt: A universal indicator test strip showing the colour for an acidic solution, tested with lemon juice.
lessons.sceneCaption: Universal indicator test for lemon juice, an acidic solution.

sceneCredit.text: Universal Indicator set for an acidic solution by Rupal Dugar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Salts, families and chemicals from common salt

activities.prompt: Why do some salts belong to the same family?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Salt families and salt secrets
activities.body: Salts with the same positive or negative radical belong to one family. So NaCl and KCl are both chloride family salts. A salt made from a strong base and a weak acid is basic in nature. Common salt comes from rock salt, which has large brown crystals. Common salt is a raw material for many things we use daily. The chlor-alkali process uses it to make useful products.
keyPoints: Salts with the same radical belong to a family.
NaCl and KCl are chloride family salts.
A salt of a strong base and weak acid is basic.
Common salt is a raw material for daily-use materials.
activities.explanation: One small crystal of salt opens the door to a whole family of chemicals!

activities.title: Chemicals hiding in common salt
activities.body: Common salt is a raw material for many materials of daily use. The chlor-alkali process gets its name from the products it forms. From salt chemistry we also get baking soda, which is sodium hydrogencarbonate, and washing soda, which is Na2CO3.10H2O. So the humble salt in your kitchen is a busy factory helper!
keyPoints: Common salt is a raw material for daily-use materials.
The chlor-alkali process is named for its products.
Baking soda is sodium hydrogencarbonate.
Washing soda is Na2CO3.10H2O.
activities.explanation: Your kitchen salt is the starting point for many useful chemicals.

activities.prompt: NaCl and KCl have the same negative radical. Which family do they belong to?
options: The chloride family
The sodium family
The potassium family
The rock salt family
activities.explanation: Both salts share the same negative radical, chloride. Salts with the same radical sit in one family.

activities.prompt: Bleaching powder is made when chlorine acts on dry slaked ______.
activities.hint: Think of the white powder used to make walls white.
activities.explanation: Chlorine acting on dry slaked lime gives us bleaching powder.

activities.prompt: Rock salt is made of large crystals that are often brown because of impurities.
activities.explanation: Well done! Rock salt has large crystals, and impurities give it a brown colour.

activities.prompt: Match each salt to what you have learnt about it.
pairs: A raw material for daily use
activities.explanation: Each salt has its own identity. Spotting them is a useful skill!

activities.prompt: Why is the chlor-alkali process called by this name?
options: Because of the products formed
Because it needs lots of heat
Because it was found near a sea
Because it uses rock salt only
activities.explanation: The name comes from the products formed in the process. Good thinking!

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order, from start to finish.
items: Start with common salt as a raw material
Use the chlor-alkali process
Chlorine is formed as a product
Chlorine acts on dry slaked lime
Bleaching powder is produced
activities.explanation: Common salt goes through the chlor-alkali process, chlorine is formed, and it then acts on dry slaked lime to make bleaching powder.

activities.prompt: Ravi has NaCl and KCl. He puts each salt in water and tests them. He wants to sort them into families. He looks at the negative part of each salt. What should he find?
options: Both have chloride, so both go in one family
Both have sodium, so both go in one family
They have different radicals, so they need two families
They look different, so families cannot be used here

why.Both have sodium, so both go in one fami: He looked at the wrong part. KCl has no sodium in it.
why.They have different radicals, so they ne: He forgot that the shared chloride radical puts them together.
why.They look different, so families cannot: He thinks family means looking similar, not sharing a radical.

activities.explanation: Right. Same negative radical means same family, so both are chlorides.

activities.prompt: A shop sells rock salt in big crystals. Meena sees the crystals are brown. Her friend says the salt is spoiled. What is the truth?
options: The brown colour comes from impurities in the crystals
The brown colour means the salt has gone bad
The brown colour means it is not a salt at all
The brown colour means the crystals are too small

why.The brown colour means the salt has gone: She thinks any colour change means spoilage, which is wrong here.
why.The brown colour means it is not a salt: She thinks only white things can be salts.
why.The brown colour means the crystals are: She mixes up crystal size with colour.

activities.explanation: Right. Rock salt is often brown because of impurities.

activities.prompt: A student says common salt is useless in industry. His teacher points to a factory. The factory takes in common salt every day. What does this show?
options: Common salt is a raw material for many daily-use materials
Common salt is only useful for cooking food
The factory must be making only common salt
The factory is wasting money by buying common salt

why.Common salt is only useful for cooking f: He thinks salt has only one use, in the kitchen.
why.The factory must be making only common s: He confuses using a material with making it.
why.The factory is wasting money by buying c: He thinks buying a cheap material means waste.

activities.explanation: Right. Common salt is a starting material for daily-use things.

activities.prompt: A worker makes bleaching powder. He has wet slaked lime and dry slaked lime. Chlorine gas is ready. Which lime should he use, and why?
options: Dry slaked lime, because chlorine acts on dry slaked lime
Wet slaked lime, because chlorine needs water to act
Dry slaked lime, because dry things are always stronger
Wet slaked lime, because bleaching powder needs extra water

why.Wet slaked lime, because chlorine needs: He adds his own idea that water is always needed.
why.Dry slaked lime, because dry things are: He thinks dry means better, without knowing the real reason.
why.Wet slaked lime, because bleaching powde: He thinks the product must contain the water he adds.

activities.explanation: Right. Bleaching powder forms when chlorine acts on dry slaked lime.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Water of Crystallisation and Plaster of Paris

activities.prompt: How can a 'dry' crystal secretly hold water inside it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Water Hiding Inside Crystals
activities.body: Some crystals look dry but hold water inside them. This hidden water is called water of crystallisation. Blue copper sulphate crystals hold five water molecules in each formula unit. Heat them, and the water leaves, so the crystals turn white. Add water again, and the blue colour returns. Gypsum holds two water molecules. Heat gypsum to 373 K and you get Plaster of Paris, used for broken bones and toys.
keyPoints: Water of crystallisation is water trapped inside crystals.
Heating blue copper sulphate makes it white; water makes it blue again.
Plaster of Paris is made by heating gypsum and sets into gypsum with water.
activities.explanation: Crystals can hold water even when they look perfectly dry.

activities.prompt: Priya finds blue copper sulphate crystals in a bottle. They look completely dry. She says there is no water in them. Is she right?
steps: The crystals look dry, so Priya thinks they hold no water.
But looking dry does not prove anything, because water can hide inside a solid.
If we heat the crystals, the hidden water leaves and the blue colour turns white.
So the crystals are not really dry. They carry water of crystallisation inside them.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Blue copper sulphate crystals look dry. What do they really contain inside?
options: Salt and sugar
Water of crystallisation
Melted ice cubes
Small air bubbles
activities.explanation: The crystals seem dry, but water of crystallisation is hidden inside them.

activities.prompt: One formula unit of copper sulphate contains ______ water molecules.
activities.hint: Count the H2O part in CuSO4.5H2O.
activities.explanation: The formula CuSO4.5H2O shows five water molecules in each formula unit.

activities.prompt: Match each salt with its formula.
activities.explanation: Copper sulphate holds five water molecules and gypsum holds two. Their formulas show this clearly.

activities.prompt: Gypsum is heated at 373 K. What is made?
options: Copper sulphate
Common salt
Calcium sulphate hemihydrate
Blue vitriol crystals
activities.explanation: Heating gypsum at 373 K gives calcium sulphate hemihydrate, which is Plaster of Paris.

activities.prompt: A doctor sets a broken arm. Why choose Plaster of Paris for the cast?
options: It becomes gypsum and holds the bone firmly
It stays soft and runny forever
It melts away when the bone heals
It turns into copper sulphate
activities.explanation: Plaster of Paris changes to gypsum with water, so it sets hard and supports the fractured bone.

activities.prompt: Put the copper sulphate experiment steps in the right order.
items: Start with blue copper sulphate crystals
Heat the crystals strongly
Water of crystallisation leaves the salt
The crystals turn white
Moisten with water and blue returns
activities.explanation: Heat drives the water out and the salt turns white. Adding water brings the blue colour back.

activities.prompt: Amit heated blue copper sulphate. It became a white powder. Now he adds a few drops of water to it. The blue colour comes back. Why does this happen?
options: The water cools the hot powder down again.
The water goes back inside and joins the salt again.
The water washes the white dust off the surface.
The water makes a new salt with a new colour.

why.The water cools the hot powder down agai: He thinks colour depends only on temperature, not on water.
why.The water washes the white dust off the: He thinks the blue was hiding under white dust, which is wrong.
why.The water makes a new salt with a new co: He thinks water always makes a new substance, but here the same salt returns.

activities.explanation: Right. Water of crystallisation returns, so the salt becomes blue again.

activities.prompt: Meena says copper sulphate crystals hold no water at all. Her reason is that the crystals look completely dry. What is the flaw in her claim?
options: Looking dry does not show what is hidden inside the crystals.
She should have tasted the crystals to check for water.
Crystals are always wet, so her whole claim is wrong.
A blue colour always proves that water is present outside.

why.She should have tasted the crystals to c: Tasting is not a safe test and would not prove her claim either.
why.Crystals are always wet, so her whole cl: Crystals are not always wet, so this reason is not correct.
why.A blue colour always proves that water i: The colour does not tell where the water is, inside or outside.

activities.explanation: Right. Water of crystallisation hides inside, so looks alone cannot decide.

activities.prompt: A toy maker mixes Plaster of Paris powder with water. He pours the soft mix into a toy mould. He waits for some time. What will happen inside the mould?
options: The mix will stay a soft powder at the bottom.
The mix will change to gypsum and take the toy's shape.
The mix will turn blue like copper sulphate crystals.
The mix will turn into clear water and drain away.

why.The mix will stay a soft powder at the b: He forgot that mixing with water starts a change, not just settling.
why.The mix will turn blue like copper sulph: He is mixing up two different salts from the same lesson.
why.The mix will turn into clear water and d: He thinks the powder dissolves away, but it sets instead.

activities.explanation: Right. Plaster of Paris changes to gypsum with water, so it sets into the toy shape.

activities.context: During lunch, Meera spilled curry on her white school shirt. Remembering her science lesson, she scrubbed the stain with soap, and the yellow mark slowly turned reddish-brown. Her friend said the shirt was ruined, but Meera took the shirt home and washed it with plenty of water. She told her friend that the stain would not stay reddish-brown, because the colour in the curry was behaving like a special kind of substance she had studied in class.
activities.prompt: After Meera washes the shirt with plenty of water, what will most likely happen to the stain?
options: It will become yellow again
It will stay reddish-brown permanently
It will turn deep blue
It will become darker reddish-brown

why.It will stay reddish-brown permanently: Wrong: the reddish-brown shade is not permanent once the cloth is rinsed well.
why.It will turn deep blue: Wrong: nothing in this situation turns the stain blue.
why.It will become darker reddish-brown: Wrong: washing with plenty of water lightens and reverses the colour, it does not deepen it.

activities.explanation: Correct: plenty of water reverses the colour change, so the stain returns to yellow.

activities.context: During lunch, Meera spilled curry on her white school shirt. Remembering her science lesson, she scrubbed the stain with soap, and the yellow mark slowly turned reddish-brown. Her friend said the shirt was ruined, but Meera took the shirt home and washed it with plenty of water. She told her friend that the stain would not stay reddish-brown, because the colour in the curry was behaving like a special kind of substance she had studied in class.
activities.prompt: Why did the stain change colour when Meera scrubbed soap on it?
options: The colouring in curry acts as an indicator, and it responded to the soap
The soap dissolved the curry completely out of the cloth
The friction of scrubbing heated the cloth and burnt the stain
The white fabric changed colour on its own when wet

why.The soap dissolved the curry completely: Wrong: if the curry had dissolved away, the stain would fade, not change to reddish-brown.
why.The friction of scrubbing heated the clo: Wrong: scrubbing does not burn the cloth; the change is a colour change of the stain.
why.The white fabric changed colour on its o: Wrong: plain white fabric does not change colour by itself when it gets wet.

activities.explanation: Correct: turmeric in the curry is an indicator, so its colour changed when soap was applied.

activities.context: During lunch, Meera spilled curry on her white school shirt. Remembering her science lesson, she scrubbed the stain with soap, and the yellow mark slowly turned reddish-brown. Her friend said the shirt was ruined, but Meera took the shirt home and washed it with plenty of water. She told her friend that the stain would not stay reddish-brown, because the colour in the curry was behaving like a special kind of substance she had studied in class.
activities.prompt: Meera wants to show her friend another household material that can behave the same way as the curry stain. Which should she pick?
options: Leaves of red cabbage
A stainless steel spoon
A piece of plain white cloth
A colourless sugar solution

why.A stainless steel spoon: Wrong: a metal spoon has no colour that changes to signal acid or base.
why.A piece of plain white cloth: Wrong: plain white cloth has no colour that can change to indicate anything.
why.A colourless sugar solution: Wrong: a colourless solution shows no colour change, so it cannot act as an indicator.

activities.explanation: Correct: red cabbage leaves are a natural material that can indicate acid or base by colour change.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Turmeric can be used to tell whether a substance is acidic or basic.
Reason (R): Turmeric is a natural indicator.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Because turmeric is a natural indicator, it shows a colour change that reveals whether a substance is acidic or basic.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Washing a curry-stained cloth with plenty of water turns the stain reddish-brown.
Reason (R): Scrubbing soap on a curry stain makes it reddish-brown.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Plenty of water actually turns the stain yellow again, while the statement about soap scrubbing is true.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between natural and synthetic indicators? Give one example of each.
activities.answer: Natural indicators are materials obtained from natural sources, such as plants, that show a colour change to tell us whether a substance is acidic or basic. Examples are litmus, which is a purple dye extracted from lichen, and turmeric. Red cabbage leaves and coloured petals of some flowers can also act this way, and such natural materials are called acid-base indicators. Synthetic indicators, on the other hand, are prepared indicators like methyl orange and phenolphthalein. Both kinds do the same job of indicating acidic or basic substances through a change in colour.
points: Natural indicators come from natural sources like plants.
Examples: litmus (from lichen) and turmeric.
Synthetic indicators include methyl orange and phenolphthalein.
Both indicate acidic or basic nature by colour change.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a lab activity, Aditi places zinc granules in dilute hydrochloric acid and sees bubbles of a gas rising. In a second test tube she adds sodium hydrogencarbonate to the same acid and again sees bubbles. Her teacher then asks her to add a little copper oxide to a third tube of the acid and warm it gently. The solid slowly disappears and the solution in the tube turns blue-green.
activities.prompt: Aditi wonders what she would observe if she repeated the first test using sodium hydroxide instead of hydrochloric acid, with the same zinc granules. What should she expect?
options: No reaction at all, because zinc only reacts with acids
Bubbles of gas again, since zinc with sodium hydroxide gives a salt and hydrogen
Bubbles of carbon dioxide, since sodium hydroxide is a carbonate
A blue-green solution, since zinc oxide would dissolve

why.No reaction at all, because zinc only re: Wrong: zinc is not limited to acids; it also reacts with sodium hydroxide
why.Bubbles of carbon dioxide, since sodium: Wrong: sodium hydroxide is a base, not a carbonate, so no carbon dioxide forms
why.A blue-green solution, since zinc oxide: Wrong: the blue-green colour is linked to copper oxide in acid, not to zinc here

activities.explanation: Correct: sodium hydroxide with zinc gives sodium zincate and hydrogen gas

activities.context: During a lab activity, Aditi places zinc granules in dilute hydrochloric acid and sees bubbles of a gas rising. In a second test tube she adds sodium hydrogencarbonate to the same acid and again sees bubbles. Her teacher then asks her to add a little copper oxide to a third tube of the acid and warm it gently. The solid slowly disappears and the solution in the tube turns blue-green.
activities.prompt: If Aditi now adds the same dilute acid to a metal carbonate instead of sodium hydrogencarbonate, what should she predict about the products?
options: Only a salt, with no gas or water formed
A salt, carbon dioxide and water, just as with the hydrogencarbonate
Only hydrogen gas, since carbonates behave like metals
Nothing, since carbonates do not react with acids

why.Only a salt, with no gas or water formed: Wrong: carbonates with acids also give carbon dioxide and water, not a salt alone
why.Only hydrogen gas, since carbonates beha: Wrong: hydrogen gas comes from metals displacing hydrogen, not from carbonates
why.Nothing, since carbonates do not react w: Wrong: metal carbonates do react with acids

activities.explanation: Correct: all metal carbonates react with acids to give a salt, carbon dioxide and water

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): When zinc granules are placed in sodium hydroxide, hydrogen gas is evolved.
Reason (R): Sodium hydroxide reacts with zinc to form sodium zincate and hydrogen.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason correctly states the reaction that produces the hydrogen gas, so it explains the assertion.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): When copper oxide is added to hydrochloric acid, the solution becomes blue-green.
Reason (R): Copper oxide is a non-metallic oxide.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but copper oxide is a metallic oxide, so the reason is false.

activities.prompt: Explain why the solution turns blue-green when copper oxide is added to dilute hydrochloric acid.
activities.answer: Copper oxide is a metallic oxide, and metallic oxides are basic oxides. When a base reacts with an acid, the reaction is called neutralisation, and it gives a salt and water. So when copper oxide is added to hydrochloric acid, the basic oxide reacts with the acid in a neutralisation reaction, forming a salt and water. As this happens, the copper oxide dissolves in the acid, and the resulting solution becomes blue-green in colour. The colour change is therefore the visible sign that the basic metallic oxide has dissolved in the acid during neutralisation.
points: Copper oxide is a metallic oxide
Metallic oxides are basic oxides
Acid plus base gives salt and water (neutralisation)
Copper oxide dissolves in HCl and the solution becomes blue-green
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A base that dissolves easily in water can be called an alkali.
Reason (R): All bases react with metals to produce hydrogen gas.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true because soluble bases are alkalis, but the reason is false since it is acids, not bases, that produce hydrogen gas with metals.

activities.prompt: Explain why an electric current can pass through an acidic solution, and describe what the ions in the solution are.
activities.answer: An acidic solution conducts electricity because the current is carried through it by ions. When an acid is dissolved in water, it produces hydrogen ions, H+(aq), in the solution. An acid contains H+ as its cation along with an anion. In water, the H+ combines with H2O to form H3O+. Since these charged ions are present and free to move in the solution, they carry the electric current through it.
points: Current through an acidic solution is carried by ions
Acids produce hydrogen ions, H+(aq), in solution
Acid contains H+ as cation and an anion
H+ combines with H2O to form H3O+
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After a heavy spicy dinner, Meera felt a burning feeling in her chest. Her mother said her stomach was making too much acid and gave her an antacid from the medical box, which made her feel better. The next afternoon, while watering the garden plants, a bee stung Meera on her arm. She remembered her science lesson and began to think about what the sting had left on her skin and what she should put on it to stop the pain.
activities.prompt: Why did the antacid make Meera's burning feeling go away?
options: It is a base that acts on the excess acid her stomach was making
It is an acid that adds to the acid already in her stomach
It raises the amount of acid in the stomach so digestion speeds up
It lowers the pH of the stomach contents further

why.It is an acid that adds to the acid alre: Wrong: adding more acid would make the burning worse, not better
why.It raises the amount of acid in the stom: Wrong: the problem was too much acid, so speeding up acid action cannot help
why.It lowers the pH of the stomach contents: Wrong: a lower pH means more acid, which would increase the burning

activities.explanation: Correct: during indigestion the stomach makes too much acid, and bases called antacids are used for this

activities.context: After a heavy spicy dinner, Meera felt a burning feeling in her chest. Her mother said her stomach was making too much acid and gave her an antacid from the medical box, which made her feel better. The next afternoon, while watering the garden plants, a bee stung Meera on her arm. She remembered her science lesson and began to think about what the sting had left on her skin and what she should put on it to stop the pain.
activities.prompt: What should Meera put on the bee sting to reduce the pain and irritation?
options: A paste of the antacid, since it is a base that can act on the acid left by the sting
Lemon juice, since sour things are soothing on the skin
Vinegar, since it cleans the wound
Nothing at all, since the sting leaves no substance on the skin

why.Lemon juice, since sour things are sooth: Wrong: lemon juice is acidic, so it would add to the acid rather than act on it
why.Vinegar, since it cleans the wound: Wrong: vinegar is also acidic and would not cancel the acid of the sting
why.Nothing at all, since the sting leaves n: Wrong: the sting does leave an acid behind, which is what causes the pain

activities.explanation: Correct: a bee-sting leaves an acid, so applying a base like the antacid paste is the right move

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A universal indicator shows different colours at different concentrations of hydrogen ions.
Reason (R): A universal indicator is a mixture of several indicators.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Because it is a mixture of several indicators, it is able to show different colours at different hydrogen ion concentrations.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Acid rain is rain water with a pH greater than 5.6.
Reason (R): On the pH scale, values less than 7 mean an acidic solution.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Acid rain actually has a pH less than 5.6, so the assertion is false, while the reason about values below 7 being acidic is true.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid, and how does the pH scale show this difference?
activities.answer: Acids differ in how many H+ ions they give in a solution. Acids that give more H+ ions are strong acids, while acids that give fewer H+ ions are weak acids. The pH scale measures the hydrogen ion concentration in a solution, and a higher hydronium ion concentration means a lower pH. So a strong acid, which gives more H+ ions, will show a lower pH on the scale, while a weak acid will show a pH that is higher, though still less than 7.
points: States that strong acids give more H+ ions
States that weak acids give fewer H+ ions
Links higher hydronium ion concentration to lower pH
Concludes that a strong acid has a lower pH than a weak acid, both below 7
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Acids, Bases and Salts

activities.prompt: Priya dips a red litmus paper into an unknown liquid. The paper turns blue. What is the liquid?
options: An acid
A base
A salt
Pure water
activities.explanation: Bases change red litmus to blue. You spotted the clue well!

activities.prompt: When soap is scrubbed on a curry stain on white cloth, the stain becomes reddish-brown.
activities.explanation: Soap is basic, and turmeric changes colour in a base. Well remembered!

activities.prompt: When an acid and a base react, they give a salt and ______. This reaction is called neutralisation.
activities.hint: Think of what you drink on a hot day.
activities.explanation: Neutralisation always gives a salt and water. You know the pattern!

activities.prompt: Ravi adds a metal to dilute acid and hears fizzing. Which gas bubbles out?
options: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Hydrogen
Nitrogen
activities.explanation: Metals push hydrogen out of acids as hydrogen gas. Great thinking!

activities.prompt: Match each indicator with what you know about it.
pairs: Its smell changes in acid or base
activities.explanation: Indicators can be natural, synthetic, or smell-based. You matched them all!

activities.prompt: Meera tests rain water and finds its pH is below 5.6. What should she call it?
options: Pure water
Acid rain
A basic solution
A neutral solution
activities.explanation: Rain with pH below 5.6 is acid rain. Sharp observation!

activities.prompt: Put the copper sulphate experiment steps in the right order.
items: Blue copper sulphate crystals look dry but hold water
Heating removes the water and the crystals turn white
The crystals are moistened with water
The blue colour comes back
activities.explanation: Heat drives the water out, and water brings the blue back. Perfect order!

activities.prompt: Non-metallic oxides are basic in nature.
activities.explanation: It is the other way round: metallic oxides are basic, non-metallic oxides are acidic. Good catch!

activities.prompt: A neutral solution has a pH of ______ on the pH scale.
activities.hint: Right in the middle of the scale.
activities.explanation: Seven is the middle of the pH scale, so the solution is neutral. Well done!

activities.prompt: Match each salt with its identity or use.
activities.explanation: Each salt has its own story and use. You have mastered this chapter!

chapters.title: Metals and Non-metals
chapters.summary: In this chapter: physical properties of metals and non-metals; chemical properties: metals with air and water; chemical properties: acids, salts and the reactivity series; how metals and non-metals react.

lessons.title: Physical properties of metals and non-metals

activities.prompt: Why can gold be stretched into wires while sulfur crumbles into powder?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Metals and non-metals
activities.body: Elements around us can be sorted into two groups: metals and non-metals. We sort them by looking at their properties. Metals usually shine, can be beaten into sheets, can be pulled into wires, conduct heat, and ring like a bell when struck. Non-metals are usually dull and soft, and they can be solids or gases. Only bromine is a liquid non-metal.
keyPoints: Elements are classified as metals or non-metals by their properties.
Metals are shiny, malleable, ductile, good conductors of heat and sonorous.
Non-metals are solids or gases, except bromine, which is a liquid.
activities.explanation: Sorting elements by their properties helps us study and use them.

activities.prompt: Amma's old gold bangle looks dull. She rubs it with a cloth and it shines again. Why does rubbing bring back the shine?
steps: Metals in pure state have a shining surface called metallic lustre, so the shine belongs to the metal itself.
Dust and dirt sit on top of the surface, so they hide the lustre from our eyes.
Rubbing removes the dirt layer, so the shining metal surface can show again.
So the bangle shines again because the lustre was always there under the dirt.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: A pure metal surface shines brightly. What is this shine called?
options: Metallic lustre
Sonorous sound
Ductility
Malleability
activities.explanation: Metals in pure state have a shining surface called metallic lustre. Well done!

activities.prompt: A blacksmith beats a metal piece into a thin sheet. This property of metals is called ______.
activities.hint: It comes from the word 'hammer'.
activities.explanation: Metals can be beaten into thin sheets. This property is malleability.

activities.prompt: A jeweller draws a metal into a very thin wire for a necklace. Which metal can be drawn into the thinnest wire?
options: Gold
Bromine
Carbon
Iron
activities.explanation: Gold is the most ductile metal, so it can be drawn into very thin wires.

activities.prompt: Match each property with its meaning.
activities.explanation: These four words describe special properties of metals. Great matching!

activities.prompt: Carbon can exist in different forms called ______.
activities.hint: Same element, different forms.
activities.explanation: Carbon can exist in different forms, and these forms are called allotropes.

activities.prompt: Put these substances in order from hardest to softest.
items: Diamond, the hardest natural substance
Iron, a hard metal
An alkali metal, cut with a knife
activities.explanation: Diamond is the hardest natural substance, iron is a hard metal, and alkali metals are so soft that a knife can cut them.

activities.prompt: Iron and coal are hit with the same hammer. Iron flattens into a thin sheet. Coal breaks into small pieces. Why does iron flatten but coal break?
options: Iron is malleable, so it can be beaten into sheets.
Iron is sonorous, so it makes a sound when hit.
Coal is ductile, so it cannot change its shape.
Iron has lustre, so shining things always flatten.

why.Iron is sonorous, so it makes a sound wh: Sonorous means making sound, not changing shape when hit.
why.Coal is ductile, so it cannot change its: Ductility is about wires, and coal is not ductile here.
why.Iron has lustre, so shining things alway: Lustre is about shine, not about how a metal behaves when hit.

activities.explanation: Right: malleability means a metal can be beaten into thin sheets.

activities.prompt: Gold and sulfur are pulled to make wires. Gold makes a very thin wire. Sulfur breaks into pieces. Why can gold do this?
options: Gold is the most ductile metal, so it draws into wires.
Gold is malleable, so hammering turns it into wires.
Gold is sonorous, so it rings and stretches without breaking.
Sulfur has no lustre, so it cannot become shiny wire.

why.Gold is malleable, so hammering turns it: Malleability is beating into sheets, not pulling into wires.
why.Gold is sonorous, so it rings and stretc: Sonorous is about sound when struck, not about stretching.
why.Sulfur has no lustre, so it cannot becom: Lustre is about shine, not about whether a wire can form.

activities.explanation: Right: ductility is drawing into wires, and gold is the most ductile.

activities.prompt: A school bell is made of metal. A wooden block is the same size. Both are struck hard. Only the bell makes a ringing sound. Why?
options: Metals are sonorous, so they make sound when struck.
Metals are malleable, so being beaten makes them ring.
Metals are ductile, so they vibrate like thin wires.
Wood is sonorous too, but this block is too soft.

why.Metals are malleable, so being beaten ma: Malleability is about flattening into sheets, not about ringing.
why.Metals are ductile, so they vibrate like: Ductility is about drawing wires, not about making sound.
why.Wood is sonorous too, but this block is: The fact says metals are sonorous; wood being soft is not the reason.

activities.explanation: Right: sonorous means a metal makes a sound on striking a hard surface.

activities.prompt: A steel spoon stands in a pot of hot soup. After some time the handle feels hot. Why does the handle get hot?
options: Steel is a metal, and metals conduct heat well.
Steel has a high melting point, so it heats up fast.
Steel is sonorous, so heat travels along with sound.
Steel is malleable, so heat gets beaten into the handle.

why.Steel has a high melting point, so it he: A high melting point means it melts at heat, not that it passes heat.
why.Steel is sonorous, so heat travels along: Sonorous is about sound when struck, not about heat moving.
why.Steel is malleable, so heat gets beaten: Malleability is about hammering into sheets, not about heat flow.

activities.explanation: Right: metals are good conductors of heat, so heat moves along the spoon.

activities.prompt: Ravi says every metal is hard. His teacher cuts a soft alkali metal easily with a knife. What is wrong with Ravi's claim?
options: One soft metal is enough to show not all metals are hard.
The knife is also metal, so Ravi's claim must be true.
Ravi is wrong only if the metal does not shine at all.
The claim is fine because most metals are hard anyway.

why.The knife is also metal, so Ravi's claim: What the knife is made of does not tell us how hard the alkali metal is.
why.Ravi is wrong only if the metal does not: Shine is about lustre, not about how hard a metal is.
why.The claim is fine because most metals ar: Even if most metals are hard, one soft metal still breaks 'every'.

activities.explanation: Right: one clear example of a soft metal is enough to break the claim.

lessons.sceneCaption: Reels of gold-plated, silver-plated and copper jewellery wire, showing how metals can be drawn into thin wires.

lessons.title: Chemical properties: metals with air and water

activities.prompt: Why do some metals catch fire in water while gold ignores it completely?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Metals meet air and water
activities.body: Metals like to join with oxygen in the air. Almost all metals form metal oxides this way. Heat some copper in air and it turns black, because copper(II) oxide forms. Metal oxides are basic in nature. Metals also react with water, making a metal oxide and hydrogen gas. But a few metals, like gold, will not touch water at all.
keyPoints: Almost all metals combine with oxygen to form metal oxides.
Metal oxides are basic in nature.
Metals react with water to give a metal oxide and hydrogen gas.
activities.explanation: Air and water can both change metals, but each metal reacts in its own way.

activities.prompt: A shop keeps potassium metal in a bottle of oil, not in open air. Why does the shop do this?
steps: Potassium reacts so strongly that it catches fire, so open air is dangerous for it.
Air has oxygen, and the metal would quickly combine with it and heat up.
Oil keeps air away from the metal, so the fast reaction cannot start.
So the oil is there to stop potassium from touching air and catching fire.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Ravi heats a piece of copper in air. What will he see?
options: The copper turns black
The copper turns green
The copper melts away
The copper stays shiny
activities.explanation: Copper heated in air joins with oxygen and forms black copper(II) oxide. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: When a metal reacts with water, it forms a metal oxide and ______ gas.
activities.hint: Think of the light gas that bubbles off in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Metals reacting with water give a metal oxide and hydrogen gas. Nice work!

activities.prompt: Match each metal to what happens with water.
pairs: Does not react with water at all
activities.explanation: Different metals react with water in very different ways. Great matching!

activities.prompt: Aluminium oxide is special. Why?
options: It reacts with both acids and bases
It reacts only with strong acids
It reacts only with water
It never reacts with anything
activities.explanation: Aluminium oxide is amphoteric, so it reacts with both acids and bases. Superb thinking!

activities.prompt: Put these metals in order, from the most vigorous reaction with water to the least.
items: Potassium catches fire with cold water
Magnesium reacts with hot water
Silver does not react with water
activities.explanation: Potassium and sodium are the most vigorous, magnesium needs hot water, and silver ignores water. Brilliant ordering!

activities.prompt: Some metals form a protective oxide layer. What does this layer do?
options: It stops more oxygen from attacking the metal
It makes the metal dissolve in water
It turns the metal into an alkali
It helps the metal catch fire faster
activities.explanation: The oxide layer acts like a shield and prevents further oxidation. You cracked the tricky one!

activities.prompt: A student says: 'All metal oxides must be acids, because oxides sound like acids.' Aluminium oxide is put in a test with an acid and also with a base. It reacts in both. What does this test show about the claim?
options: The claim is wrong, because some oxides react with acids and bases both
The claim is right, because the oxide reacted with the base
The claim is right, because all oxides react with acids
The claim cannot be checked without heating the oxide first

why.The claim is right, because the oxide re: Wrong: reacting with a base shows basic behaviour, not that the claim is right.
why.The claim is right, because all oxides r: Wrong: reacting with an acid alone does not prove every oxide is an acid.
why.The claim cannot be checked without heat: Wrong: the two test tubes already give a clear answer, no heating is needed.

activities.explanation: Right: amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases, so not all oxides are acids.

activities.prompt: Two identical iron nails are left out. One is coated with a clear layer that stops air touching the iron. After a week, the plain nail is dull but the coated nail is still shiny. The coated nail stays shiny because
options: its oxide layer blocks air from reaching the metal below
its oxide layer makes the nail stronger than the other
the coating cools the nail so reactions slow down
the coating feeds the nail and keeps it fresh

why.its oxide layer makes the nail stronger: Wrong: strength has nothing to do with staying shiny here.
why.the coating cools the nail so reactions: Wrong: temperature is not the reason; blocking air is the reason.
why.the coating feeds the nail and keeps it: Wrong: a coating does not feed a metal; it only covers it.

activities.explanation: Right: a protective oxide layer stops air from getting in, so oxidation stops.

activities.prompt: A student plans to compare how fast magnesium and sodium react with water. She uses cold water for sodium and hot water for magnesium. Her friend says the test is not fair. The friend is right because
options: both metals must be tested in water at the same temperature
the metals must be the same size before any test can work
sodium must always be tested in hot water like magnesium
water can never be used to compare how metals react

why.the metals must be the same size before: Wrong: size matters too, but the clear flaw here is the different temperatures.
why.sodium must always be tested in hot wate: Wrong: sodium in hot water is unsafe and does not make the test fair.
why.water can never be used to compare how m: Wrong: water can be used; the problem is only the unfair temperatures.

activities.explanation: Right: a fair test changes only the metal, so water temperature must be the same.

lessons.sceneAlt: A piece of silvery-white sodium metal, a soft metal that reacts fiercely with water.
lessons.sceneCaption: Sodium is a silvery white, very soft metal which reacts fast and fiercely with water.

lessons.title: Chemical properties: acids, salts and the reactivity series

activities.prompt: Why do some metals fizzle in acid while others stay silent?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Metals meet acids
activities.body: When a metal meets an acid, something exciting happens. The metal and acid make a salt, and bubbles of hydrogen gas appear. But not every metal reacts the same way. Some metals fizz quickly, some react slowly, and some do not react at all. Scientists put metals in a list from most reactive to least reactive. This list is called the reactivity series. It helps you guess how each metal will behave.
keyPoints: Metals react with acids to give salt and hydrogen gas.
Metals can be ranked from most reactive to least reactive.
This ranked list is called the reactivity series.
activities.explanation: Acids and metals make salt and hydrogen, and every metal reacts at its own speed.

activities.prompt: Riya puts a magnesium strip in dilute hydrochloric acid. Her friend puts an iron nail in the same acid. Why do the bubbles come out much faster from the magnesium strip?
steps: Both metals react with dilute acid to give salt and hydrogen gas, so both will make bubbles.
The bubbles are hydrogen gas, so faster bubbles mean the metal is reacting faster.
Magnesium is more reactive than iron, so magnesium gives up electrons more easily and reacts faster.
So the magnesium strip makes bubbles faster because it is higher in the reactivity series than iron.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The pushing game
activities.body: Think of a queue where stronger children can push weaker ones out. Metals play this game too. A more reactive metal can push a less reactive metal out of its salt solution. This is called displacement. If metal A pushes metal B out of a solution, you know at once that A is more reactive than B. Doing many such tests lets scientists build the reactivity series, the ranked list of metals.
keyPoints: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution.
If metal A displaces metal B, then A is more reactive than B.
The reactivity series lists metals from most to least reactive.
activities.explanation: Displacement is a strength contest, and the winner tells you who is more reactive.

activities.title: What does a metal give with an acid?
activities.prompt: A metal reacts with an acid. What are the two things made?
options: Salt and hydrogen gas
Salt and oxygen gas
Water and carbon dioxide
activities.explanation: Well done! Metals and acids always make a salt, and hydrogen gas bubbles out.

activities.title: Keeping sodium safe
activities.prompt: Sodium is kept dipped in ______ so that it cannot catch fire by accident.
activities.hint: Think of the oily liquid in a lamp.
activities.explanation: Yes! Kerosene keeps air away from sodium, so accidental fires cannot start.

activities.title: Nitric acid is different
activities.prompt: Hydrogen gas is released when a metal reacts with nitric acid.
activities.explanation: Good thinking! Nitric acid is special. It does not give hydrogen gas with a metal.

activities.title: Match the metal to its behaviour
activities.prompt: Match each metal or acid to what the lesson says about it.
pairs: Reacts fastest with dilute hydrochloric acid
Does not react with dilute HCl
A mix of concentrated HCl and concentrated nitric acid
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each metal has its own speed, and aqua regia is a special acid mix.

activities.title: Line them up!
activities.prompt: Put these metals in order, from the most reactive to the least reactive.
items: Magnesium (Mg)
Aluminium (Al)
Zinc (Zn)
Iron (Fe)
activities.explanation: Perfect order! Magnesium is the fastest of these four, and iron is the slowest.

activities.title: What happens in the beaker?
activities.prompt: Metal A displaces metal B from B's salt solution. What does this prove?
options: A is more reactive than B
B is more reactive than A
A and B are equally reactive
activities.explanation: Well done! Only the stronger metal can push the weaker one out of the solution.

activities.prompt: A student dips an iron nail in dilute hydrochloric acid. Bubbles rise from the nail. The student says the bubbles are oxygen gas. What is the correct answer to give the student?
options: The bubbles are hydrogen gas made by the reaction.
The bubbles are oxygen gas from the acid breaking up.
The bubbles are air that was trapped inside the nail.
The bubbles are salt changing into a gas form.

why.The bubbles are oxygen gas from the acid: Wrong: this forgets that metals with acids give hydrogen, not oxygen.
why.The bubbles are air that was trapped ins: Wrong: the bubbles keep coming out, so they are made by the reaction, not trapped air.
why.The bubbles are salt changing into a gas: Wrong: the salt stays dissolved in the solution; it does not turn into gas.

activities.explanation: Right: a metal with an acid gives salt and hydrogen gas, so the bubbles are hydrogen.

activities.prompt: Four students test the same metal strips in dilute hydrochloric acid. They all use the same acid, the same size strips and the same temperature. Only Riya warms her acid more than the others. She says her metal is the most reactive because her bubbles are fastest. What is the flaw in her claim?
options: She warmed her acid, so her test was not fair.
She used a bigger strip than the other students.
Her metal was different from the metals of others.
She watched the bubbles for a longer time than others.

why.She used a bigger strip than the other s: Wrong: the question says all strips were the same size, so this did not happen.
why.Her metal was different from the metals: Wrong: the question says all strips were the same metal, so this did not happen.
why.She watched the bubbles for a longer tim: Wrong: watching longer does not change how fast the bubbles come out.

activities.explanation: Right: a fair test needs everything the same except the metal, and warming changed one thing.

activities.prompt: A student puts copper in dilute hydrochloric acid and waits. No bubbles come out. The student says the acid must be too weak. Another student says copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series. Which student is right, and why?
options: The second student, because copper cannot push hydrogen out of the acid.
The first student, because every metal makes bubbles if the acid is strong.
The first student, because copper always reacts slowly with any acid.
The second student, because the acid has already been used up by the copper.

why.The first student, because every metal m: Wrong: this thinks strength alone decides; copper does not react with dilute HCl at all.
why.The first student, because copper always: Wrong: copper does not react slowly with dilute HCl; it does not react at all.
why.The second student, because the acid has: Wrong: the acid was never used up because no reaction happened at all.

activities.explanation: Right: copper does not react with dilute HCl, and metals below hydrogen cannot displace hydrogen.

activities.prompt: A strip of zinc is placed in a solution of a salt of iron. After some time, iron starts appearing on the zinc strip. A friend says this shows iron is more reactive than zinc. What should the student reply?
options: No, zinc is more reactive because it pushed the iron out of its salt.
Yes, iron is more reactive because iron appeared on the strip.
No, both metals are equally reactive because both changed place.
Yes, iron is more reactive because iron was in the solution first.

why.Yes, iron is more reactive because iron: Wrong: seeing iron appear does not mean iron did the displacing; zinc did the work.
why.No, both metals are equally reactive bec: Wrong: only zinc displaced iron; nothing shows they are equal.
why.Yes, iron is more reactive because iron: Wrong: being in the solution first does not decide which metal is more reactive.

activities.explanation: Right: the metal that displaces another from its salt is the more reactive one.

activities.prompt: A student reads that metals give hydrogen gas with acids. She tries this with nitric acid on a metal and gets no hydrogen. She says the fact is wrong. What is the best reply to her?
options: The fact holds for many acids, but nitric acid is a special case.
She is right, because every metal must give hydrogen with every acid.
The metal she used must have been copper, which never reacts at all.
The acid was too old, so it had lost its power to react with metals.

why.She is right, because every metal must g: Wrong: she is not right; the rule is true, but nitric acid behaves differently.
why.The metal she used must have been copper: Wrong: the reason is the nitric acid itself, not which metal she picked.
why.The acid was too old, so it had lost its: Wrong: old acid is not the reason; nitric acid never gives hydrogen with metals.

activities.explanation: Right: metals give hydrogen with acids, but nitric acid is the exception that does not.

lessons.sceneAlt: A student uses magnesium and hydrochloric acid in a test tube to produce hydrogen gas.
lessons.sceneCaption: Magnesium reacting with hydrochloric acid releases hydrogen gas, which burns with a flame.
