lessons.title: How metals and non-metals react

activities.prompt: Why does salt taste nothing like the dangerous metal and gas it comes from?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why atoms react
activities.body: Atoms react to fill their outermost shell, called the valence shell. Noble gases already have a full valence shell, so they stay calm and hardly react. Sodium gives away one electron. Chlorine needs one electron. Sodium and chlorine make a give-and-take deal. This transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal forms an ionic compound, like sodium chloride.
keyPoints: Reactivity is the wish to get a completely filled valence shell.
Noble gases have full valence shells, so they show little chemical activity.
Electrons transfer from metal to non-metal, making ionic compounds.
activities.explanation: Atoms react to complete their outermost shell, and electron transfer makes ionic compounds.

activities.prompt: Salt is on the table every day. Why does it melt only at a very high heat, and not like ice?
steps: Salt is not made of single molecules, but of many oppositely charged ions packed together.
Each ion is pulled by all the ions around it, so the pulls are strong in every direction.
Melting means pulling these ions apart, and strong pulls need a lot of heat to break.
So salt melts at a high heat because strong electrostatic forces hold its ions in place.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Why do noble gases show little chemical activity?
options: They have a completely filled valence shell
They have very light atoms
They are always in a solid state
They have no electrons at all
activities.explanation: A full valence shell means an atom is already satisfied, so it need not react. Well done!

activities.prompt: When a sodium atom loses one electron from its M shell, it forms a sodium ______.
activities.hint: It is the name for a positive ion.
activities.explanation: Losing one electron gives sodium a positive charge, so it becomes a cation.

activities.prompt: Sodium meets chlorine. What kind of deal do they make?
options: A give-and-take deal with electrons
They share all their protons
They swap their shells completely
They refuse to react at all
activities.explanation: Sodium gives one electron and chlorine takes it. This give-and-take joins them together.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its partner.
activities.explanation: Each partner shows how atoms behave when shells are full or nearly full. Great matching!

activities.prompt: Why do ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points?
options: Strong electrostatic forces hold the ions
The ions are very light in weight
The ions move very fast always
The compounds contain noble gases
activities.explanation: The oppositely charged ions attract each other with strong electrostatic forces. Breaking them takes lots of heat.

activities.prompt: Put these statements about an ionic compound in the correct order, from its formation to its use.
items: Electrons transfer from the metal to the non-metal
Oppositely charged ions attract each other
The ionic compound forms as a hard solid
The solid is melted
The molten compound conducts electricity
activities.explanation: First electrons transfer, then ions attract and form a solid. Only when melted can it conduct electricity.

activities.prompt: A sodium atom has one electron in its outer shell. A chlorine atom has seven electrons in its outer shell. Sodium and chlorine are brought close together. What will most likely happen?
options: Sodium gives its one electron to chlorine.
Chlorine gives one electron to sodium.
Both atoms lose all their outer electrons.
Nothing happens, both shells are already full.

This mixes it up; chlorine already has seven and wants to gain, not give away.
why.Both atoms lose all their outer electron: This goes too far; each atom only needs to reach a full outer shell, not empty it.
why.Nothing happens, both shells are already: This treats them like noble gases, but their outer shells are not full yet.

activities.explanation: Right. Sodium loses one electron easily and chlorine needs exactly one, so a give-and-take works.

activities.prompt: A student tests two samples with a battery and a bulb. One sample is solid salt. The other is the same salt melted hot. The bulb glows only with the melted salt. Why?
options: Heat makes the salt change into a new substance.
In solid salt the charged ions cannot move freely.
The bulb only works when the salt is very hot.
Solid salt has no charged ions inside it at all.

why.Heat makes the salt change into a new su: Heating melts the salt but does not turn it into a new substance.
why.The bulb only works when the salt is ver: The bulb glows because charges can move, not because of the temperature itself.
why.Solid salt has no charged ions inside it: The ions are there in the solid too; they are just stuck in place.

activities.explanation: Right. In the solid the ions are held fixed; melting lets them move and carry current.

activities.prompt: A friend says: salt must be made of separate molecules, so it should melt easily like ice. But salt needs a very high heat to melt. What is the flaw in the claim?
options: Salt is actually a liquid at room temperature.
Salt is a gas, so it needs high heat to melt.
Salt is made of ions held by strong forces, not molecules.
Salt has no charges, so heat cannot act on it.

why.Salt is actually a liquid at room temper: Salt is a solid at room temperature, so this cannot be the reason.
why.Salt is a gas, so it needs high heat to: Salt is not a gas; this confuses melting with boiling.
why.Salt has no charges, so heat cannot act: Salt does have charged ions; the claim fails for a different reason.

activities.explanation: Right. Salt is aggregates of oppositely charged ions, and strong forces need high heat to break.

activities.prompt: A student melts an ionic compound and finds it conducts electricity. She says: it is the same compound, so the solid must conduct too. But the solid does not conduct. What is wrong with her claim?
options: Melting destroys the ions, so new ions form.
The solid has no ions, only the melt has them.
In the solid the ions are fixed and cannot move.
Electricity only flows through hot things, never cold.

why.Melting destroys the ions, so new ions f: Melting does not destroy the ions; it only frees them to move.
why.The solid has no ions, only the melt has: The same ions are present in both states; only their movement changes.
why.Electricity only flows through hot thing: Temperature is not the rule; being able to move is what matters.

activities.explanation: Right. Conduction needs moving charges, and solid ions are locked by strong forces.

lessons.sceneAlt: A diagram showing sodium giving its outer electron to chlorine, forming charged ions that attract each other in a lattice.
lessons.sceneCaption: Sodium donates its valence electron to chlorine; the resulting ions attract, forming an ionic bond and a lattice.

lessons.title: Occurrence and extraction of metals

activities.prompt: Why do we dig so deep just to get a shiny piece of metal?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Where do metals come from?
activities.body: Metals are found inside the earth's crust, which is the hard outer layer of the ground. Minerals occur naturally in this crust. Some minerals hold a lot of metal and are worth digging up. These are called ores. Before we can use a metal, we must separate it from its ore. How we do this depends on how reactive the metal is.
keyPoints: The earth's crust is the major source of metals.
Minerals occur naturally in the earth's crust.
Ores are minerals with a high percentage of metal that can be profitably extracted.
How we extract a metal depends on where it sits in the activity series.
activities.explanation: Metals live inside rocks in the ground, and ores are the richest rocks to dig.

activities.prompt: Riya finds a shiny golden-looking stone in a river bed. Her friend says it must be gold. How can the activity series help us think about this?
steps: Gold is at the bottom of the activity series, so it is the least reactive metal.
Because it is least reactive, it does not combine easily with things around it, so it can stay free in nature.
A very reactive metal would have already joined with other substances, so it would never be found free like this.
So a free shiny metal found in nature is likely to be a low-reactivity metal like gold, not a reactive one.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Spot the ore
activities.prompt: A miner finds two rocks. Rock P has a high percentage of metal and can be profitably extracted. Rock Q has only a tiny trace of metal. Which rock is an ore?
options: Rock P
Rock Q
Both rocks
Neither rock
activities.explanation: An ore is a mineral with a high percentage of metal that can be profitably extracted. Rock Q has too little metal to be worth it.

activities.title: What is gangue?
activities.prompt: You dig up an ore and find soil and sand mixed in with it. What is this unwanted material called?
options: Gangue
Alloy
Ore
Mineral
activities.explanation: Gangue is the impurities, such as soil and sand, found in an ore.

activities.title: Why some metals hide in compounds
activities.prompt: Metals at the top of the activity series are never found free in nature. Why is this?
options: They are very reactive, so they join with other things
They are too heavy to stay on the surface
They melt deep inside the earth
They are too rare to be found at all
activities.explanation: Metals at the top of the activity series are the most reactive. They combine with other elements, so they are never found as free elements.

activities.title: Match the process
activities.prompt: Match each word with what it means.
pairs: Heating a sulphide ore strongly to make an oxide
Heating a carbonate ore strongly in limited air
Soil and sand impurities in an ore
A mineral rich in metal worth extracting
activities.explanation: Roasting and calcination both turn ores into oxides by strong heating. They differ in the type of ore and the air supply.

activities.title: Getting the most reactive metals
activities.prompt: Metals high in the activity series are obtained by ______ reduction.
activities.hint: Think of the method that uses electricity to pull the metal out.
activities.explanation: Metals high in the activity series are so reactive that we need electrolytic reduction to obtain them.

activities.title: Put the steps in order
activities.prompt: Put these steps for getting a metal from its ore in the correct order.
items: Dig up the ore from the earth's crust
Remove the gangue, such as soil and sand
Heat the ore strongly to change it into an oxide
Reduce the oxide to get the metal
activities.explanation: First the ore is mined, then the gangue is removed, then heating makes the oxide, and finally the oxide is reduced to the metal.

activities.prompt: Two ores are dug from the same mine. Ore A has only a little metal mixed with lots of rock. Ore B has a high percentage of the same metal. Mining costs the same for both. Which ore should the company choose to make money?
options: Ore A, because it is easier to dig up
Ore B, because more metal comes from the same work
Both, because all minerals give the same profit
Neither, because rock always blocks the metal

why.Ore A, because it is easier to dig up: Thinks digging cost is the only thing that matters, but profit depends on metal got out.
why.Both, because all minerals give the same: Thinks all minerals are equally useful, but a mineral with little metal may not be worth extracting.
why.Neither, because rock always blocks the: Thinks rock makes extraction impossible, but ore is exactly rock rich enough in metal to be worth it.

activities.explanation: Right: with the same cost, the ore rich in metal gives more metal, so it can be extracted profitably.

activities.prompt: A student says: 'Every shiny metal found in the ground must have come from a compound that broke apart.' Her friend digs up a piece of copper metal directly from the earth. Who is thinking correctly, and why?
options: The student, because all metals hide inside compounds
The friend, because copper is low in the activity series and can be found free
The student, because copper always reacts with air at once
The friend, because copper is at the top of the activity series

why.The student, because all metals hide ins: Thinks every metal must be in a compound, but least reactive metals can stay free.
why.The student, because copper always react: Thinks copper reacts instantly, but its low reactivity lets it survive free.
why.The friend, because copper is at the top: Right idea about copper being free, but places it wrongly at the top, where metals are never free.

activities.explanation: Right: metals low in the activity series are least reactive, so copper can exist free in nature.

activities.prompt: An ore is a sulphide. A worker heats it strongly in plenty of air. Another ore is a carbonate. The worker heats it strongly but keeps the air very limited. What is the worker trying to do in both cases?
options: Turn both ores into oxides before reducing them
Wash the gangue out of both ores with air
Melt both ores so the metal flows out as liquid
Make both ores free metals without any further step

why.Wash the gangue out of both ores with ai: Thinks heating removes gangue, but gangue is soil and sand, not removed by these heating steps.
why.Melt both ores so the metal flows out as: Thinks the aim is melting, but the aim is changing the ore's chemical form, not melting it.
why.Make both ores free metals without any f: Thinks heating alone gives the metal, but an oxide still needs reduction to become metal.

activities.explanation: Right: roasting and calcination both convert sulphide and carbonate ores into oxides, the step before reduction.

activities.prompt: A student heats a metal compound that is low in the activity series. Her friend heats a compound of a metal high in the activity series in the same way. Only the first student gets the free metal. Why did the friend fail?
options: The friend used too little heat for any metal ever
The friend's metal is so reactive that heating alone cannot reduce it
The friend's ore had no gangue, so heating did nothing
The friend's compound was an oxide, so it could not change

why.The friend used too little heat for any: Thinks heat amount is the only issue, but the real reason is the metal's high reactivity.
why.The friend's ore had no gangue, so heati: Thinks gangue is needed for heating to work, but gangue is just an impurity, not the reason.
why.The friend's compound was an oxide, so i: Thinks oxides cannot be reduced, but oxides of low-reactivity metals are reduced by heating.

activities.explanation: Right: metals high in the activity series need electrolytic reduction, not just heating.

activities.prompt: A railway worker needs to join two broken rail ends. A chemist suggests using a thermit reaction instead of ordinary welding. What will happen to the molten metal produced?
options: It will cool and join the two rail ends firmly
It will sink into the ground and leave a gap
It will turn back into ore because it came from one
It will float away as gas because thermit makes gases

why.It will sink into the ground and leave a: Thinks the metal disappears, but molten metal is poured exactly where the join is needed.
why.It will turn back into ore because it ca: Thinks metal turns back into ore, but reduction goes from ore towards free metal, not backwards.
why.It will float away as gas because thermi: Thinks thermit gives a gas, but it is used precisely because it gives molten metal.

activities.explanation: Right: the thermit reaction produces molten metal that fills the gap and joins the parts when it cools.

activities.prompt: A student claims: 'Since minerals occur naturally in the crust, every mineral in the crust is an ore we can mine for profit.' What is the flaw in this claim?
options: Minerals are found only deep down, never near the surface
Some minerals have too little metal to extract profitably
Minerals stop forming once people start mining them
Ores are man-made, so no natural mineral can be an ore

why.Minerals are found only deep down, never: Thinks location decides profit, but the claim is about every mineral, wherever it is.
why.Minerals stop forming once people start: Thinks mining changes how minerals form, which does not answer the claim about profit.
why.Ores are man-made, so no natural mineral: Reverses the idea: ores come from natural minerals, not the other way round.

activities.explanation: Right: an ore must have a high percentage of metal, so a mineral with little metal is not an ore.

lessons.title: Corrosion, prevention and alloys

activities.prompt: Why does shiny metal slowly lose its sparkle, and how can we stop it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: When metals get tired
activities.body: Metals can change when air touches them. Silver turns black. Copper reacts with moist carbon dioxide in the air. Iron gets a brown flaky coat called rust. We can stop this by painting, oiling, greasing, galvanising, chrome plating, anodising or making alloys. An alloy mixes metals together. Alloying makes metals stronger and better than before.
keyPoints: Silver turns black in air; copper reacts with moist carbon dioxide.
Iron in moist air gets a brown flaky coat called rust.
Rusting can be prevented by painting, oiling, greasing, galvanising and more.
An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of metals, and alloying improves a metal's properties.
activities.explanation: Air and moisture slowly change metals, but we can protect them.

activities.prompt: Grandma's old silver coin looks black, but a new silver coin looks shiny. Both coins are made of silver. Why do they look so different?
steps: The old coin has stayed in air for many years, but the new coin has not.
Silver slowly reacts with things in the air, so its surface turns black over time.
The new coin has not had enough time in air, so its surface is still shiny.
So the colour difference comes from time spent in air, not from different metals.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Iron left in moist air grows a brown flaky coat. What is this coat called?
options: Rust
Dust
Silver shine
Zinc layer
activities.explanation: Iron in moist air gets a brown flaky substance called rust. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: Galvanisation protects steel and iron by coating them with a thin layer of ______.
activities.hint: A grey metal used on coated gates and buckets.
activities.explanation: A thin zinc layer keeps steel and iron safe. That is galvanisation!

activities.prompt: Iron mixed with which two metals gives stainless steel?
options: Nickel and chromium
Zinc and copper
Silver and gold
Tin and lead
activities.explanation: Iron plus nickel and chromium makes stainless steel, which resists rusting.

activities.prompt: Match each metal to what happens to it in air.
activities.explanation: Each metal meets air in its own way. You matched them all!

activities.prompt: Put the story of a rusty gate in order.
items: Iron gate is left in moist air
A brown flaky coat of rust forms
The gate is given a coat of paint
The rusting is prevented
activities.explanation: Moist air causes rust, and painting stops it from spreading.

activities.prompt: The iron pillar near the Qutub Minar has stood for over 1600 years. What does this show about Indian iron workers of that time?
options: They understood how to make iron that resists rust
They painted the pillar every single year
They coated the pillar with gold
They kept the pillar wrapped in cloth
activities.explanation: The pillar was built over 1600 years ago and still stands strong. Those workers knew their iron well!

activities.prompt: Two iron nails are left outside in moist air. One nail is coated with a thin layer of zinc. One nail has no coating. What will you see after a week?
options: Both nails are covered with rust
The plain nail rusts, the zinc-coated one does not
The zinc-coated nail rusts, the plain one does not
Neither nail rusts because nails are hard

why.Both nails are covered with rust: Wrong: thinks a zinc coating makes no difference at all.
why.The zinc-coated nail rusts, the plain on: Wrong: thinks the coating causes rust instead of stopping it.
why.Neither nail rusts because nails are har: Wrong: thinks hard metals cannot rust.

activities.explanation: Right: zinc coating protects iron, while plain iron rusts in moist air.

activities.prompt: A bangle made of 24 carat gold bends out of shape in one day. The shopkeeper offers gold mixed with other metals instead. Why is the mixed gold better for a bangle?
options: It is harder, so the bangle keeps its shape
It is cheaper, so bending does not matter
It is heavier, so it cannot bend at all
It melts faster, so it sets into shape well

why.It is cheaper, so bending does not matte: Wrong: thinks price is the reason, not the property of the metal.
why.It is heavier, so it cannot bend at all: Wrong: thinks heavy things cannot bend.
why.It melts faster, so it sets into shape w: Wrong: mixes up melting with staying hard.

activities.explanation: Right: pure gold is very soft, and mixing metals improves its properties.

activities.prompt: A friend says: iron always rusts away in a few years, so an iron pillar cannot stand for 1600 years. The pillar near the Qutub Minar was built more than 1600 years ago and still stands. What is wrong with the friend's claim?
options: The pillar is not really made of iron
The pillar was painted fresh every year
The pillar itself shows iron can last very long
Rust stops growing on its own after a few years

why.The pillar is not really made of iron: Wrong: throws away the fact instead of using it.
why.The pillar was painted fresh every year: Wrong: invents a reason that was never given.
why.Rust stops growing on its own after a fe: Wrong: thinks rusting stops by itself with time.

activities.explanation: Right: a real iron pillar standing over 1600 years proves the claim wrong.

lessons.sceneAlt: Two open boxes holding reels of jewellery wire, including gold-plated, silver-plated and coloured copper wire.
lessons.sceneCaption: Reels of gold-plated, silver-plated and copper jewellery wire, showing how metals can be drawn into thin wires.

activities.context: Ravi visits his uncle's workshop where a goldsmith is pulling a glowing metal rod through a small hole, turning it into a very fine wire for a bracelet. On the shelf lies a small cutting tool used to slice pieces of a soft metal kept under oil. Nearby, a worker taps a metal sheet and a clear ringing sound fills the room. Ravi notices the goldsmith polishing a ring until its surface shines brightly.
activities.prompt: The goldsmith chooses gold for making the very fine wire in the bracelet. What property of gold is he mainly depending on, and what would happen if he tried the same with a metal lacking this property?
options: He is using ductility; a metal without it would snap instead of stretching into a wire
He is using malleability; a metal without it would not shine when polished
He is using sonority; a metal without it would not make a ringing sound
He is using lustre; a metal without it could not be drawn through the hole

why.He is using malleability; a metal withou: Malleability is about beating into sheets, not pulling wires, and shine is a separate property.
why.He is using sonority; a metal without it: Sonority is about sound on striking, which has nothing to do with forming a wire.
why.He is using lustre; a metal without it c: Lustre is the shining surface; it does not decide whether a metal can be drawn into a wire.

activities.explanation: Correct: drawing into thin wires is ductility, and gold is the most ductile metal, so a metal lacking it would break rather than stretch.

activities.context: Ravi visits his uncle's workshop where a goldsmith is pulling a glowing metal rod through a small hole, turning it into a very fine wire for a bracelet. On the shelf lies a small cutting tool used to slice pieces of a soft metal kept under oil. Nearby, a worker taps a metal sheet and a clear ringing sound fills the room. Ravi notices the goldsmith polishing a ring until its surface shines brightly.
activities.prompt: The worker slices a piece of the soft metal with the cutting tool. Based on what kind of metals behave this way, what is this metal most likely to be, and what should Ravi expect if he struck it hard?
options: An alkali metal; it would not give the strong ringing sound that harder metals give
A non-metal like bromine; it would flow like a liquid when struck
Diamond; it would scratch the cutting tool instead of being cut
Gold; it would stretch into a wire the moment it is tapped

why.A non-metal like bromine; it would flow: Bromine is the liquid non-metal, but the item being cut is a solid piece of metal, not a liquid.
why.Diamond; it would scratch the cutting to: Diamond is the hardest natural substance, so it cannot be the soft metal being sliced.
why.Gold; it would stretch into a wire the m: Ductility means drawing into wires by pulling, not by tapping, so this prediction is wrong.

activities.explanation: Correct: alkali metals are so soft they can be cut with a knife, and being soft, they would not behave like the sonorous harder metals.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Bromine is grouped with non-metals even though it is not a solid or a gas.
Reason (R): Non-metals are solids or gases, with bromine being the only exception because it is a liquid.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the exception stated in the reason directly explains why bromine still counts as a non-metal.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Diamond is used where an extremely hard natural material is needed.
Reason (R): Diamond is a form in which carbon can exist.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both are true, but the reason diamond is valued is that it is the hardest natural substance known, not merely that it is an allotrope of carbon.

activities.prompt: Explain why a metal sheet is chosen over a non-metal sheet for an application where the sheet must be beaten into shape, carry heat, and ring clearly when struck.
activities.answer: A metal sheet is chosen because metals show a set of properties the non-metal sheet cannot match. Metals are malleable, so the sheet can be beaten into the required shape without breaking. Metals are good conductors of heat, so heat will travel through the sheet as needed. Metals are also sonorous, meaning they make a ringing sound when struck, which the application requires. A non-metal sheet, being solid or gas in nature and lacking these metallic properties, would fail in all three roles.
points: States that metals are malleable, so the sheet can be beaten into shape
States that metals are good conductors of heat
States that metals are sonorous, making a sound on striking a hard surface
Notes that non-metals do not show these metallic properties
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a science club activity, Riya heats a piece of copper in air and watches it slowly turn black. Later the club receives small pieces of potassium and sodium for a demonstration, and the teacher warns that these must never touch water. Another member suggests leaving them in an open dish on the table to save time.
activities.prompt: If the member's suggestion is followed and water accidentally splashes into the open dish, what is the most likely result?
options: Nothing would happen, as these metals ignore water at room temperature
The metals would dissolve slowly, giving a clear solution
The metals would react violently and could even catch fire
A protective coating would form on the metals, making them safe

why.Nothing would happen, as these metals ig: Wrong: potassium and sodium react violently with cold water, they do not ignore it
why.The metals would dissolve slowly, giving: Wrong: their reaction with water is violent, not slow and quiet
why.A protective coating would form on the m: Wrong: a protective layer idea does not apply here; these metals are highly reactive with water

activities.explanation: Correct: potassium and sodium react so vigorously with cold water that they catch fire

activities.context: During a science club activity, Riya heats a piece of copper in air and watches it slowly turn black. Later the club receives small pieces of potassium and sodium for a demonstration, and the teacher warns that these must never touch water. Another member suggests leaving them in an open dish on the table to save time.
activities.prompt: Aluminium also combines with oxygen, yet it does not keep getting used up by air. Why is this?
options: Aluminium is too unreactive to combine with oxygen at all
The oxide formed on its surface acts as a shield, stopping further attack by air
Aluminium reacts only with water, never with oxygen
Its oxide is amphoteric, so air cannot affect it

why.Aluminium is too unreactive to combine w: Wrong: almost all metals, including aluminium, combine with oxygen
why.Aluminium reacts only with water, never: Wrong: aluminium does combine with oxygen; the question states this
why.Its oxide is amphoteric, so air cannot a: Wrong: being amphoteric concerns reaction with acids and bases, not protection from air

activities.explanation: Correct: the protective oxide layer prevents further oxidation

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Potassium catches fire when it is put in cold water.
Reason (R): Potassium reacts with cold water so vigorously that the reaction sets it on fire.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true and the vigorous reaction with cold water is exactly why potassium catches fire.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Magnesium reacts vigorously with cold water to give hydrogen.
Reason (R): Magnesium needs hot water in order to react with water.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because magnesium reacts with hot water, not cold water, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain why sodium oxide is described as basic in nature while zinc oxide is described as amphoteric.
activities.answer: Sodium oxide dissolves in water to produce an alkali, which shows that it is basic in nature, like metal oxides in general. Zinc oxide, however, does not behave only as a base; it reacts with both acids and bases, and in each case the products are a salt and water. Because it shows both acidic and basic behaviour in this way, zinc oxide is called amphoteric, unlike sodium oxide which behaves only as a base.
points: Sodium oxide dissolves in water to produce an alkali
Metal oxides are basic in nature
Amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases
The products of such reactions are salts and water
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Riya sets up four test tubes containing dilute hydrochloric acid and drops similar-sized pieces of magnesium, aluminium, zinc and iron into them. She notices fizzing in all four tubes, but the fizzing is fastest in the tube with magnesium and slowest in the tube with iron. Her lab partner wonders what would happen if a piece of copper were added to a fifth tube of the same acid.
activities.prompt: If Riya adds a piece of copper to a fifth tube of the same dilute hydrochloric acid, what is she most likely to observe?
options: Fizzing faster than in the magnesium tube
Fizzing slower than in the iron tube
No bubbles of gas appearing at all
Bubbles appearing only after the acid is heated

why.Fizzing faster than in the magnesium tub: Wrong: copper is less reactive than magnesium, so it cannot beat the fastest metal.
why.Fizzing slower than in the iron tube: Wrong: this would suggest copper has some reactivity, but it is even less reactive than iron.
why.Bubbles appearing only after the acid is: Wrong: heating is not part of the given facts; copper simply does not react with this acid.

activities.explanation: Correct: copper does not react with dilute HCl, so no hydrogen gas is released.

activities.context: Riya sets up four test tubes containing dilute hydrochloric acid and drops similar-sized pieces of magnesium, aluminium, zinc and iron into them. She notices fizzing in all four tubes, but the fizzing is fastest in the tube with magnesium and slowest in the tube with iron. Her lab partner wonders what would happen if a piece of copper were added to a fifth tube of the same acid.
activities.prompt: Riya's friend claims the iron tube must have a mistake because iron fizzed least. Based on the order of reactivity, what should Riya conclude?
options: The friend is right; iron should have fizzed fastest
The friend is right; all four metals should fizz equally
The friend is wrong; iron is the least reactive of the four metals tested
The friend is wrong; iron should have shown no reaction at all

why.The friend is right; iron should have fi: Wrong: magnesium, not iron, is the most reactive of the four, so iron cannot fizz fastest.
why.The friend is right; all four metals sho: Wrong: the metals differ in reactivity, so their fizzing rates are not expected to be equal.
why.The friend is wrong; iron should have sh: Wrong: iron does react with dilute HCl, just more slowly than the others, so some fizzing is expected.

activities.explanation: Correct: reactivity decreases in the order Mg > Al > Zn > Fe, so iron fizzing least fits the expected order.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Sodium is stored by keeping it immersed in kerosene oil.
Reason (R): Sodium is kept in kerosene oil to prevent accidental fires.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the reason correctly explains why sodium is stored in kerosene oil.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Zinc can displace iron from a solution of an iron compound.
Reason (R): Copper reacts vigorously with dilute hydrochloric acid to release hydrogen gas.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true because zinc is more reactive than iron, but the reason is false since copper does not react with dilute HCl.

activities.prompt: Explain why a more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from its salt solution, using the idea of the reactivity series.
activities.answer: The reactivity series is a list of metals arranged in order of decreasing activities. A metal higher in this series is more active than a metal below it. Reactive metals can displace less reactive metals from their compounds, so when a more reactive metal is placed in the salt solution of a less reactive metal, the more reactive metal pushes the less reactive one out and takes its place. For example, if metal A displaces metal B from solution, A is more reactive than B. This is why displacement happens only from the more reactive metal towards the less reactive one, and never the reverse.
points: Defines the reactivity series as metals arranged in order of decreasing activities
States that reactive metals can displace less reactive metals from their compounds
Applies the rule: if A displaces B from solution, A is more reactive than B
Concludes displacement occurs only from more reactive to less reactive metal
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Riya reads that a sodium atom has a single electron in its outermost M shell, while a chlorine atom has seven electrons in its outermost shell. When the two elements react, sodium hands over its outer electron to chlorine. The white solid formed melts only at a very high temperature. Riya notices something strange: the solid does not conduct electricity at all, but the same substance conducts well once it is melted.
activities.prompt: Riya's melted sample conducts electricity but the solid did not. What is the best explanation for this change?
options: Melting frees the oppositely charged ions to move, while in the solid they are locked in place
Melting creates the ions, which were missing in the solid
Electricity flows through electrons in the solid, and melting removes them
The solid is too hard for current, and melting makes it soft enough

why.Melting creates the ions, which were mis: The oppositely charged ions already exist in the solid; melting does not create them
why.Electricity flows through electrons in t: Conduction here is due to ions, not free electrons in the solid
why.The solid is too hard for current, and m: Hardness is not the reason; the key is whether the charged particles can move

activities.explanation: Correct: ions are held by strong electrostatic forces in the solid, and the molten state allows conduction

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Sodium chloride is a hard solid that melts at a high temperature.
Reason (R): Its oppositely charged ions are held together by strong electrostatic forces.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The strong electrostatic forces holding the ions explain both the hardness and the high melting point.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Metals and Non-metals

activities.prompt: A goldsmith hammers a metal into a thin sheet. Which property is she using?
options: Ductility
Sonorous sound
Malleability
Metallic lustre
activities.explanation: Metals that can be beaten into thin sheets show malleability. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: All non-metals are solids or gases.
activities.explanation: Almost! Bromine is a non-metal that is a liquid. Nearly there.

activities.prompt: ______ is the most ductile metal of all.
activities.hint: Think of the shiny metal used in jewellery.
activities.explanation: Gold can be drawn into the thinnest wires, so it is the most ductile metal.

activities.prompt: Match each metal property with what it means.
activities.explanation: Each property has its own name. You matched them all like a champion!

activities.prompt: Aluminium oxide reacts with acids AND with bases. What do we call such an oxide?
options: Basic oxide
Amphoteric oxide
Acidic oxide
Noble oxide
activities.explanation: Amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases to give salt and water.

activities.prompt: Sodium is kept immersed in kerosene oil to prevent accidental fires.
activities.explanation: Sodium catches fire so easily that kerosene keeps it safely away from air and water.

activities.prompt: Put these metals in order from MOST reactive to LEAST reactive with dilute hydrochloric acid.
items: Magnesium
Aluminium
Zinc
Iron
activities.explanation: Reactivity decreases in the order Mg, then Al, then Zn, then Fe. Superb ordering!

activities.prompt: When a metal reacts with nitric acid, the gas ______ is not evolved.
activities.hint: It is the lightest gas and pops with a squeak.
activities.explanation: With most acids metals give hydrogen, but nitric acid is different. Tricky one, well done!

activities.prompt: An iron gate is coated with a thin layer of zinc to stop it rusting. What is this method called?
options: Anodising
Alloying
Galvanisation
Calcination
activities.explanation: Galvanisation protects steel and iron with a thin zinc coat. Great recall!

activities.prompt: Match each idea from the chapter with what you learnt about it.
activities.explanation: You connected ideas from the whole chapter. A brilliant finish to your challenge!

chapters.title: Carbon and its Compounds
chapters.summary: In this chapter: carbon and covalent bonding; versatile nature of carbon and saturated/unsaturated compounds; chains, branches, rings and functional groups; homologous series and nomenclature.

lessons.title: Carbon and Covalent Bonding

activities.title: Carbon and Covalent Bonding
activities.body:
Carbon is important to us in both its elemental form and in compounds.

Many things we use, like food, clothes, medicines and books, are based on carbon.

All living structures are made of carbon-based substances.
keyPoints: The earth’s crust has only 0.02% carbon in the form of minerals.
The atmosphere has 0.03% carbon dioxide.
activities.explanation: Now try some questions.

activities.prompt: Why does carbon hold the secret to everything alive around you?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.prompt: Carbon has four electrons in its outermost shell. Why does carbon share electrons instead of losing or gaining them?
steps: Carbon has four electrons in its outermost shell.
Carbon wants to become stable, so it must deal with these four outer electrons.
Instead of losing or gaining them, carbon shares its valence electrons with other atoms.
Each shared pair of electrons forms a single covalent bond, so sharing makes carbon stable.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which of these is based on carbon?
options: The gold in a ring
The book you read
The iron in a nail
The copper in a wire
activities.explanation: Well done! Books, like food, clothes and medicines, are based on carbon.

activities.prompt: Carbon has ______ electrons in its outermost shell.
activities.hint: Count the electrons carbon needs to share to become stable.
activities.explanation: Carbon has four electrons in its outermost shell, so it shares to fill up.

activities.prompt: All living structures are made of carbon-based substances.
activities.explanation: Yes! Every living thing, including you, is built from carbon-based substances.

activities.prompt: Why does carbon share its electrons with other atoms?
options: To lose all its electrons
To gain a big electric charge
To become stable
To become heavier
activities.explanation: Carbon shares its valence electrons with other atoms so it can become stable.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of forming a covalent bond in order.
items: Two atoms come near each other
Each atom has electrons in its outermost shell
The atoms share a pair of electrons
The shared pair forms a single covalent bond
Both atoms become stable
activities.explanation: Spot on! Sharing an electron pair makes the bond, and both atoms end up stable.

activities.prompt: Riya builds a circuit with a covalent compound in the gap. What will she most likely see, and why?
options: The bulb glows, as covalent bonds share electrons freely
The bulb stays dim or off, as covalent compounds are poor conductors
The bulb glows brightly, as carbon makes compounds conduct well
The bulb stays dim or off, as covalent bonds break in a circuit
activities.explanation: Covalent compounds are generally poor conductors, so little current flows and the bulb stays off.

activities.prompt: Priya joins a battery to a bulb with wires. She dips the wire ends into a liquid. The liquid is a carbon compound. Carbon compounds are covalent compounds. What will Priya see?
options: The bulb stays off because covalent compounds are poor conductors.
The bulb glows brightly because all liquids conduct well.
The bulb glows dimly because carbon compounds conduct a little.
The bulb stays off because the bulb has become faulty.

why.The bulb glows brightly because all liqu: Wrong. This assumes every liquid conducts electricity, which is not true.
why.The bulb glows dimly because carbon comp: Wrong. This thinks poor conductors still let the bulb glow, but they generally do not.
why.The bulb stays off because the bulb has: Wrong. This blames the equipment instead of thinking about the liquid being tested.

activities.explanation: Right. Covalent compounds are generally poor conductors, so little current flows.

activities.prompt: The earth's crust has only 0.02% carbon as minerals. Ravi says, 'Carbon is so little in the crust. So my body cannot be made of carbon-based substances.' What is wrong with Ravi's claim?
options: All living structures are made of carbon-based substances.
The 0.02% number for the crust is wrong.
Carbon-based substances can only be found in rocks.
Bodies are made of minerals, not of any substances.

Wrong. This doubts the given fact instead of connecting it to living things.
why.Carbon-based substances can only be foun: Wrong. This thinks carbon-based matter exists only in the crust, forgetting living things.
why.Bodies are made of minerals, not of any: Wrong. This confuses minerals in the crust with what living bodies are made of.

activities.explanation: Right. All living structures are made of carbon-based substances, so his body can be too.

activities.prompt: Meera eats food, wears clothes, takes medicine and reads books. Many things we use are based on carbon. Meera says, 'Food, clothes, medicines and books share nothing with each other.' What is the flaw in her claim?
options: All these things she uses are based on carbon.
She uses too many things every single day.
Medicines and books are related, but food is not.
Clothes and books are related, but medicines are not.

why.She uses too many things every single da: Wrong. This talks about how many things she uses, not what they share.
why.Medicines and books are related, but foo: Wrong. This picks only some items, but all the listed things are carbon based.
why.Clothes and books are related, but medic: Wrong. This picks only some items, but all the listed things are carbon based.

activities.explanation: Right. Many things we use, like food, clothes, medicines and books, are all based on carbon.

activities.prompt: The atmosphere has 0.03% carbon dioxide. Arjun says, 'That number is so tiny. So there is no carbon dioxide around us at all.' Is Arjun right?
options: No, the atmosphere does contain carbon dioxide.
Yes, a tiny number means a thing is absent.
No, because carbon dioxide is found only in the crust.
Yes, because only gases can exist in the atmosphere.

why.Yes, a tiny number means a thing is abse: Wrong. This thinks a small percentage means zero, but a small amount is still present.
why.No, because carbon dioxide is found only: Wrong. This moves carbon dioxide to the wrong place, the crust instead of the atmosphere.
why.Yes, because only gases can exist in the: Wrong. This adds a made-up rule about gases instead of using the given fact.

activities.explanation: Right. The atmosphere has 0.03% carbon dioxide, so it is present even in a small amount.

lessons.sceneAlt: A Bohr model diagram of a carbon atom showing six protons, six neutrons, six electrons and four valence electrons.
lessons.sceneCaption: A carbon atom has six protons, six neutrons and six electrons, with four electrons in its outermost shell.

lessons.title: Versatile Nature of Carbon and Saturated/Unsaturated Compounds

activities.prompt: Why does carbon form more compounds than every other element combined?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why carbon is special
activities.body: Carbon is a champion of chemistry. Compounds of carbon outnumber compounds of all other elements put together. Carbon can join hands with other carbon atoms. This special trick is called catenation. Carbon also has a valency of four, so it can bond with four other atoms. It happily bonds with oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine and many more elements.
keyPoints: Carbon compounds outnumber all other compounds put together.
Catenation is carbon joining with other carbon atoms.
Carbon has a valency of four, so it forms four bonds.
activities.explanation: Carbon's strong bonds and valency of four make it build more compounds than any other element.

activities.prompt: Priya sees a long necklace made of many beads joined one by one. Her teacher says carbon atoms can also join into long chains. Priya wonders how carbon can build such long chains.
steps: Carbon can join with other carbon atoms, so a chain can keep growing.
This joining of carbon to carbon is called catenation.
The carbon-carbon bond is very strong and stable, so the chain does not break easily.
So catenation plus strong bonds lets carbon build long chains of many atoms.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Saturated or unsaturated?
activities.body: Look at the bonds between carbon atoms. If they are all single bonds, the compound is saturated. If there is a double or triple bond, it is unsaturated. Ethane has only single bonds. Ethene and ethyne are unsaturated. The carbon-carbon bond is very strong and stable, so these chains hold together well.
keyPoints: Only single bonds means saturated.
Double or triple bonds means unsaturated.
The carbon-carbon bond is very strong and stable.
activities.explanation: Count the bonds between carbon atoms to decide: single means saturated, double or triple means unsaturated.

activities.prompt: Carbon atoms can join with other carbon atoms. What is this property called?
options: Valency
Catenation
Saturation
Bonding
activities.explanation: Catenation is the special ability of carbon to bond with other carbon atoms. Well done!

activities.prompt: Carbon compounds are fewer than the compounds made by all other elements put together.
activities.explanation: It is the other way round! Carbon compounds outnumber all the others put together.

activities.prompt: A carbon compound has only single bonds between its carbon atoms. What is it called?
options: Saturated
Unsaturated
Catenated
Branched
activities.explanation: Only single bonds between carbon atoms means the compound is saturated.

activities.prompt: Match each carbon compound with its formula.
activities.explanation: Ethane is C2H6, ethene is C2H4 and ethyne is C2H2. Spot the pattern!

activities.prompt: Put these compounds in order, from most hydrogen atoms to fewest.
items: Ethane (C2H6)
Ethene (C2H4)
Ethyne (C2H2)
activities.explanation: Ethane has six hydrogens, ethene has four and ethyne has two. Great ordering!

activities.prompt: Ethane has the formula C2H6. Ethene has the formula C2H4. Ethyne has the formula C2H2. Ethene and ethyne have fewer hydrogen atoms. Which compound is saturated?
options: Ethane, because all its bonds are single bonds.
Ethene, because it has a double bond.
Ethyne, because it has the fewest hydrogen atoms.
All three, because they all contain hydrogen.

Double bonds make a compound unsaturated, not saturated.
why.Ethyne, because it has the fewest hydrog: Fewer hydrogens means fewer bonds are used, so it is unsaturated.
why.All three, because they all contain hydr: Having hydrogen does not make a compound saturated.

activities.explanation: Right. Saturated compounds have only single bonds between carbon atoms.

activities.prompt: A student draws a carbon chain with a double bond in it. Her friend says this compound is saturated. What is the flaw in the friend's claim?
options: She is right, because double bonds are very strong.
She is wrong, because double bonds make it unsaturated.
She is right, because the chain is very long.
She is wrong, because the chain should be a ring.

why.She is right, because double bonds are v: Strength of a bond does not decide if a compound is saturated.
why.She is right, because the chain is very: Chain length has nothing to do with being saturated.
why.She is wrong, because the chain should b: A chain shape does not decide saturation; the bond type does.

activities.explanation: Right. Unsaturated compounds have double or triple bonds between carbon atoms.

activities.prompt: Ravi builds a long chain of carbon atoms with a model kit. The carbon-carbon bond is very strong and stable. What can Ravi predict about his long chain?
options: It will break apart into single atoms very easily.
It will stay joined and keep its shape well.
It will curl into a ring on its own.
It will join with oxygen and change at once.

why.It will break apart into single atoms ve: Strong bonds do not break easily, so this is wrong.
Rings are one possible shape, but chains do not curl by themselves.
why.It will join with oxygen and change at o: Carbon can bond with oxygen, but that needs a reaction, not just time.

activities.explanation: Right. Strong, stable bonds hold the chain of carbon atoms together.

activities.prompt: Two carbon compounds are made of the same atoms. One has a straight chain of atoms. One has all its atoms in a ring. What does this show about carbon compounds?
options: Carbon compounds can only form straight chains.
Carbon compounds can form chains, branched chains and rings.
Carbon compounds always have double bonds between atoms.
Carbon compounds cannot join with other elements.

why.Carbon compounds can only form straight: Chains are one shape, but carbon compounds are not limited to chains.
why.Carbon compounds always have double bond: Some carbon compounds have only single bonds, so this is wrong.
why.Carbon compounds cannot join with other: Carbon forms compounds with oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen and many elements.

activities.explanation: Right. Carbon compounds may have long chains, branched chains or rings.

lessons.sceneAlt: A ball-and-stick model of an ethane molecule with two carbon atoms joined by a single bond, each carrying three hydrogen atoms.
lessons.sceneCaption: Ball-and-stick model of the ethane molecule, C2H6, a saturated compound with a single bond between its carbon atoms.

lessons.title: Chains, Branches, Rings and Functional Groups

activities.prompt: Why can the same atoms join in chains, branches, and rings?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Carbon loves to build
activities.body: Carbon atoms can join in different ways. They may form a long chain, and chains can hold many more carbon atoms. Sometimes a chain branches, like a tree. Butane can have two different carbon skeletons. Some compounds even close into a ring, like a bangle. Carbon can also join with other elements, such as oxygen or nitrogen.
keyPoints: Carbon chains can contain many more carbon atoms.
Butane can have two different carbon skeletons.
Some carbon compounds have atoms arranged in a ring.
An element that replaces hydrogen in a chain is called a heteroatom.
activities.explanation: Carbon is a great builder: it makes chains, branches and rings.

activities.title: Saturated or unsaturated?
activities.body: A compound made of only carbon and hydrogen is a hydrocarbon. If it has only single bonds, it is saturated, and we call it an alkane. If it has one or more double bonds, it is an alkene. If it has one or more triple bonds, it is an alkyne. Double and triple bonds make it unsaturated.
keyPoints: Saturated hydrocarbons are called alkanes.
Unsaturated hydrocarbons with double bonds are alkenes.
Unsaturated hydrocarbons with triple bonds are alkynes.
activities.explanation: Single bonds mean saturated; double or triple bonds mean unsaturated.

activities.prompt: A compound is made of only two kinds of elements. When do we call it a hydrocarbon?
options: Only carbon and oxygen
Only hydrogen and nitrogen
Only carbon and hydrogen
Only carbon and sulphur
activities.explanation: A hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen, nothing else. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: In a hydrocarbon chain, the element that takes the place of a hydrogen atom is called a ______.
activities.hint: It starts with 'h' and means 'different atom'.
activities.explanation: A heteroatom is any element that replaces a hydrogen in the chain. You remembered it!

activities.prompt: A chain of carbon atoms can contain many more carbon atoms.
activities.explanation: Yes! Carbon chains can grow very long. Great thinking.

activities.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.
pairs: An unsaturated hydrocarbon with double bonds
An unsaturated hydrocarbon with triple bonds
An element replacing hydrogen in a chain
activities.explanation: Each family name tells you about the bonds in the chain. Superb matching!

activities.prompt: Cyclohexane is a carbon compound whose atoms form a ring. Which formula belongs to cyclohexane?
options: C6H14
C6H12
C6H6
C12H6
activities.explanation: Cyclohexane has the formula C6H12. You are getting really good at this!

activities.prompt: Compounds that have the same molecular formula but different structures are called ______ isomers.
activities.hint: The word describes the structure of the compound.
activities.explanation: Same formula, different structure: that is what structural isomers means. Brilliant work!

activities.prompt: Cyclohexane has the formula C6H12. Sami says its six carbon atoms must sit in a straight line. Priya says they can join into a ring. Find the flaw in Sami's idea.
options: Some carbon compounds have carbons arranged in a ring
Rings can only hold carbon compounds with more atoms
A ring would break all the bonds between carbons
Cyclohexane is not really a compound of carbon

why.Rings can only hold carbon compounds wit: Wrong: thinks rings have a size limit bigger than six atoms.
why.A ring would break all the bonds between: Wrong: thinks making a ring destroys the carbon-carbon bonds.
why.Cyclohexane is not really a compound of: Wrong: thinks cyclohexane lacks carbon, which the formula shows is false.

activities.explanation: Right: carbon atoms can join in a ring, so a straight line is not forced.

activities.prompt: Gas P has only single bonds. Gas Q has one double bond. Both gases contain only carbon and hydrogen. Which gas is an alkene?
options: Gas Q, because alkenes have one or more double bonds
Gas P, because single bonds are what make alkenes
Both gases, because both of them are hydrocarbons
Neither gas, because alkenes need triple bonds

why.Gas P, because single bonds are what mak: Wrong: mixes up saturated single bonds with alkene double bonds.
why.Both gases, because both of them are hyd: Wrong: thinks being a hydrocarbon alone decides the alkene name.
why.Neither gas, because alkenes need triple: Wrong: swaps the double-bond and triple-bond families.

activities.explanation: Right: an unsaturated hydrocarbon with a double bond is an alkene.

activities.prompt: Ravi says a hydrocarbon with one double bond is an alkane. His book says alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons. Find the flaw in Ravi's claim.
options: Alkanes are saturated, so they have no double bonds
Alkanes can have double bonds but never triple bonds
A double bond makes the hydrocarbon formula wrong
Only triple bonds can make a hydrocarbon unsaturated

why.Alkanes can have double bonds but never: Wrong: thinks alkanes allow double bonds but not triple bonds.
why.A double bond makes the hydrocarbon form: Wrong: thinks a double bond breaks the formula instead of the family name.
why.Only triple bonds can make a hydrocarbon: Wrong: thinks double bonds do not cause unsaturation, only triple bonds do.

activities.explanation: Right: saturated means only single bonds, so a double bond cannot be an alkane.

lessons.sceneCaption: A molecular model set shows cyclohexane, a ring of six carbon atoms with the formula C6H12.

lessons.title: Homologous Series and Nomenclature

activities.prompt: How do chemists name millions of carbon compounds without getting hopelessly confused?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Families of Carbon Compounds
activities.body: Carbon compounds come in families called homologous series. In a family, every member has the same functional group taking the place of hydrogen in a carbon chain. Neighbours in the family differ by just one –CH2- unit. As molecular mass grows, melting and boiling points rise too. Best of all, members of a family behave alike in chemical reactions, because the functional group decides their chemical properties.
keyPoints: A homologous series has the same functional group in every member.
Successive members differ by a –CH2- unit.
Melting and boiling points rise as molecular mass rises.
Members of a series have similar chemical properties.
activities.explanation: One functional group, many compounds that behave like cousins.

activities.prompt: Two bottles on a shelf hold compounds from the same homologous series. One molecule is bigger than the other. Kavya wonders which one will melt at a higher temperature, and why.
steps: Both compounds are in one series, so both carry the same functional group on their carbon chains.
Successive members of a series differ by one -CH2- unit, so the bigger molecule has more mass.
In a homologous series, melting and boiling points rise as molecular mass rises.
So the bottle with the bigger molecule will melt at the higher temperature, because more mass means a higher melting point.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How Names Are Built
activities.body: Naming a carbon compound follows clear steps. First, count the carbon atoms in the chain. The name is based on this basic carbon chain. Then the functional group is shown by a prefix or a suffix. One neat rule: if a suffix begins with a vowel, the final e of the chain name is deleted. So the chain name and the group name fit together smoothly.
keyPoints: First count the number of carbon atoms.
The name is based on the basic carbon chain.
A prefix or suffix shows the functional group.
A suffix starting with a vowel removes the final e.
activities.explanation: Count the carbons, name the chain, then attach the group.

activities.prompt: Two neighbouring compounds in a homologous series differ by which unit?
options: A –CH2- unit
A –CH3- unit
An oxygen atom
activities.explanation: Each step up the family ladder adds one –CH2- unit. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: The general formula for alkenes is CnH____.
activities.hint: Think of how the hydrogen count grows with the carbon count.
activities.explanation: For alkenes, the number of hydrogen atoms is twice the number of carbon atoms.

activities.prompt: Compounds in the same homologous series have similar chemical properties.
activities.explanation: The functional group decides chemical properties, and it is the same all through the series.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with its correct partner.
pairs: Three carbons with a double bond
Three carbons with a triple bond
replace ane with ene or yne
activities.explanation: Double bonds give -ene names, triple bonds give -yne names, and vowel suffixes drop the final e.

activities.prompt: A suffix begins with a vowel. What happens to the name of the carbon chain?
options: Its final e is deleted
Its first letter is doubled
It stays exactly the same
activities.explanation: When the suffix starts with a vowel, the final e of the chain name is dropped so the name reads smoothly.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for naming a carbon compound in order.
items: Identify the number of carbon atoms
Build the name on the basic carbon chain
Show the functional group with a prefix or suffix
activities.explanation: Count the carbons first, then name the chain, then attach the group. You have cracked the naming recipe!

activities.prompt: Two liquids belong to the same homologous series. The second liquid has a bigger molecule. Its mass is higher. Which liquid boils at a higher temperature?
options: The bigger one, because its larger mass needs more heat to boil
The smaller one, because small things always heat up faster
Both at the same heat, because they sit in one series
Neither one boils, because series liquids cannot boil at all

why.The smaller one, because small things al: Thinks small size means faster heating, mixing heating speed with boiling point.
why.Both at the same heat, because they sit: Thinks one series means everything is equal, but only chemical properties stay similar.
why.Neither one boils, because series liquid: Thinks being in a series stops boiling, which is not what a series means.

activities.explanation: Right: in a series, boiling point rises as molecular mass rises.

activities.prompt: Ravi drips a test liquid into two bottles. Both bottles hold compounds from one homologous series. Both bottles give the same result in the test. Why do both compounds act the same way?
options: Both carry the same functional group, which controls their reactions
Both carry the same number of carbon atoms in their chains
Both have the same boiling point, so they react the same way
Both have the same mass, so they must behave the same way

why.Both carry the same number of carbon ato: Thinks carbon count controls reactions, but members differ by a -CH2- unit.
why.Both have the same boiling point, so the: Thinks boiling point fixes reactions, but boiling is a physical property.
why.Both have the same mass, so they must be: Thinks equal mass means equal behaviour, but masses differ along a series.

activities.explanation: Right: the functional group decides chemical properties, and it stays the same in a series.

activities.prompt: A carbon chain holds three carbon atoms. The chain has a triple bond, not only single bonds. Arjun writes the name with the ending ane. What is the flaw in Arjun's name?
options: The ending ane is wrong, because a triple bond needs yne
The ending ane is wrong, because a double bond needs yne
The name is fine, because three carbons always end with ane
The name is fine, because bonds never change the chain name

why.The ending ane is wrong, because a doubl: Mixes up the double bond ending with the triple bond ending.
why.The name is fine, because three carbons: Thinks carbon count alone fixes the ending, ignoring the bond.
why.The name is fine, because bonds never ch: Thinks bonds play no part in naming, but unsaturation changes the ending.

activities.explanation: Right: an unsaturated chain replaces ane, and a triple bond takes yne.

activities.prompt: An alkene has three carbon atoms in its chain. The general formula for alkenes is CnH2n. How many hydrogen atoms does this alkene carry?
options: Six, because the formula doubles the number of carbons
Three, because the formula keeps hydrogens equal to carbons
Eight, because the formula adds two to the carbon number
Nine, because the formula squares the number of carbons

why.Three, because the formula keeps hydroge: Misreads the formula as one hydrogen for every carbon.
why.Eight, because the formula adds two to t: Misreads 2n as n plus two instead of n times two.
why.Nine, because the formula squares the nu: Misreads 2n as n squared instead of n times two.

activities.explanation: Right: CnH2n means hydrogens equal two times n, so two times three is six.

lessons.sceneAlt: Two small glass vials side by side, one holding methanol and the other ethanol, in front of their commercial stock bottles.
lessons.sceneCaption: Methanol and ethanol are neighbouring members of the alcohol homologous series, differing by one CH2 unit.

lessons.title: Chemical Properties of Carbon Compounds

activities.prompt: Why do some flames burn yellow and smoky while others burn clean and blue?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Carbon compounds love to burn
activities.body: Carbon compounds take part in many reactions. When carbon burns in oxygen, it forms carbon dioxide. Most carbon compounds give out lots of heat and light as they burn. Burning is a kind of oxidation, which means oxygen is added. This is why fuels give us warmth and light.
keyPoints: Carbon burns in oxygen to give carbon dioxide.
Most carbon compounds release much heat and light on burning.
Burning is oxidation, where oxygen is added.
activities.explanation: Burning is the most common reaction of carbon compounds.

activities.prompt: Riya lights a candle in a closed box. Soon the flame turns yellow and gives black smoke. Why?
steps: The box has only a little air, so oxygen runs out fast.
Little oxygen means even a saturated fuel cannot burn fully, so combustion becomes incomplete.
Incomplete burning makes unburnt carbon, which we see as black smoke.
So the yellow smoky flame happens because the closed box limits the air supply.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Adding and swapping atoms
activities.body: Carbon compounds react in other ways too. Unsaturated hydrocarbons can add hydrogen with the help of catalysts like palladium or nickel. A catalyst changes the rate of a reaction but stays unchanged itself. In sunlight, chlorine can replace hydrogen atoms in a hydrocarbon, one by one. Such a swap is called a substitution reaction.
keyPoints: Unsaturated hydrocarbons add hydrogen using catalysts like palladium or nickel.
A catalyst changes the rate of a reaction without being affected.
In sunlight, chlorine replaces hydrogen atoms one by one. This is substitution.
activities.explanation: Some reactions add atoms, and some swap one atom for another.

activities.prompt: Meera burns some charcoal in a pan. Which gas is made when carbon burns in oxygen?
options: Oxygen
Nitrogen
Carbon dioxide
Hydrogen
activities.explanation: Carbon in all its forms burns in oxygen to give carbon dioxide. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: A saturated hydrocarbon is burning, but its flame turns yellow with lots of black smoke. Why?
options: The compound has no carbon in it.
The air supply to the flame is limited.
The compound is unsaturated instead.
The flame is too cold to burn.
activities.explanation: Limited air causes incomplete combustion, even of saturated hydrocarbons. That makes a sooty flame.

activities.prompt: A substance that adds oxygen to another substance is called an ______ agent.
activities.hint: It begins like the word 'oxygen'.
activities.explanation: Substances that add oxygen to others are called oxidising agents. You remembered it!

activities.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.
pairs: One atom takes the place of another
Replaces hydrogen atoms one by one
activities.explanation: Each helper has its own job in a reaction. You matched them all!

activities.prompt: Fuels like coal and petroleum contain small amounts of which two substances?
options: Oxygen and helium
Iron and copper
Nitrogen and sulphur
Water and sand
activities.explanation: Coal and petroleum contain some nitrogen and sulphur. Careful thinking!

activities.prompt: Put the steps of burning a carbon compound in the right order.
items: A carbon compound is burnt in air
Oxygen is added to the compound by oxidation
Carbon dioxide is formed
A large amount of heat and light is given out
activities.explanation: Burning adds oxygen first, carbon dioxide forms, then heat and light come out. Perfect order!

activities.prompt: A kerosene stove gives a clean flame in the open. Priya covers it partly with a lid. What happens to the flame?
options: It burns even cleaner because the lid traps the heat inside
It goes out at once because kerosene is not a fuel
It turns yellow and smoky because less air reaches the flame
It stays exactly the same because the fuel has not changed

why.It burns even cleaner because the lid tr: She thinks heat alone makes burning clean, but air supply is what matters.
why.It goes out at once because kerosene is: She thinks any change must stop burning, but limited air only makes it incomplete.
why.It stays exactly the same because the fu: She forgets the flame depends on air, not only on the fuel itself.

activities.explanation: Right, because limiting air makes even saturated fuel burn incompletely and smoke.

activities.prompt: Two lamps burn the same amount of fuel. One gives a clean flame. One gives black smoke. A girl says the smoky lamp must use a different kind of fuel. Is her test fair?
options: Yes, because smoke always proves the fuel is a different kind
No, because the same fuel can smoke if its air supply is limited
Yes, because a clean flame and a smoky flame cannot come from one fuel
No, because smoke only shows that the lamp is very old

why.Yes, because smoke always proves the fue: She links smoke only to fuel type and forgets air supply matters too.
why.Yes, because a clean flame and a smoky f: She thinks one fuel can only ever burn one way, which is not true.
why.No, because smoke only shows that the la: She blames the lamp instead of thinking about the air reaching the flame.

activities.explanation: Right, because limited air makes even saturated hydrocarbons burn with smoke.

activities.prompt: A friend says coal is a bad fuel because it makes smoke and harmful gases. You know coal has some nitrogen and sulphur. What is the best reason to agree with him?
options: Burning coal releases a large amount of heat, which is always wasteful
Coal cannot burn in oxygen, so it never burns fully at all
Its nitrogen and sulphur also burn, adding unwanted things to the air
Coal is saturated, so it must always give a very dirty flame

why.Burning coal releases a large amount of: He confuses giving out heat with being wasteful; heat is what fuels are for.
why.Coal cannot burn in oxygen, so it never: He forgets carbon burns in oxygen to give carbon dioxide.
why.Coal is saturated, so it must always giv: He wrongly links the word saturated with a dirty flame.

activities.explanation: Right, because the nitrogen and sulphur in coal also burn and pollute the air.

activities.prompt: A student passes hydrogen through an unsaturated hydrocarbon with nickel powder. Another student does the same test but uses plain sand instead of nickel. What is wrong with the second test?
options: Sand is a catalyst too, so the second test is exactly the same
Sand cannot change the rate of the reaction, so hydrogen will not add on
Sand adds oxygen to the hydrocarbon, so it acts as an oxidising agent
Sand replaces hydrogen atoms, so a substitution reaction happens instead

why.Sand is a catalyst too, so the second te: He thinks any powder works as a catalyst, but only catalysts like nickel do.
why.Sand adds oxygen to the hydrocarbon, so: He mixes up adding hydrogen with adding oxygen to a substance.
why.Sand replaces hydrogen atoms, so a subst: He mixes up adding hydrogen with replacing atoms in sunlight.

activities.explanation: Right, because without a catalyst like nickel, hydrogen does not add on.

activities.prompt: A gas flame in a kitchen suddenly turns yellow and starts giving soot on the pot. The gas pipe has not changed. What should the family check first?
options: Whether the gas has changed from saturated to unsaturated
Whether the gas has stopped releasing heat and light
Whether something is blocking the air holes of the burner
Whether the pot has become an oxidising agent

why.Whether the gas has changed from saturat: The fuel has not changed, so its kind cannot be the reason.
why.Whether the gas has stopped releasing he: The flame still gives heat, so heat release is not the problem.
why.Whether the pot has become an oxidising: An oxidising agent adds oxygen to others; a pot cannot do that.

activities.explanation: Right, because blocked air limits oxygen and makes even saturated fuel burn incompletely.

lessons.sceneCaption: Bunsen burner flames change from yellow and sooty to clean blue as the air supply increases.
