lessons.title: Ethanol, Ethanoic Acid, Soaps and Detergents

activities.prompt: Why does soap fail in hard water, and what really works instead?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Carbon Friends and Two Cleaners
activities.body: Ethanol is the alcohol in drinks. Heat it with concentrated sulphuric acid and it turns into ethene. Ethanoic acid is also called acetic acid. Mixed with water, it becomes the vinegar in your kitchen. Soaps are salts of long chain carboxylic acids. Detergents are their clever cousins that beat hard water.
keyPoints: Ethanol is the alcohol in drinks.
Ethanoic acid in water makes vinegar.
Soaps are salts of long chain carboxylic acids.
Detergents work well even in hard water.
activities.explanation: These four substances appear often in daily life, from the kitchen to the wash basin.

activities.title: Mix acid and base

tasks.then: More base than acid: litmus turns blue.

activities.takeaway: Equal amounts of acid and base cancel out and make a neutral solution.
activities.explanation: Equal amounts of acid and base cancel out and make a neutral solution.

activities.prompt: Ravi washes his hands with soap using well water. Hardly any lather forms, and a sticky grey layer appears. His friend uses detergent in the same water and gets lots of lather. Why?
steps: Well water is hard, so it contains things that react with soap.
This reaction makes scum, an insoluble solid, so the soap gets used up instead of making lather.
Detergents do not form scum in hard water, so they keep working and give lather.
So Ravi's soap is not bad; the hard water is what stopped it from lathering.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Your kitchen has a bottle of vinegar. What is vinegar?
options: A 5-8% solution of acetic acid in water
Pure acetic acid with no water
A solution of ethanol in water
A salt of a carboxylic acid
activities.explanation: Vinegar is simply acetic acid mixed with water in a 5-8% solution. You have been using an acid in your food!

activities.prompt: When ethanol reacts with sodium, bubbles of ______ gas come out.
activities.hint: Think of the lightest gas, the one that makes balloons rise.
activities.explanation: Sodium pushes ethanol to give off hydrogen gas. A nice fizzy sign that a reaction is happening!

activities.prompt: Match each substance with its common name or special feature.
pairs: Pure acid that freezes in winter
activities.explanation: Each name tells a small story. Glacial means the pure acid freezes during winter, like ice.

activities.prompt: Ethanol meets ethanoic acid, and an acid catalyst helps. What is made?
options: An ester
Ethene
Hydrogen
A micelle
activities.explanation: With an acid catalyst, ethanol and ethanoic acid join to give an ester. Esters often smell pleasant.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for making an ester in the correct order.
items: Take ethanol
Add ethanoic acid
Add an acid catalyst
An ester forms
activities.explanation: First gather the two reactants, then add the catalyst, and the ester forms. You are a chemist now!

activities.prompt: Soap is added to hard water and to soft water. What happens in each?
options: Micelles in soft water, scum in hard water
Scum in soft water, micelles in hard water
Micelles in both waters
Scum in both waters
activities.explanation: In water, soap molecules gather into micelles that trap dirt. But hard water makes soap form scum, an insoluble substance. That is why detergents are handy in hard water areas.

activities.prompt: Soap molecules form micelles in water. Hands have oily dirt on them. Water alone cannot wash oil off. How does soap remove the oil?
options: Micelles trap the oil inside, so water can rinse it away
Soap melts the oil with heat, so it mixes into water
Soap turns the oil into soap, so the oil dissolves
Micelles push the oil deep into the skin, hiding it

why.Soap melts the oil with heat, so it mixe: Thinks soap works by heating or melting the oil.
why.Soap turns the oil into soap, so the oil: Thinks soap chemically changes oil into more soap.
why.Micelles push the oil deep into the skin: Thinks the oil just gets hidden rather than removed.

activities.explanation: Right: micelles hold the oil inside, so rinsing water carries it off.

activities.prompt: Vinegar is a 5-8% solution of acetic acid in water. Two bottles stand in a cold room in winter. The pure ethanoic acid bottle freezes solid. The vinegar bottle stays liquid. Why?
options: Pure ethanoic acid freezes in winter; vinegar has water mixed in
Vinegar stays warm because its acid makes heat inside it
The pure bottle froze because its glass pulled the cold in
Vinegar cannot freeze because acids never freeze in winter

why.Vinegar stays warm because its acid make: Thinks acids give out heat and so cannot get cold.
why.The pure bottle froze because its glass: Blames the bottle instead of thinking about the liquid inside.
why.Vinegar cannot freeze because acids neve: Thinks being an acid stops a liquid from freezing.

activities.explanation: Right: pure ethanoic acid freezes in winter, and vinegar is mostly water.

activities.prompt: Carboxylic acids are weak acids. A friend says, 'Glacial acetic acid froze solid in winter, so it must be a very strong acid.' What is the flaw in this claim?
options: Freezing shows the acid is pure, not that it is strong
The friend is right, because frozen acids are strong acids
Acetic acid is strong, but freezing made it become weak
Weak acids never freeze, so the bottle held something else

why.The friend is right, because frozen acid: Thinks how easily something freezes tells you its acid strength.
why.Acetic acid is strong, but freezing made: Thinks freezing can change how strong an acid is.
why.Weak acids never freeze, so the bottle h: Thinks weak acids cannot freeze, so doubts the bottle's label.

activities.explanation: Right: freezing in winter only shows purity; ethanoic acid is still a weak acid.

lessons.sceneAlt: A Bohr model diagram of a carbon atom showing six protons, six neutrons, six electrons and four valence electrons.
lessons.sceneCaption: A carbon atom has six protons, six neutrons and six electrons, with four electrons in its outermost shell.

activities.context: During a science club activity, Aditi and Rohan test different liquids with a simple circuit that has a bulb and two electrodes. The bulb glows brightly in salt water, glows weakly in lemon juice, but stays completely dark when they dip the electrodes in a solution of a carbon-based compound. Aditi is puzzled because the solution looks just like the others. Meanwhile, their teacher reminds them that carbon has four electrons in its outermost shell and that the earth's crust contains very little carbon, yet almost everything around them — food, clothes, medicines and books — depends on it.
activities.prompt: Why did the bulb stay dark when the electrodes were dipped in the carbon-based solution?
options: Because the solution had no dissolved material in it at all
Because compounds formed by sharing electron pairs generally do not carry electricity through them
Because the bulb needed a stronger battery to work with any liquid
Because carbon compounds conduct electricity only when heated

why.Because the solution had no dissolved ma: Wrong — the passage gives no reason to think the solution was empty; the issue is how it conducts, not what is dissolved.
why.Because the bulb needed a stronger batte: Wrong — the bulb worked in other liquids with the same setup, so the battery is not the problem.
why.Because carbon compounds conduct electri: Wrong — nothing in the lesson links heating to conduction; this is an invented condition.

activities.explanation: Correct — the compound is covalent, and such compounds are generally poor conductors, so the circuit stays incomplete.

activities.context: During a science club activity, Aditi and Rohan test different liquids with a simple circuit that has a bulb and two electrodes. The bulb glows brightly in salt water, glows weakly in lemon juice, but stays completely dark when they dip the electrodes in a solution of a carbon-based compound. Aditi is puzzled because the solution looks just like the others. Meanwhile, their teacher reminds them that carbon has four electrons in its outermost shell and that the earth's crust contains very little carbon, yet almost everything around them — food, clothes, medicines and books — depends on it.
activities.prompt: Rohan argues that carbon should be rare and unimportant since the crust holds only 0.02% of it as minerals. What is the flaw in his reasoning?
options: He forgot that the atmosphere's carbon dioxide share is much larger than the crust's share
He ignored that living structures and many everyday materials are built from carbon-based substances
He assumed carbon in mineral form conducts electricity
He counted the crust's carbon twice, once as minerals and once as compounds

why.He forgot that the atmosphere's carbon d: Wrong — the atmosphere figure (0.03% carbon dioxide) is also tiny, so it does not rescue his argument.
why.He assumed carbon in mineral form conduc: Wrong — conduction of carbon compounds has nothing to do with why carbon matters to us.
why.He counted the crust's carbon twice, onc: Wrong — there is no double counting; the crust figure is a single stated percentage.

activities.explanation: Correct — importance does not depend on how much carbon the crust holds; all living structures and many things we use are carbon-based.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Carbon becomes stable by sharing its valence electrons with other atoms.
Reason (R): Carbon has four electrons in its outermost shell.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and having four outer electrons is exactly why carbon needs to share electrons to become stable.

activities.prompt: Explain why most carbon compounds are poor conductors of electricity.
activities.answer: In carbon compounds, the atoms are joined by covalent bonds. A covalent bond is formed when two atoms share a pair of electrons, and each shared pair counts as a single covalent bond. Since the bonds in these compounds are formed by sharing electron pairs in this way, covalent compounds generally do not conduct electricity. Therefore, most carbon compounds, being covalent in nature, behave as poor conductors when tested in a circuit.
points: States that atoms in carbon compounds are joined by covalent bonds.
Defines a covalent bond as a shared pair of electrons forming a single bond.
Links covalent compounds to being generally poor conductors.
Concludes that this is why most carbon compounds do not conduct.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a science exhibition, Aditi sets up three sealed models labelled C2H6, C2H4 and C2H2. Her friend Rohan claims all three must behave the same because each contains only carbon and hydrogen. Aditi disagrees and asks visitors to decide, using bond types, which models show saturated compounds and which show unsaturated ones, and why carbon can build such a huge variety of compounds in the first place.
activities.prompt: A visitor asks why carbon alone manages to form more compounds than all other elements put together. What should Aditi answer?
options: Because carbon can join with other carbon atoms and also bonds with four other atoms at a time
Because carbon is the only element that can bond with hydrogen
Because carbon compounds are always found as rings
Because carbon has a valency of two, letting it bond easily

why.Because carbon is the only element that: Wrong: many elements form compounds with hydrogen; this is not special to carbon.
why.Because carbon compounds are always foun: Wrong: carbon compounds may be long chains, branched chains or rings, not only rings.
why.Because carbon has a valency of two, let: Wrong: carbon's valency is four, not two, so this states the fact incorrectly.

activities.explanation: Correct: catenation (carbon joining with carbon) together with a valency of four explains the enormous variety.

activities.context: During a science exhibition, Aditi sets up three sealed models labelled C2H6, C2H4 and C2H2. Her friend Rohan claims all three must behave the same because each contains only carbon and hydrogen. Aditi disagrees and asks visitors to decide, using bond types, which models show saturated compounds and which show unsaturated ones, and why carbon can build such a huge variety of compounds in the first place.
activities.prompt: Suppose the bonds between the carbon atoms in the C2H4 model were changed to single bonds only. What would the model then represent?
options: A saturated compound, since only single bonds would remain between the carbon atoms
An unsaturated compound, since changing bonds always keeps a compound unsaturated
A compound that is no longer made of carbon and hydrogen
A compound of carbon with oxygen, nitrogen or sulphur instead

why.An unsaturated compound, since changing: Wrong: saturation depends on the bonds present; single bonds make it saturated, not unsaturated.
why.A compound that is no longer made of car: Wrong: changing the carbon-carbon bond type does not change which elements make up the compound.
why.A compound of carbon with oxygen, nitrog: Wrong: the elements in the compound stay the same; only the bond between the carbon atoms changes.

activities.explanation: Correct: with only single bonds between carbon atoms, the compound becomes saturated.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Ethyne (C2H2) is classified as an unsaturated compound.
Reason (R): Ethyne has double or triple bonds between its carbon atoms.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the triple bond between the carbon atoms is exactly why ethyne is unsaturated.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The carbon-carbon bond is very strong and stable.
Reason (R): Carbon has a valency of four.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but a valency of four tells how many atoms carbon can bond with, not why the bond is strong.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Ethane (C2H6) is an unsaturated compound.
Reason (R): Compounds with only single bonds between carbon atoms are called saturated.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Ethane has only single bonds, so it is saturated, making the assertion false while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain why carbon forms far more compounds than all other elements put together.
activities.answer: Carbon has a unique ability to form bonds with other carbon atoms, a property called catenation. Because of catenation, carbon atoms can join to form long chains, branched chains or rings, giving a huge number of possible structures. In addition, carbon has a valency of four, so each carbon atom can bond with four other atoms. Carbon also forms compounds with oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine and many other elements. Together, catenation, four valency and bonding with many elements make the number of carbon compounds larger than all other compounds put together.
points: States catenation: carbon bonds with other carbon atoms
Mentions long chains, branched chains and rings
States valency of four allows bonding with four atoms
Mentions bonding with oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine and other elements
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: For the school science fair, Riya is building molecule models with a ball-and-stick kit. She has made a four-carbon chain, a six-carbon ring with formula C6H12, and a long chain made only of carbon and hydrogen. Her friend Arjun joins a chlorine atom in place of one hydrogen on the long chain, and then challenges Riya to name and classify everything she has built before the judge arrives.
activities.prompt: Riya makes a second model with the same four carbons and the same number of hydrogens as her first four-carbon model, but joined in a different arrangement. What should she tell the judge about the two models?
options: They are structural isomers of each other
They are the same compound, so one model should be dismantled
One of them must actually contain a ring
They are different hydrocarbons because their formulas differ

why.They are the same compound, so one model: Different structures mean they are different compounds, so one cannot be discarded
why.One of them must actually contain a ring: A different arrangement of a chain does not mean the atoms form a ring
why.They are different hydrocarbons because: Their molecular formulas are the same, not different, so they are not different hydrocarbons on that count

activities.explanation: Same molecular formula but different structures is exactly what structural isomers are

activities.context: For the school science fair, Riya is building molecule models with a ball-and-stick kit. She has made a four-carbon chain, a six-carbon ring with formula C6H12, and a long chain made only of carbon and hydrogen. Her friend Arjun joins a chlorine atom in place of one hydrogen on the long chain, and then challenges Riya to name and classify everything she has built before the judge arrives.
activities.prompt: The judge asks Riya to add one more model showing an unsaturated hydrocarbon with a triple bond. What should she build?
options: A chain in which every carbon is joined by single bonds
A chain containing a triple bond between carbon atoms
A chain containing a double bond between carbon atoms
A six-carbon ring with the formula C6H12

why.A chain in which every carbon is joined: All single bonds would give a saturated alkane, not an unsaturated model
why.A chain containing a double bond between: A double bond would make an alkene, not a compound with a triple bond
why.A six-carbon ring with the formula C6H12: Her ring model has no triple bond, so it would not answer the judge's request

activities.explanation: An unsaturated hydrocarbon with a triple bond is an alkyne

activities.context: For the school science fair, Riya is building molecule models with a ball-and-stick kit. She has made a four-carbon chain, a six-carbon ring with formula C6H12, and a long chain made only of carbon and hydrogen. Her friend Arjun joins a chlorine atom in place of one hydrogen on the long chain, and then challenges Riya to name and classify everything she has built before the judge arrives.
activities.prompt: Arjun replaced one hydrogen on the long chain with a chlorine atom. What should Riya conclude about his new model?
options: It is no longer a hydrocarbon, and the chlorine is a heteroatom
It is still a hydrocarbon, just with a shorter chain
It has become an alkene because an atom was replaced
It is now a structural isomer of the original chain

why.It is still a hydrocarbon, just with a s: No carbon atom was removed, so the chain length has not changed
why.It has become an alkene because an atom: Replacing an atom does not create a double bond, so it is not an alkene
why.It is now a structural isomer of the ori: Structural isomers must have the same molecular formula, but replacing hydrogen with chlorine changes the formula

activities.explanation: The model no longer contains only carbon and hydrogen, and the replacing element is a heteroatom

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The two different carbon skeletons of butane are an example of structural isomerism.
Reason (R): Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason states the definition, which directly explains why butane's two skeletons are structural isomers.

activities.prompt: Explain why butane can exist in two different forms, and state what these forms are called.
activities.answer: Carbon chains can be arranged in more than one way. With four carbon atoms, butane's atoms can be joined into two different carbon skeletons. Both forms have the same molecular formula, but the atoms are connected in different structures. Compounds that share a molecular formula but differ in structure are called structural isomers. So the two forms of butane are structural isomers: their formula is identical, yet their carbon skeletons, and therefore their structures, are different.
points: Carbon atoms can be joined in more than one arrangement
Both forms have the same molecular formula
The structures (carbon skeletons) are different
Such compounds are called structural isomers
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a science exhibition, Aditi displays three bottles from one homologous series. Each label shows one more –CH2– unit than the bottle before it, and she has written the boiling points beside them, which rise from the first bottle to the third. A visitor notices that all three liquids give the same result in a chemical test, and asks Aditi why the liquids behave alike chemically, why the boiling points differ, and how the third liquid, a three-carbon chain with a triple bond, received its name.
activities.prompt: Why do all three liquids give the same result in the chemical test?
options: Because each liquid carries the same functional group that decides its chemical behaviour
Because all three liquids have exactly the same molecular mass
Because their boiling points are close to one another
Because each liquid differs from the next by a –CH2– unit

why.Because all three liquids have exactly t: Wrong: molecular mass actually increases along the series, so it is not the same
why.Because their boiling points are close t: Wrong: boiling points rise along the series, so they are not close or responsible here
why.Because each liquid differs from the nex: Wrong: the –CH2– difference explains changing physical properties, not similar chemical behaviour

activities.explanation: Correct: the functional group governs chemical properties, so members of the series react alike

activities.context: During a science exhibition, Aditi displays three bottles from one homologous series. Each label shows one more –CH2– unit than the bottle before it, and she has written the boiling points beside them, which rise from the first bottle to the third. A visitor notices that all three liquids give the same result in a chemical test, and asks Aditi why the liquids behave alike chemically, why the boiling points differ, and how the third liquid, a three-carbon chain with a triple bond, received its name.
activities.prompt: Aditi adds a fourth bottle containing the next member of the same series. What should she expect for its boiling point compared with the third bottle?
options: It will be higher, since the added –CH2– unit raises the molecular mass
It will be lower, since longer chains hold less heat
It will be exactly the same, since the functional group is unchanged
It cannot be predicted from the information on the labels

why.It will be lower, since longer chains ho: Wrong: this reverses the trend; heavier members boil at higher temperatures
why.It will be exactly the same, since the f: Wrong: the functional group staying the same affects chemical properties, not boiling point
why.It cannot be predicted from the informat: Wrong: the series pattern given is enough to predict the direction of change

activities.explanation: Correct: melting and boiling points rise with molecular mass in a homologous series

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Carbon and its Compounds

activities.prompt: Why does carbon share electrons instead of giving them away or taking them?
options: It has four electrons in its outermost shell
It has no electrons at all in its shell
It has eight electrons in its outermost shell
activities.explanation: Carbon has four outer electrons, so sharing helps it become stable. Well done!

activities.prompt: Most carbon compounds are good conductors of electricity.
activities.explanation: Covalent compounds are generally poor conductors. Keep going!

activities.prompt: Carbon compounds outnumber all other elements' compounds put together. What makes this possible?
options: Carbon can bond with other carbon atoms
Carbon is found in huge amounts in the crust
Carbon melts easily in warm weather
activities.explanation: This special bonding with other carbon atoms is called catenation. Great thinking!

activities.prompt: Compounds with double or triple bonds between carbon atoms are called ______ compounds.
activities.hint: Think of the opposite of 'saturated'.
activities.explanation: Single bonds mean saturated; double or triple bonds mean unsaturated. You remembered it!

activities.prompt: Match each hydrocarbon family to its bond type.
activities.explanation: Each family is named by the kind of bond it holds. Superb matching!

activities.prompt: Butane can have two different carbon skeletons with the same formula. What are such compounds called?
options: Structural isomers
Heteroatoms
Oxidising agents
activities.explanation: Same formula but different structures means structural isomers. Spot on!

activities.prompt: In a homologous series, melting and boiling points rise as molecular mass rises.
activities.explanation: Heavier compounds in the series need more heat to melt or boil. Correct!

activities.prompt: A three-carbon chain with a double bond is called ______.
activities.hint: The chain has three carbons, and 'ene' shows a double bond.
activities.explanation: Three carbons give 'prop', and a double bond gives 'ene'. Lovely work!

activities.prompt: Put these naming steps in the correct order.
items: Count the number of carbon atoms in the chain
Show the functional group with a prefix or suffix
Delete the final e if the suffix begins with a vowel
activities.explanation: First count the carbons, then mark the group, then fix the ending. Perfect order!

activities.prompt: An unsaturated carbon compound burns in air. What flame would you expect to see?
options: A yellow flame with lots of black smoke
A clean flame with no smoke at all
A blue flame that gives no light
activities.explanation: Unsaturated compounds burn with a yellow flame and black smoke. Excellent recall!

activities.prompt: Even a saturated hydrocarbon gives a dirty flame if the air supply is limited.
activities.explanation: Limited air causes incomplete combustion, even for saturated fuels. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: Match each substance or mixture to what the lesson says about it.
pairs: Ethanol heated with concentrated sulphuric acid
activities.explanation: Each reaction and mixture has its own special result. Brilliant matching!

activities.prompt: In hard water, soap forms an insoluble substance called ______.
activities.hint: It is a four-letter word starting with 's'.
activities.explanation: Scum forms when soap meets hard water, so detergents work better there. Superb!

activities.prompt: Successive compounds in a homologous series differ by a fixed unit. Which one?
options: A –CH2- unit
A –CH4- unit
A –C2H6- unit
activities.explanation: Each step in the series adds one –CH2- unit. You cracked it!

chapters.title: Life Processes
chapters.summary: In this chapter: life processes and maintenance; nutrition and autotrophic nutrition; heterotrophic nutrition and human digestion; respiration.

lessons.title: Life processes and maintenance

activities.prompt: Why doesn't a sleeping tree still need to eat or breathe?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What keeps living things alive?
activities.body: Living things move, breathe and grow. But tiny movements inside the body matter even more. These molecular movements keep life going. A living body is a well-ordered structure, and the world around it keeps trying to break that order. So the body must repair and maintain itself all the time. The processes that do this maintenance job are called life processes.
keyPoints: Visible movement alone cannot define life.
Living bodies must keep repairing their structures.
Life processes together do the maintenance job.
activities.explanation: Life is not just about moving. It is about keeping the body's order safe.

activities.prompt: A girl says her moving toy car is alive because it moves. Why is she wrong?
steps: The car shows big visible movement, so her idea seems fair at first.
But living things also have tiny molecular movements happening inside them.
The car has no such tiny movements inside, because it is not a living thing.
So visible movement alone cannot define life, and the car is not alive.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: You see a plant that is not moving at all. What should you think?
options: It cannot be alive
It may still be alive
It is growing fast
It is taking in oxygen
activities.explanation: Visible movement alone cannot define life. A thing can be alive without moving.

activities.prompt: Taking food in from outside the body is called ______.
activities.hint: It starts with the letter n.
activities.explanation: Food is an outside energy source. Taking it in is called nutrition.

activities.prompt: Why must living creatures keep repairing their structures?
options: Because the environment keeps breaking their order down
Because they want to grow bigger and taller
Because they must make new cells every day
Because food gives them extra energy to spare
activities.explanation: The environment can break down the ordered structure of a body. If order breaks down fully, the organism will no longer be alive.

activities.prompt: Match each word with what it means.
pairs: Using oxygen to break down food
Processes that do the maintenance job
Show no molecular movement until they infect a cell
activities.explanation: Each word names one key idea from the lesson. Well done for linking them.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order, from where energy starts to where it is used.
items: Energy comes from outside the body
Food is taken in, which is called nutrition
Oxygen is taken in to break down the food
Cells get energy from the broken-down food
The energy is used to maintain the body
activities.explanation: Energy enters as food, nutrition takes it in, respiration breaks it down, and the body uses it for maintenance.

activities.prompt: A virus is sitting outside a cell. Why is it not showing molecular movement?
options: It only shows molecular movement after infecting a cell
It has used up all the food it stored inside
It is too small to show any movement at all
It is waiting for oxygen to start respiration
activities.explanation: Viruses do not show molecular movement until they infect a cell. That is why they look lifeless outside a cell.

activities.prompt: A toy robot walks and waves its arms. It is not alive. A dog moves too. Why is moving alone not enough to prove life?
options: Robots move only when a living person presses their buttons.
Everything alive moves, so anything that moves must be alive.
Moving things may not be alive, so movement alone cannot prove life.
Robots move faster than dogs, so their movement is different.

why.Robots move only when a living person pr: Thinks the source of movement matters, but the real issue is that movement alone cannot define life.
why.Everything alive moves, so anything that: Reverses the rule by assuming movement always proves life.
why.Robots move faster than dogs, so their m: Focuses on speed of movement, which misses the point completely.

activities.explanation: Right, because visible movement alone cannot define life.

activities.prompt: A virus sits on a door handle for hours. Nothing happens inside it. Then it gets inside a person's cell. What starts inside the virus then?
options: Molecular movements begin inside the virus.
Nothing changes inside the virus at all.
The virus grows much bigger very quickly.
The virus starts making its own food.

Thinks viruses never change, even inside a cell.
why.The virus grows much bigger very quickly: Thinks infection means growing bigger, which is not what happens.
Thinks viruses make food, but that is not given here.

activities.explanation: Right, because viruses show molecular movement only after infecting a cell.

activities.prompt: Wind and rain keep hitting a bird every day. Its body parts can slowly break down. What must the bird do to stay alive?
options: Keep repairing and maintaining its body structures.
Stop flying so the wind cannot touch it.
Grow bigger feathers to block all damage.
Find a new nest in a safer place.

Tries to avoid the environment instead of fixing the damage inside.
why.Grow bigger feathers to block all damage: Thinks bigger parts stop damage, but order still breaks down.
Thinks changing its home repairs its body, which it does not.

activities.explanation: Right, because living creatures must keep repairing and maintaining their structures.

activities.prompt: A boy sleeps all night and does nothing. His body still works inside. Why does his body keep working while he rests?
options: Maintenance jobs never stop, even when he does nothing.
His body waits for morning before it starts working.
Sleeping gives his body brand new parts overnight.
His body only works when he is eating food.

why.His body waits for morning before it sta: Thinks body work can pause and restart later, which is wrong.
why.Sleeping gives his body brand new parts: Thinks sleep creates new parts, which is not the reason.
why.His body only works when he is eating fo: Thinks the body needs eating to work at every moment.

activities.explanation: Right, because maintenance functions go on even when an organism is not doing anything particular.

activities.prompt: A girl stops eating for many days. Her body still needs energy for maintenance. Where must this energy come from?
options: From outside her body, like the food she eats.
From inside her body, made fresh from nothing.
From her bones, which store movement for later.
From her school, which gives her daily power.

why.From inside her body, made fresh from no: Thinks the body can create energy from nothing inside.
why.From her bones, which store movement for: Thinks bones store energy, which is not given here.
why.From her school, which gives her daily p: Confuses a place she visits with a source of body energy.

activities.explanation: Right, because energy for maintenance comes from outside the body, and food is that source.

lessons.sceneAlt: A bright microscope photo of living moss leaf cells filled with green chloroplasts and elongated starch granules inside them.
lessons.sceneCaption: Living leaf cells of a moss, showing green chloroplasts with accumulated starch granules inside them.

sceneCredit.creator: Des_Callaghan

lessons.title: Nutrition and Autotrophic Nutrition

activities.prompt: How do plants make their own food from just sunlight, water, and air?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Where does food come from?
activities.body: Food gives you energy and materials to grow and repair your body. All living things need food, but they get it in different ways. Green plants make their own food from carbon dioxide and water. They are called autotrophs. Animals eat ready-made food, so they are called heterotrophs. Plants use sunlight and a green colouring called chlorophyll to make their food. This process is called photosynthesis.
keyPoints: Food gives energy and materials for growth and repair.
Autotrophs make food from carbon dioxide and water.
Heterotrophs depend on other living things for food.
Photosynthesis needs sunlight and chlorophyll.
activities.explanation: Plants cook their own food using sunlight, while animals must eat theirs.

activities.prompt: A cow eats grass, but a green plant makes its own food from air and water. Why does the cow need the plant?
steps: The cow cannot make food from air and water, so it must eat ready-made food.
Grass is a green plant, so it makes its own food using sunlight, carbon dioxide and water.
The food in grass holds energy, and the cow gets that energy by eating the grass.
So the cow depends on the plant, because the plant is the one that first makes food from simple things.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Why does your body need food?
options: To give energy and help you grow
To make you sleep longer
To change your eye colour
To make your hair curly
activities.explanation: Food is the source of energy and materials for growth and repair.

activities.prompt: A cow eats grass instead of making its own food. What is the cow?
options: An autotroph
A heterotroph
A bacterium
A chlorophyll
activities.explanation: Heterotrophs cannot make their own food, so they eat other living things.

activities.prompt: Green plants are autotrophs because they make their own food.
activities.explanation: Well done! Autotrophs use simple materials like carbon dioxide and water to make food.

activities.prompt: The green colouring in leaves that absorbs light is called ______.
activities.hint: It starts with 'chlor' and it is green.
activities.explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy during photosynthesis. Great job!

activities.prompt: Match each word with what it means.
activities.explanation: These four words are the keys to this lesson. You matched them all!

activities.prompt: A heterotroph eats complex food. What helps to break it into simpler substances?
options: Chlorophyll
Starch
Enzymes
Sunlight
activities.explanation: Enzymes are bio-catalysts that break down complex substances into simpler ones.

activities.prompt: A pot of green algae is kept in a dark cupboard for many days. It gets water and air. It slowly dies. Why?
options: It could not absorb light energy to make its food
It could not break down complex food with enzymes
It could not get enough water from the soil
It could not store starch in its green cells

why.It could not break down complex food wit: This mixes it up with heterotrophs, which break down complex food; algae make food instead.
why.It could not get enough water from the s: The pot was watered, so water was not the missing thing.
why.It could not store starch in its green c: Starch storage happens after food is made; the real problem was making food at all.

activities.explanation: Right. Algae are autotrophs, and without light chlorophyll cannot absorb energy to make food.

activities.prompt: Riya says a mushroom growing on dead wood is a green plant. Her friend says it is not. Who is right and why?
options: Riya, because it grows from simple things like water
Riya, because it makes food using sunlight
The friend, because it feeds on complex dead matter
The friend, because it needs enzymes to make starch

why.Riya, because it grows from simple thing: Autotrophs use carbon dioxide and water, but a mushroom takes complex food, not simple things.
why.Riya, because it makes food using sunlig: Mushrooms are not green and cannot make food from sunlight like plants do.
why.The friend, because it needs enzymes to: Enzymes break down food in heterotrophs; they are not used to make starch in plants.

activities.explanation: Right. It breaks down complex substances, so it is a heterotroph, not a green plant.

activities.prompt: Two identical green pots get sunlight and water. One pot also gets extra carbon dioxide. After some weeks, which pot has more stored starch?
options: The pot with extra carbon dioxide, it made more food
Both pots, because water alone makes all the starch
The normal pot, because extra gas blocks the sunlight
Neither pot, because starch comes only from the soil

why.Both pots, because water alone makes all: Carbon dioxide is also needed to make carbohydrates, so the pots will not be the same.
why.The normal pot, because extra gas blocks: Extra carbon dioxide does not block light; light and gas are both used together.
why.Neither pot, because starch comes only f: Starch is made inside the plant from carbon dioxide and water, not taken from soil.

activities.explanation: Right. More carbon dioxide means more raw material, so more food is made and stored as starch.

activities.prompt: A student says: 'A lion is a heterotroph, so it does not depend on plants at all.' What is the flaw?
options: Lions are autotrophs, so they make their own food
The lion's prey ate plants, so plants feed it indirectly
Lions use enzymes to make food from carbon dioxide
Lions store starch, so they need green leaves daily

why.Lions are autotrophs, so they make their: Lions cannot make food from carbon dioxide and water; that mistake flips the two groups.
why.Lions use enzymes to make food from carb: Enzymes break down complex food; they do not make food from carbon dioxide.
why.Lions store starch, so they need green l: Starch is the energy reserve of plants, not of lions.

activities.explanation: Right. Heterotrophs depend on autotrophs directly or indirectly, here through the prey.

activities.prompt: A boy covers one leaf of a green plant with thick black paper. Both leaves get water and air. After days, the covered leaf is weak. Why?
options: The paper stopped chlorophyll from absorbing light energy
The paper stopped enzymes from breaking down its food
The paper stopped water from reaching the leaf veins
The paper stopped starch from leaving the green cells

why.The paper stopped enzymes from breaking: Enzymes break down complex food in heterotrophs; the leaf makes its own food instead.
why.The paper stopped water from reaching th: The plant still got water; the covered leaf was blocked from light, not water.
why.The paper stopped starch from leaving th: Starch storage is not the first step; without light, food cannot be made at all.

activities.explanation: Right. No light reached the leaf, so chlorophyll could not absorb energy to make food.

activities.prompt: A girl wants to test if light is needed for photosynthesis. She has two similar green plants. Which is the fair test?
options: Give one plant light and water, the other light and no water
Give one plant light and water, the other darkness and water
Give one plant darkness and no water, the other light and no water
Give both plants darkness and water, then check their starch

why.Give one plant light and water, the othe: This changes two things, light and water, so we cannot tell which one caused the result.
why.Give one plant darkness and no water, th: This changes two things as well, and neither plant gets water, so the test is unfair.
why.Give both plants darkness and water, the: With no light on either plant, there is nothing to compare, so no test happens.

activities.explanation: Right. Only light is different, so any change in food made must be due to light.

lessons.sceneCaption: Sunlight on a green leaf (India)

lessons.title: Heterotrophic Nutrition and Human Digestion

activities.prompt: What really happens to the sandwich you eat, step by step?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different Ways of Taking In Food
activities.body: Living things get food in different ways, depending on what food is around. Some organisms break down food outside their bodies and then absorb it. Amoeba takes in food using tiny finger-like extensions of its cell surface. Humans digest food inside a long tube called the alimentary canal. It runs from the mouth all the way to the anus.
keyPoints: The form of nutrition depends on the type and availability of food.
Some organisms digest food outside the body and then absorb it.
Amoeba uses finger-like extensions of its cell surface to take in food.
The alimentary canal is a long tube from mouth to anus.
activities.explanation: Every living thing has its own clever way of getting food.

activities.prompt: Two rubber tubes carry sugared water. One tube is smooth inside. The other has many tiny folds inside, like villi. Which tube takes up more sugar, and why?
steps: Digested food can only pass in through the inner surface of the gut.
Folds make the same tube have much more inner surface than a smooth one.
More surface means more places where sugar can pass through at once.
So the folded tube absorbs more sugar, just like villi do in the small intestine.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Inside the Stomach and Small Intestine
activities.body: When food enters your stomach, the stomach expands to hold it. Gastric glands in its wall release hydrochloric acid, pepsin and mucus. The acid makes an acidic medium so pepsin can work. Next, food reaches the small intestine, where carbohydrates, proteins and fats are completely digested. Tiny villi increase the surface area, so absorption happens quickly.
keyPoints: The stomach expands when food enters it.
Gastric glands release hydrochloric acid, pepsin and mucus.
The small intestine completely digests carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
Villi increase the surface area for absorption.
activities.explanation: The stomach churns and the small intestine finishes the digesting job.

activities.prompt: How does Amoeba take in its food?
options: With a long tube from mouth to anus
With strong acid inside a stomach
With finger-like extensions of its cell surface
With green leaves that trap sunlight
activities.explanation: Amoeba is a single cell, so it uses temporary finger-like extensions to wrap around food. Well done!

activities.prompt: In your mouth, salivary amylase breaks down starch into simple ______.
activities.hint: Think of the sweet taste in ripe fruit.
activities.explanation: Salivary amylase in saliva turns starch into simple sugar right in your mouth.

activities.prompt: Some organisms break down food outside their bodies and then absorb it.
activities.explanation: Yes! Not every organism swallows food first. Some digest it outside and then soak it up.

activities.prompt: What do peristaltic movements do in your gut?
options: They push food forward along the gut
They make the stomach expand wider
They turn starch into simple sugar
They increase the surface area for absorption
activities.explanation: Peristaltic movements are waves in the gut wall that gently push food along its journey.

activities.prompt: Match each helper to its job in digestion.
pairs: Makes an acidic medium for pepsin
Increase the surface area for absorption
Push food forward along the gut
activities.explanation: Each part of the canal has its own special job. You matched them all!

activities.prompt: Put these parts in the order that food travels through the alimentary canal.
items: Mouth
Stomach
Small intestine
Large intestine
activities.explanation: Food starts at the mouth, is digested fully in the small intestine, and unabsorbed food is sent into the large intestine.

activities.prompt: An amoeba is a tiny blob with no mouth. It floats near a food particle. It must take the food inside. How will it do this?
options: It wraps finger-like parts of its surface around the food.
It opens a fixed mouth hole and sucks the food in.
It waits until the food dissolves into its body water.
It sends acid out to melt the food into pieces.

why.It opens a fixed mouth hole and sucks th: Wrong: thinks every eater must have a fixed mouth like us.
why.It waits until the food dissolves into i: Wrong: confuses this with digesting food outside the body.
why.It sends acid out to melt the food into: Wrong: thinks acid outside the cell is how amoeba feeds.

activities.explanation: Right: it uses temporary finger-like extensions of the cell surface.

activities.prompt: Mould grows on a piece of bread. It is too small to eat big pieces. It gives out juices onto the bread first. Why does it do this?
options: So the bread breaks down outside and can then be soaked in.
So the bread becomes soft and easier to sit on.
So the mould can grow bigger and look stronger.
So the bread stays fresh for a longer time.

why.So the bread becomes soft and easier to: Wrong: thinks softness is the goal, not taking food in.
why.So the mould can grow bigger and look st: Wrong: thinks the juices are for growth, not for digesting.
why.So the bread stays fresh for a longer ti: Wrong: thinks the mould is helping the bread, not feeding on it.

activities.explanation: Right: it breaks down food outside the body and then absorbs it.

activities.prompt: Ravi chews plain bread for a long time. It slowly begins to taste sweet. Nothing sweet was added. Why does it taste sweet?
options: Saliva has amylase that turns bread starch into sugar.
Chewing presses the sweet parts to the tongue.
The bread changes into sugar when it touches air.
His tongue makes sugar when he chews for long.

why.Chewing presses the sweet parts to the t: Wrong: thinks sweetness was already hidden inside the bread.
why.The bread changes into sugar when it tou: Wrong: blames air instead of the saliva acting on starch.
why.His tongue makes sugar when he chews for: Wrong: thinks the tongue itself makes sugar during chewing.

activities.explanation: Right: salivary amylase breaks down starch into simple sugar.

activities.prompt: Meera eats her dinner lying with her head lower than her stomach. The food still reaches her stomach. Why?
options: The wall of the food pipe pushes food with wave-like movements.
Gravity pulls the food down even when she lies down.
The stomach pulls the food towards it like a magnet.
The food is light, so it floats down the pipe.

why.Gravity pulls the food down even when sh: Wrong: thinks gravity alone moves food, so it should fail here.
why.The stomach pulls the food towards it li: Wrong: imagines the stomach pulling like a magnet.
why.The food is light, so it floats down the: Wrong: thinks light food floats down on its own.

activities.explanation: Right: peristaltic movements push food forward along the gut.

activities.prompt: A medicine makes the stomach less acidic for some hours. Now pepsin works very slowly there. Why does pepsin slow down?
options: Pepsin needs the acidic medium to act on food.
Pepsin gets washed away by the extra water.
Pepsin turns into mucus when acid becomes less.
Pepsin only works when the stomach is empty.

why.Pepsin gets washed away by the extra wat: Wrong: thinks the medicine adds water that washes pepsin out.
why.Pepsin turns into mucus when acid become: Wrong: thinks pepsin and mucus change into each other.
why.Pepsin only works when the stomach is em: Wrong: thinks fullness, not acidity, controls pepsin.

activities.explanation: Right: hydrochloric acid makes the acidic medium pepsin needs.

lessons.sceneAlt: A labelled diagram of the human digestive tract, the alimentary canal, showing the organs from mouth to anus.
lessons.sceneCaption: The gastrointestinal tract, also called the digestive tract or alimentary canal, digests food to extract energy and nutrients.

lessons.title: Respiration

activities.prompt: Where does the energy in your food actually come from?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Your Cells Get Energy
activities.body: The food you eat travels to your cells. There, it is used to give you energy. Glucose, a sugar from food, is broken down. When oxygen is present, glucose breaks fully into carbon dioxide and water. This releases lots of energy. The energy is stored as ATP, the energy currency of the cell. Your body spends ATP to do everything, like running and thinking.
keyPoints: Food is broken down in cells to release energy.
With oxygen, glucose breaks into carbon dioxide and water.
ATP is the energy currency for most cellular processes.
activities.explanation: Respiration is how food turns into energy inside your cells.

activities.prompt: Riya runs fast to catch her school bus. After sitting down, her legs ache and she breathes heavily for a while. Why do her legs ache?
steps: Running fast needs lots of energy, so her muscles work very hard.
Her muscles could not get enough oxygen during the fast run.
Without enough oxygen, pyruvate in her muscles turns into lactic acid.
So the lactic acid built up in her legs is why they ache.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Your cell needs energy to work. Which substance is called the energy currency of the cell?
options: Glucose
ATP
Pyruvate
Lactic acid
activities.explanation: ATP stores and gives out energy for most cellular processes. Well done!

activities.prompt: The first step of respiration breaks glucose into ______ in the cytoplasm.
activities.hint: It is the substance named in this lesson that comes after glucose.
activities.explanation: Glucose is first split into pyruvate in the cytoplasm. Great job!

activities.prompt: Match each place or living thing with what happens there.
activities.explanation: Each part of the body, and each organism, handles respiration in its own way.

activities.prompt: Two cells break the same amount of glucose. One uses oxygen. One does not. Which cell gets more energy?
options: The cell using oxygen
The cell without oxygen
Both get the same energy
Neither gets any energy
activities.explanation: Aerobic respiration releases much more energy than anaerobic respiration. Oxygen helps break glucose fully.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of aerobic respiration in the correct order.
items: Glucose breaks into pyruvate in the cytoplasm
Pyruvate breaks into carbon dioxide and water using oxygen
The released energy is stored as ATP
activities.explanation: First glucose splits into pyruvate, then oxygen finishes the job, and ATP stores the energy.

activities.prompt: You run a fast race. Your leg muscles do not get enough oxygen. What happens to the pyruvate in them?
options: It turns into lactic acid
It turns into ethanol
It turns into glucose
It stays the same
activities.explanation: When muscles lack oxygen, pyruvate changes into lactic acid. That is why legs can ache after hard running!

activities.prompt: A baker makes bread using yeast. The dough is kept in a closed box. The dough slowly rises and smells a little like beer. What is happening inside the dough?
options: Yeast is breaking glucose without oxygen, making ethanol and carbon dioxide
Yeast is breaking glucose with oxygen, making carbon dioxide and water
Yeast is turning lactic acid into pyruvate, so the dough rises
Yeast is turning ethanol into glucose, so bubbles fill the dough

why.Yeast is breaking glucose with oxygen, m: This mixes up anaerobic yeast fermentation with aerobic respiration, which needs oxygen.
why.Yeast is turning lactic acid into pyruva: This confuses yeast with muscles; yeast makes ethanol, not lactic acid.
why.Yeast is turning ethanol into glucose, s: This reverses the process; yeast makes ethanol from glucose, not glucose from ethanol.

activities.explanation: Right: yeast in a closed box has no oxygen, so it does fermentation, making ethanol and carbon dioxide.

activities.prompt: A student says: 'Anaerobic respiration is better than aerobic respiration because it works without oxygen.' What is the flaw in this claim?
options: Anaerobic respiration breaks glucose fully, so it needs no oxygen at all
Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy, so it is not better
Anaerobic respiration makes more pyruvate, so it gives more energy
Anaerobic respiration happens in the cytoplasm, so it gives more energy

why.Anaerobic respiration breaks glucose ful: Wrong: anaerobic respiration does not break glucose fully; that is the aerobic way.
why.Anaerobic respiration makes more pyruvat: Pyruvate is made in the first step either way; it does not give extra energy.
why.Anaerobic respiration happens in the cyt: Where it happens does not decide the energy; the oxygen use does.

activities.explanation: Right: the claim forgets that aerobic respiration releases much more energy.

activities.prompt: A cell needs energy all day. A student claims: 'The cell can store ATP made at night and use it next week.' Why is this claim wrong?
options: ATP is used up by cellular processes as they happen, so it cannot be stored long
ATP turns into lactic acid without oxygen, so it cannot last in cells
ATP needs alveoli to work, so it cannot be used deep inside cells
ATP breaks glucose into pyruvate, so it gets used up in the cytoplasm

why.ATP turns into lactic acid without oxyge: Lactic acid comes from pyruvate in muscles, not from stored ATP.
why.ATP needs alveoli to work, so it cannot: Alveoli are for gas exchange in lungs; ATP works inside all cells.
why.ATP breaks glucose into pyruvate, so it: Glucose breaks into pyruvate; ATP does not break glucose itself.

activities.explanation: Right: ATP is the energy currency spent by cellular processes as they happen.

lessons.sceneAlt: A simple diagram showing the formula for cellular respiration with glucose and oxygen.
lessons.sceneCaption: Simple formula for cellular respiration, showing how glucose and oxygen produce energy.

lessons.title: Transport in Human Beings

activities.prompt: How does food you eat reach your toes?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Your Body's Delivery Service
activities.body: Think of blood as a delivery van moving through your body. It carries food, oxygen and waste materials to where they are needed. The pale liquid part, called plasma, carries food, carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes in dissolved form. Oxygen travels in a special way: red blood corpuscles pick it up and deliver it, just like a dedicated courier.
keyPoints: Blood transports food, oxygen and waste materials.
Plasma carries food, carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes in dissolved form.
Red blood corpuscles carry oxygen.
activities.explanation: Blood is the body's transport system, and each part has its own job.

activities.prompt: After a running race, Priya's legs hurt and feel heavy. Her friend says her blood is 'tired'. Priya wonders: what is her blood actually carrying to her legs, and what is it taking away?
steps: Running muscles work hard, so they need a lot of oxygen and food to keep going.
Blood is the delivery service of the body, so it must carry oxygen and food to the leg muscles.
Hard-working muscles also make waste, so the same blood must carry the waste away.
So Priya's blood is not tired; it is busy delivering oxygen and food and removing waste from her legs.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Blood moves around your body like a delivery van. What does it carry?
options: Food, oxygen and waste materials
Only water and salt
Only oxygen
Only waste materials
activities.explanation: Blood is a busy carrier: it takes food and oxygen to cells and carries waste away. Well done if you picked the full list!

activities.prompt: Arteries carry blood ______ from the heart.
activities.hint: Think of the direction: does blood leave the heart or arrive at it?
activities.explanation: Arteries are the exit roads. They carry blood away from the heart to the rest of the body.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the heart with its job.
pairs: Receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs
Pumps blood out to the body
activities.explanation: Each chamber has its own job: receive from the lungs, pump to the body, or pump to the lungs. You matched them all!

activities.prompt: Put the journey of oxygen-rich blood in the correct order.
items: Oxygen-rich blood comes from the lungs
It enters the left atrium
The left ventricle pumps the blood
The blood travels out to the body
activities.explanation: Blood arrives from the lungs at the left atrium, is pumped by the left ventricle, and then travels out to the body. You traced the whole route!

activities.prompt: Capillaries are tiny vessels with very thin walls. Why are they built this way?
options: So materials can be exchanged through them easily
So blood can flow backwards through them
So they can hold more blood than arteries
So they can pump blood to the lungs
activities.explanation: Capillaries are only one cell thick, so materials can pass through them easily. That is where the exchange happens!

activities.prompt: Blood is flowing inside a thin tube in a hospital. The nurse says this blood is moving away from the heart. Which vessel is inside the tube?
options: A vein, because veins hold the most blood
An artery, because arteries carry blood away from the heart
A capillary, because capillaries are the thinnest vessels
A valve, because valves control where blood goes

why.A vein, because veins hold the most bloo: Veins bring blood back to the heart, the opposite direction.
why.A capillary, because capillaries are the: Being thin tells us nothing about the direction of flow.
why.A valve, because valves control where bl: Valves are flaps inside vessels, not vessels carrying blood.

activities.explanation: Right: arteries carry blood away from the heart.

activities.prompt: A student says, 'The heart pushes blood forward strongly, so valves are not needed.' What is wrong with this claim?
options: The heart is too weak to push blood without valves
Valves make the blood pick up more oxygen
Without valves, blood could flow backwards
Valves are needed to make new blood cells

why.The heart is too weak to push blood with: The problem is direction of flow, not strength of the heart.
why.Valves make the blood pick up more oxyge: Valves control flow direction; they do not add oxygen.
why.Valves are needed to make new blood cell: Valves have nothing to do with making blood cells.

activities.explanation: Right: valves stop blood from flowing backwards.

activities.prompt: Food and oxygen in the blood must reach the cells of your toes. The blood must also collect wastes from them. At which vessels does this exchange happen?
options: Arteries, because they carry blood away from the heart
Veins, because they carry blood back to the heart
Capillaries, because their walls are one cell thick
The heart chambers, because blood is pumped from there

why.Arteries, because they carry blood away: Arteries just carry blood away; exchange is not their job.
why.Veins, because they carry blood back to: Veins just carry blood back; exchange is not their job.
why.The heart chambers, because blood is pum: The heart pumps blood; exchange happens far from it.

activities.explanation: Right: capillaries are one cell thick, so materials are exchanged there.

lessons.sceneCaption: Diagram of the human circulatory system, showing how blood travels around the body.

lessons.title: Transport in Plants and Excretion

activities.prompt: How does a tree drink water without a mouth?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Plants Move Things, How Bodies Clean Up
activities.body: Plants pull water and minerals from the soil through their roots. Two tubes carry things inside a plant. Xylem carries water and minerals upwards. Phloem carries food made in the leaves to other parts. Plants do not need much energy, so slow transport is fine for them. In your body, kidneys clean the blood. They filter out harmful wastes and make urine.
keyPoints: Roots take in water and minerals from the soil.
Xylem carries water and minerals; phloem carries food.
Kidneys filter waste from blood and make urine.
activities.explanation: Plants use slow tubes to move water and food, while kidneys clean your blood.

activities.prompt: A girl waters a plant near its roots. How does the water reach the leaves high up, when the plant never moves or pumps anything?
steps: The roots touch the wet soil, so they can soak up the water and minerals.
The plant does not run or jump, so it needs very little energy each day.
Because its energy needs are low, a slow transport system is enough for it.
So the xylem slowly carries the water and minerals upward to the leaves.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which tube carries water and minerals from the soil inside a plant?
options: Xylem
Phloem
Nephron
Root hair
activities.explanation: Xylem is the tube that moves water and minerals taken from the soil. Well done!

activities.prompt: A plant's ______ absorb substances because they touch the soil.
activities.hint: This part of the plant grows underground.
activities.explanation: Roots are in contact with the soil, so they can take in what the plant needs.

activities.prompt: What is transpiration in a plant?
options: Loss of water vapour from aerial parts
Transport of food from the leaves
Filtering of waste from the blood
activities.explanation: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant.

activities.prompt: Match each part with its job.
activities.explanation: Each part has its own special job in transport or cleaning the body.

activities.prompt: Put the journey of water through a plant in the correct order.
items: Water and minerals are in the soil
Roots absorb the water
Xylem carries the water upwards
Water reaches the leaves
activities.explanation: Water starts in the soil, is soaked up by roots, then travels up the xylem to the leaves.

activities.prompt: Excretion means removing harmful metabolic wastes from the body. Which part does the filtering to make urine?
options: The kidneys, using nephrons as filter units
The phloem, using xylem as filter units
The roots, using soil as a filter
activities.explanation: Kidneys filter waste from the blood to make urine, and the nephron is their filtration unit.

activities.prompt: Ravi puts a plant in a dry pot with no soil touching the roots. What will happen to the water and minerals the plant needs?
options: The roots will still take them in from the air around.
The roots cannot take them in without touching wet soil.
The leaves will make the water and minerals themselves.
The xylem will pull them in from the dry air.

why.The roots will still take them in from t: Thinks roots can absorb from anywhere, but they need soil contact.
why.The leaves will make the water and miner: Thinks leaves make everything, but leaves make food, not minerals.
why.The xylem will pull them in from the dry: Thinks xylem pulls from air, but xylem only moves what roots take in.

activities.explanation: Right: roots absorb substances only because they touch the soil.

activities.prompt: On a hot day, water vapour leaves a plant through its leaves. What good does this loss do for the water in the roots?
options: It helps pull water and minerals upward from the roots.
It pushes water and minerals downward to the roots.
It stops the roots from taking in any more water.
It turns the minerals in the roots into food.

why.It pushes water and minerals downward to: Reverses the direction, thinking loss pushes things down.
why.It stops the roots from taking in any mo: Thinks losing water blocks the roots, but it actually helps flow.
why.It turns the minerals in the roots into: Confuses transport with food-making in the leaves.

activities.explanation: Right: transpiration helps water and minerals move up from the roots.

activities.prompt: A leaf makes sugar-rich food on a sunny day. The roots cannot make food. Which path carries the food to the roots?
options: The xylem carries the food down to the roots.
The phloem carries the food down to the roots.
The roots pull the food up from the soil instead.
The food stays in the leaf and never moves at all.

why.The xylem carries the food down to the r: Mixes up the two tubes, thinking xylem carries food.
why.The roots pull the food up from the soil: Thinks roots take in food, but they take in water and minerals.
why.The food stays in the leaf and never mov: Thinks food stays put, but plants move it to all parts.

activities.explanation: Right: phloem carries food made in leaves to other parts.

activities.prompt: A student says the xylem carries food from leaves to roots. Her test shows water going up instead. What is wrong with her claim?
options: Nothing is wrong, xylem carries food in both directions.
Xylem carries water and minerals, not food from leaves.
Xylem carries food only at night when there is no sun.
The test was wrong, water really does carry food up.

why.Nothing is wrong, xylem carries food in: Thinks one tube does both jobs, but the tubes have different jobs.
why.Xylem carries food only at night when th: Invents a day-and-night rule that is not how plants work.
why.The test was wrong, water really does ca: Blames the test instead of fixing the wrong idea about xylem.

activities.explanation: Right: xylem moves water and minerals from the soil, not food.

activities.prompt: A boy says his sweat on a hot day is like a plant losing water vapour. He also says his skin then works like kidneys. Is he right about the kidneys?
options: Yes, because both skin and kidneys remove water from the body.
Yes, because sweat and urine are exactly the same liquid.
No, because kidneys filter waste from blood to make urine.
No, because the body has no way to remove wastes at all.

why.Yes, because both skin and kidneys remov: Thinks removing water is enough, but kidneys have a special job.
why.Yes, because sweat and urine are exactly: Thinks sweat and urine are the same, which is a wrong guess.
why.No, because the body has no way to remov: Goes too far, saying the body removes nothing, which is wrong.

activities.explanation: Right: kidneys filter blood wastes to make urine, a different job.

lessons.sceneCaption: Diagram showing water and minerals transported in xylem, and organic nutrients transported separately in phloem.
