activities.prompt: When you smell fresh mango pickle, ______ receptors in your nose detect the smell.
activities.hint: These receptors are found in sense organs and their name starts with 'o'.
activities.explanation: Olfactory receptors detect smell, while gustatory receptors detect taste.

activities.prompt: Match each hormone to what it does or where it comes from.
activities.explanation: Each hormone has its own gland and job. Together they form the endocrine system.

activities.prompt: Put the journey of a nerve impulse through a neuron in the correct order.
items: The impulse starts at the dendritic tip
It travels to the cell body
It moves along the axon
Chemicals are released at the end of the axon
activities.explanation: A chemical reaction at the tip starts the electrical impulse. It flows dendrite to cell body to axon, then chemicals are released.

activities.prompt: You touch a chhui-mui plant and its leaves fold up. Later, you watch a seedling bend as it grows. How are these two movements different?
options: Both movements are caused by growth
The leaf movement is quick with no growth; the seedling movement is caused by growth
The leaf movement is caused by growth; the seedling movement has no growth
Neither movement has anything to do with growth
activities.explanation: The sensitive plant's leaf movement is quick and has no growth. The seedling's directional movement is caused by growth.

activities.prompt: Blood pressure, salivation and vomiting are controlled by the ______.

activities.explanation: The medulla controls involuntary actions like blood pressure, salivation and vomiting.

activities.prompt: You are in a scary situation and your body prepares to fight or run away. What does adrenaline do to help?
options: It makes the heart beat faster and diverts blood to skeletal muscles
It sends more blood to the digestive system and skin
It slows the heart so you can stay calm and still
It makes the muscle cells grow longer like a shoot tip
activities.explanation: Adrenaline makes the heart beat faster. Blood to the digestive system and skin is reduced and diverted to skeletal muscles.

activities.prompt: Inside its bony box, the brain sits in a fluid-filled balloon that absorbs shocks.
activities.explanation: The brain sits inside a bony box, and the fluid-filled balloon inside protects it from shocks.

chapters.title: How do Organisms Reproduce?
chapters.summary: In this chapter: why organisms reproduce and copy dna; variation and survival; fission and fragmentation; regeneration, budding, vegetative propagation and spores.

lessons.title: Why Organisms Reproduce and Copy DNA

activities.prompt: Why do living things bother to reproduce at all?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why do living things reproduce?
activities.body: You eat, breathe and remove waste to stay alive. These life processes keep one organism going, but reproduction is not needed for that. So why do organisms reproduce? At its most basic, reproduction makes copies of the blueprints of body design. That blueprint is DNA, found inside the cell nucleus. A copy of the DNA is made, new cell equipment is built, and one cell divides into two.
keyPoints: Reproduction is not needed to keep one individual alive.
Reproduction makes copies of the body design blueprints.
DNA in the nucleus holds the information for inheritance.
A DNA copy is made, then the cell divides into two cells.
activities.explanation: Reproduction passes body designs to the next generation, one DNA copy at a time.

activities.prompt: A puppy grows up looking just like its mother. Why does it look so similar, when the puppy is a brand new living thing?
steps: The puppy is new, so its body was built from a set of instructions, not from old body parts.
Similar body designs need similar blueprints, so the puppy must have got a copy of the mother's blueprint.
Reproduction at its most basic level makes copies of the blueprints of body design, so copying happened when the puppy began.
So the puppy looks like its mother because reproduction copied the blueprint of body design before the puppy's body was built.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which of these is NOT needed to keep one individual organism alive?
options: Nutrition
Reproduction
Respiration
Excretion
activities.explanation: Nutrition, respiration and excretion keep you alive. Reproduction helps the species, not one body.

activities.prompt: A basic event in reproduction is the creation of a DNA ______.
activities.hint: Think of what the blueprint makes first.
activities.explanation: Yes! Copying the DNA is the most basic event in reproduction.

activities.prompt: Where in a cell do we find DNA?
options: In the cell wall
In the nucleus, on chromosomes
In the food vacuole
Outside the cell
activities.explanation: Chromosomes sit in the nucleus, and they carry the inheritance information in DNA.

activities.prompt: Match each item with what it does.
pairs: Found in the nucleus of a cell
Makes copies of body design blueprints
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each part has its own special job in reproduction.

activities.prompt: Put these steps of basic reproduction in the correct order.
items: A copy of the DNA is created
An additional cellular apparatus is created
The cell divides to give rise to two cells
activities.explanation: Spot on! First the DNA is copied, then new cell equipment is built, then the cell divides in two.

activities.prompt: The information in a cell's DNA changes. What happens next?
options: Different proteins are made and body designs change
The DNA copy stops being made
The cell divides into four cells at once
The nucleus moves out of the cell
activities.explanation: Changed information means different proteins, and different proteins alter the body design.

activities.prompt: A cat is fed well and stays healthy all its life. One day someone says the cat must reproduce to stay alive. What is wrong with this claim?
options: The cat will die soon because it has not reproduced yet
The cat can stay alive without reproducing, like it does now
The cat must reproduce only when it feels hungry
The cat will stop breathing if it does not reproduce

why.The cat will die soon because it has not: Wrong: staying alive depends on life processes, not on reproducing.
why.The cat must reproduce only when it feel: Wrong: food is for nutrition, not a signal to reproduce.
why.The cat will stop breathing if it does n: Wrong: breathing is a separate life process from reproducing.

activities.explanation: Right: reproduction is not needed to keep an individual organism alive.

activities.prompt: In a pond, tiny organisms appear in huge numbers after a few days. A student says they were always there but hidden. Another says they got noticed because they multiplied. Which explanation fits better?
options: They were hidden, because small things can never be seen first
They multiplied, because organisms are noticed when they reproduce in large numbers
They were hidden, because water hides everything living in it
They multiplied, because big numbers make organisms heavier to see

why.They were hidden, because small things c: Wrong: hiding does not explain why they suddenly appear everywhere.
why.They were hidden, because water hides ev: Wrong: water does not hide all living things all the time.
why.They multiplied, because big numbers mak: Wrong: numbers do not change how heavy or visible a thing is.

activities.explanation: Right: reproducing in large numbers is why organisms get noticed.

activities.prompt: Two birds of the same species have very similar beaks. A student says this happened by luck. What is the better reason?
options: Similar beaks happened by luck in each bird separately
Similar body designs need similar blueprints, so their blueprints match
The beaks became similar because both birds ate the same food
The beaks match because both birds fly at the same speed

why.Similar beaks happened by luck in each b: Wrong: luck does not explain why the same species matches so well.
why.The beaks became similar because both bi: Wrong: food does not change the blueprint of body design.
why.The beaks match because both birds fly a: Wrong: flying speed does not decide beak shape.

activities.explanation: Right: similar body designs need similar blueprints, so members of a species share them.

activities.prompt: A cell divides and gives rise to two cells. A student says each new cell got only half a blueprint. What should the student expect instead?
options: Each new cell got a full copy, because a DNA copy is made in reproduction
Each new cell got half a blueprint, so both cells will be weak
Each new cell got no blueprint, because the old one was used up
Each new cell shares one blueprint between them after dividing

why.Each new cell got half a blueprint, so b: Wrong: the blueprint is copied, not cut into halves.
why.Each new cell got no blueprint, because: Wrong: the blueprint is copied, not used up and destroyed.
why.Each new cell shares one blueprint betwe: Wrong: each cell gets its own copy, not one shared copy.

activities.explanation: Right: a basic event in reproduction is the creation of a DNA copy, so each cell gets a copy.

lessons.title: Variation and Survival

activities.prompt: Why do some individuals survive big changes while others don't?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why copies are not perfect
activities.body: When DNA is copied, the new copies are similar to the original but may not be exactly the same. This happens because no bio-chemical reaction is absolutely reliable. Most small changes do no harm, but a drastic change can make a copy unable to work, and that cell dies. The cells that survive are similar yet subtly different. This inbuilt tendency for variation during reproduction is the basis for evolution.
keyPoints: DNA copies are similar but may not be identical.
Some drastic variations kill the cell.
Variation during reproduction is the basis for evolution.
activities.explanation: Small copying changes are normal, and they help species over time.

activities.prompt: A bacteria colony lives in a warm pond. One summer, the pond water becomes very hot. Why might some bacteria survive when most die?
steps: When bacteria copy their DNA, the copies are similar but not always identical, so small changes appear.
Most copies still work well, but a few copies carry a change that helps in hot water.
When the pond suddenly becomes hot, bacteria with the old design cannot live there any more.
So the few bacteria with a helpful change survive, and this shows why variation saves the species.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: A new DNA copy is made. How does it compare with the original?
options: It is always exactly identical
It is similar but may not be identical
It is always completely different
activities.explanation: Copies are close to the original, but small changes can creep in.

activities.prompt: Each population fills a well-defined place in the ecosystem, called a ______.
activities.hint: It is the special place or role a population has in its surroundings.
activities.explanation: A niche is the well-defined place a population fills in the ecosystem.

activities.prompt: Which of these can cause a niche to change?
options: A change in water levels
A new name for the niche
Animals moving to a zoo
activities.explanation: Temperatures, water levels or meteorite hits can vary, and this changes the niche.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with what it means.
pairs: A well-defined place in the ecosystem
activities.explanation: Steady copying keeps body design safe, while variation gives a chance when the niche changes.

activities.prompt: Put these events in order, from first to last.
items: The niche changes, as temperatures or water levels vary
The niche is drastically altered, so the population could be wiped out
A few individuals with variations get some chance to survive
The species survives over time, helped by variation
activities.explanation: First the niche changes, then the population is at risk, then varied individuals survive, and over time the species is saved.

activities.prompt: Why is variation during reproduction so important in the long run?
options: It makes every cell die slowly
It is the basis for evolution
It stops niches from ever changing
activities.explanation: The inbuilt tendency for variation during reproduction is the basis for evolution, and it helps species survive over time.

activities.prompt: A student says: 'If copying were always perfect, variation would still happen anyway.' What is the flaw?
options: Perfect copying would still allow changes because cells want variety
Perfect copying would remove the main source of small differences
Perfect copying would make more variations because copies are faster
Perfect copying would push variations in from the outside world

why.Perfect copying would still allow change: Wrong: this thinks cells choose to vary; variation comes from imperfect copying, not choice.
why.Perfect copying would make more variatio: Wrong: this links speed to variation; speed of copying does not create differences.
why.Perfect copying would push variations in: Wrong: this says variation comes from outside; the source here is the copying itself.

activities.explanation: Right: small differences in copies come from copying not being perfectly reliable.

activities.prompt: A beetle population lives in one niche in a forest. A flood changes that niche drastically. Why might the species still survive?
options: A few beetles had variations that fit the new conditions
All beetles quickly change their design on purpose to fit
The flood makes every beetle copy its DNA more carefully
The forest niche stays exactly the same after a big flood

why.All beetles quickly change their design: Wrong: beetles cannot choose their design; survival depends on variations already present.
why.The flood makes every beetle copy its DN: Wrong: careful copying reduces variation, and the flood does not change how copying works.
why.The forest niche stays exactly the same: Wrong: the question says the niche changed drastically, so it cannot stay the same.

activities.explanation: Right: variation in a few individuals gives the species some chance to survive a big change.

activities.prompt: A student claims: 'Variation is bad for a species, so species would be safer without it.' What is the flaw?
options: Variation is bad only when the niche stays the same forever
Variation is the only thing that keeps body design the same
Variation gives some individuals a chance when niches change
Variation matters only for single cells, not for whole species

why.Variation is bad only when the niche sta: Wrong: niches rarely stay the same forever, so variation is needed, not bad.
why.Variation is the only thing that keeps b: Wrong: this mixes up variation with consistent copying, which keeps body design.
why.Variation matters only for single cells,: Wrong: variation helps the whole species over time, not just single cells.

activities.explanation: Right: when a niche changes, individuals with helpful variations can survive and save the species.

lessons.sceneAlt: A bacterium copying its DNA and dividing into two daughter cells, each with a complete copy of the genetic material.
lessons.sceneCaption: DNA replicates as a bacterium divides, giving each daughter cell a complete copy of the genetic material.

sceneCredit.text: XBio illustration – Bacterial Cell Division by explorebiology, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: explorebiology

lessons.title: Fission and Fragmentation

activities.prompt: How can a tiny creature split itself in two and become two?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Simple Ways to Make New Life
activities.body: How an organism reproduces depends on its body design. Tiny single-celled beings like bacteria and Amoeba simply split into two. This is called fission. Some, like Plasmodium, split into many cells at once. Flat green Spirogyra breaks into pieces, and each piece grows into a new plant. This is fragmentation. Simple body plans allow such simple methods.
keyPoints: The way an organism reproduces depends on its body design.
Fission: a single cell splits into two, or into many cells.
Fragmentation: a body breaks into pieces, and each piece grows into a new individual.
activities.explanation: Simple bodies can use simple ways to reproduce.

activities.prompt: A drop of pond water has many tiny Amoeba. A friend says each Amoeba must split the same way a flat chapati is cut, always down the middle in one fixed line. Is your friend right?
steps: Amoeba is a single cell, so its whole body design is just one blob with no fixed shape.
Because it has no fixed shape, it does not need one fixed line to divide along.
So it can split in any plane, not just one middle line like a chapati.
So your friend is wrong: Amoeba splits in any plane because its body has no fixed shape.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: In a tiny single-celled organism, what creates new individuals?
options: Growing flowers
Cell division or fission
Bud picking
activities.explanation: For single-celled organisms, cell division or fission makes new individuals.

activities.prompt: Plasmodium divides into many daughter cells. What is this called?
options: Multiple fission
Fragmentation
Budding
activities.explanation: When one cell splits into many daughter cells, it is multiple fission.

activities.prompt: When Spirogyra matures, it breaks up into smaller pieces called ______, and each one grows into a new individual.
activities.hint: Think of something breaking into parts.
activities.explanation: Spirogyra breaks into fragments, and each fragment grows into a new individual.

activities.prompt: Match each organism with its special way of reproducing.
activities.explanation: Each organism has its own simple method, suited to its body design.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of reproduction in Spirogyra in the correct order.
items: Spirogyra matures
It breaks up into smaller pieces
Each fragment grows into a new individual
activities.explanation: First it matures, then it breaks into fragments, then each fragment grows into a new individual.

activities.prompt: Why can simple reproductive methods still work in some multicellular organisms?
options: They have simple body organisation
They are very large in size
They live only in water
activities.explanation: Simple methods work when the body organisation is simple. Body design decides the method of reproduction.

activities.prompt: Amoeba and Plasmodium are both single-celled. Amoeba splits into two cells. Plasmodium splits into many cells at once. A student watches both under a microscope. What will the student see?
options: Both split into two cells each time
Both split into many cells each time
Amoeba makes two cells, Plasmodium makes many
Amoeba makes many cells, Plasmodium makes two

why.Both split into two cells each time: Thinks all single-celled organisms must divide in the same way.
why.Both split into many cells each time: Thinks one example of splitting applies to every organism.
why.Amoeba makes many cells, Plasmodium make: Swaps the two organisms and how each one divides.

activities.explanation: Right: Amoeba splits into two, but Plasmodium divides into many daughter cells.

activities.prompt: A thread-like water plant, Spirogyra, is cut into three small pieces by a fish. Each piece has healthy cells. What will most likely happen to the pieces?
options: All three pieces die because they were cut apart
Each piece grows into a new Spirogyra plant
The pieces join back into one single plant
Only the biggest piece survives and grows

why.All three pieces die because they were c: Thinks being cut always harms an organism badly.
why.The pieces join back into one single pla: Thinks broken pieces must always rejoin like a broken toy.
why.Only the biggest piece survives and grow: Thinks size decides survival, not the ability of fragments to grow.

activities.explanation: Right: fragments of Spirogyra grow into new individuals.

activities.prompt: A boy says: 'Every living thing can just split into two halves to make babies, like bacteria do.' His friend shows him a cow. Why does the cow not simply split into two calves?
options: Because cows are too big to split into halves
Because cows have a complex body, not a simple one
Because cows live on land and not in water
Because cows do not make babies at all

why.Because cows are too big to split into h: Thinks size is the reason, not body design.
why.Because cows live on land and not in wat: Brings in a wrong reason about where the animal lives.
why.Because cows do not make babies at all: Wrong fact; cows do reproduce, just not by splitting.

activities.explanation: Right: many multicellular organisms cannot divide cell-by-cell because their bodies are complex.

lessons.sceneAlt: A microscope image of yeast cells, the tiny single-celled organisms that reproduce by budding.
lessons.sceneCaption: Microscope view of yeast, the fungus that grows small buds which separate and grow into new individuals.

sceneCredit.creator: Nbnidhi

lessons.title: Regeneration, Budding, Vegetative Propagation and Spores

activities.prompt: Can a tiny piece of a broken animal grow into a whole new one?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: New Plants and Animals from Old Parts
activities.body: Some living things can grow a whole new body from a small piece. This is called regeneration, and special cells do this work. Hydra grows tiny buds that become new individuals. Roots, stems and leaves can grow into new plants too. Spores wear thick coats that keep them safe.
keyPoints: Regeneration means a body part grows into a new individual.
Hydra and Planaria can be cut into pieces, and each piece grows whole again.
Roots, stems and leaves can grow into new plants.
Spores have thick walls that protect them.
activities.explanation: Life finds clever ways to make more of itself, even from one small piece.

activities.prompt: A boy cuts a Planaria into two pieces by accident while washing it. He thinks both pieces will die. What will really happen, and why?
steps: The boy thinks a cut body part must die, because his own cut skin just heals.
But Planaria is an organism whose body parts can make new individuals.
Its specialised cells carry out regeneration, so each piece can rebuild the missing parts.
So both pieces will not die; each piece grows into a complete Planaria.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Planaria is cut into two pieces. What happens to each piece?
options: Each piece dies at once
Each piece grows into a complete organism
Each piece stays the same size forever
activities.explanation: Well done! Hydra and Planaria can be cut into pieces, and each piece grows into a complete organism.

activities.prompt: Hydra uses ______ cells for reproduction in budding.
activities.hint: Think of the word for cells that can rebuild and renew.
activities.explanation: Hydra uses regenerative cells to grow buds. Each bud can become a new Hydra.

activities.prompt: Match each living thing or plant with how it makes new ones.
activities.explanation: Each living thing has its own clever way of making new individuals. Great matching!

activities.prompt: A farmer grows plants by vegetative propagation instead of seeds. What good thing can she expect?
options: The plants will bear flowers and fruits earlier
The plants will grow taller leaves only
The plants will never need water
activities.explanation: Plants raised by vegetative propagation can bear flowers and fruits earlier than seed plants. A handy trick for farmers!

activities.prompt: Put the steps of budding in Hydra in the correct order.
items: Regenerative cells start a bud on Hydra
The bud develops into a tiny individual
The tiny individual grows fully mature
The mature bud detaches from Hydra
activities.explanation: First the bud forms, then it grows into a tiny individual, matures, and finally detaches. You traced the whole journey!

activities.prompt: A girl cuts a Planaria into three small pieces in water. Each piece has its specialised cells. What will happen to the pieces?
options: Each piece grows into a complete Planaria.
Only the piece with the head grows into a Planaria.
All three pieces stay alive as small incomplete worms.
All three pieces slowly die because they were cut.

why.Only the piece with the head grows into: Wrong: she thinks only the head part matters, but every piece can regenerate.
why.All three pieces stay alive as small inc: Wrong: she thinks pieces just stay as pieces, but they rebuild missing parts.
why.All three pieces slowly die because they: Wrong: she thinks cutting always kills, but these pieces can regenerate.

activities.explanation: Right: each piece grows into a complete organism by regeneration.

activities.prompt: A farmer wants mango fruits as early as possible. He can grow trees from seeds or by vegetative propagation. Which should he choose, and why?
options: Seeds, because seed plants grow much taller than other plants.
Vegetative propagation, because those plants bear fruits earlier.
Seeds, because seed plants need much less water to grow.
Vegetative propagation, because those plants make bigger leaves.

why.Seeds, because seed plants grow much tal: Wrong: he links seeds with height, but height is not the goal here.
why.Seeds, because seed plants need much les: Wrong: he links seeds with less water, but water is not the goal here.
why.Vegetative propagation, because those pl: Wrong: he links propagation with leaf size, but leaf size is not the goal.

activities.explanation: Right: vegetatively propagated plants bear flowers and fruits earlier.

activities.prompt: Grapes are grown by grafting, not from seeds. A boy says, 'So grape plants must give fruits later than grape plants grown from seeds.' What is the flaw in his claim?
options: Grafting is only used for plants that never give any fruits.
Grafting makes plants weaker, so they cannot make fruits at all.
Vegetatively grown plants can bear fruits earlier than seed plants.
Seed plants always give fruits earlier than any other plants.

why.Grafting is only used for plants that ne: Wrong: he thinks grafted plants make no fruits, but they do bear fruits.
why.Grafting makes plants weaker, so they ca: Wrong: he thinks grafting weakens plants, but that is not the flaw here.
why.Seed plants always give fruits earlier t: Wrong: he thinks seeds are always fastest, but vegetative plants are earlier.

activities.explanation: Right: vegetatively propagated plants bear flowers and fruits earlier than seed plants.

lessons.sceneAlt: An illustration of a freshwater hydra reproducing by budding, with a cloned offspring growing from its body.
lessons.sceneCaption: Hydra are fresh water invertebrates that can reproduce by budding, producing cloned offspring.

sceneCredit.text: Hydra Budding by SadiesBurrow, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: SadiesBurrow

lessons.title: Sexual Reproduction and Flowering Plants

activities.prompt: How does a tiny flower manage to create a whole new plant?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Parents, One New Plant
activities.body: Sexual reproduction needs two individuals. It mixes DNA from two different parents, so the young one is not an exact copy of either. Special cells called germ-cells carry only half the DNA. In flowering plants, the flower holds the reproductive parts: the stamens and the pistil. When germ-cells join, a new life begins.
keyPoints: Sexual reproduction needs two individuals.
It combines DNA from two different individuals.
Germ-cells carry half the DNA.
The flower holds the reproductive parts: stamens and pistil.
activities.explanation: Mixing DNA from two parents gives each new plant its own special set of features.

activities.prompt: Ravi cuts open an apple and finds seeds inside. He asks: how did this big juicy fruit grow from a small flower?
steps: First, pollen must land on the stigma, because that transfer is pollination.
The pollen's germ-cell fuses with the egg cell in the ovule, because that fusion is fertilisation.
Fertilisation makes a zygote, and the zygote divides to form an embryo inside the ovule.
Then the ovary grows fast and ripens, because the ovary is what becomes the fruit.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which parts of a flower take part in reproduction?
options: Petals and sepals
Stamens and pistil
Stem and leaves
Roots and buds
activities.explanation: Well done! The stamens and the pistil are the reproductive parts of a flower.

activities.prompt: Pollen moves from the stamen to the stigma. This step is called ______.
activities.hint: It starts with the letter P.
activities.explanation: Great! Moving pollen from stamen to stigma is called pollination.

activities.prompt: What does the ovary of a flower contain?
options: Ovules, each with an egg cell
Seeds, each with a fruit
Pollen, each with a grain
Petals, each with a colour
activities.explanation: Yes! The ovary holds ovules, and every ovule has an egg cell inside.

activities.prompt: Match each word with what it means.
pairs: Germ-cells fuse to form a zygote
Grows from the zygote in the ovule
activities.explanation: Lovely matching! You have linked each step with its meaning.

activities.prompt: Put these steps of a flower's story in the right order.
items: Pollen moves from stamen to stigma
Germ-cells fuse and form a zygote
The zygote divides and forms an embryo in the ovule
The ovary ripens and becomes a fruit
activities.explanation: Perfect order! Pollen first, then fertilisation, then the embryo, and finally the fruit.

activities.prompt: Why do germ-cells carry only half the DNA?
options: So two germ-cells can combine their DNA
So the cell can grow bigger
So the flower can make more pollen
So the fruit can ripen faster
activities.explanation: Exactly! Half from each parent adds up, so the new individual gets DNA from both.

activities.prompt: A germ-cell has half the DNA of a body cell. During fertilisation, two germ-cells fuse into one zygote. Why does the zygote have the full amount of DNA?
options: Each germ-cell brings half, so together they make the full amount
The zygote quickly copies DNA from the food around it
Each germ-cell doubles its DNA just before they fuse
Half the DNA is thrown away because it is not needed

why.The zygote quickly copies DNA from the f: Food gives energy, not DNA; DNA comes from the two germ-cells.
why.Each germ-cell doubles its DNA just befo: Germ-cells stay at half; they do not double before fusing.
why.Half the DNA is thrown away because it i: No DNA is thrown away; the two halves join to make the full set.

activities.explanation: Right: half plus half makes the full amount in the zygote.

activities.prompt: A boy says: 'The pollen grain itself grows into the fruit.' Pollen lands on the stigma. The ovary sits below it. What is wrong with his claim?
options: Pollen only carries germ-cells; the ovary is what ripens into the fruit
Pollen does become the fruit, but only when the sun is strong
The stigma grows into the fruit and the pollen is thrown away
Pollen becomes the fruit only if many grains land together

why.Pollen does become the fruit, but only w: Sunlight is not the reason; the fruit comes from the ovary, not the pollen.
why.The stigma grows into the fruit and the: The stigma receives pollen; it is the ovary that becomes the fruit.
why.Pollen becomes the fruit only if many gr: The number of grains does not matter; the fruit still comes from the ovary.

activities.explanation: Right: pollen's job is fertilisation; the ovary grows and ripens into the fruit.

activities.prompt: A girl has her mother's eyes and her father's smile. She grew from one zygote. Why does she look like both parents?
options: She copied the looks of the parent she lives with
Her body picked looks from the parent she likes more
The zygote got DNA from both parents when germ-cells fused
She looks like both because she eats the same food as them

why.She copied the looks of the parent she l: Living together cannot change DNA; DNA was fixed at fertilisation.
why.Her body picked looks from the parent sh: Liking someone does not change DNA; DNA came from both germ-cells.
why.She looks like both because she eats the: Food helps the body grow, but it does not give DNA from parents.

activities.explanation: Right: sexual reproduction combines DNA from two individuals in the zygote.

activities.prompt: A student cuts off all the stamens from one flower. The pistil is left alone. The flower is kept far from all other flowers. What will happen?
options: The pistil will make its own pollen and a fruit forms
The stamens grow back, so a fruit forms as usual
No fruit forms because no pollen reaches the stigma
The egg cell turns into pollen and a fruit forms

why.The pistil will make its own pollen and: The pistil receives pollen; it does not make pollen.
why.The stamens grow back, so a fruit forms: Cut stamens do not grow back in time for pollination.
why.The egg cell turns into pollen and a fru: Egg cells and pollen are different things; an egg cell cannot become pollen.

activities.explanation: Right: stamens make the pollen, so without them pollination cannot happen.

lessons.sceneAlt: A labelled cutaway drawing of a flower showing the ovary with ovules, the style, and the stamens.
lessons.sceneCaption: Longitudinal cut of a flower showing the ovary, ovules, style and stamens, the reproductive parts where egg cells form.

lessons.title: Human Reproduction and Reproductive Health

activities.prompt: How does a tiny cell grow into a baby inside the mother?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Humans Reproduce
activities.body: Humans use a sexual mode of reproduction. During adolescence, puberty begins. This is when reproductive tissues mature. Girls notice their breast size increasing. Boys grow thick hair on the face and their voices crack. Sperms form in the testes. Each month, one ovary releases an egg. The egg travels to the womb, where a baby can grow.
keyPoints: Humans use a sexual mode of reproduction.
Puberty is when reproductive tissues mature.
Sperms form in the testes; one egg is released each month.
activities.explanation: Puberty prepares the body so that reproduction can happen later in life.

activities.prompt: In which body part do sperms form?
options: Ovary
Testes
Womb
Oviduct
activities.explanation: Well done! Sperms form in the testes.

activities.prompt: The egg is carried from the ovary to the womb through the ______, also called the fallopian tube.
activities.hint: It starts with the letter 'o'.
activities.explanation: Great! The oviduct is the tube that carries the egg to the womb.

activities.prompt: Rahul has noticed new thick hair on his face. His voice cracks when he speaks. What is happening to him?
options: He is unwell and needs rest
He is going through puberty
He has grown too tall
He is losing his baby teeth
activities.explanation: These are normal puberty changes in boys as reproductive tissues mature.

activities.prompt: Match each body part or event with what it does.
pairs: Womb lining breaks and comes out
activities.explanation: Each part has its own special job in reproduction.

activities.prompt: Put the journey of the egg in the correct order.
items: An egg is released by one ovary
The egg travels through the oviduct
The fertilised egg divides and forms an embryo
The embryo settles in the lining of the uterus
activities.explanation: The egg travels from the ovary, through the oviduct, then grows in the womb.

activities.prompt: An embryo has settled in the lining of the uterus. What does the placenta do for the growing foetus?
options: It makes the voice crack
It releases one egg each month
It provides nutrition from the mother's blood
It carries the egg to the ovary
activities.explanation: The placenta feeds the growing foetus with nutrition from the mother's blood.

activities.prompt: A sperm and an egg meet inside the fallopian tube. The sperm comes from the testes. The egg comes from the ovary. What happens to the fertilised egg next?
options: It stays in the tube and grows into a foetus
It moves back into the ovary and waits
It divides, forms an embryo, and implants in the uterus
It breaks into pieces and leaves the body at once

why.It stays in the tube and grows into a fo: Wrong: the tube only carries the egg; the embryo grows in the uterus lining.
why.It moves back into the ovary and waits: Wrong: the egg travels one way, from the ovary towards the womb, never back.
why.It breaks into pieces and leaves the bod: Wrong: a fertilised egg does not break; an unfertilised one leaves with the lining.

activities.explanation: Right: the zygote divides into an embryo, which implants in the uterus lining.

activities.prompt: A baby grows inside its mother. The baby cannot eat food. The mother eats good food every day. How does the baby get food?
options: The baby drinks water that the mother drinks
The placenta passes nutrition from the mother's blood
The baby makes its own food inside the womb
The baby stores food before it entered the womb

why.The baby drinks water that the mother dr: Wrong: water has no nutrition; food reaches the baby through the blood, not by drinking.
why.The baby makes its own food inside the w: Wrong: a baby cannot make its own food; it depends on the mother.
why.The baby stores food before it entered t: Wrong: a baby cannot store months of food; it needs a steady supply.

activities.explanation: Right: the placenta connects the baby to the mother's blood and passes nutrition.

activities.prompt: Meera learns that one egg leaves an ovary each month. If no sperm meets the egg, the uterus lining is not needed. What happens to the lining then?
options: It stays and grows thicker every month
It turns into an egg for the next month
It breaks and comes out as menstruation
It hardens and stays inside forever

why.It stays and grows thicker every month: Wrong: without a fertilised egg, the body does not keep building the lining up.
why.It turns into an egg for the next month: Wrong: eggs come from the ovary, not from the uterus lining.
why.It hardens and stays inside forever: Wrong: the lining does not harden; it breaks and leaves the body.

activities.explanation: Right: menstruation is the monthly cycle when the lining breaks and comes out.

activities.prompt: A shop sells condoms, oral pills, and copper-T. A couple wants to avoid pregnancy. They ask which choice is a method of contraception. What should they pick?
options: Only the copper-T, because pills do not work
Any of the three, because all prevent pregnancy
Only condoms, because other methods do not exist
None of them, because nothing can prevent pregnancy

why.Only the copper-T, because pills do not: Wrong: oral pills are also a working contraception method.
why.Only condoms, because other methods do n: Wrong: pills and copper-T do exist as contraception methods too.
why.None of them, because nothing can preven: Wrong: contraception is possible; several methods are available.

activities.explanation: Right: condoms, oral pills, and copper-T are all listed contraception methods.

activities.prompt: A student claims: 'Sperms and eggs are made in the same place, so boys and girls work the same way.' Another student disagrees. What is the flaw in the claim?
options: Sperms form in testes, eggs form in ovaries
Sperms and eggs both form in the womb
Eggs form daily, sperms form once a year
Boys make eggs, girls make sperms after puberty

why.Sperms and eggs both form in the womb: Wrong: the womb holds a baby; it does not make sperms or eggs.
why.Eggs form daily, sperms form once a year: Wrong: one egg is released each month; sperms are not made once a year.
why.Boys make eggs, girls make sperms after: Wrong: boys never make eggs and girls never make sperms.

activities.explanation: Right: sperms form in the testes and eggs form in the ovaries, so the places differ.

lessons.sceneCaption: The earliest stages of human life, from a single fertilized oocyte to the blastocyst within five days.

activities.context: Aditi visits her grandmother's village pond. Last month the pond water looked clear, but now it is greenish and crowded with countless tiny living things. Her grandmother says the same tiny creatures appeared in the pond every year after the rains. Aditi also notices that a nearby family's three children all look remarkably alike, and she wonders how both observations could be connected to reproduction.
activities.prompt: Why did the tiny creatures in the pond become so noticeable within a few weeks?
options: Because they reproduce in large numbers, so their presence becomes easy to notice
Because they stopped reproducing and grew individually much bigger
Because they moved into the pond from the nearby soil one by one
Because they changed into a completely different species after the rains

why.Because they stopped reproducing and gre: Wrong: growing bigger without reproducing would not create huge numbers.
why.Because they moved into the pond from th: Wrong: gradual arrival from outside does not explain sudden crowding by reproduction.
why.Because they changed into a completely d: Wrong: changing species is not needed; the same creatures multiply.

activities.explanation: Correct: large numbers produced through reproduction make organisms noticeable.

activities.context: Aditi visits her grandmother's village pond. Last month the pond water looked clear, but now it is greenish and crowded with countless tiny living things. Her grandmother says the same tiny creatures appeared in the pond every year after the rains. Aditi also notices that a nearby family's three children all look remarkably alike, and she wonders how both observations could be connected to reproduction.
activities.prompt: The three children in the family look very much alike. What is the most likely reason for this?
options: They eat the same food, so their bodies take identical shapes
They belong to the same species, so their body designs follow similar blueprints
They exercise together, which makes their features match
They copied each other's habits, so their appearance became similar

why.They eat the same food, so their bodies: Wrong: food affects health, not the basic blueprint of body design.
why.They exercise together, which makes thei: Wrong: exercise cannot make unrelated features identical.
why.They copied each other's habits, so thei: Wrong: habits change behaviour, not inherited body design.

activities.explanation: Correct: members of one species share similar blueprints, so they look alike.

activities.context: Aditi visits her grandmother's village pond. Last month the pond water looked clear, but now it is greenish and crowded with countless tiny living things. Her grandmother says the same tiny creatures appeared in the pond every year after the rains. Aditi also notices that a nearby family's three children all look remarkably alike, and she wonders how both observations could be connected to reproduction.
activities.prompt: If the information for body design in these creatures got changed during copying, what would most likely happen next?
options: The creatures would immediately stop reproducing altogether
The creatures would make different proteins and show altered body designs
The creatures would keep exactly the same body design as before
The creatures would leave the pond and live on land

why.The creatures would immediately stop rep: Wrong: changed information does not stop reproduction itself.
why.The creatures would keep exactly the sam: Wrong: the whole point of changed information is that designs can differ.
why.The creatures would leave the pond and l: Wrong: nothing in the change of information forces a shift in habitat.

activities.explanation: Correct: changed information leads to different proteins and altered body designs.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): An organism can survive even if it does not reproduce.
Reason (R): Reproduction is not needed to keep an individual organism alive.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly states why the assertion is true.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): DNA copying must be accompanied by creation of an additional cellular apparatus.
Reason (R): A dividing cell gives rise to two cells, so each new cell needs its own cellular equipment.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Cell division into two cells explains why extra cellular apparatus is created.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Nutrition and respiration are more essential for an individual's survival than reproduction.
Reason (R): Reproduction produces large numbers of organisms that are easily noticed.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but being noticed in large numbers does not explain why reproduction is less essential for survival.

activities.prompt: Explain why organisms are noticed because of reproduction even though reproduction is not needed for an individual organism's survival.
activities.answer: An individual organism stays alive through life processes like nutrition, respiration and excretion, which are essential for its own survival. Reproduction is not one of these, so a single organism does not need it to keep living. However, reproduction produces organisms in large numbers, and it is these large numbers that make organisms easily noticed by us. So reproduction matters for the continued presence and visibility of a kind of organism, not for the life of one individual.
points: Names nutrition, respiration, excretion as essential life processes
States reproduction is not needed for individual survival
Links large numbers from reproduction to being noticed
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A shallow pond is home to a large population of tiny green organisms. Each time they reproduce, their DNA is copied, and the copying is usually consistent, so the body design features of the population stay stable. However, no bio-chemical reaction is absolutely reliable, so a few copies come out subtly different. One dry season, the water level of the pond falls sharply and the niche changes drastically.
activities.prompt: During reproduction, most daughter cells in the pond resemble the parents, but a few are subtly different. What is the most likely reason for this?
options: The DNA copies made during reproduction are similar but not always identical to the original
The daughter cells copy their DNA twice to correct all differences
The parent cells choose to produce different offspring on purpose
The water level change altered every cell's DNA in the same way

why.The daughter cells copy their DNA twice: Wrong: nothing in the process corrects all differences; copying is simply not absolutely reliable.
why.The parent cells choose to produce diffe: Wrong: cells do not choose their variations; variations arise during DNA copying.
why.The water level change altered every cel: Wrong: the water level change happened after reproduction and did not cause the copying differences.

activities.explanation: Correct: DNA copying is not perfectly reliable, so copies are similar but may not be identical.

activities.context: A shallow pond is home to a large population of tiny green organisms. Each time they reproduce, their DNA is copied, and the copying is usually consistent, so the body design features of the population stay stable. However, no bio-chemical reaction is absolutely reliable, so a few copies come out subtly different. One dry season, the water level of the pond falls sharply and the niche changes drastically.
activities.prompt: The water level drops drastically and most of the population is wiped out, but a few individuals survive. Why did those few survive?
options: They were subtly different from the others, and this variation gave them some chance of survival
They were exactly identical to every other individual in the population
They stopped reproducing, so their DNA stopped changing
They moved the pond's niche back to its original state

why.They were exactly identical to every oth: Wrong: if they were identical to all others, they would face the same fate as the rest.
why.They stopped reproducing, so their DNA s: Wrong: stopping reproduction does not protect them; survival came from their variation.
why.They moved the pond's niche back to its: Wrong: individuals cannot restore a niche; the niche changed because water levels varied.

activities.explanation: Correct: variations in a few individuals give some of them a chance to survive when the niche changes.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The inbuilt tendency for variation during reproduction is the basis for evolution.
Reason (R): DNA copying during reproduction produces copies that are similar but may not be identical to the original.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The slight differences in DNA copies create variations, and this inbuilt tendency for variation is what evolution is based on.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Reproduction is linked to the stability of populations of species.
Reason (R): Niches in an ecosystem can change because temperatures, water levels or meteorite hits can vary.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but niche change explains risk to populations, not why reproduction maintains their stability.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): If a population's niche is drastically altered, every individual in it will always survive.
Reason (R): Consistent DNA copying is important for maintaining body design features.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because drastic niche change could wipe out the population, while the reason about consistent DNA copying is true.

activities.prompt: How does consistent DNA copying help a species, and what could happen if the species had no variation at all?
activities.answer: Consistent DNA copying is important because it maintains the body design features that allow the population to occupy its well-defined niche in the ecosystem, and reproduction is linked to the stability of populations of species. However, no bio-chemical reaction is absolutely reliable, so copies are similar but subtly different, and this inbuilt tendency for variation is the basis for evolution. If a species had no variation at all, every individual would be identical. Then, if the niche changed drastically through altered temperatures, water levels or a meteorite hit, no individual would have any chance of surviving, and the whole population could be wiped out.
points: Consistent copying maintains body design features and the population's niche
Reproduction is linked to stability of populations of species
Copying is never perfectly reliable, so variation arises and is the basis for evolution
Without variation, a drastic niche change could wipe out the entire population
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a lab activity, Ravi prepares two wet slides. On the first slide he finds a single-celled organism, and he watches its body split into two equal halves. On the second slide he sees a green filament that has snapped into several short lengths after maturing. His teacher asks the class to predict what each slide will show if the samples are kept under observation for a few more days.
activities.prompt: What should Ravi expect to see on the first slide after a few days?
options: Small outgrowths separating from each cell and growing further
The two halves living independently as separate individuals
The short lengths from the other slide appearing on this slide too
One cell producing many daughter cells all at the same time

why.Small outgrowths separating from each ce: Buds separating and growing is how yeast reproduces, not what Ravi observed here.
why.The short lengths from the other slide a: Fragmentation belongs to the filament slide; the two slides show different organisms.
why.One cell producing many daughter cells a: Division into many daughter cells at once is a different mode of fission from splitting into two halves.

activities.explanation: Correct - when a unicellular organism splits into two equal halves, each half continues as a new individual.

activities.context: During a lab activity, Ravi prepares two wet slides. On the first slide he finds a single-celled organism, and he watches its body split into two equal halves. On the second slide he sees a green filament that has snapped into several short lengths after maturing. His teacher asks the class to predict what each slide will show if the samples are kept under observation for a few more days.
activities.prompt: What will most likely happen to the broken pieces on the second slide if Ravi keeps observing them?
options: Each piece will slowly die because it is no longer attached to the whole filament
Each piece will grow into a complete new individual
Each piece will put out buds that detach and grow
Each piece will divide into many daughter cells simultaneously

why.Each piece will slowly die because it is: Breaking up on maturation is a normal step, not a sign that the pieces are lost.
why.Each piece will put out buds that detach: Budding is not the method by which this filament produces new individuals.
why.Each piece will divide into many daughte: Many daughter cells at once describes multiple fission, not what happens to fragments.

activities.explanation: Correct - fragments of the filament grow into new individuals.

activities.context: During a lab activity, Ravi prepares two wet slides. On the first slide he finds a single-celled organism, and he watches its body split into two equal halves. On the second slide he sees a green filament that has snapped into several short lengths after maturing. His teacher asks the class to predict what each slide will show if the samples are kept under observation for a few more days.
activities.prompt: If Ravi later finds a slide on which one cell is producing many daughter cells at the same time, which organism is he most likely observing?
options: Amoeba
Spirogyra
Plasmodium
Yeast

why.Amoeba: Amoeba splits into two equal halves, not into many cells at once.
why.Spirogyra: Spirogyra is a filament that breaks into pieces; it is not seen as one cell forming many daughters.
why.Yeast: Yeast puts out buds that separate, rather than forming many daughter cells at once.

activities.explanation: Correct - Plasmodium divides into many daughter cells by multiple fission.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Amoeba can divide in any plane of its body.
Reason (R): The body design of Amoeba does not fix one particular plane along which it must split.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the reason correctly explains why any plane of splitting is possible.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Every multicellular organism can reproduce by simply dividing cell-by-cell into new individuals.
Reason (R): Many multicellular organisms have body designs that do not allow the whole body to divide cell-by-cell.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because many multicellular organisms cannot divide this way, while the reason itself is true.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: How do Organisms Reproduce?

activities.prompt: Which life process is NOT needed to keep one individual organism alive?
options: Nutrition
Respiration
Reproduction
Excretion
activities.explanation: Food, breathing and removing waste keep you alive. Reproduction keeps the species going, not one body.

activities.prompt: DNA copies are always exactly identical to the original.
activities.explanation: Copies are similar, but no reaction in the body is perfectly reliable. Small differences can creep in, and that is good news for the species.

activities.prompt: Plasmodium divides into many daughter cells during ______ fission.
activities.hint: The word means 'many'.
activities.explanation: Many bacteria and protozoa split into two, but Plasmodium splits into many cells at once.

activities.prompt: Match each organism with the way it reproduces.
activities.explanation: Each body design suits a different mode. Amoeba can split any way, but Spirogyra snaps into pieces that grow anew.

activities.prompt: A gardener grows roses by layering instead of from seeds. What can she expect?
options: The plants will never grow flowers
The plants will flower earlier than seed plants
The plants will flower later than seed plants
The plants cannot grow any roots
activities.explanation: Plants raised by vegetative propagation can bear flowers and fruits earlier than plants grown from seeds.

activities.prompt: Put these events in a flowering plant in the correct order.
items: Pollen is transferred from stamen to stigma
Germ-cells fuse to form a zygote
The zygote divides and forms an embryo
The ovary ripens to form a fruit
activities.explanation: First pollen lands on the stigma, then fertilisation makes a zygote, the zygote becomes an embryo, and finally the ovary swells into a fruit.

activities.prompt: A niche changes drastically, say a big shift in water level. Why does variation help the species?
options: Variation makes every individual identical
Variation stops niches from ever changing
A few varied individuals may survive the change
Variation removes all the old body designs
activities.explanation: If a niche is wiped out, identical copies would all be at risk. Variation gives some individuals a chance to survive.

activities.prompt: Regeneration is carried out by specialised cells.
activities.explanation: That is why Hydra and Planaria can regrow a whole body from a cut piece. Specialised cells do this clever work.

activities.prompt: During fertilisation, the fusion of germ-cells gives rise to a ______.
activities.hint: It is the very first cell of the new individual.
activities.explanation: When two germ-cells meet and fuse, a zygote is formed. It then divides to form an embryo.

activities.prompt: Match each part with its job in human reproduction.
pairs: carries the egg to the womb
activities.explanation: Each part has its own task, from making germ-cells to feeding the growing foetus.

chapters.title: Heredity
chapters.summary: In this chapter: accumulation of variation during reproduction; heredity and inherited traits; mendel's experiments with one trait; independent inheritance of two traits.

lessons.title: Accumulation of Variation during Reproduction

activities.prompt: Why do siblings look alike but never exactly the same?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why are you like your family, but not a copy?
activities.body: When living things reproduce, the new ones are similar to their parents. But they are not exact copies. Small changes, called variations, creep in every time. Inheritance keeps the basic body design the same, while tiny changes are added. Asexual reproduction makes very similar individuals. Sexual reproduction makes much more variety.
keyPoints: Reproduction makes new individuals similar to their parents.
Small changes called variations appear in every generation.
Inheritance keeps the basic body design, with subtle changes.
Sexual reproduction creates greater diversity than asexual reproduction.
activities.explanation: You inherit a body design from your parents, plus a few small changes of your own.

activities.prompt: A sugarcane field looks like rows of twins. But no two people in your family look exactly the same. Both grow by reproduction. Why is one so uniform and the other so varied?
steps: Reproduction always makes new individuals that are similar, so both fields and families start from a shared design.
Sugarcane grows by asexual reproduction, and its DNA copying makes only tiny mistakes, so the plants stay almost identical.
Humans use sexual reproduction, which mixes parents and creates much bigger variation, so family members differ more.
So the difference is not luck; the type of reproduction decides how much variation appears.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: You walk through a sugarcane field. How much variation do you expect among the plants?
options: A huge range of different plants
Very little variation among plants
No two plants look alike
Every plant is a new species
activities.explanation: Sugarcane is grown by asexual reproduction, so the plants stay very similar. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: Bacteria that reproduce asexually produce very different individuals.
activities.explanation: Asexual reproduction in bacteria gives very similar individuals. Only tiny differences appear.

activities.prompt: The small differences in asexual reproduction come from mistakes during DNA ______.
activities.hint: Think of the word for when DNA makes a copy of itself.
activities.explanation: DNA copying is not perfect, so tiny errors slip in. These errors create the small differences.

activities.prompt: Match each case with the amount of variation it shows.
activities.explanation: Asexual reproduction gives little change, while sexual reproduction gives much more variety.

activities.prompt: Why does sexual reproduction create more variety than asexual reproduction?
options: It copies DNA perfectly every time
It makes individuals without any change
It generates even greater diversity
It stops variations from appearing
activities.explanation: Sexual reproduction brings together more changes, so it creates greater diversity. Good thinking!

activities.prompt: Every variation has an equal chance of helping an individual survive.
activities.explanation: Variations do not have equal chances of surviving. Some help in a place, others do not.

activities.prompt: A heat wave strikes. Which bacteria will survive better, and what does this lead to?
options: Heat-tolerant bacteria survive; selection of variants forms the basis for evolution
Heat-sensitive bacteria survive; evolution stops completely
All bacteria survive equally; nothing changes at all
Only new bacteria survive; the old ones evolve faster
activities.explanation: Bacteria that can bear the heat survive better. When the environment selects variants like this, it forms the basis for evolution.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order, from first to last.
items: New individuals are born with small variations
The environment tests each variation
Variants that suit the conditions survive better
Selection of variants forms the basis for evolution
activities.explanation: Variations appear first, then the environment selects the ones that survive, and this selection drives evolution.

activities.prompt: A hot spring is home to many bacteria. Only a few bacteria there can bear heat. The heat never goes away. After a very long time, most bacteria in the spring can bear heat. Why?
options: The hot environment kept picking the heat-bearing survivors.
The bacteria slowly learned to enjoy the hot water.
The heat changed every bacterium at the same moment.
The bacteria moved away and new ones came each day.

why.The bacteria slowly learned to enjoy the: Wrong: bacteria cannot learn traits; only the already heat-bearing ones survived.
why.The heat changed every bacterium at the: Wrong: heat does not rewrite all bacteria at once; it only kills the ones that cannot cope.
why.The bacteria moved away and new ones cam: Wrong: the change happened among the bacteria already living there, not by swapping crowds.

activities.explanation: Right: environmental factors select the variants that survive, and this selection over time is the basis of evolution.

lessons.title: Heredity and Inherited Traits

activities.prompt: Why don't you look exactly like your parents?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Like Parent, Like Child... But Not Quite!
activities.body: When living things reproduce, the young ones are mostly like their parents. This passing on of features is called heredity. Rules of heredity decide how traits pass from parents to children. A child has all the basic human features, yet never looks exactly like its parents. Small differences, called variation, appear in every population. Mendel worked out the main rules of such inheritance.
keyPoints: Heredity is the passing of traits from parents to children.
A child shows all basic human features but is not an exact copy of its parents.
Human populations show a great deal of variation.
Mendel worked out the main rules of inheritance.
activities.explanation: Children resemble their parents, yet small differences make each person unique.

activities.prompt: Riya looks like her mother's eyes but her nose looks like her father's nose. Why is she a mix, and why is she still not exactly like either parent?
steps: Both the father and the mother give almost equal genetic material to the child, so Riya gets instructions from both sides.
Each trait in Riya has two versions, one from each parent, so both sides can show up in her.
That is why each trait, like her nose, can be shaped by both paternal and maternal DNA.
But the two versions mix in new ways, so she does not look exactly like either parent, while still being fully human.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Why does a child not look exactly like its parents?
options: Because children copy their friends
Because traits come only from the father
Because it gets traits from both parents
Because parents hide their features
activities.explanation: Traits come from both parents, so the child is similar but not identical. Well done for thinking it through!

activities.prompt: The lowest part of the ear is called the ______.
activities.hint: Think of the soft bottom part of your ear.
activities.explanation: That soft lowest part is the earlobe. Great memory!

activities.prompt: A child bears all the basic features of a human being.
activities.explanation: Yes! Every child shows the basic features that make us human.

activities.prompt: How much genetic material does each parent give to a child?
options: More from the mother
More from the father
Equal amounts from both
None at all
activities.explanation: Father and mother contribute practically equal amounts of genetic material. Both matter equally!

activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct partner.
pairs: Closely fixed to the side of the head
activities.explanation: Earlobes come in two variants, and Mendel gave us the rules of inheritance. Super matching!

activities.prompt: A trait in a child can be influenced by which DNA?
options: Only the mother's DNA
Both paternal and maternal DNA
Only the father's DNA
Neither parent's DNA
activities.explanation: Both paternal and maternal DNA can influence each trait. That is why you are a blend of both sides!

activities.prompt: A baby boy has his mother's smile and his father's ears. He is still clearly a human baby. Why does he match both parents in different traits?
options: Only the father's DNA decides most traits in a child.
Both parents give equal genetic material, so both can show in traits.
The baby copies one parent fully and the other partly.
Traits from the mother appear first and father's traits appear later.

why.Only the father's DNA decides most trait: This thinks only one parent matters, but both give nearly equal genetic material.
why.The baby copies one parent fully and the: This thinks a child is a copy of one parent, but a child gets two versions of each trait.
why.Traits from the mother appear first and: This thinks traits appear in a time order, but both sides act together from the start.

activities.explanation: Right: father and mother contribute practically equal genetic material, so each trait can be influenced by both.

activities.prompt: A boy's earlobes hang free like his mother's. His sister's earlobes are closely attached to the side of the head. Both have the same parents. Why can the two children differ in this trait?
options: Each child got two versions of the trait, and the mix can differ.
The sister's earlobes will become free when she grows older.
The parents passed earlobe traits only to the son, not the daughter.
Attached earlobes happen when a child sleeps pressing the ear.

why.The sister's earlobes will become free w: This thinks the trait changes with age, but the inherited version stays the same.
why.The parents passed earlobe traits only t: This thinks parents choose traits per child, but both children get versions from both parents.
why.Attached earlobes happen when a child sl: This blames a habit, but earlobe type is inherited, not caused by sleeping position.

activities.explanation: Right: each trait has two versions in each child, so different mixes give free or attached earlobes.

activities.prompt: A girl says: 'My parents look alike, so my brother and I must look exactly like them too.' Her brother looks quite different from both parents. What is wrong with her claim?
options: Brothers always look different from sisters, so her rule fails.
Children get two versions of each trait, so new mixes appear.
Her brother is younger, so his traits have not settled yet.
Parents hide their real traits and pass different ones to children.

why.Brothers always look different from sist: This uses a gender rule, but the reason works for any two children.
why.Her brother is younger, so his traits ha: This blames age, but inherited traits are already set in the child.
why.Parents hide their real traits and pass: This thinks parents hide traits, but children simply get two versions that mix in new ways.

activities.explanation: Right: each trait has two versions in each child, so children can get mixes unlike either parent.

activities.prompt: In a class photo, no two students have exactly the same face, even though all are humans with the same basic features. What does this show about human populations?
options: Faces change a little every year in every person.
Students copy features from friends they sit near.
Human populations show a great deal of variation.
Only children of tall parents can look different from others.

why.Faces change a little every year in ever: This blames time, but the differences are inherited, not yearly changes.
why.Students copy features from friends they: This thinks friends share traits, but traits come from parents, not friends.
why.Only children of tall parents can look d: This links difference to height only, but variation appears in all kinds of traits.

activities.explanation: Right: human populations show a great deal of variation, so faces differ.

activities.prompt: A student claims: 'Since a child gets traits from both parents, the child must be a half-copy of the mother and a half-copy of the father.' What is the flaw in this claim?
options: The claim is right; children are always exact half-copies.
Each trait gets two versions that mix, not whole halves of a person.
Children copy only the parent they live with more.
The claim fails because parents never pass any traits at all.

why.The claim is right; children are always: This accepts the claim, but children are not exact copies of either parent.
why.Children copy only the parent they live: This brings living habits in, but traits come from genetic material, not time spent together.
why.The claim fails because parents never pa: This swings to the opposite error; parents do pass genetic material to children.

activities.explanation: Right: each trait has two versions, one from each side, so traits mix trait by trait.

activities.prompt: A teacher shows the lowest part of the ear in a picture. Some students have that part hanging free, and some have it closely attached to the side of the head. Both types are in the same family. What is this lowest part of the ear, and why do both types exist?
options: It is the earlobe; both versions are inherited in populations.
It is the eardrum; use decides if it stays free or attached.
It is the earlobe; attached ones come from wearing heavy earrings.
It is the ear canal; both versions appear only in adults.

why.It is the eardrum; use decides if it sta: This names the wrong part; the eardrum is deep inside, not the lowest part.
why.It is the earlobe; attached ones come fr: This blames earrings, but the type is inherited, not caused by jewellery.
why.It is the ear canal; both versions appea: This names the wrong part and adds an age rule that is not true.

activities.explanation: Right: the lowest part is the earlobe, and free and attached are two inherited variants in populations.

lessons.sceneCaption: Four generations of one family in 1900: similar features passed down, yet each person looks a little different.
