lessons.title: Mendel's Experiments with One Trait

activities.prompt: If two tall pea plants have a short baby, what happened?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Mendel and his pea plants
activities.body: Mendel studied garden peas. He picked pairs of plants with opposite looks, like tall and short. He crossed a tall plant with a short one. The first generation, called F1, was all tall. No plant was halfway! Then he let the F1 plants self-pollinate. In the next generation, F2, one quarter of the plants were short. So the shortness trait had been hiding inside the tall F1 plants.
keyPoints: Mendel used contrasting characters of garden peas.
All F1 plants were tall, with no halfway features.
One quarter of the F2 plants were short.
Both traits were inherited in F1, but only tallness showed.
activities.explanation: A hidden trait can skip a generation and appear again later.

activities.prompt: A girl crosses a tall pea plant with a short pea plant. All the baby plants are tall. She wonders: did the shortness trait disappear forever?
steps: The F1 plants look tall, so tallness is the trait that shows itself.
But shortness could still be hiding inside, just not visible.
So she self-pollinates the F1 plants and waits for the next generation.
Some F2 plants come out short, so the shortness trait was there all along, only hidden.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What plant did Mendel choose for his experiments?
options: Garden peas
Mango trees
Wheat crops
activities.explanation: Mendel used garden peas with contrasting visible characters.

activities.prompt: The F1 plants were all tall. What height did they show?
options: Halfway between tall and short
Tall
Short
activities.explanation: The F1 generation had no halfway characteristics. They were all tall.

activities.prompt: Mendel self-pollinated the F1 tall plants. In the F2 progeny, one ______ of the plants were short.
activities.hint: Think of a cake cut into four equal pieces.
activities.explanation: Great thinking! One quarter of the F2 plants were short.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its meaning.
activities.explanation: T is dominant and t is recessive. A single T makes a plant tall, but both copies must be t to be short.

activities.prompt: Put Mendel's steps in the order he did them.
items: Cross a tall plant with a short plant
Get F1 progeny, all tall
Self-pollinate the F1 tall plants
Get F2 progeny, with one quarter short
activities.explanation: Spot on! Mendel crossed, then grew F1, then self-pollinated them to get F2.

activities.prompt: Why did some F2 plants become short even though the F1 plants were tall?
options: Shortness appears only in warm weather
Both their copies were t, so shortness showed
The tallness trait got lost in the seeds
activities.explanation: Mendel said traits are controlled by two copies of a factor. Both copies must be t for a plant to be short.

activities.prompt: A boy says the shortness trait died out in the F1 tall plants. He self-pollinates them and grows F2. What will show him the truth?
options: All F2 plants will be tall, proving him right
Some F2 plants will be short, so shortness was hiding
All F2 plants will be medium height
The F2 plants will be taller than the F1 plants

why.All F2 plants will be tall, proving him: Thinks the hidden trait is gone, but it was inherited in F1.
why.All F2 plants will be medium height: Thinks traits blend, but F2 plants are tall or short, not halfway.
why.The F2 plants will be taller than the F1: Thinks crossing makes plants stronger, which is not how traits work here.

activities.explanation: Right: both traits were inherited in F1, only tallness was expressed.

activities.prompt: Two tall F1 pea plants are self-pollinated. Their F2 seeds grow. Why do some F2 plants turn out short?
options: Because shortness was hiding in the F1 plants all along
Because the soil made those plants weak and short
Because tallness got used up in the other plants
Because shortness jumped in from plants outside

why.Because the soil made those plants weak: Blames the environment, but the trait was inherited from the parents.
why.Because tallness got used up in the othe: Thinks traits run out like fuel, but copies of factors are passed on.
why.Because shortness jumped in from plants: Thinks traits come from outside, but they come from the parent plants.

activities.explanation: Right: both traits were inherited in F1, but only tallness was expressed.

activities.prompt: A friend claims: a pea plant with one T copy and one t copy must be short, because it carries t. Is his test of the plant fair?
options: Yes, because every t copy always makes plants short
Yes, because carrying t always hides tallness
No, because one T copy is enough to make it tall
No, because the plant will be medium height instead

why.Yes, because every t copy always makes p: Thinks t always wins, but t needs both copies to show.
why.Yes, because carrying t always hides tal: Thinks carrying a trait forces it to show, but t stays hidden.
why.No, because the plant will be medium hei: Thinks traits blend, but there is no halfway height here.

activities.explanation: Right: a single copy of T is enough to make the plant tall.

activities.prompt: A boy wants a pea plant to be short. He learns how the copies of the factor work. Which plant should he choose?
options: One with two T copies, so tallness is doubled
One with one T and one t, so both act together
One with two t copies, the only way to be short
One with one t copy alone, since t causes shortness

why.One with two T copies, so tallness is do: Thinks more T means shorter, but T makes plants tall.
why.One with one T and one t, so both act to: Thinks mixed copies give shortness, but T hides t.
why.One with one t copy alone, since t cause: Thinks one t is enough, but a single T copy makes it tall.

activities.explanation: Right: both copies have to be t for the plant to be short.

lessons.title: Independent Inheritance of Two Traits

activities.prompt: Can a tall plant end up with wrinkled seeds like its grandparents?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Traits at Once
activities.body: Mendel bred pea plants that differed in two traits at once: tall or short plants, and round or wrinkled seeds. All the F1 children were tall with round seeds. When the F1 plants self-pollinated, the F2 family held a surprise. Some plants were tall with wrinkled seeds, and some were short with round seeds. The two traits are inherited independently of each other.
keyPoints: Crossing tall round with short wrinkled gave all tall round F1 progeny.
Self-pollinating F1 plants produced the F2 progeny.
F2 progeny showed new combinations, like tall wrinkled and short round.
The two traits are inherited independently.
activities.explanation: Two traits can travel separately from parent to child, so new mixes appear.

activities.prompt: You pack one bag with shirts and another bag with shoes. Your friend asks: if I borrow your shirt bag, must I also get your shoe bag? You say no, because the bags are separate. In a plant, the tall trait and the seed trait are like those two bags. So can a baby plant get tall from one parent and wrinkled seeds from the other?
steps: The shirt bag and the shoe bag are packed separately, so taking one does not force you to take the other.
In the plant, the tall trait and the seed trait also sit on separate pieces, so they do not have to travel together.
That is why a baby plant can be tall like one parent but wrinkled like the other parent.
So the two traits are inherited independently, each one on its own.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Mendel bred tall round plants with short wrinkled plants. What were all the F1 progeny like?
options: All short and wrinkled
All tall and round
Half tall and half short
activities.explanation: Tallness and round seeds are dominant traits, so they showed in every F1 plant. Well done!

activities.prompt: The F1 progeny were self-pollinated to generate the ______ progeny.
activities.hint: It is the next generation after F1.
activities.explanation: Self-pollinating the F1 plants gave the F2 generation. You remembered the steps!

activities.prompt: Which of these new combinations appeared in the F2 progeny?
options: Short plants with round seeds
Tall plants with green seeds
Short plants with big seeds
activities.explanation: Some F2 plants were short but had round seeds, a mix not seen in the parents. Nice thinking!

activities.prompt: Put Mendel's two-trait experiment in order.
items: Breed tall round plants with short wrinkled plants
All F1 progeny are tall and round
Self-pollinate the F1 plants
F2 progeny show old pairs and new combinations
activities.explanation: First the cross, then the F1, then self-pollination, then the mixed F2. You got the whole story!

activities.prompt: Why can the tall/short trait and the seed shape trait be inherited independently?
options: Because each gene set is on separate chromosomes
Because both traits are always linked together
Because F1 plants are always short and wrinkled
activities.explanation: Each gene set sits on separate independent pieces called chromosomes, so traits can recombine freely. Brilliant reasoning!

activities.prompt: A gardener breeds a tall plant that has round seeds. She breeds it with a short plant that has wrinkled seeds. Every baby plant looks the same. Tallness and round seeds are the strong traits. What do the baby plants look like?
options: All are tall with round seeds
All are short with wrinkled seeds
All are tall with wrinkled seeds
Half are tall and half are short

why.All are short with wrinkled seeds: This child thinks the weaker traits must show in the babies.
why.All are tall with wrinkled seeds: This child thinks one trait comes from each parent, which is not how it works here.
why.Half are tall and half are short: This child thinks babies must split evenly between the two parents.

activities.explanation: Right: the strong traits show up, so all babies are tall with round seeds.

activities.prompt: The gardener self-pollinates those baby plants to make the F2 plants. Some F2 plants are tall with round seeds. Some F2 plants show new mixes. What is one new mix she can see?
options: A tall plant with wrinkled seeds
Only tall plants with round seeds
Only short plants with wrinkled seeds
Plants that grow no seeds at all

why.Only tall plants with round seeds: This child thinks F2 must look exactly like F1.
why.Only short plants with wrinkled seeds: This child thinks only the grandparent mixes can appear.
why.Plants that grow no seeds at all: This child thinks self-pollination stops seeds from forming.

activities.explanation: Right: tall with wrinkled is a new mix that appears in F2.

activities.prompt: In the F2 plants, some are short but have round seeds. The grandparents were tall-round and short-wrinkled. Why can a short plant have round seeds?
options: The two traits are inherited on their own
The tall trait slowly turned into the seed trait
The short plant copied one grandparent fully
Round seeds can only grow on short plants

why.The tall trait slowly turned into the se: This child thinks one trait changes into another trait.
why.The short plant copied one grandparent f: This child thinks a plant must copy one whole grandparent.
why.Round seeds can only grow on short plant: This child thinks seed shape depends on plant height.

activities.explanation: Right: the traits are inherited independently, so they can mix in new ways.

activities.prompt: A boy saw the F1 plants. All of them were tall with round seeds. He says tall and round must always travel together forever. What is wrong with his claim?
options: F2 plants show tall with wrinkled seeds too
F1 plants were too small to count properly
Round seeds cannot be seen on tall plants
Tall plants always make wrinkled seeds later

why.F1 plants were too small to count proper: This child blames the size of the plants, not the mixing.
why.Round seeds cannot be seen on tall plant: This child thinks you cannot see seeds on tall plants.
why.Tall plants always make wrinkled seeds l: This child thinks tall plants change their seeds later on.

activities.explanation: Right: F2 shows new mixes, so the traits do not always travel together.

activities.prompt: Two traits called R and y sit together on the same piece. They always move as one single unit. A plant has R and y together. What will its babies get?
options: Always R and y together, never apart
R and y split up evenly between babies
Only y, and never R at all
New mixes like R without y

why.R and y split up evenly between babies: This child thinks linked traits still separate like free traits.
why.Only y, and never R at all: This child thinks one linked trait gets lost completely.
why.New mixes like R without y: This child thinks new mixes can form even when traits are linked.

activities.explanation: Right: linked traits cannot be inherited independently, so they stay together.

lessons.title: Sex Determination

activities.prompt: Why isn't everyone born a boy or a girl by chance alone?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Who decides: boy or girl?
activities.body: How is a boy or a girl decided? Different species use very different strategies. Some animals rely entirely on the environment around them. In some reptiles, the temperature of the eggs decides the sex. Snails can even change sex! In humans, sex is largely decided by genes. We each carry chromosomes, and one special pair, called sex chromosomes, holds the answer.
keyPoints: Different species use very different strategies for sex determination.
In some reptiles, egg temperature decides sex; snails can change sex.
In humans, sex is largely genetically determined.
Sex chromosomes are a special pair that is not always a perfect match.
activities.explanation: Nature has many ways to decide sex, and humans use genes to do it.

activities.prompt: A baby boy is born. His friend says the mother decided his sex. Is the friend right?
steps: Every child gets an X from the mother, so the mother always gives X.
The father can give X or Y, because his pair is XY.
So the child's sex depends on which one the father gives.
So the friend is wrong; the father decides the sex.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: In some reptiles, what decides whether a fertilised egg becomes male or female?
options: The size of the egg
The colour of the egg
The temperature where the egg is kept
The age of the mother reptile
activities.explanation: Well done! In some reptiles, the temperature at which the eggs are kept decides the sex.

activities.prompt: Which pair of sex chromosomes does a woman have?
options: XX
XY
YY
XO
activities.explanation: A woman has a perfect pair: two X chromosomes, so we say XX.

activities.prompt: Every child inherits an ______ chromosome from their mother.
activities.hint: It is the chromosome that every woman has two of.
activities.explanation: That's right! All children get an X chromosome from their mother.

activities.prompt: Match each living thing to how its sex is decided.
pairs: Sex is largely decided by genes
activities.explanation: Great matching! Different species use very different strategies for sex determination.

activities.prompt: A man has a mismatched pair of sex chromosomes. What is it called?
options: XX
XY
YY
XXX
activities.explanation: Yes! Men have one normal-sized X and one short Y, so we write XY.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to show how a baby's sex is decided.
items: Every child inherits an X chromosome from the mother
The father gives either an X or a Y chromosome
XX becomes a girl and XY becomes a boy
Half the children will be boys and half will be girls
activities.explanation: Brilliant ordering! The mother always gives an X, so the father's chromosome decides the sex, giving half boys and half girls.

activities.prompt: A farmer keeps some turtle eggs in warm sand and some in cool sand. The babies hatch. What will he most likely see?
options: The warm-sand babies and cool-sand babies may be different sexes.
All the babies will be boys, because sand cannot change sex.
All the babies will match the mother turtle's sex.
Half the babies will be boys and half will be girls.

why.All the babies will be boys, because san: Wrong: thinks genes must always decide sex, like in humans.
why.All the babies will match the mother tur: Wrong: thinks the mother's sex passes on, but temperature is the cue here.
why.Half the babies will be boys and half wi: Wrong: applies the human 50-50 rule to an animal that uses temperature.

activities.explanation: Right: in some reptiles, egg temperature decides the sex, so warm and cool can give different sexes.

activities.prompt: A snail is male this year. Next year it is female. A student says its sex genes must have changed. What is the flaw?
options: The snail's sex was never fixed by genes, so genes need not change.
The student is right, because only genes can change an animal's sex.
The snail must have mated, and that changed its sex genes.
The snail's genes changed because the weather changed its body.

why.The student is right, because only genes: Wrong: assumes genes always control sex, but snails show this is not true.
why.The snail must have mated, and that chan: Wrong: invents a mating cause; snails can change sex on their own.
why.The snail's genes changed because the we: Wrong: blames weather changing genes; the point is genes were never in charge.

activities.explanation: Right: in snails sex is not genetically determined, so a sex change does not need gene change.

activities.prompt: A mother is XX. A baby girl is born. A baby boy is born later. What did both babies get from her?
options: Both babies got an X chromosome from her.
The girl got an X and the boy got a Y from her.
The girl got both her X chromosomes, the boy got none.
The boy got nothing from her, because fathers pass on Y.

why.The girl got an X and the boy got a Y fr: Wrong: thinks she can pass a Y, but she has no Y at all.
why.The girl got both her X chromosomes, the: Wrong: thinks she gives her whole pair; she gives one chromosome only.
why.The boy got nothing from her, because fa: Wrong: thinks mothers pass nothing for boys; every child gets her X.

activities.explanation: Right: she has only X chromosomes, so every child gets an X from her.

activities.prompt: Two families each have four girls. One father says mothers decide a baby's sex. Does his claim fit what children inherit?
options: No, because the father's chromosome, X or Y, decides the sex.
Yes, because mothers have a perfect pair, so they choose.
Yes, because four girls in a row proves the mother decided.
No, because having four girls means the father has no Y.

why.Yes, because mothers have a perfect pair: Wrong: thinks a perfect pair gives the mother the deciding power.
why.Yes, because four girls in a row proves: Wrong: reads a run of luck as proof of a rule.
why.No, because having four girls means the: Wrong: thinks four girls erase the father's Y; he still carries it.

activities.explanation: Right: all children get X from mother, so the father's X or Y decides.

activities.context: A gardener grows a large bed of sugarcane in which every plant looks almost identical, since the plants arose through asexual reproduction. In a nearby pond, a population of bacteria also reproduces asexually, so its members are very similar too. One summer, an unusual heat wave strikes the area. The gardener expects the sugarcane bed to stay much the same, while a visiting observer predicts that within the pond, not all bacteria will cope equally well with the sudden heat.
activities.prompt: During the heat wave, what is most likely to happen among the bacteria in the pond?
options: The bacteria that can withstand heat will survive in greater numbers
Every bacterium will face exactly the same chance of surviving
The whole population will instantly become identical to each other
The bacteria will develop a completely new basic body design

why.Every bacterium will face exactly the sa: Wrong: this treats all variations as equal, but survival chances differ.
why.The whole population will instantly beco: Wrong: reproduction cannot make a varied population suddenly identical.
why.The bacteria will develop a completely n: Wrong: inheritance gives a common basic body design; it is not replaced in one event.

activities.explanation: Correct: variations do not have equal chances of surviving, and heat-tolerant bacteria survive a heat wave better.

activities.context: A gardener grows a large bed of sugarcane in which every plant looks almost identical, since the plants arose through asexual reproduction. In a nearby pond, a population of bacteria also reproduces asexually, so its members are very similar too. One summer, an unusual heat wave strikes the area. The gardener expects the sugarcane bed to stay much the same, while a visiting observer predicts that within the pond, not all bacteria will cope equally well with the sudden heat.
activities.prompt: If the gardener's sugarcane had instead arisen through sexual reproduction, what would the bed most likely show?
options: Greater diversity among the plants than is actually seen
Even less difference between plants than now
No inheritance of the basic body design at all
Identical plants with no subtle changes whatsoever

why.Even less difference between plants than: Wrong: this reverses the effect; sexual reproduction maximises successful variations.
why.No inheritance of the basic body design: Wrong: inheritance still gives a common basic body design with subtle changes.
why.Identical plants with no subtle changes: Wrong: even asexual reproduction produces some variation, so total absence is impossible.

activities.explanation: Correct: sexual reproduction generates even greater diversity, so more distinct variations would appear.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): All variations in a population have equal chances of surviving.
Reason (R): Environmental factors select which variants survive.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because survival chances differ, while the reason is true and forms the basis for evolution.

activities.prompt: Explain why sexually reproducing animals, including humans, show distinct variations, while a sugarcane field shows very little variation among its plants.
activities.answer: A sugarcane field arises from asexual reproduction, which gives rise to new individuals that are very similar; the only minor differences come from small inaccuracies in DNA copying, so very little variation is seen. In contrast, sexual reproduction generates even greater diversity and maximises successful variations. So sexually reproducing animals, including humans, show distinct variations, while still sharing a common basic body design inherited from their parents, along with subtle changes.
points: Sugarcane field is produced asexually, so individuals are very similar
Minor differences in asexual reproduction come from DNA copying inaccuracies
Sexual reproduction generates greater diversity and maximises successful variations
Inheritance gives a common basic body design with subtle changes
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Riya is looking through her family album. She notices that everyone in the photos is clearly a human being, yet no two faces are exactly alike. Her cousin has a free earlobe — the lowest part of the ear hangs loose — while Riya's earlobe is closely attached to the side of her head. Her teacher tells the class that a father and mother pass on practically equal amounts of genetic material to each child. Riya wonders why she and her cousin differ in this trait.
activities.prompt: Why does Riya have an attached earlobe while her cousin's hangs free, even though both are clearly human?
options: Each child carries two versions of a trait, and the combination received can differ from one child to another
Only the father's genetic material decides how a trait appears in a child
A trait is always copied exactly from one single parent
Children receive all their traits from the parent they resemble most

why.Only the father's genetic material decid: Wrong: both parents contribute practically equal genetic material, so the father alone does not decide
why.A trait is always copied exactly from on: Wrong: traits are influenced by both paternal and maternal DNA, not copied from just one parent
why.Children receive all their traits from t: Wrong: inheritance follows fixed rules of heredity, not resemblance to one parent

activities.explanation: Correct: with two versions per trait, different children can end up with different combinations, so cousins can differ

activities.context: Riya is looking through her family album. She notices that everyone in the photos is clearly a human being, yet no two faces are exactly alike. Her cousin has a free earlobe — the lowest part of the ear hangs loose — while Riya's earlobe is closely attached to the side of her head. Her teacher tells the class that a father and mother pass on practically equal amounts of genetic material to each child. Riya wonders why she and her cousin differ in this trait.
activities.prompt: Riya's teacher asks the class why human populations show a great deal of variation. What should a student conclude?
options: Because heredity passes traits on through rules that allow different combinations of the two versions of each trait in different children
Because the reproductive process produces individuals of a completely different design every time
Because children receive traits only from their mothers, so fathers add variety
Because the basic features of a human being change in every new child

why.Because the reproductive process produce: Wrong: reproduction mainly produces individuals of a similar design, not a different design each time
why.Because children receive traits only fro: Wrong: father and mother contribute practically equal amounts of genetic material
why.Because the basic features of a human be: Wrong: the basic features of a human being stay the same; only details vary

activities.explanation: Correct: the rules of heredity reliably pass on traits, and two versions per trait allow different combinations, producing variation

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A child does not look exactly like its parents.
Reason (R): Each trait in a child can be influenced by both paternal and maternal DNA.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Since both parents' DNA influences each trait and the child has two versions of each trait, the combination need not match either parent exactly.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Mendel worked out the main rules of such inheritance.
Reason (R): The reproductive process produces individuals of a completely different design each time.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because reproduction mainly produces individuals of a similar design.

activities.prompt: Explain why a child bears all the basic features of a human being but still does not look exactly like its parents.
activities.answer: The reproductive process mainly produces individuals of a similar design, so every child bears all the basic features of a human being. However, the rules of heredity decide how traits are reliably inherited. The father and mother contribute practically equal amounts of genetic material, and each trait can be influenced by both paternal and maternal DNA. Since every child has two versions of each trait, the combination a child receives can differ from the combination seen in either parent. This is why human populations show a great deal of variation, and children resemble their parents without being exact copies of them.
points: Reproduction produces individuals of similar design, so basic human features are present
Father and mother contribute practically equal amounts of genetic material
Each trait is influenced by both paternal and maternal DNA, with two versions per trait
Different combinations of versions explain variation and why the child is not an exact copy
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A school gardener sows seeds from a cross between a tall pea plant and a short pea plant. Every plant that grows from this first generation is tall — none is short or halfway in between. Curious, she lets these tall plants self-pollinate and collects seeds from them. When the next generation grows, she counts the plants and notices that some are short, even though no short parent took part in the original cross.
activities.prompt: Why did none of the first-generation plants look short even though the short parent took part in the cross?
options: The copy for shortness was inherited but stayed hidden, because one copy for tallness was enough
The copy for shortness was destroyed when the two plants were crossed
The short parent passed on nothing to the first generation
Shortness could not show because the first-generation plants had not self-pollinated yet

why.The copy for shortness was destroyed whe: Factors are not destroyed in a cross; the shortness copy was still carried.
why.The short parent passed on nothing to th: The short parent did contribute — its trait reappeared in the next generation.
why.Shortness could not show because the fir: Self-pollination affects the next generation, not whether a trait shows in F1.

activities.explanation: Correct — both traits were inherited but only tallness was expressed, since a single T is enough.

activities.context: A school gardener sows seeds from a cross between a tall pea plant and a short pea plant. Every plant that grows from this first generation is tall — none is short or halfway in between. Curious, she lets these tall plants self-pollinate and collects seeds from them. When the next generation grows, she counts the plants and notices that some are short, even though no short parent took part in the original cross.
activities.prompt: The gardener wants seeds that will grow into only short plants. What should she do?
options: Collect seeds from a short second-generation plant, since such a plant carries only the shortness copy
Collect seeds from any tall first-generation plant, since all first-generation plants looked tall
Cross the tall parent with the short parent again and pick the tallest seedlings
Grow the first-generation plants close together so tallness cannot spread to them

why.Collect seeds from any tall first-genera: Tall F1 plants also carry the shortness copy, so their offspring will not all be short.
why.Cross the tall parent with the short par: Repeating the original cross again gives all tall first-generation plants, not short ones.
why.Grow the first-generation plants close t: Growing plants close together does not change which copies of the factor they carry.

activities.explanation: Correct — both copies must be t for a plant to be short, so a short plant passes only t on.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): In the first generation, the shortness trait was present in the plants even though no plant looked short.
Reason (R): A single copy of the factor for tallness is enough to make a pea plant tall.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The tallness copy hides shortness, which is why both traits were inherited but only tallness was expressed.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A pea plant with two copies of the factor for shortness would grow tall.
Reason (R): Traits that stay hidden in the first generation, like shortness here, are called recessive traits.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both copies have to be t for the plant to be short, so the assertion is false, though shortness is indeed recessive.

activities.prompt: Explain why the first generation had no halfway plants, yet shortness appeared again in the second generation.
activities.answer: When the tall and short parents were crossed, each first-generation plant received one copy of the factor for tallness and one copy of the factor for shortness. Since a single copy of T is enough to make the plant tall, every F1 plant looked tall and no halfway characteristic appeared. However, both copies were still carried inside the plants. When the F1 tall plants self-pollinated, some offspring received the t copy from both parents; with no T present, these plants were short, so one quarter of the F2 progeny were short.
points: F1 plants received one copy of each factor from the two parents
A single copy of T is enough, so all F1 plants were tall with no halfway character
Both copies were still inherited, only tallness was expressed
Self-pollination of F1 allowed offspring with both copies t, giving one quarter short in F2
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student crosses pea plants that differ in two characteristics: plant height and seed shape. One parent is tall with round seeds, the other is short with wrinkled seeds. All the first-generation plants look alike. The student then self-pollinates these first-generation plants and waits to see what the next generation looks like before writing her observation notebook.
activities.prompt: Why did every plant in the first generation look tall with round seeds?
options: Because tallness and round seeds are the dominant traits, so they appeared over the short and wrinkled forms
Because the short and wrinkled traits were stronger and hid the others
Because the two traits had already formed new combinations in this generation
Because the factors for seed shape and seed colour recombined at this stage

why.Because the short and wrinkled traits we: Wrong: it reverses the dominance; short and wrinkled are the hidden forms, not the stronger ones.
why.Because the two traits had already forme: Wrong: new combinations appear only in the next generation after self-pollination, not here.
why.Because the factors for seed shape and s: Wrong: recombination of factors explains the later generation, not the uniform first generation.

activities.explanation: Correct: dominance of tallness and round seeds explains why only these forms show.

activities.context: A student crosses pea plants that differ in two characteristics: plant height and seed shape. One parent is tall with round seeds, the other is short with wrinkled seeds. All the first-generation plants look alike. The student then self-pollinates these first-generation plants and waits to see what the next generation looks like before writing her observation notebook.
activities.prompt: After self-pollinating the first-generation plants, the student finds some short plants with round seeds. What should she conclude?
options: The seeds got mixed up, since short plants can only have wrinkled seeds
A new combination has appeared, showing the two traits are inherited independently
The traits R and y must be linked on the same piece, so they moved together
Self-pollination always produces plants identical to the original short parent

why.The seeds got mixed up, since short plan: Wrong: the case shows short plants with round seeds really occur, so nothing was mixed up.
why.The traits R and y must be linked on the: Wrong: if the traits were linked they could NOT be independently inherited, so new combinations would not appear.
why.Self-pollination always produces plants: Wrong: self-pollination of the first generation produces several kinds of plants, not copies of one parent.

activities.explanation: Correct: short with round seeds is one of the new combinations, which shows independent inheritance.

activities.context: A student crosses pea plants that differ in two characteristics: plant height and seed shape. One parent is tall with round seeds, the other is short with wrinkled seeds. All the first-generation plants look alike. The student then self-pollinates these first-generation plants and waits to see what the next generation looks like before writing her observation notebook.
activities.prompt: Suppose the factors for these two characteristics were linked instead of being on separate independent pieces. What would change in the second generation?
options: All plants would be tall with round seeds, exactly like the first generation
New combinations like tall with wrinkled seeds would become more common than before
The new combinations would not appear, because linked factors could not be independently inherited
Every plant would be short with wrinkled seeds, like the second parent

why.All plants would be tall with round seed: Wrong: the first generation was tall and round because of dominance, not because of linkage; this does not follow.
why.New combinations like tall with wrinkled: Wrong: linkage would prevent recombination, so new combinations would not become more common.
why.Every plant would be short with wrinkled: Wrong: dominance of tallness and round seeds would still operate; nothing here makes all plants short and wrinkled.

activities.explanation: Correct: if two characteristics were linked, they could not be independently inherited, so the new combinations would not form.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): In the second generation, some pea plants were tall with wrinkled seeds.
Reason (R): The factors for seed shape and seed colour recombine, so new combinations can appear.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and recombination of factors is exactly why the new combination appeared.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Heredity

activities.prompt: Mendel crossed a tall pea plant with a short one. What did every plant in the first generation look like?
options: All were short
All were tall
Half tall, half short
All were halfway in height
activities.explanation: The first generation had no halfway plants. All of them were tall, so tallness hid shortness.

activities.prompt: Asexual reproduction makes new individuals that are exactly alike, with no variation at all.
activities.explanation: Even asexual reproduction makes some variation. In bacteria, small DNA copying mistakes cause tiny differences.

activities.prompt: A trait like T, which shows its effect even when only one copy is present, is called a ______ trait.
activities.hint: It is the opposite of recessive.
activities.explanation: One copy of T is enough to make a plant tall. That is why T is called dominant.

activities.prompt: Match each living thing with how its sex is decided.
activities.explanation: Different species use very different ways to decide sex. Some use genes, some use the surroundings.

activities.prompt: Put Mendel's pea experiment in the correct order.
items: Cross a tall plant with a short plant
All F1 plants grow tall
Self-pollinate the F1 tall plants
One quarter of the F2 plants are short
activities.explanation: First came the cross, then the all-tall F1, then self-pollination, and finally short plants reappeared in F2.

activities.prompt: In the F2 generation, some plants were tall with wrinkled seeds. Why could such new combinations appear?
options: The traits were inherited independently
The plants were all short at first
The seeds were copied inaccurately
The tall trait had disappeared
activities.explanation: The tall/short trait and the seed trait are inherited independently. So the factors can recombine in new ways.

activities.prompt: In humans, the mother's chromosome decides whether a child is a boy or a girl.
activities.explanation: Every child gets an X from the mother. The sex is decided by what the child inherits from the father.

activities.prompt: When Mendel self-pollinated the F1 tall plants, ______ of the F2 progeny were short.
activities.hint: Think of four equal parts of the F2 plants.
activities.explanation: Both copies must be t for a plant to be short. That happened in one quarter of the F2 progeny.

activities.prompt: A heat wave strikes. Which bacteria are most likely to survive?
options: Those that can withstand heat
Those that copy DNA fastest
Those that are most varied
Those that reproduce asexually
activities.explanation: Variations do not have equal chances of surviving. In a heat wave, the heat-tolerant bacteria do best.

activities.prompt: A child shows all the basic features of a human being, yet does not look exactly like its parents.
activities.explanation: Inheritance gives a common basic body design with subtle changes. Both parents contribute nearly equal genetic material, so the child is similar but not identical.

chapters.title: Light Reflection and Refraction
chapters.summary: In this chapter: light and reflection; spherical mirrors; images by spherical mirrors and uses; mirror formula and sign convention.

lessons.title: Light and Reflection

activities.prompt: Why can you see yourself in a mirror but not in a dark room?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How do we see things?
activities.body: Think of a dark room at night. You cannot see your toys until you switch on a light. That is because light bounces off objects and travels to your eyes. This bouncing back of light is called reflection. Light seems to travel in straight lines, like an arrow. A mirror is a smooth, shiny surface that reflects most of the light that falls on it. That is why you can see your face in it!
keyPoints: We see an object when light from it reaches our eyes.
Light appears to travel in straight lines.
A mirror reflects most of the light falling on it.
activities.explanation: Light travels to your eyes after bouncing off things, so no light means no sight.

activities.prompt: You open your school bag in a closed cupboard. It is fully dark inside. You cannot see your pencil box at all. Then you switch on a small torch. Now you see it clearly. Why did the pencil box 'appear' only after the torch was on?
steps: In the dark, no light is falling on the pencil box, so no light can bounce off it towards your eyes.
We only see an object when light from that object actually reaches our eyes, so in darkness there is nothing reaching us.
When the torch is switched on, light travels in straight lines from the torch to the box and then bounces off it to your eyes.
So the pencil box did not appear by magic; it became visible because light reflected from it finally reached your eyes.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: A mirror is a polished surface that ______ most of the light falling on it.
activities.hint: Think of what a mirror does with light.
activities.explanation: A mirror reflects most of the light that falls on it. That is why it shines!

activities.prompt: A small bulb makes a shadow of your toy on the wall. What kind of shadow will you see?
options: A sharp shadow
A very faint shadow
No shadow at all
activities.explanation: A small light source makes a sharp shadow of an opaque object. Nice thinking!

activities.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.
pairs: Light bouncing back off a surface
A polished surface that reflects most light
The ray of light that strikes the mirror
The ray of light that bounces off the mirror
activities.explanation: These words describe how light bounces off a mirror. Super matching!

activities.prompt: You stand 2 metres in front of a plane mirror. Where does your image appear to be?
options: 2 metres behind the mirror
Right on the surface of the mirror
1 metre behind the mirror
activities.explanation: A plane mirror image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Brilliant!
derived: 2 metres = the distance given in the question

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to show how you see your face in a mirror.
items: Light from a lamp strikes your face
Light bounces off your face towards the mirror
The mirror reflects the light
The reflected light reaches your eyes and you see your face
activities.explanation: Light travels from the lamp to you, then to the mirror, and back to your eyes. Superb ordering!

activities.prompt: You make a shadow of your hand on a wall. First you use a tiny torch bulb. Then you use a big tube light. Which shadow will be sharper?
options: The big tube light gives the sharper shadow.
Both lights give shadows that are equally sharp.
The tiny torch bulb gives the sharper shadow.
The big tube light makes no shadow at all.

why.The big tube light gives the sharper sha: Wrong: the child thinks a bigger light is 'stronger', but a big source blurs the shadow edges instead of sharpening them.
why.Both lights give shadows that are equall: Wrong: the child thinks the source size does not matter, but the size of the light source changes how sharp the shadow is.
why.The big tube light makes no shadow at al: Wrong: the child thinks big lights cannot make shadows, but any light makes a shadow; a big one just makes it blurry.

activities.explanation: Right: a small light source makes a sharp shadow of an opaque object like the hand.

activities.prompt: You point a torch at a flat mirror. The beam hits the mirror slanting from your left side. Where does the beam go after it bounces off?
options: It goes straight back to the torch.
It keeps going straight through the mirror.
It slants away on the other side, equally slanting.
It spreads in all directions from the mirror.

Wrong: the child thinks light always bounces straight back, but the bounce keeps the same slant as the incoming beam.
why.It keeps going straight through the mirr: Wrong: the child forgets the mirror reflects light, so the beam cannot pass through it.
why.It spreads in all directions from the mi: Wrong: the child thinks mirrors scatter light everywhere, but a mirror sends the beam in one fixed reflected direction.

activities.explanation: Right: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, so the beam leaves at the same slant on the other side.

activities.prompt: Sara stands far away from a plane mirror. Then she walks slowly closer to it. What happens to the size of her image?
options: The image grows bigger as she comes closer.
The image stays the same size as Sara.
The image grows smaller as she comes closer.
The image becomes flat when she stands close.

why.The image grows bigger as she comes clos: Wrong: the child judges by how the image looks and thinks closer means bigger, but the actual image size does not change.
why.The image grows smaller as she comes clo: Wrong: the child mixes up 'far away looks small' with the real image size, which never changes in a plane mirror.
why.The image becomes flat when she stands c: Wrong: the child invents a strange effect, but a plane mirror image is always the same size and upright.

activities.explanation: Right: a plane mirror always forms an image the same size as the object, so the image stays exactly Sara's size.

activities.prompt: Ravi stands facing a plane mirror. He raises his right hand. Which hand of his image seems to be raised?
options: The image raises its right hand too.
The image raises its left hand.
The image raises both of its hands.
The image raises no hand at all.

Wrong: the child thinks the mirror copies him exactly like a photo, but a plane mirror image is laterally inverted.
Wrong: the child thinks the mirror doubles the movement, but the image shows only one raised hand, on the opposite side.
Wrong: the child thinks mirrors cannot show hands moving, but the image copies the action with left and right swapped.

activities.explanation: Right: a plane mirror image is laterally inverted, so right becomes left and the image seems to raise its left hand.

lessons.sceneAlt: A diagram showing a light ray hitting a mirror, with the incident ray, normal and reflected ray all in the same plane.
lessons.sceneCaption: The law of reflection: the incident ray, normal and reflected ray all lie in one plane.

lessons.title: Spherical Mirrors

activities.prompt: Why does a spoon make your face look different on each side?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Mirrors that bend like a ball
activities.body: Some mirrors are not flat. A spherical mirror has a reflecting surface that is part of a sphere. If the surface curves inwards, like the inside of a bowl, it is a concave mirror. If it curves outwards, like the back of a spoon, it is a convex mirror. Both types are all around you. Let us meet their special points next.
keyPoints: A spherical mirror has a reflecting surface that is part of a sphere.
A concave mirror curves inwards.
A convex mirror curves outwards.
activities.explanation: Curved mirrors are pieces of a big invisible sphere.

activities.prompt: A spoon is shiny. One side shows your face big and close. The other side shows your face small. Both sides are curved metal. Why do the two sides look so different?
steps: The inside of the spoon curves inwards, so it acts like a concave mirror.
The outside of the spoon curves outwards, so it acts like a convex mirror.
A concave mirror curves inwards, so light from your face comes back in a different way than from a convex mirror.
So the two sides look different because one is concave and the other is convex.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Special points and lines
activities.body: Every spherical mirror has special points and lines. The centre of curvature is the centre of the sphere. It lies outside the reflecting surface. For a concave mirror it is in front; for a convex mirror it is behind. The principal axis is a straight line through the pole and the centre of curvature. The focal length is the distance from the pole to the principal focus. The aperture is the diameter of the reflecting surface.
keyPoints: The centre of curvature lies outside the reflecting surface.
The principal axis is a straight line through the pole and the centre of curvature.
The focal length is the distance between the pole and the principal focus.
The aperture is the diameter of the reflecting surface.
activities.explanation: These points and lines help us draw how mirrors bend light.

activities.prompt: You look at a mirror whose reflecting surface curves inwards, like the inside of a bowl. Which mirror is it?
options: Concave mirror
Convex mirror
Flat mirror
Broken mirror
activities.explanation: A surface that curves inwards makes it a concave mirror. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: The reflecting surface of a spherical mirror is part of a ______.
activities.hint: Think of a round ball shape.
activities.explanation: That is why we call it a spherical mirror.

activities.prompt: Where does the centre of curvature of a convex mirror lie?
options: Behind the mirror
In front of the mirror
On the pole
On the aperture
activities.explanation: For a convex mirror, the centre of curvature sits behind the reflecting surface.

activities.prompt: Match each mirror word with its meaning.
pairs: Distance from pole to principal focus
activities.explanation: Four new words, each with its own job. You matched them all!

activities.prompt: Put the words in order to build the meaning of focal length.
items: The focal length is
the distance between
the pole
and the principal focus
activities.explanation: Focal length measures the gap from the pole to the principal focus. Nicely built!

activities.prompt: The principal axis is normal to the mirror at one special point. At which point is this?
options: The pole
The principal focus
The centre of curvature
The aperture
activities.explanation: The principal axis meets the mirror at right angles at the pole. Great thinking!

activities.prompt: A shiny ball is cut in half. The inside bowl shape is used as a mirror. The bowl curves inwards. What kind of mirror is this bowl?
options: A concave mirror, because the surface curves inwards
A convex mirror, because the ball was round before
A plane mirror, because the bowl is smooth
A spherical mirror, because it is made of metal

why.A convex mirror, because the ball was ro: Wrong. The old ball shape does not matter; the curved-in surface makes it concave.
why.A plane mirror, because the bowl is smoo: Wrong. A plane mirror is flat, but this surface is curved.
why.A spherical mirror, because it is made o: Wrong. Being metal does not decide the type; the inward curve does.

activities.explanation: Right. A reflecting surface curved inwards is a concave mirror.

activities.prompt: Riya holds a spoon. The back of the spoon curves outwards and shines. She looks at her face in it. What kind of mirror is the back of the spoon?
options: A concave mirror, because spoons are used for eating
A convex mirror, because the surface curves outwards
A plane mirror, because she can see her face in it
A concave mirror, because the spoon is small

why.A concave mirror, because spoons are use: Wrong. The use of a spoon does not decide the mirror type.
why.A plane mirror, because she can see her: Wrong. Seeing your face does not make it flat; the surface is curved.
why.A concave mirror, because the spoon is s: Wrong. Small size does not make it concave; the outward curve makes it convex.

activities.explanation: Right. A reflecting surface curved outwards is a convex mirror.

activities.prompt: A concave mirror is hanging on a wall. A student says its centre of curvature is behind the wall. Is the student right?
options: Yes, because the centre is always behind a mirror
Yes, because the wall hides the centre
No, because the centre of a concave mirror lies in front of it
No, because the centre is always inside the mirror glass

why.Yes, because the centre is always behind: Wrong. The centre is not always behind; it depends on the mirror type.
why.Yes, because the wall hides the centre: Wrong. Hiding a point does not decide where the point is.
why.No, because the centre is always inside: Wrong. The centre is not inside the glass; it lies in front of a concave mirror.

activities.explanation: Right. The centre of curvature of a concave mirror lies in front of it.

activities.prompt: Two mirrors hang side by side. One is concave and one is convex. Both are the same size. Where are their centres of curvature?
options: Both in front, because both mirrors face the room
Both behind, because centres are always behind mirrors
Concave in front, convex behind, because of their curves
Concave behind, convex in front, because of their curves

why.Both in front, because both mirrors face: Wrong. Facing the room does not fix the centre for both mirrors.
why.Both behind, because centres are always: Wrong. The centre is not always behind; it depends on the curve.
why.Concave behind, convex in front, because: Wrong. This swaps the two; concave has its centre in front.

activities.explanation: Right. A concave mirror has its centre in front, a convex mirror behind it.

activities.prompt: A student says: the focal length of a mirror is the distance from the pole to the centre of curvature. What is the flaw in this claim?
options: The claim is right, because both distances are the same
The claim is wrong, because focal length is measured to the focus
The claim is wrong, because focal length is measured to the aperture
The claim is wrong, because focal length is measured along the mirror surface

why.The claim is right, because both distanc: Wrong. The centre of curvature and the focus are not the same point.
why.The claim is wrong, because focal length: Wrong. The aperture is a width of the surface, not a distance for focal length.
Wrong. Focal length is a straight distance along the axis, not along the surface.

activities.explanation: Right. Focal length is the distance between the pole and the principal focus.

lessons.sceneCaption: A convex mirror diagram showing the focus, focal length, centre of curvature, principal axis and other basic parts.

lessons.title: Images by Spherical Mirrors and Uses

activities.prompt: Why do dentists and car side mirrors use such different mirrors?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Spherical Mirrors Make Images
activities.body: A concave mirror can make different kinds of images. It depends on where you place the object near the mirror. The image can be real or virtual. It can be magnified, reduced or the same size. To find where the image forms, we follow reflected rays. At least two reflected rays must meet at one point. Concave mirrors are used in torches, headlights and solar furnaces. Convex mirrors are used as rear-view mirrors in vehicles.
keyPoints: A concave mirror's image depends on the object's position.
The image can be real or virtual, and magnified, reduced or the same size.
At least two reflected rays must meet to fix the image position.
Concave mirrors work in torches and solar furnaces; convex mirrors work as rear-view mirrors.
activities.explanation: Mirrors bend rays of light in fixed ways, and that is what builds the image you see.

activities.prompt: A torch shines a straight beam far ahead. Inside, the small bulb sits near a curved concave mirror. Why does the beam go straight ahead instead of spreading out in all directions?
steps: The bulb sits at the principal focus of the concave mirror.
Light from the bulb hits the mirror and gets reflected.
A ray coming from the focus always leaves parallel to the principal axis.
So all the reflected rays travel together straight ahead, making a strong beam.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Ravi looks in the mirror fixed inside a bus to see the road behind. Which mirror is used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles?
options: A concave mirror
A plane mirror
A convex mirror
A broken mirror
activities.explanation: Convex mirrors are used as rear-view mirrors in vehicles. They give an erect, diminished image, so the driver sees a wide view.

activities.prompt: A ray of light travels parallel to the principal axis and strikes a concave mirror. Where does it go after reflection?
options: It bounces back along the same path
It passes through the principal focus
It spreads out and disappears
It stops at the pole of the mirror
activities.explanation: A ray parallel to the principal axis passes through the principal focus after reflection. This rule helps us draw images.

activities.prompt: A ray that passes through the centre of curvature of a concave mirror is reflected back along the ______ path.
activities.hint: Think of a ball thrown straight at a wall. It comes straight back.
activities.explanation: A ray through the centre of curvature hits the mirror head-on. So it retraces its own path.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to find the image made by a concave mirror.
items: Draw a ray from the object parallel to the principal axis
After reflection, the ray passes through the principal focus
Draw a second reflected ray from the object
The point where the two reflected rays meet gives the image position
activities.explanation: Well done! The intersection of at least two reflected rays gives the image position. The parallel-ray rule tells you where the first ray goes.

activities.prompt: In a torch, the bulb is kept at the focus of a concave mirror. Rays from the bulb hit the mirror. What kind of beam comes out of the torch?
options: A parallel beam going straight ahead
A beam that spreads out in all directions
A beam that stops at the mirror surface
A beam that bends back into the bulb

why.A beam that spreads out in all direction: This treats the mirror like an open bulb with no reflecting shape.
why.A beam that stops at the mirror surface: This forgets the mirror reflects the light back out of the torch.
why.A beam that bends back into the bulb: This confuses reflection with light going backwards into the source.

activities.explanation: Right. A ray from the focus leaves parallel to the principal axis.

activities.prompt: You bring your face very close to a concave mirror, nearer than the focus. You look for your image. What do you see?
options: A virtual image that cannot be caught on a screen
A real image shining on the wall behind you
No image at all, because you are too close
An upside-down image deep inside the mirror

why.A real image shining on the wall behind: Real images form only for some other object positions, not this one.
why.No image at all, because you are too clo: An image still forms; the position only changes its type.
why.An upside-down image deep inside the mir: Inverted images come from other positions, not from very close ones.

activities.explanation: Right. Very close objects give a virtual image in a concave mirror.

activities.prompt: Riya draws one reflected ray from a concave mirror. She marks one point on it and says, 'This is where the image is.' What is wrong with her claim?
options: She needs at least two reflected rays crossing at one point
She needs to draw the ray with a sharper pencil
She needs to measure the mirror with a scale first
One ray is enough if she draws it very long

why.She needs to draw the ray with a sharper: Neat drawing helps, but one ray alone can never fix the image point.
why.She needs to measure the mirror with a s: Measuring the mirror does not tell her where the rays actually meet.
why.One ray is enough if she draws it very l: A longer single ray still gives many points, not one image point.

activities.explanation: Right. The image forms where at least two reflected rays intersect.

lessons.title: Mirror Formula and Sign Convention

activities.prompt: Why do mirrors use plus and minus signs for distances?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Rule for Signs
activities.body: Spherical mirrors follow a rule for signs called the New Cartesian Sign Convention. The pole of the mirror is the origin, like zero on a number line. The principal axis is taken as the x-axis. The object always sits to the left of the mirror. Distances are measured from the pole. To the right is positive. To the left is negative.
keyPoints: The pole is the origin of the sign convention.
The principal axis is the x-axis.
Right of the origin is positive, left is negative.
activities.explanation: One fixed rule keeps every mirror answer in agreement.

activities.prompt: A candle stands to the left of a mirror. Its distance gets measured from the pole. Why does that distance come out negative?
steps: The object is always placed to the left of the mirror, so the candle must be on the left side.
Distances along the principal axis are measured from the pole, so the pole is the starting point, like the zero mark on a ruler.
Distances to the left of the origin are negative, so moving from the pole towards the candle means moving in the negative direction.
So the candle's distance is always written with a minus sign, because the object always sits on the negative side.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Mirror Formula and Magnification
activities.body: The mirror formula connects three things: object distance, image distance and focal length. It works for every spherical mirror and every position of the object. Magnification compares the height of the image with the height of the object. A negative magnification means the image is real. A positive magnification means the image is virtual.
keyPoints: The mirror formula links object distance, image distance and focal length.
Magnification is image height divided by object height.
Negative magnification means real; positive means virtual.
activities.explanation: The sign of magnification quickly tells you the kind of image.

activities.prompt: Which point is taken as the origin in the sign convention for mirrors?
options: The focus of the mirror
The centre of curvature
The pole of the mirror
The top of the object
activities.explanation: Well done! The pole is the starting point, like zero on a number line.

activities.prompt: A point lies to the left of the origin. Its distance is taken as...
options: Positive
Negative
Zero
activities.explanation: Left of the origin means negative, just like numbers left of zero.

activities.prompt: The object is always placed to the left of the mirror.
activities.explanation: Yes! Placing the object on the left keeps every problem the same.

activities.prompt: Distances parallel to the principal axis are always measured from the ______ of the mirror.
activities.hint: It is the middle point where the axis meets the mirror.
activities.explanation: The pole is the origin, so all these distances start from it.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the sign convention with its meaning.
activities.explanation: Great matching! These four rules cover the whole sign convention.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of setting up the sign convention in order.
items: Take the pole as the origin
Take the principal axis as the x-axis
Place the object to the left of the mirror
Measure all distances from the pole
activities.explanation: Perfect order! Fix the origin and axis first, then place the object and measure.

activities.prompt: You place a candle to the left of a mirror. You measure from the pole to the candle. What sign does this distance get?
options: Negative, because left of the pole is the negative side.
Positive, because the candle is a real object.
Negative, because the candle is far away.
Positive, because the candle gives out light.

why.Positive, because the candle is a real o: Wrong: being a real object does not decide the sign; the side of the pole does.
why.Negative, because the candle is far away: Wrong: the sign depends on direction, not on how far away the candle is.
why.Positive, because the candle gives out l: Wrong: giving light does not make a distance positive; direction from the pole decides it.

activities.explanation: Right: the object is always on the left, and left of the origin is the negative side.

activities.prompt: Distances along the axis are all measured from the pole. Why is the pole chosen as the starting point?
options: The pole is the fixed origin, so every distance starts there.
The pole is the brightest point of the mirror.
The pole is where the object must always stand.
The pole is the only part that reflects light.

why.The pole is the brightest point of the m: Wrong: brightness is not the reason; the pole is chosen as the origin.
why.The pole is where the object must always: Wrong: the object stands to the left of the mirror, not at the pole.
why.The pole is the only part that reflects: Wrong: the whole mirror surface reflects light, not just the pole.

activities.explanation: Right: the pole is taken as the origin, so it is the single starting point for all distances.

activities.prompt: An image forms to the right of a mirror. You measure from the pole to the image. What sign does the image distance get?
options: Negative, because images are always negative.
Positive, because the image is upside down.
Positive, because right of the pole is the positive side.
Negative, because the image is far away.

why.Negative, because images are always nega: Wrong: images are not always negative; the side of the pole decides the sign.
why.Positive, because the image is upside do: Wrong: upside down is about magnification, not about the sign of distance.
Wrong: how far away the image is does not change the sign.

activities.explanation: Right: distances to the right of the origin are positive, so this image distance is positive.

lessons.title: Refraction and Refractive Index

activities.prompt: Why does a pencil look bent when dipped in water?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Light Changes Direction
activities.body: Have you seen a pencil look bent in a glass of water? That is refraction. When light travels slantwise from one medium, like air, into another, like water or glass, its direction changes. This happens because light travels at different speeds in different media. The light bends towards or away from a line called the normal.
keyPoints: Light changes direction when it passes slantwise from one medium to another.
This bending of light is called refraction.
Refraction happens because the speed of light changes in different media.
activities.explanation: Light bends whenever it crosses slantwise into a medium where its speed is different.

activities.title: Snell's Law and Refractive Index
activities.body: The bending of light follows a rule. The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal all lie in one plane. Snell's law says: divide the sine of the angle of incidence by the sine of the angle of refraction. You always get the same constant. This constant is called the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first.
keyPoints: The incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in the same plane.
Snell's law: sine of angle of incidence divided by sine of angle of refraction is constant.
This constant is the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first.
activities.explanation: Snell's law gives a fixed number for each pair of media, called the refractive index.

activities.prompt: A straw in a glass of water looks bent at the water surface. What is this change in the direction of light called?
options: Reflection
Refraction
Absorption
activities.explanation: The change of direction of light when it passes from one medium to another is called refraction. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: Why does the bottom of a pond look raised to you?
options: Because the water makes light bend
Because the water soaks up the light
Because the pond is very shallow
activities.explanation: Light bends as it passes through the water, so the bottom appears raised. You are getting the hang of refraction!

activities.prompt: A pencil partly dipped in water looks shifted at the place where it meets the water surface.
activities.explanation: Yes! Light bends at the air-water surface, so the pencil looks displaced there. Great thinking.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with what happens.
pairs: Emergent ray from a glass slab
activities.explanation: Light bends towards the normal entering glass, and away from it leaving glass. Superb matching!

activities.prompt: In Snell's law, the constant you get is called the ______ index of the second medium with respect to the first.
activities.hint: It tells you how much the light bends between the two media.
activities.explanation: The constant in Snell's law is the refractive index. You remembered it well!

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order as light passes through a rectangular glass slab.
items: The incident ray strikes the glass slab
The ray bends towards the normal as it enters the glass
The ray bends away from the normal as it leaves the glass
The emergent ray travels parallel to the incident ray
activities.explanation: Light bends towards the normal on entering glass, away on leaving, and comes out parallel. Brilliant ordering!

activities.prompt: A student says: 'Light bends at the water surface because water pushes the light sideways.' A friend tests the idea with a glass slab too. Why is the student's claim wrong?
options: Because light only bends when it enters water, not glass.
Because bending happens when light speed changes, not from a push.
Because light never changes direction in any transparent material.
Because a push would make the light bend the same way both ways.

why.Because light only bends when it enters: Light bends in glass too, so this reason does not fix the claim.
why.Because light never changes direction in: Light does change direction when it crosses obliquely into a new medium.
why.Because a push would make the light bend: This argues about pushes but misses the real cause, the speed change.

activities.explanation: Right. Refraction happens because the speed of light changes in different media.

activities.prompt: Two students measure angles for light going from air into glass. Both divide sine of the incidence angle by sine of the refraction angle. They use different angles of incidence. What should they find, and what does the number mean?
options: Different numbers each time; each number is a new speed of light.
The same number each time; it is the refractive index of glass in air.
The same number each time; it is the speed of light in glass.
Different numbers each time; the angles do not follow any rule.

why.Different numbers each time; each number: Snell's law says the ratio stays constant, so the numbers should not differ.
why.The same number each time; it is the spe: The ratio is a refractive index, not a speed of light.
why.Different numbers each time; the angles: The incident ray, refracted ray and normal follow Snell's law, so a rule exists.

activities.explanation: Right. The constant ratio is the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first.

activities.prompt: A student draws a refraction experiment. She draws the incident ray and the refracted ray, but she draws the normal on a different table surface, tilted away from both rays. What is wrong with her drawing?
options: The normal must be drawn longer than both rays.
The normal must touch the refracted ray only.
The normal must lie in the same plane as both rays.
The normal must always point along the incident ray.

why.The normal must be drawn longer than bot: Length of the normal line does not matter for refraction.
why.The normal must touch the refracted ray: The normal matters for the incident ray too, not just one ray.
why.The normal must always point along the i: The normal is not along the incident ray; it has its own direction.

activities.explanation: Right. The incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in the same plane.
