lessons.title: Lenses and Power

activities.prompt: Why do some glasses make things look bigger and others smaller?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is a lens?
activities.body: A lens is a clear material with one or both surfaces curved like a ball. A convex lens is fatter in the middle and thin at the edges. It bends light rays inward, so we say it converges them. A concave lens is the opposite: thin in the middle and fat at the edges. It bends light rays outward, so we say it diverges them.
keyPoints: A lens is transparent with spherical surface or surfaces.
A convex lens is thicker at the middle and converges light.
A concave lens is thicker at the edges and diverges light.
activities.explanation: The shape of a lens decides which way it bends light.

activities.prompt: Priya finds two lenses with no labels. She sends parallel torch rays through each one. Rays through lens A meet at one point. Rays through lens B spread apart. How can she tell which lens is convex?
steps: A convex lens converges light rays, so it makes parallel rays come together at one point.
So lens A must be the convex lens, because its rays meet at a point.
A concave lens diverges light rays, so it makes parallel rays spread apart.
So lens B is the concave lens, and Priya can now label both lenses correctly.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Special points on a lens
activities.body: The optical centre is the central point of a lens. A ray that goes through it passes straight on without bending. Parallel rays that hit a convex lens meet at its principal focus. Parallel rays hitting a concave lens seem to spread out from its principal focus. A concave lens always makes a virtual, erect and diminished image. The power of a lens tells us how strong it is.
keyPoints: A ray through the optical centre goes straight without deviation.
Parallel rays meet at the principal focus of a convex lens.
A concave lens always gives a virtual, erect and diminished image.
activities.explanation: Every lens has special points and rules that help us draw its rays.

activities.prompt: You hold a lens and feel that it is thicker at the middle than at the edges. Which lens is it?
options: Concave lens
Convex lens
A broken lens
A flat mirror
activities.explanation: A convex lens is thicker at the middle than at the edges. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: A convex lens brings parallel light rays together, so we say it ______ them.
activities.hint: Think of the opposite of spreading out.
activities.explanation: A convex lens converges light rays, pulling them together at one point.

activities.prompt: A concave lens makes light rays spread outward.
activities.explanation: A concave lens diverges light rays, which means it makes them spread out.

activities.prompt: Match each lens word with what it means.
activities.explanation: Each word tells you about a lens shape or what it does to light. Great matching!

activities.prompt: A light ray passes straight through the optical centre of a lens. What happens to it?
options: It bends towards the middle
It bounces back
It passes without any deviation
It stops at the lens
activities.explanation: A ray through the optical centre passes without any deviation, so it goes straight on.

activities.prompt: The power of a lens is linked to its focal length. How?
options: It is the reciprocal of the focal length
It is double the focal length
It is the same as the focal length
It is half the focal length
activities.explanation: The power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length. You have cracked the big idea of this lesson!

activities.prompt: A torch sends parallel rays through lens A. The rays meet at one point after the lens. Through lens B, the rays spread apart. Which lens is the convex lens?
options: Lens A, because it brings the rays together
Lens B, because it spreads the rays apart
Lens A, because its rays travel straight
Lens B, because its rays bend the most

why.Lens B, because it spreads the rays apar: This child thinks spreading rays means bending more, but spreading is diverging.
why.Lens A, because its rays travel straight: This child thinks all rays pass straight, but only the optical centre ray does.
why.Lens B, because its rays bend the most: This child picked the lens with the wrong effect, since spreading means concave.

activities.explanation: Right: a convex lens converges light rays, so parallel rays meet at one point.

activities.prompt: Meera wants to focus sunlight on paper. She picks a lens thicker at the edges than at the middle. Why will the paper not get a hot spot?
options: This lens spreads rays out, so they never meet
This lens blocks sunlight, so no rays pass through
The lens is too thick, so the light gets weaker
Sunlight is too weak, so no lens can heat paper

why.This lens blocks sunlight, so no rays pa: This child thinks the lens stops light, but lenses are transparent.
why.The lens is too thick, so the light gets: This child blames thickness itself, but the shape of thickness matters.
why.Sunlight is too weak, so no lens can hea: This child blames the sunlight, but a convex lens could focus it.

activities.explanation: Right: a concave lens diverges rays, so they cannot come together at one point.

activities.prompt: Lens P has a short focal length. Lens Q has a long focal length. Which lens has more power?
options: Lens P, because power grows when focal length gets shorter
Lens Q, because power grows when focal length gets longer
Lens P, because a short lens is always made stronger
Lens Q, because a long lens bends light more strongly

why.Lens Q, because power grows when focal l: This child thinks power and focal length grow together, but they go opposite ways.
why.Lens P, because a short lens is always m: This child guesses from the word short, not from the reciprocal rule.
why.Lens Q, because a long lens bends light: This child thinks a long lens bends more, but a long focal length means less bending.

activities.explanation: Right: power is the reciprocal of focal length, so a short focal length means more power.

activities.context: Meera walks into a windowless storeroom and switches on a small torch. She holds up a cardboard cutout and sees its sharp shadow on the far wall. She then stands facing a mirror mounted on the wall and raises her right hand, noticing that the figure in the mirror raises the hand on her left side. Curious, she takes a few steps back from the mirror and keeps watching the figure.
activities.prompt: If Meera replaces the small torch with a much bigger light source, what is she most likely to notice about the shadow on the wall?
options: The shadow will look blurred at its edges instead of sharp.
The shadow will become even sharper with clearer edges.
The shadow will vanish completely from the wall.
The shadow will stay exactly as sharp as it was before.

why.The shadow will become even sharper with: Wrong: sharpness comes from a small source; a bigger source works the other way.
why.The shadow will vanish completely from t: Wrong: an opaque object still blocks light, so a shadow still forms.
why.The shadow will stay exactly as sharp as: Wrong: the size of the source is what controls sharpness, so it will change.

activities.explanation: Correct: a small source gives a sharp shadow, so a bigger source will not keep the edges sharp.

activities.context: Meera walks into a windowless storeroom and switches on a small torch. She holds up a cardboard cutout and sees its sharp shadow on the far wall. She then stands facing a mirror mounted on the wall and raises her right hand, noticing that the figure in the mirror raises the hand on her left side. Curious, she takes a few steps back from the mirror and keeps watching the figure.
activities.prompt: Meera steps back from the mirror. What will happen to her image?
options: It moves back too, staying as far behind the mirror as she is in front.
It stays fixed in the same spot behind the mirror.
It comes closer to the mirror as she moves away.
It becomes smaller than her as the distance increases.

why.It stays fixed in the same spot behind t: Wrong: the image position is tied to the object's position, so it cannot stay fixed.
why.It comes closer to the mirror as she mov: Wrong: moving away increases the object distance, so the image distance increases too.
why.It becomes smaller than her as the dista: Wrong: a plane mirror image is always the same size as the object.

activities.explanation: Correct: the image is always as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): In a completely dark room, a book lying on the table cannot be seen.
Reason (R): We see an object only when light reflected from it reaches our eyes.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: In darkness no light is reflected from the book to the eyes, so the reason correctly explains the assertion.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A small light source produces a sharp shadow of an opaque object.
Reason (R): Light appears to travel in curved paths that bend around obstacles.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but light travels in straight lines, so the reason is false.

activities.prompt: Explain why you cannot see anything the moment you enter a dark room, and what changes when a light is switched on.
activities.answer: We see an object only when light reflected from it reaches our eyes. In a dark room there is no light, so nothing is reflected from the objects around me into my eyes, and I cannot see anything. When a light is switched on, light falls on the objects in the room, and this light is reflected from their surfaces to my eyes. That reflected light lets me make out the objects, which is why the room becomes visible the moment the light comes on.
points: Seeing requires light reflected from an object to reach the eyes.
In a dark room no light is available, so nothing is reflected to the eyes.
Switching on a light lets objects reflect light to the eyes, making them visible.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a lab activity, Riya is given two spherical mirrors. Mirror A has its reflecting surface curved inwards, while Mirror B has its reflecting surface curved outwards. Her teacher asks her to mark the centre of curvature of each mirror on a diagram, draw the straight line through the pole and centre of curvature, and then measure the distance from the pole to the principal focus of Mirror A.
activities.prompt: Riya marks the centre of curvature of Mirror B on the same side as its shining surface. What should she correct in her diagram?
options: She should shift the mark to the side behind the mirror, away from its reflecting surface
She should shift the mark onto the reflecting surface itself
She should shift the mark onto the pole of the mirror
She should erase the mark, since a convex mirror has no centre of curvature

why.She should shift the mark onto the refle: Wrong: the centre of curvature always lies outside the reflecting surface, never on it
why.She should shift the mark onto the pole: Wrong: the pole is the point the principal axis passes through, not the centre of curvature
why.She should erase the mark, since a conve: Wrong: every spherical mirror has a centre of curvature; only its position differs

activities.explanation: Correct: for a mirror curved outwards, the centre of the sphere lies on the non-reflecting side, behind the mirror

activities.context: During a lab activity, Riya is given two spherical mirrors. Mirror A has its reflecting surface curved inwards, while Mirror B has its reflecting surface curved outwards. Her teacher asks her to mark the centre of curvature of each mirror on a diagram, draw the straight line through the pole and centre of curvature, and then measure the distance from the pole to the principal focus of Mirror A.
activities.prompt: Riya measures across the widest part of Mirror A's shining surface and records this as its focal length. What has she actually measured, and what should she measure instead?
options: She has measured the aperture; she should measure the distance between the pole and the principal focus
She has measured the focal length correctly; no change is needed
She has measured the aperture; she should measure the distance from the centre of curvature to the focus
She has measured the principal axis; she should measure the distance from the pole to the edge of the mirror

why.She has measured the focal length correc: Wrong: a distance across the surface is not the pole-to-focus distance that defines focal length
why.She has measured the aperture; she shoul: Wrong: the focal length is measured from the pole, not from the centre of curvature
why.She has measured the principal axis; she: Wrong: a straight line through pole and centre of curvature is the principal axis, and pole-to-edge is not the focal length either

activities.explanation: Correct: the diameter of the reflecting surface is the aperture, while the focal length is the pole-to-focus distance

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The centre of curvature of a concave mirror lies in front of its reflecting surface.
Reason (R): A concave mirror has its reflecting surface curved inwards, towards the centre of the sphere.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Because the surface caves inwards, the centre of the sphere of which it is a part falls on the front, reflecting side.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The aperture of a spherical mirror is the distance between its pole and its principal focus.
Reason (R): The focal length of a spherical mirror is measured along the straight line through its pole and centre of curvature.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The aperture is the diameter of the reflecting surface, not the pole-to-focus distance, though the reason about focal length is true.

activities.prompt: Explain why the centre of curvature of a concave mirror lies in front of it, while that of a convex mirror lies behind it.
activities.answer: A spherical mirror is part of a sphere, so its centre of curvature is the centre of that sphere, and it always lies outside the reflecting surface. In a concave mirror the reflecting surface is curved inwards, towards the centre of the sphere. Since the hollow, reflecting side faces the centre, the centre of curvature lies in front of the mirror. In a convex mirror the reflecting surface bulges outwards, so the reflecting side faces away from the centre of the sphere; the centre therefore lies on the other side, behind the mirror.
points: Centre of curvature is the centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part
It always lies outside the reflecting surface
Concave surface curves inwards, so the centre is in front
Convex surface curves outwards, so the centre is behind
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Meera is helping her uncle on a long drive. She notices that the mirror mounted on the side of the car shows the vehicles behind as upright but noticeably smaller than they look in the small mirror inside. Later, at a community centre, she sees a huge curved dish mirror facing the sun, with a pot placed at one spot in front of it, heating up strongly. That night, her torch throws a bright, straight beam of light onto a distant wall.
activities.prompt: Why should Meera's uncle still turn his head before overtaking, even though the side mirror shows the road behind clearly?
options: Because the mirror makes the vehicles behind look smaller than they really are, so their actual distance is hard to judge
Because the mirror inverts the image of the vehicles behind, so they appear upside down
Because the mirror shows only a real image that disappears when a vehicle comes close
Because the mirror magnifies the vehicles behind, making them look much closer than they are

why.Because the mirror inverts the image of: Wrong: the image in such a mirror is erect, not inverted
why.Because the mirror shows only a real ima: Wrong: the image is not a real one that vanishes; it is always visible and upright
why.Because the mirror magnifies the vehicle: Wrong: the image is diminished, not magnified, so this is the opposite of what happens

activities.explanation: Correct: a diminished erect image makes objects seem farther away, so judging distance needs care

activities.context: Meera is helping her uncle on a long drive. She notices that the mirror mounted on the side of the car shows the vehicles behind as upright but noticeably smaller than they look in the small mirror inside. Later, at a community centre, she sees a huge curved dish mirror facing the sun, with a pot placed at one spot in front of it, heating up strongly. That night, her torch throws a bright, straight beam of light onto a distant wall.
activities.prompt: Meera's torch gives a straight, strong beam. What would happen to the beam if the tiny bulb were shifted away from the special point inside the curved reflector?
options: The reflected light would no longer go out as a parallel beam, so the spot on the wall would spread out and become dimmer
The reflected light would bend back into the torch, so nothing at all would be seen on the wall
The reflected light would travel along the same path back to the bulb, making the torch hotter
The reflected light would become brighter and sharper, since moving the bulb always improves the beam

why.The reflected light would bend back into: Wrong: reflected rays do not turn back into the torch; they simply lose their parallel arrangement
why.The reflected light would travel along t: Wrong: rays return along the same path only when they pass through the centre of curvature, not when the bulb shifts
why.The reflected light would become brighte: Wrong: moving the bulb away from the focus spoils the parallel beam rather than improving it

activities.explanation: Correct: only a bulb at the principal focus gives reflected rays parallel to the principal axis, producing a tight beam

activities.context: Meera is helping her uncle on a long drive. She notices that the mirror mounted on the side of the car shows the vehicles behind as upright but noticeably smaller than they look in the small mirror inside. Later, at a community centre, she sees a huge curved dish mirror facing the sun, with a pot placed at one spot in front of it, heating up strongly. That night, her torch throws a bright, straight beam of light onto a distant wall.
activities.prompt: At the community centre, why is the cooking pot kept at one particular spot in front of the large curved mirror?
options: Because sunlight striking the mirror is directed so that the reflected rays pass through the principal focus, where the heating is strongest
Because the mirror reflects sunlight equally in all directions, and the pot simply marks the centre of the setup
Because the pot blocks the reflected rays and stores their energy as it slowly turns upside down
Because the mirror sends sunlight back towards the sun, and the pot catches the heat bouncing off the sky

why.Because the mirror reflects sunlight equ: Wrong: the mirror does not scatter light equally everywhere; the rays are brought together at one point
why.Because the pot blocks the reflected ray: Wrong: the pot does not work by blocking or flipping; it works by sitting where the reflected rays meet
why.Because the mirror sends sunlight back t: Wrong: the heat comes from rays reflected by the mirror itself, not from anything bouncing off the sky

activities.explanation: Correct: parallel sunlight after reflection passes through the focus, so concentrating the heat there is exactly why the pot sits at that spot

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A concave mirror can form a real image of an object.
Reason (R): For some positions of the object, the reflected rays from the mirror meet at a point, and the meeting point of at least two reflected rays gives the image position.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the meeting of reflected rays is exactly why the image formed is a real one.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A convex mirror always forms an image that is larger than the object.
Reason (R): Convex mirrors are used as rear-view mirrors in vehicles.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because a convex mirror always gives a diminished image, while the reason is a true fact about its use.

activities.prompt: Explain why the same concave mirror can give a magnified image of an object at one position and a reduced image at another position.
activities.answer: The nature of the image formed by a concave mirror depends on where the object is placed relative to the pole, the principal focus and the centre of curvature. As the object is moved between and beyond these points, the mirror can produce an image that is magnified, reduced or the same size as the object. The image position in each case is found where at least two reflected rays intersect, using rays such as one parallel to the principal axis that passes through the focus after reflection. Since different object positions change where these reflected rays meet, the same mirror gives different image sizes.
points: Image depends on object position relative to P, F and C
Image can be magnified, reduced or the same size
Image position found by intersection of at least two reflected rays
Example ray: parallel ray passes through the focus after reflection
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a science lab session, Meera sets up a spherical mirror on an optical bench to study image formation. Her teacher reminds the class that every measurement must follow the New Cartesian Sign Convention. Meera places her object on the left side of the mirror and records distances carefully in her practical file. Later, she calculates a magnification value and must decide what it tells her about the image before writing her conclusion.
activities.prompt: Meera first measures the object distance starting from the outer edge of the mirror stand instead of the marked point on the mirror. According to the convention she is following, what should she do?
options: Keep the measurement, since any point near the mirror works equally well
Re-measure starting from the pole of the mirror
Re-measure starting from the right side of the mirror
Keep the measurement but change its sign to negative

why.Keep the measurement, since any point ne: Wrong: the convention fixes one reference point, not any convenient point
why.Re-measure starting from the right side: Wrong: the reference point is the pole, not simply the right side
why.Keep the measurement but change its sign: Wrong: changing the sign does not fix measuring from the wrong starting point

activities.explanation: Correct: distances parallel to the principal axis must be measured from the pole, which is the origin

activities.context: During a science lab session, Meera sets up a spherical mirror on an optical bench to study image formation. Her teacher reminds the class that every measurement must follow the New Cartesian Sign Convention. Meera places her object on the left side of the mirror and records distances carefully in her practical file. Later, she calculates a magnification value and must decide what it tells her about the image before writing her conclusion.
activities.prompt: Meera's calculation gives a positive image distance. Using the sign convention, what does this tell her about where the image lies?
options: On the left side, the same side as the object
To the right of the pole
Exactly at the pole
The sign of the distance gives no information about position

why.On the left side, the same side as the o: Wrong: the object side is the left, where distances are negative
why.Exactly at the pole: Wrong: a distance of zero would mean the image is at the origin, not a positive distance
why.The sign of the distance gives no inform: Wrong: the whole purpose of the sign convention is to encode position through signs

activities.explanation: Correct: distances to the right of the origin are positive, so a positive image distance means the image is on the right

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Light Reflection and Refraction

activities.prompt: It is night and all the lights are off. Why can you not see your book on the table?
options: Your eyes switch off at night
No light reflects from the book to your eyes
The book soaks up darkness around it
Books can only be seen in daylight
activities.explanation: We see an object when light reflected from it reaches our eyes. With no light in the room, nothing reaches your eyes. Switch on the lamp and the book appears!

activities.prompt: The image formed by a plane mirror is the same size as the object.
activities.explanation: A plane mirror always makes a virtual, erect image that matches the object in size. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: When light bounces off a mirror, the angle of incidence equals the angle of ______.
activities.hint: It is the name for light bouncing back.
activities.explanation: This is the first law of reflection. The two angles are always equal.

activities.prompt: Which mirror is used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles?
options: Concave mirror
Plane mirror
Convex mirror
Broken mirror
activities.explanation: Convex mirrors always give an erect, though diminished, image. That wide view helps the driver see traffic behind.

activities.prompt: A pencil stands in a glass of water. It looks bent at the water surface. Why?
options: Light bounces off the water surface
Light changes direction as it passes from water to air
The pencil really bends inside water
Water washes away the pencil's colour
activities.explanation: This change of direction of light is called refraction. It happens when light travels obliquely from one medium to another.

activities.prompt: Match each mirror word with its meaning.
pairs: Distance from pole to principal focus
activities.explanation: These four words describe spherical mirrors. Knowing them helps you read every ray diagram.

activities.prompt: Put these steps of light passing through a glass slab in order.
items: Light strikes the glass slab from air
Inside the glass, the ray bends towards the normal
Leaving the glass, the ray bends away from the normal
The emergent ray runs parallel to the incident ray
activities.explanation: Light bends towards the normal entering glass and away from it leaving glass. So the emergent ray ends up parallel to the incident ray.

activities.prompt: In the New Cartesian Sign Convention, distances to the left of the pole are taken as ______.
activities.hint: The opposite of positive.
activities.explanation: Distances to the right of the origin are positive, and distances to the left are negative. The pole is the origin.

activities.prompt: A concave lens can form a magnified image of an object.
activities.explanation: A concave lens always gives a virtual, erect and diminished image. It can never make things look bigger.

activities.prompt: Match each lens fact with its partner.
activities.explanation: Convex lenses bring rays together and concave lenses spread them out. A ray through the optical centre never deviates.

boss.sceneAlt: A diagram showing a light ray hitting a mirror, with the incident ray, normal and reflected ray all in the same plane.
boss.sceneCaption: The law of reflection: the incident ray, normal and reflected ray all lie in one plane.

chapters.title: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the human eye; power of accommodation and eye conditions; defects of vision and their correction; refraction of light through a prism.

lessons.title: The Human Eye

activities.prompt: How does your eye turn light into the pictures you see?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Your Eye: A Living Camera
activities.body: Your eye is a very valuable and sensitive sense organ. It works like a camera. Light first enters through the cornea, a thin, transparent bulge at the front. The pupil controls how much light comes in. The lens makes fine adjustments to focus. Then the lens makes an inverted image on the retina. Retina cells send signals to the brain through the optic nerves.
keyPoints: The eye works like a camera.
Light enters through the thin cornea, where most refraction happens.
The retina gets the image and sends signals to the brain.
activities.explanation: Your eye gathers light, focuses it, and tells your brain what it sees.

activities.prompt: Riya reads her book clearly. Then she looks up and sees a far mountain clearly too. Her camera needs a new lens for that. Why can her eye do it without any change?
steps: The eye works like a camera, so both make a picture on a light-sensitive screen.
The eye's screen is the retina, and the lens makes the picture on it.
A camera needs a new lens for a new distance, but the eye's crystalline lens makes fine adjustments instead.
So Riya's eye refocuses by itself, and both the book and the mountain look clear.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Through which part does light first enter your eye?
options: The retina
The cornea
The optic nerve
The pupil
activities.explanation: Light enters the eye through the thin cornea at the front. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: On a bright sunny day, which part controls how much light enters your eye?
options: The pupil
The cornea
The retina
The optic nerve
activities.explanation: The pupil controls how much light enters the eye. That is why it changes in bright light.

activities.prompt: The eye lens makes an image on the light-sensitive ______ at the back of the eye.
activities.hint: This part sends signals to the brain.
activities.explanation: The lens system makes an image on the light-sensitive retina. Great thinking!

activities.prompt: Match each eye part to its job.
pairs: Gets the image of what you see
activities.explanation: Each part has its own job, and together they help you see.

activities.prompt: Put the journey of light through the eye in the correct order.
items: Light enters through the cornea
The pupil controls how much light passes
The lens focuses the light
An image forms on the retina
Signals travel to the brain through the optic nerve
activities.explanation: Light enters, gets controlled, gets focused, forms an image, then the brain gets the message. Perfect order!

activities.prompt: What kind of image does the eye lens form on the retina?
options: An upright real image
An inverted real image
An inverted shadow
A blurred picture
activities.explanation: The eye lens forms an inverted real image on the retina. Your brain sorts it out for you!

activities.prompt: You walk from bright sunlight into a dark room. At first you see very little. Soon you see much better. The pupil controls how much light enters the eye. What did your pupil most likely do?
options: It grew bigger, to let more light enter.
It grew smaller, to let more light enter.
It grew bigger, to let less light enter.
It stayed the same size the whole time.

why.It grew smaller, to let more light enter: Wrong. This child mixed up the sizes; a smaller opening lets in less light.
Wrong. This child forgot that a bigger opening cannot let in less light.
Wrong. This child forgot the pupil must change size to control the light.

activities.explanation: Right. A bigger opening lets more light in, so the dark room becomes visible.

activities.prompt: The eye lens makes an inverted real image on the retina. Retina cells send signals to the brain through optic nerves. A baby sees her mother standing upright. Why does the baby not see her upside down?
options: Her brain understands the signals and shows her mother upright.
Her retina flips the image upright before sending the signals.
Her eye lens really makes an upright image, not inverted.
Her cornea flips the image back before the lens sees it.

why.Her retina flips the image upright befor: Wrong. This child thinks the retina fixes the image; it only sends signals.
why.Her eye lens really makes an upright ima: Wrong. This child forgot the lens image on the retina is truly inverted.
why.Her cornea flips the image back before t: Wrong. This child thinks the cornea flips images; it only bends light.

activities.explanation: Right. The brain receives the signals and makes sense of them for her.

activities.prompt: Most refraction of light entering the eye happens at the cornea's outer surface. The crystalline lens only makes fine adjustments to focus. Your friend says the eye lens does most of the bending of light. What is the flaw in his claim?
options: He forgot that the lens sits behind the pupil.
He mixed up which part bends the light the most.
He forgot the lens changes focus for near and far.
He forgot the retina needs an inverted image to work.

why.He forgot that the lens sits behind the: Wrong. Where the lens sits does not decide how much it bends light.
why.He forgot the lens changes focus for nea: Wrong. That is a true fact, but it is not the flaw in his claim.
why.He forgot the retina needs an inverted i: Wrong. The image direction has nothing to do with his claim.

activities.explanation: Right. The cornea bends light most; the lens only makes fine adjustments.

activities.prompt: Light enters the eye through the thin cornea. The cornea is a transparent bulge on the front of the eyeball. A friend covers the white sides of her eye, but not the front bulge. Can she still see?
options: Yes, light still enters through the clear front bulge.
No, light can only enter through the white sides.
Yes, because the pupil makes its own light inside.
No, because the cornea blocks all light from entering.

why.No, light can only enter through the whi: Wrong. This child thinks the white sides are the entry door for light.
why.Yes, because the pupil makes its own lig: Wrong. This child thinks the eye makes light; eyes only receive light.
why.No, because the cornea blocks all light: Wrong. This child forgot the cornea is transparent, so light passes through.

activities.explanation: Right. The transparent cornea at the front still lets light enter.

activities.prompt: The eyeball is roughly spherical and about 2.3 cm across. Your friend says your eyeball is as wide as a big cricket ball. A cricket ball is far wider than 2.3 cm. What is wrong with his claim?
options: The eyeball is much smaller than a cricket ball.
The eyeball really is as wide as a cricket ball.
The eyeball is flat, so it cannot be compared.
The eyeball looks big because it holds a big lens.

why.The eyeball really is as wide as a crick: Wrong. This child forgot the real size of the eyeball.
why.The eyeball is flat, so it cannot be com: Wrong. This child forgot the eyeball is roughly spherical, not flat.
why.The eyeball looks big because it holds a: Wrong. This child thinks the lens size sets the eyeball size.

activities.explanation: Right. 2.3 cm is far less than the width of a cricket ball.

lessons.sceneCaption: A labelled diagram of the human eye showing the cornea, lens and retina that make an image.

lessons.title: Power of Accommodation and Eye Conditions

activities.prompt: How does your eye instantly focus on a bird and then your book?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Your Eye Can Change Shape!
activities.body: The lens in your eye is made of a fibrous, jelly-like material. Around it are ciliary muscles. These muscles can change the curvature of the lens. When the curvature changes, the focal length of the lens changes too. This clever trick lets you see both a faraway kite and a book in your lap clearly.
keyPoints: The eye lens is fibrous and jelly-like.
Ciliary muscles change the curvature of the lens.
Changing the curvature changes the focal length.
activities.explanation: Your eye adjusts its lens like a camera adjusts its focus.

activities.prompt: Kabir reads a comic book close to his face. Then he looks up at a bird flying far away. He wonders: how can the same eye see both clearly?
steps: The lens is jelly-like, so it is soft and can change shape.
For the near book, the ciliary muscles contract, so the lens gets thick and its focal length becomes short.
For the far bird, the ciliary muscles relax, so the lens gets thin and its focal length becomes long.
So the same eye sees both clearly because it can adjust its focal length. This power is called accommodation.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Limits of the Eye
activities.body: The lens cannot make its focal length shorter and shorter forever. There is a minimum limit. So a normal eye sees clearly from 25 cm away up to infinity. Also, in old age the crystalline lens can turn milky and cloudy. This condition is called cataract, and it makes vision blurry.
keyPoints: The focal length cannot decrease below a minimum limit.
A normal eye sees clearly between 25 cm and infinity.
A cloudy, milky lens in old age is called cataract.
activities.explanation: Even a healthy eye has limits, and age can cloud the lens.

activities.prompt: Which part of the eye changes the curvature of the lens?
options: The ciliary muscles
The retina
The optic nerve
The pupil
activities.explanation: Ciliary muscles squeeze or relax to change the lens shape.

activities.prompt: Accommodation is the power of the eye lens to adjust its ______.
activities.hint: It is what changes when the lens curvature changes.
activities.explanation: Well done! Accommodation means the lens can change its focal length.

activities.prompt: When the ciliary muscles relax, the lens becomes thin and its focal length increases.
activities.explanation: Relaxed muscles let the lens go thin, so the focal length grows. That helps you see distant objects.

activities.prompt: You look at a small ant crawling near your feet. What do your ciliary muscles do?
options: They contract
They relax
They disappear
They stay still
activities.explanation: For nearby objects, the muscles contract, the lens grows thicker and the focal length drops.

activities.prompt: Match each action with what happens in the eye.
activities.explanation: Relaxed muscles suit far things; contracted muscles suit near things.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order when your eye looks at a nearby object.
items: You look at a nearby object
Ciliary muscles contract
The eye lens becomes thicker
The focal length decreases
You see the nearby object clearly
activities.explanation: Great ordering! Contracting muscles thicken the lens, shortening the focal length for near vision.

activities.prompt: Sara reads a book close to her eyes. Then she looks at a faraway tree. What happens inside her eye?
options: The ciliary muscles relax, the lens gets thin, its focal length increases.
The ciliary muscles contract, the lens gets thick, its focal length increases.
The ciliary muscles relax, the lens gets thick, its focal length decreases.
The ciliary muscles contract, the lens keeps its shape, its focal length stays same.

why.The ciliary muscles contract, the lens g: This child reused the near-reading action and mixed up how focal length changes.
why.The ciliary muscles relax, the lens gets: This child thinks relaxing makes the lens thick, but relaxing makes it thin.
why.The ciliary muscles contract, the lens k: This child thinks the lens never changes shape when muscles act.

activities.explanation: Right. For far objects the muscles relax, the lens thins, and focal length grows.

activities.prompt: Ravi holds his book 5 cm from his eyes. The letters look blurry. Why?
options: The lens cannot make its focal length shorter than a minimum limit.
The lens cannot make its focal length longer than a maximum limit.
The ciliary muscles get too relaxed to work on near objects.
The lens has already become milky and cloudy like in old age.

why.The lens cannot make its focal length lo: This child flipped the direction; near seeing needs a shorter focal length, not longer.
why.The ciliary muscles get too relaxed to w: This child blames the muscles, but the real limit is the lens's shortest focal length.
why.The lens has already become milky and cl: This child jumps to cataract, but cloudiness is an old-age change, not a near-reading limit.

activities.explanation: Right. Near objects need a short focal length, but it cannot go below a minimum.

activities.prompt: Grandma says everything looks cloudy, even in bright light. The doctor checks her eye lens. What is most likely found?
options: The lens has become milky and cloudy, which is called cataract.
The ciliary muscles have become too strong and keep squeezing the lens.
The lens has become too thin, so its focal length is too long.
The lens material has turned hard like bone, so light cannot pass.

why.The ciliary muscles have become too stro: This child blames the muscles, but the cloudiness is in the lens itself.
why.The lens has become too thin, so its foc: This child links cloudiness to lens thickness, but thickness is not the cause here.
why.The lens material has turned hard like b: This child invents a hardening idea; the given change is milkiness and cloudiness.

activities.explanation: Right. In old age the lens can turn milky and cloudy; this is cataract.

activities.prompt: You look up from your notebook and gaze at the blackboard far away. What happens to your eye lens?
options: It becomes thinner, so its focal length increases.
It becomes thicker, so its focal length increases.
It becomes thinner, so its focal length decreases.
It stays the same thickness, so its focal length stays same.

why.It becomes thicker, so its focal length: This child mixes up thickness; far seeing makes the lens thin, not thick.
why.It becomes thinner, so its focal length: This child pairs thinning with a shorter focal length, but thinning makes it longer.
why.It stays the same thickness, so its foca: This child thinks the lens never changes when the viewing distance changes.

activities.explanation: Right. Relaxing muscles thin the lens, and a thinner lens has a longer focal length.

activities.prompt: A normal eye sees a far mountain and also a small coin 25 cm away. Why can one eye do both?
options: The lens can adjust its focal length; this power is called accommodation.
The eye makes two lenses, one for far things and one for near things.
The lens stays fixed, and the ciliary muscles do the seeing for it.
The eye sees near things clearly only when the muscles fully relax.

why.The eye makes two lenses, one for far th: This child imagines two lenses, but there is one lens that changes its focal length.
why.The lens stays fixed, and the ciliary mu: This child thinks muscles see and the lens does nothing, which is not how it works.
why.The eye sees near things clearly only wh: This child reverses the muscle action; relaxing helps far seeing, not near seeing.

activities.explanation: Right. Accommodation is the lens's ability to adjust its focal length for near and far.

lessons.sceneCaption: A labelled diagram of the human eye showing the ciliary muscle and the lens changing form during accommodation.

lessons.title: Defects of Vision and Their Correction

activities.prompt: Why do some people see blurry, and how do glasses fix it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: When the Eye Needs Help
activities.body: Sometimes the eye slowly loses its power of accommodation. Then vision becomes blurred. These are called refractive defects of the eye. There are three common ones. In myopia, or near-sightedness, distant things look blurry. In hypermetropia, or far-sightedness, close things look blurry. Presbyopia comes with ageing. The right lens can fix each defect, so you can see clearly again.
keyPoints: There are three common refractive defects of vision.
In myopia the image of a distant object forms in front of the retina; a concave lens corrects it.
In hypermetropia light from a close object focuses behind the retina; a convex lens corrects it.
Presbyopia happens when the power of accommodation decreases with ageing.
Bi-focal lenses can help people with both myopia and hypermetropia.
activities.explanation: Blurred vision has a reason, and a suitable lens can fix it.

activities.prompt: Grandma can read the far street sign easily, but she holds her sewing thread far away to see it. Why does she do this?
steps: She sees far things well, so her eye is not myopic, because myopia blurs distant objects.
She struggles with close work, so light from near objects focuses behind her retina, because that is what hypermetropia does.
She is old, so her power of accommodation has decreased, because ageing weakens the eye's ability to change the lens.
So her eye cannot bend light enough for near objects, and this defect of old age is presbyopia.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Myopia is also called which of these?
options: Far-sightedness
Near-sightedness
Bi-focal sight
Sharp sight
activities.explanation: Well done! Myopia has another name: near-sightedness.

activities.prompt: In hypermetropia, light from a close object focuses ______ the retina.
activities.hint: The image lands too far back in the eye.
activities.explanation: Great! In hypermetropia the focus falls behind the retina, so close things look blurry.

activities.prompt: Myopia may happen because of which change in the eye?
options: The eyeball becomes elongated
The retina becomes thicker
The eye changes its colour
The eyelid becomes heavier
activities.explanation: Correct! Too much curvature of the lens or an elongated eyeball can cause myopia.

activities.prompt: Match each defect or name with its correct partner.
activities.explanation: Nice matching! Concave lenses help myopia, and convex lenses help hypermetropia.

activities.prompt: Put these image positions in order, from the front of the eye to the back.
items: In front of the retina
On the retina
Behind the retina
activities.explanation: Perfect order! In myopia the image falls in front of the retina, and in hypermetropia it falls behind.

activities.prompt: A person has both myopia and hypermetropia. Which lens may be needed?
options: Only a concave lens
Only a convex lens
A bi-focal lens
A plain glass lens
activities.explanation: Well done! A bi-focal lens can handle both defects at once.

activities.prompt: Ravi reads his book easily. But the blackboard looks blurry to him. Which defect does Ravi have?
options: Myopia, because his eye makes the image before the retina
Hypermetropia, because his eye makes the image behind the retina
Presbyopia, because ageing has weakened his power of accommodation
No defect, because clear near vision means the eye is perfect

why.Hypermetropia, because his eye makes the: He mixed up the two defects; hypermetropia blurs near objects, not far ones.
why.Presbyopia, because ageing has weakened: Presbyopia comes with ageing, but Ravi is young and his near vision is fine.
why.No defect, because clear near vision mea: He thinks clear near vision means all is well, but myopia only blurs distant objects.

activities.explanation: Right: the board is far, and in myopia a distant object's image forms in front of the retina.

activities.prompt: Meera sees the far bus number clearly. But her book looks blurry. Which lens will help her read?
options: A concave lens, because it spreads the light more
A convex lens, because it bends the light more
A bi-focal lens, because she has two defects together
No lens, because her eye can fix itself with effort

why.A concave lens, because it spreads the l: She mixed up the lenses; a concave lens corrects myopia, which blurs far objects.
why.A bi-focal lens, because she has two def: Bi-focal lenses are for people with both defects, but Meera has only one.
why.No lens, because her eye can fix itself: Her eye cannot fix this by effort, because the light already focuses behind the retina.

activities.explanation: Right: in hypermetropia light focuses behind the retina, so a convex lens bends it more.

activities.prompt: An uncle has both myopia and hypermetropia. His friend says one single lens can fix him. What is the flaw?
options: One lens is too weak, so he needs two of the same lens
One lens bends light one way, but he needs both corrections
One lens works only for children, so adults need surgery
One lens is fine, because both defects have the same fix

why.One lens is too weak, so he needs two of: The problem is not lens strength; a single lens cannot correct two opposite defects.
why.One lens works only for children, so adu: The type of lens matters, not the age of the person wearing it.
why.One lens is fine, because both defects h: The defects need opposite lenses, so they do not share the same fix.

activities.explanation: Right: myopia needs a concave lens and hypermetropia needs a convex one, so he needs bi-focal lenses.

activities.prompt: A student makes a model eye with an eyeball longer than normal. She shines light from a far object into it. Where does the image form?
options: Behind the retina, because the eyeball is too short
On the retina, because the lens still works normally
In front of the retina, because the eyeball is too long
Outside the eye, because the light cannot enter at all

why.Behind the retina, because the eyeball i: She mixed up the two defects; a longer eyeball focuses light too soon, not too late.
why.On the retina, because the lens still wo: The lens may work fine, but the long eyeball still puts the image too early.
why.Outside the eye, because the light canno: Light enters a longer eye easily; length does not block the light.

activities.explanation: Right: an elongated eyeball causes myopia, so the image forms in front of the retina.

activities.prompt: A friend claims a concave lens can correct every refractive defect of vision. What is wrong with his claim?
options: Concave lenses only suit myopia, but hypermetropia needs a convex lens
Concave lenses are too strong, so they blur every eye that wears them
Concave lenses work only for old people, so young eyes need convex ones
Concave lenses fix the eyeball shape, so no other lens is ever needed

why.Concave lenses are too strong, so they b: A concave lens does not blur every eye; it is the right fix for myopia.
why.Concave lenses work only for old people,: The defect decides the lens, not the age of the person.
why.Concave lenses fix the eyeball shape, so: A lens corrects vision but cannot change the shape of the eyeball itself.

activities.explanation: Right: a concave lens corrects myopia, while hypermetropia needs a convex lens of suitable power.

lessons.sceneAlt: A diagram showing myopia, hypermetropia and presbyopia and how each is corrected with glasses.
lessons.sceneCaption: Diagram of sight defects and their corrections, showing myopia, hypermetropia and presbyopia with correction lenses.

lessons.title: Refraction of Light Through a Prism

activities.prompt: Why does a glass prism bend light differently than a glass slab?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What a Prism Does to Light
activities.body: A prism is a piece of glass shaped like a triangle. It has two triangular bases and three rectangular side faces. When light passes through it, the ray bends at both surfaces. So the ray that comes out is not parallel to the ray that goes in. The angle between them is called the angle of deviation.
keyPoints: A prism has two triangular bases and three rectangular side faces.
Light bends towards the normal when it enters the glass, and away from the normal when it leaves.
The emergent ray makes an angle with the incident ray. This is the angle of deviation.
activities.explanation: The prism's shape bends the ray twice, so the light leaves in a new direction.

activities.prompt: Sunlight goes through a glass slab and then through a triangular prism. In the slab the light comes out going the same way it went in. In the prism the light comes out going a different way. Why does the shape of the glass change what happens?
steps: In the slab, light bends towards the normal going in and away coming out, so the two bends cancel and the ray comes out parallel.
In the prism, the two surfaces are not parallel, so the normals at the two surfaces point in different directions.
Because the normals differ, the bend towards the normal at the first surface and the bend away at the second do not cancel.
So the prism's shape makes the emergent ray bend at an angle to the incident ray, and this angle is the angle of deviation.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: How many rectangular side faces does a triangular glass prism have?
options: Two
Three
Four
Six
activities.explanation: A triangular prism has three rectangular side faces and two triangular bases. Well done!

activities.prompt: In a prism, what is the angle between the two side faces called?
options: The angle of deviation
The angle of the prism
The angle of the base
The side angle
activities.explanation: The angle between the two lateral faces is called the angle of the prism.

activities.prompt: The angle between the emergent ray and the incident ray is called the angle of ______.
activities.hint: It tells you how much the ray has been turned.
activities.explanation: The prism bends the ray, and the angle of deviation measures that turn.

activities.prompt: Light enters a prism from air into glass at the first surface. Which way does it bend?
options: Towards the normal
Away from the normal
It does not bend
It goes backwards
activities.explanation: Going from air into glass, the ray bends towards the normal at the first surface.

activities.prompt: Match each ray or angle with what it means.
pairs: Angle between the two side faces
Angle between emergent and incident rays
Emergent ray is parallel but shifted sideways
activities.explanation: Great matching! These are the key words for rays through glass.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order as light passes through a prism.
items: The incident ray PE strikes the first surface
Light enters from air to glass and bends towards the normal
The ray travels through the glass
Light enters from glass to air and bends away from the normal
The emergent ray makes an angle of deviation with the incident ray
activities.explanation: Perfect order! Two bends at the two surfaces make the ray leave at a new angle.

activities.prompt: A ray goes through a glass slab and comes out parallel to how it entered. The same ray goes through a prism and comes out at an angle. Why does the prism act differently?
options: The prism's two surfaces are not parallel, so the two bends do not cancel.
The prism glass is thicker, so light bends much more inside it.
The prism is triangular, so light gets confused and turns randomly.
The slab is smooth but a prism has rough slanted surfaces.

why.The prism glass is thicker, so light ben: Wrong: thickness is not the reason; the shape of the surfaces causes the leftover angle.
why.The prism is triangular, so light gets c: Wrong: light follows fixed rules at each surface; it never turns randomly.
why.The slab is smooth but a prism has rough: Wrong: both surfaces are smooth glass; roughness is not the cause.

activities.explanation: Right: with non-parallel surfaces, the bend towards and the bend away leave an angle left over.

activities.prompt: A student says a prism makes light bend sideways like a slab does, only more. Which test fairly checks this claim?
options: Send one ray through a slab and one through a prism, and compare the outgoing ray directions.
Send one ray through a thick prism and one through a thin prism, and compare the angles.
Send one ray through a prism and one through open air, and compare the brightness.
Send one ray through a slab twice and once through a prism, and compare the brightness.

why.Send one ray through a thick prism and o: Wrong: comparing two prisms never tests the claim about the slab.
why.Send one ray through a prism and one thr: Wrong: brightness does not measure how much the ray direction bends.
why.Send one ray through a slab twice and on: Wrong: brightness is not the thing being claimed; the direction of the ray is.

activities.explanation: Right: comparing outgoing directions of slab and prism tests the claim about bending directly.

activities.prompt: A friend says: light bends towards the normal at both surfaces of a prism. You watch a ray go in and come out. What is wrong with the claim?
options: At the second surface light goes from glass to air, so it bends away from the normal.
Nothing is wrong, because glass always bends light towards the normal.
The claim is wrong because light never bends at the second surface at all.
The claim is wrong because light bends away at both surfaces of a prism.

why.Nothing is wrong, because glass always b: Wrong: the direction of bending depends on which way the light crosses the surface.
why.The claim is wrong because light never b: Wrong: light does bend at the second surface; it bends away from the normal.
why.The claim is wrong because light bends a: Wrong: at the first surface, air to glass, light bends towards the normal.

activities.explanation: Right: glass to air bends away from the normal, so the claim fails at the second surface.

activities.prompt: A ray passes through a thick glass slab. The outgoing ray is parallel to the incoming ray. What else is true about the outgoing ray, and why?
options: It is shifted a little to the side, because the ray bent at both surfaces.
It is exactly on the same line, because parallel rays never shift.
It is shifted a lot sideways, because the slab is very thick glass.
It is shifted backwards, because the slab sends light the opposite way.

why.It is exactly on the same line, because: Wrong: parallel does not mean the same line; the ray still ends up shifted.
why.It is shifted a lot sideways, because th: Wrong: the shift is slight; thickness alone does not make it large in this lesson.
why.It is shifted backwards, because the sla: Wrong: the ray keeps going forward; it does not turn around.

activities.explanation: Right: bending at each surface makes the parallel ray come out slightly displaced sideways.

lessons.sceneCaption: Diagram shows a light ray being deflected as it enters and exits a prism.

lessons.title: Dispersion, Spectrum and Rainbow

activities.prompt: Why does sunlight hide seven colours inside a raindrop?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: White light hides a secret
activities.body: White light looks plain, but it is made of many colours. When light passes through a prism, the colours split apart and form a band. This band is called a spectrum. Splitting light into its colours is called dispersion. A rainbow in the sky is nature doing the same trick with raindrops!
keyPoints: A prism splits white light into a band of colours.
The band of colours is called a spectrum.
Splitting light into its colours is called dispersion.
activities.explanation: A prism is like a magic key that opens white light and shows the colours inside.

activities.prompt: Riya sees a rainbow after the rain. The Sun is behind her back. Why is the rainbow always on the opposite side from her shadow?
steps: Raindrops in the air act like tiny prisms and split sunlight into colours.
The sunlight must enter the raindrops first, so the drops must be on the side facing the Sun.
The light then leaves the drops and travels back towards Riya, so she must face away from the Sun to catch it.
So the rainbow always appears in the sky opposite to the Sun, on the same side as her shadow.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Light passes through a prism and splits into many colours. What is this splitting called?
options: Reflection
Dispersion
Spectrum
Shadow
activities.explanation: Splitting light into its component colours is called dispersion. You got it!

activities.prompt: You want to remember the order of colours in the spectrum. Which helper does the lesson give you?
options: ROYGBIV
VIBGYOR
RAINBOW
PRISM
activities.explanation: VIBGYOR stands for Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange and Red, in that order.

activities.prompt: When a prism splits white light, the band of coloured components is called a ______.
activities.hint: It starts with 's' and names the whole band of colours.
activities.explanation: The band of coloured components of light is called a spectrum. Well done!

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what it does.
pairs: First used a glass prism on sunlight
activities.explanation: Newton began the experiment, and raindrops repeat it in the sky every time it rains.

activities.prompt: Put the colours of the spectrum in order, starting with the one that bends the most.
items: Violet
Green
Yellow
Orange
Red
activities.explanation: Violet bends the most, so it comes first. Red bends the least, so it comes last.

activities.prompt: Newton split sunlight with one prism. What did he do with a second inverted prism?
options: Made the colours brighter
Recombined the colours into white light
Turned the colours into a rainbow
Split the light into more colours
activities.explanation: The second inverted prism joined the colours back together into white light. Clever thinking!

activities.prompt: Sunlight passes through a glass prism. A coloured band appears on the wall. Which colour is at the bottom edge, where light bent the most?
options: Red, because red light bends the least of all
Violet, because violet light bends the most of all
Green, because green light sits in the middle
Blue, because blue light is the darkest colour

why.Red, because red light bends the least o: This mixes up the colours; red bends the least, so it sits at the other edge.
why.Green, because green light sits in the m: Green is in the middle of the band, not at the bending edge.
why.Blue, because blue light is the darkest: Darkness is not the reason a colour bends more or less.

activities.explanation: Correct. The colour that bends the most ends up furthest from the straight path.

activities.prompt: A student says: 'A prism paints the light with colours.' Sunlight goes through a prism and splits. What is wrong with this claim?
options: Prisms only work at night, not in the day
The colours were already inside the white sunlight
The prism adds new colours that were never there
The wall paints the colours onto the light beam

why.Prisms only work at night, not in the da: Prisms work in daylight; that is how we see spectra from sunlight.
why.The prism adds new colours that were nev: The prism does not create colours; it only splits the ones already present.
why.The wall paints the colours onto the lig: The wall only shows the band; the splitting happens inside the prism.

activities.explanation: Correct. White light is a mixture, and the prism only separates the colours already in it.

activities.prompt: After rain, Meera sees a rainbow. Her shadow falls in front of her. Where should she look to see the rainbow again?
options: Towards the Sun, above her head
Towards her shadow, opposite the Sun
Straight up, at the top of the sky
Behind the clouds, near the rain

why.Towards the Sun, above her head: Looking towards the Sun means looking away from the rainbow.
why.Straight up, at the top of the sky: The rainbow is not always at the top of the sky.
why.Behind the clouds, near the rain: The rainbow is in the rain, but the direction is set by the Sun's position.

activities.explanation: Correct. A rainbow forms in the direction opposite to the Sun, where her shadow points.

activities.prompt: A student wants to test if different colours bend by different amounts. Sunlight goes through a prism. Which observation is the fair test for this idea?
options: Count how many colours appear in the band
Check that the band appears on a white wall
Compare where red and violet land on the wall
Time how long the band stays on the wall

why.Count how many colours appear in the ban: Counting colours shows the light splits, but not how much each colour bends.
why.Check that the band appears on a white w: A white wall just makes the band easy to see; it says nothing about bending.
why.Time how long the band stays on the wall: The time the band lasts has nothing to do with how colours bend.

activities.explanation: Correct. Comparing the positions of red and violet shows they bend through different angles.

lessons.sceneCaption: A prism splits white light into a spectrum of colours, showing dispersion.

lessons.title: Atmospheric Refraction and Scattering of Light

activities.prompt: Why do stars twinkle while planets don't?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Air Bends and Scatters Light
activities.body: The air around Earth bends light. This bending is called atmospheric refraction. It makes stars twinkle at night. It also lets you see the Sun about two minutes before sunrise. Tiny particles floating in air can scatter light too. Very fine particles scatter mainly blue light. Red light is scattered the least, so danger lights are red.
keyPoints: Atmospheric refraction is the bending of light by the air.
Twinkling of stars and early sunrise happen because of this bending.
Very fine particles scatter mainly blue light; red is scattered the least.
activities.explanation: Air bends light, and tiny particles can scatter it in different ways.

activities.prompt: Ravi sits near a campfire. He looks at a tree through the hot air above the fire. The tree seems to waver and shake. Why does this happen?
steps: The fire makes the air above it very hot.
Hot air is less dense, so it has a slightly lower refractive index.
Light from the tree bends again and again as the hot air moves.
So the tree seems to waver, and this wavering is atmospheric refraction.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Why do stars twinkle at night?
options: Atmospheric refraction of starlight
The star switches its light on and off
Clouds pass in front of the star
activities.explanation: Well done! The air bends starlight, and this bending makes stars twinkle.

activities.prompt: The scattering of light by colloidal particles is called the ______ effect.
activities.hint: It is named after a scientist, and it starts with T.
activities.explanation: Great! Colloidal particles scatter light, and this is the Tyndall effect.

activities.prompt: Danger lights are red. Why is red the best colour to use?
options: Red is scattered least by fog or smoke
Red is scattered most by fog or smoke
All colours are scattered equally in fog
activities.explanation: Red is scattered the least, so it travels well through fog and smoke.

activities.prompt: Match each thing you see with its cause in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each sight in the sky or in air has a clear cause. Super matching!

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to explain why you see the Sun before sunrise.
items: The Sun is still below the horizon
Light from the Sun enters the air of the atmosphere
The air bends the light towards the normal
The bent light reaches your eyes
You see the Sun about 2 minutes early
activities.explanation: The bending of light by air lets the Sun reach your eyes early. Brilliant ordering!

activities.prompt: Air above a fire wavers and shimmers. What happens if you look through this hot air?
options: Light bends because hot air is less dense
Light bends because hot air is more dense
Light passes straight through without bending
activities.explanation: Hot air is less dense with a lower refractive index, so light bends and wavers.

activities.prompt: Air above a road fire is hot. Hot air has a lower refractive index. Meena looks at a bus through this hot air. What will she see?
options: The bus looks steady and sharp.
The bus looks wavy and shaking.
The bus looks dark and black.
The bus looks smaller than before.

She thinks hot air does not change light, so the bus stays steady.
She confuses bending of light with loss of colour.
She thinks bending of light changes the size of the bus.

activities.explanation: Right. Light bends in moving hot air, so the bus looks wavy.

activities.prompt: Starlight bends towards the normal when it enters air. Our eyes follow the light back in a straight line. Where does the star seem to be?
options: Slightly lower than its real place.
Exactly at its real place.
Slightly higher than its real place.
Much nearer than its real place.

She thinks bending towards the normal pushes the star's image down.
She thinks bent light and straight light point to the same place.
She confuses the direction of the image with its distance.

activities.explanation: Right. The eye traces the bent ray straight, so the star looks higher.

activities.prompt: A planet is closer to us than a star. It looks like a small disc, not a point. Light comes from many points of the disc. Why does the planet not twinkle?
options: Changes from many points cancel each other out.
Planet light is too strong to ever change.
Planet light does not bend in the air at all.
Planets give their own steady light like the Sun.

why.Planet light is too strong to ever chang: She thinks brightness alone stops the twinkling effect.
why.Planet light does not bend in the air at: She thinks planet light skips atmospheric refraction completely.
why.Planets give their own steady light like: She thinks planets make light like the Sun does.

activities.explanation: Right. As an extended source, changes from many points average out, so it stays steady.

activities.prompt: Water in a glass has very fine particles mixed in. A torch beam passes through the water. Sana looks at the beam from the side of the glass. What does she mostly see?
options: Blue light scattered towards her eye.
Red light scattered towards her eye.
No light coming out of the glass.
Only a plain white beam of light.

She mixes up the least scattered colour with the most scattered one.
She thinks scattering removes all light from the beam.
She thinks the particles scatter all colours equally.

activities.explanation: Right. Fine particles scatter mainly blue light, so blue reaches her eye from the side.

activities.prompt: Fog is full of tiny particles. Red light is scattered the least by such particles. A signal is placed on a foggy hill road. Why is its danger light red?
options: Red light is the brightest colour made.
Red light travels in bent, wavy paths.
Red light stays strong and reaches far.
Red light is scattered the most in fog.

She thinks red is chosen because it is the brightest colour.
She confuses scattering of light with bending of light.
She mixes up least scattered with most scattered.

activities.explanation: Right. Least scattered red light stays strong and is seen far in fog.

lessons.sceneCaption: Light from a satellite is refracted by Earth's atmosphere, whose density increases towards the ground.
