lessons.title: Test practice
lessons.sceneAlt: A labelled 3D diagram of a human eyeball cross-section showing the cornea, lens, iris, retina and other parts.
lessons.sceneCaption: A labelled diagram of the human eye showing the cornea, lens and retina that make an image.

sceneCredit.text: Eye-diagram no circles border by Chabacano, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Chabacano

activities.context: Riya steps out of a dim room into bright afternoon sunlight and immediately squints. Later she sits in a garden, first gazing at distant hills, then reading small print on her phone. Her eyes adjust each time without her thinking about it. Light entering each eyeball, which is roughly spherical and about 2.3 cm across, finally produces a picture on the light-sensitive layer at the back.
activities.prompt: Why does Riya squint when she steps into the bright sunlight?
options: Her pupil becomes smaller so that less light enters the eye
Her cornea becomes opaque to block the extra light
Her crystalline lens thickens to stop light from passing through
Her retina stops sending signals for a few seconds

why.Her cornea becomes opaque to block the e: Wrong: the cornea is a transparent bulge and stays transparent; it does not turn opaque
why.Her crystalline lens thickens to stop li: Wrong: the crystalline lens only makes fine adjustments to focus at different distances, not to block light
why.Her retina stops sending signals for a f: Wrong: the retina keeps sending electrical signals to the brain; squinting is not caused by signals stopping

activities.explanation: Correct: the pupil controls how much light enters the eye, so it becomes smaller in bright light

activities.context: Riya steps out of a dim room into bright afternoon sunlight and immediately squints. Later she sits in a garden, first gazing at distant hills, then reading small print on her phone. Her eyes adjust each time without her thinking about it. Light entering each eyeball, which is roughly spherical and about 2.3 cm across, finally produces a picture on the light-sensitive layer at the back.
activities.prompt: The picture formed on the light-sensitive layer at the back of Riya's eye is upside down, yet she sees the hills the right way up. What most likely explains this?
options: The cornea turns the image the right way up before it reaches the retina
The pupil rotates the image as light passes through it
The retina cells send electrical signals to the brain through optic nerves, and the brain sorts out what is seen
The crystalline lens flips the image a second time before it reaches the retina

why.The cornea turns the image the right way: Wrong: the cornea only refracts most of the entering light at its outer surface; it does not turn images upright
why.The pupil rotates the image as light pas: Wrong: the pupil only controls how much light enters the eye; it does not rotate anything
why.The crystalline lens flips the image a s: Wrong: the eye lens forms an inverted real image on the retina and does not flip it again

activities.explanation: Correct: the retina sends electrical signals to the brain through optic nerves, and the brain makes sense of them

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): In bright light, the pupil of the human eye becomes smaller.
Reason (R): The pupil controls how much light enters the eye.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and because the pupil controls the amount of entering light, it becomes smaller in bright light.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The image formed on the retina of the human eye is upright.
Reason (R): The human eye works like a camera.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because the eye lens forms an inverted real image on the retina, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain why most of the bending of light entering the eye happens at the cornea, even though the eye also has a crystalline lens.
activities.answer: Light entering the eye first passes through the thin cornea, which forms a transparent bulge on the front of the eyeball. Most of the refraction of the entering light takes place at the cornea's outer surface. The crystalline lens behind it does not do the main bending of light; it only makes fine adjustments to focus objects that are at different distances. So the cornea does the major work of bending light, while the lens fine-tunes the focus so that a clear image forms on the light-sensitive retina.
points: Light enters through the thin cornea, a transparent bulge on the front of the eyeball
Most refraction happens at the cornea's outer surface
The crystalline lens only makes fine adjustments for objects at different distances
Together they let a clear image form on the light-sensitive retina
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Rohan's grandfather loves reading the newspaper in the garden, but he recently complained that distant things look hazy and his vision seems clouded. At the eye clinic, the doctor examined his eyes and explained how the lens inside the eye changes shape with the help of muscles around it, and how this ability can weaken with age. Rohan wants to understand what is happening in his grandfather's eyes.
activities.prompt: When Rohan's grandfather looks up from his newspaper at a bird flying far away, what must happen inside his eye for the bird to come into clear focus?
options: The ciliary muscles relax, making the lens thinner so its focal length becomes longer
The ciliary muscles contract, making the lens thicker so its focal length becomes shorter
The lens material changes from jelly-like to rigid, fixing the focal length permanently
The lens becomes cloudy so that light spreads evenly across the retina

why.The ciliary muscles contract, making the: This describes what happens for nearby objects like the newspaper, not distant ones
why.The lens material changes from jelly-lik: The lens stays flexible and jelly-like; its shape keeps changing during vision
why.The lens becomes cloudy so that light sp: Cloudiness blurs vision rather than bringing distant objects into focus

activities.explanation: Correct: for distant objects the muscles relax, the lens thins and focal length increases

activities.context: Rohan's grandfather loves reading the newspaper in the garden, but he recently complained that distant things look hazy and his vision seems clouded. At the eye clinic, the doctor examined his eyes and explained how the lens inside the eye changes shape with the help of muscles around it, and how this ability can weaken with age. Rohan wants to understand what is happening in his grandfather's eyes.
activities.prompt: Rohan asks why his grandfather cannot focus on the newspaper held very close to his face, closer than usual. What is the best explanation?
options: The ciliary muscles can never contract, so near objects are always unclear
The lens's focal length cannot be reduced below a certain minimum, so objects nearer than that limit stay blurred
The lens becomes thinner when looking at nearby objects, pushing the image away
Distant objects and near objects need exactly the same focal length, so distance cannot matter

why.The ciliary muscles can never contract,: Wrong: the muscles do contract for near objects; that is how near vision works
why.The lens becomes thinner when looking at: Wrong: for near objects the lens becomes thicker, not thinner, and focal length decreases
why.Distant objects and near objects need ex: Wrong: different object distances need different focal lengths, which is why accommodation exists

activities.explanation: Correct: there is a minimum limit to focal length, so anything closer than that limit cannot be focused

activities.context: Rohan's grandfather loves reading the newspaper in the garden, but he recently complained that distant things look hazy and his vision seems clouded. At the eye clinic, the doctor examined his eyes and explained how the lens inside the eye changes shape with the help of muscles around it, and how this ability can weaken with age. Rohan wants to understand what is happening in his grandfather's eyes.
activities.prompt: The doctor says Rohan's grandfather's lens has turned milky and cloudy. What is this condition, and what does it mean for his sight of both the newspaper and the bird?
options: Accommodation, which only affects seeing nearby objects while distant sight stays perfect
Cataract, in which the cloudy lens makes vision hazy for objects at any distance
Over-relaxed ciliary muscles, which can be fixed simply by looking at nearby objects more often
A lens that has become too thin, which can be corrected by contracting the ciliary muscles harder

why.Accommodation, which only affects seeing: Wrong: accommodation is the normal adjusting of focal length, not a cloudiness of the lens
why.Over-relaxed ciliary muscles, which can: Wrong: the problem is the lens becoming cloudy, not the state of the ciliary muscles
why.A lens that has become too thin, which c: Wrong: the lens is cloudy, not thin, and muscle effort cannot clear the cloudiness

activities.explanation: Correct: a milky, cloudy lens is cataract and blurs vision regardless of object distance

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): When the ciliary muscles relax, the eye lens becomes thin.
Reason (R): Relaxing the ciliary muscles decreases the focal length of the eye lens.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but relaxing the muscles increases the focal length, so the reason is false.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A normal eye can see distant objects clearly when the lens becomes thin.
Reason (R): Ciliary muscles can change the curvature of the eye lens, which changes its focal length.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the muscle's ability to reshape the lens explains how the lens thins for distant vision.

activities.prompt: Explain why you can read a page of your book clearly and then, a moment later, look up and see a tree far away clearly too. What changes inside your eye each time?
activities.answer: The eye lens can adjust its focal length, an ability called accommodation. When I read the book, nearby objects are being viewed, so the ciliary muscles contract and the lens becomes thicker, decreasing its focal length so the page is seen clearly. When I look up at the distant tree, the ciliary muscles relax, the lens becomes thin, and its focal length increases, so the far tree is seen clearly. The changing curvature of the lens makes this switching possible.
points: Names accommodation as the lens adjusting its focal length
Near object: ciliary muscles contract, lens thickens, focal length decreases
Distant object: ciliary muscles relax, lens thins, focal length increases
Links changing curvature of the lens to the change in focal length
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A person with myopia finds distant objects look blurred.
Reason (R): In a myopic eye, the image of a distant object forms in front of the retina.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the image forming before the retina directly explains the blurred distance vision.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A person with hypermetropia should be given a concave lens of suitable power.
Reason (R): In hypermetropia, light from a close object focuses behind the retina.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason is true, but hypermetropia is corrected with a convex lens, so the assertion is false.

activities.prompt: Explain why a concave lens is used to correct myopia while a convex lens is used to correct hypermetropia.
activities.answer: In myopia, the image of a distant object forms in front of the retina, so distant things look blurred. A concave lens of suitable power is placed before the eye so that the image is formed back on the retina. In hypermetropia, light from a close object focuses behind the retina, so nearby things look blurred. Here a convex lens of appropriate power is used so that the focus moves forward onto the retina. Each lens type shifts the image in the direction needed to restore clear vision.
points: States that in myopia the distant-object image forms in front of the retina.
States that the concave lens of suitable power corrects myopia.
States that in hypermetropia light from a close object focuses behind the retina.
States that the convex lens of appropriate power corrects hypermetropia.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a science fair, Riya shines a narrow beam of light, PE, onto a triangular glass prism. The beam enters the first surface, travels through the glass, and leaves from the second surface. Riya notices that the ray coming out does not continue in the same direction as the ray going in. Her friend claims the prism must be faulty. Riya decides to test a rectangular glass slab as well, to find out whether the shape of the glass piece is responsible for what she saw.
activities.prompt: Riya now wants to compare how strongly different prisms turn the ray. What should she do?
options: For each prism, measure the angle between the incoming ray and the outgoing ray
Measure the thickness of the triangular bases of the prisms
Measure the lengths of the rectangular side faces of the prisms
Compare the brightness of the beam coming out of each prism

why.Measure the thickness of the triangular: Base thickness is not the quantity that decides how much the ray is turned.
why.Measure the lengths of the rectangular s: Side-face length does not measure the turning of the ray.
why.Compare the brightness of the beam comin: Brightness is not related to the angle of deviation described here.

activities.explanation: Correct: the turning between incident and emergent rays is the angle of deviation, shown as ∠D, so comparing it compares the bending.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): At the first surface of a triangular glass prism, the ray of light bends towards the normal.
Reason (R): At the first surface, light travels from air into glass.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and entering from air into glass is exactly why the ray bends towards the normal.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A rectangular glass slab turns the emergent ray through a large angle, just like a prism does.
Reason (R): In a rectangular glass slab, the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because a slab gives a parallel, only sideways-shifted ray, while the reason is true.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: The Human Eye and the Colourful World

activities.prompt: Light enters your eye first through the cornea. Where does the lens system form the image?
options: On the retina
On the cornea
On the pupil
On the optic nerve
activities.explanation: The lens system makes an image on the light-sensitive retina. Well done!

activities.prompt: Most of the bending of light entering the eye happens at the outer surface of the cornea.
activities.explanation: Yes! The cornea does most of the refraction. The lens only makes fine adjustments.

activities.prompt: The eye lens can change its focal length. This power of the eye is called ______.
activities.hint: It starts with the letter A.
activities.explanation: Accommodation is the eye lens's ability to adjust its focal length.

activities.prompt: Ravi cannot see distant objects clearly. The image forms in front of his retina. Which lens will help him?
options: A concave lens
A convex lens
A bi-focal lens
No lens is needed
activities.explanation: This is myopia, and a concave lens of suitable power corrects it.

activities.prompt: Match each eye condition with what helps or causes it.
pairs: Power of accommodation decreases with age
activities.explanation: Each defect has its own fix. You know them all now!

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order as light passes through a glass prism.
items: Light enters the first surface from air to glass
The ray bends towards the normal
Light leaves the second surface from glass to air
The ray bends away from the normal
The emergent ray bends at an angle called the angle of deviation
activities.explanation: Light bends towards the normal entering glass, and away from it leaving glass. The result is the angle of deviation.

activities.prompt: Planets twinkle just as much as stars because they are also far away.
activities.explanation: Planets are closer and seen as extended sources, so they do not twinkle.

activities.prompt: Why are danger lights red?
options: Red is least scattered by fog or smoke
Red is scattered the most in air
Red light travels in zigzag paths
Red light has no colour components
activities.explanation: Red is least scattered by fog or smoke, so it can be seen from far away.

activities.prompt: Raindrops act like small prisms and split sunlight. A rainbow forms in a direction ______ to the Sun.
activities.hint: Turn your back to the Sun to look for it!
activities.explanation: Yes, the rainbow appears opposite the Sun, with raindrops dispersing the sunlight.

boss.sceneCaption: A labelled diagram of the human eye showing the cornea, lens and retina that make an image.

chapters.title: Electricity
chapters.summary: In this chapter: electric current and circuit; electric potential and potential difference; circuit diagram and ohm's law; factors affecting resistance.

lessons.title: Electric Current and Circuit

activities.prompt: Why does a bulb glow only when the switch is closed?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is an electric circuit?
activities.body: Electricity is a handy form of energy we can control. When electric charge flows through a conductor, we call it electric current. A cell or battery pushes charges through the bulb. A switch joins the cell and bulb in one path. This closed path is called a circuit. If the path breaks anywhere, the current stops and the bulb goes dark.
keyPoints: Electric current is the flow of electric charges through a conductor.
A cell or battery makes charges flow through the bulb.
A closed path of current is an electric circuit; if it breaks, the current stops.
In metal wires, electrons flow. Conventional current is shown opposite to electron flow.
activities.explanation: A circuit is like a round track: the current can only move if the track is complete.

activities.title: Light the bulb

tasks.then: Closing the switch completes the circuit, so current flows.
More cells for each bulb push more current through it.

activities.takeaway: Current flows only round a closed circuit; more cells push more current.
activities.explanation: Current flows only round a closed circuit; more cells push more current.

activities.prompt: Anaya's torch worked yesterday. Today she slides the switch, but the bulb stays dark. The cell is new and the bulb is fine. Why does the torch not work?
steps: The bulb glows only when charge flows through it, and charge flows only in a closed path.
The switch is the link that joins the cell and bulb into one closed path.
If the switch does not close that link, the path has a gap somewhere.
So the current stops, and the dark bulb means the circuit is not closed.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: In a torch, what makes charges flow through the bulb?
options: The glass of the bulb
The plastic cover
A cell or battery
The air around it
activities.explanation: A torch cell or battery makes charges flow through the bulb. Well done!

activities.prompt: A continuous closed path of electric current is called an electric ______.
activities.hint: It starts with the letter c.
activities.explanation: A complete, closed path for current is an electric circuit.

activities.prompt: Electric current is best described as...
options: The rate of flow of electric charges
The colour of the wire used
The weight of the battery
The heat inside the switch
activities.explanation: Current tells us how much charge flows in unit time. You have got it!

activities.prompt: Match each part or word with what it does.
pairs: Makes charges flow through the bulb
Make up the charge flow in metal wires
activities.explanation: Each part of a circuit has its own job. Great matching!

activities.prompt: One ampere is one coulomb of charge flowing per ______.
activities.hint: It is a unit of time.
activities.explanation: One coulomb of charge flowing each second is one ampere of current.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to light a torch bulb.
items: Take a torch cell
Join a wire from the cell to the bulb
Add a switch in the path
Close the switch to complete the circuit
The bulb glows as current flows
activities.explanation: The cell pushes charges, the switch closes the path, and then the bulb glows. Super ordering!

activities.prompt: A torch has a cell, wires and a bulb. The bulb is glowing. One wire comes loose from its clip. What happens to the bulb?
options: It glows brighter than before.
It glows the same as before.
It goes dark at once.
It glows for a while, then goes dark.

A loose wire cannot make the current stronger.
The path is broken, so the current cannot keep flowing.
Current does not keep flowing for a while after the path breaks.

activities.explanation: Right: a break anywhere stops the current, so the bulb cannot glow.

activities.prompt: Riya opens the switch in her torch. The path now has a gap. Why does the bulb go dark?
options: No closed path means the current stops.
The switch uses up all the charge.
The bulb becomes too cold to glow.
The cell stops making charges flow.

A switch is just a link; it does not use up charge.
The bulb goes dark because current stops, not because of cold.
The cell can still make charges flow if the path is closed again.

activities.explanation: Right: current needs a continuous closed path, and the open switch breaks it.

activities.prompt: In a metal wire, electrons are flowing to the left. The conventional current is drawn as an arrow. Which way should the arrow point?
options: To the left, like the electrons.
To the right, opposite the electrons.
It should not point any way.
It should point both ways at once.

This forgets that conventional current is opposite to electron flow.
Current has a direction we show with an arrow.
Current is shown with one arrow, not two.

activities.explanation: Right: conventional current direction is opposite to electron flow.

activities.prompt: Wire A carries more charge through it each second than wire B. Both wires are the same thickness. Which wire has the bigger current?
options: Wire A, because more charge flows each second.
Wire B, because thinner wires carry more current.
Both are equal, because both are wires.
You cannot say without seeing the wires.

why.Wire B, because thinner wires carry more: This mixes up wire thickness with charge flowing per second.
Being a wire does not make currents equal.
You can say it, because current depends on charge per second.

activities.explanation: Right: current is the amount of charge flowing in unit time, so A is bigger.

activities.prompt: Meera wants to measure the current in a bulb. The current must flow in one path through the circuit. How should she place the ammeter?
options: In the path, so the current flows through it too.
Beside the path, so the current flows around it.
Anywhere, because current is the same everywhere.
Far from the bulb, so it does not block the current.

why.Beside the path, so the current flows ar: A current flowing around the ammeter never passes through it.
why.Anywhere, because current is the same ev: Placement matters; the ammeter must be part of the path.
why.Far from the bulb, so it does not block: Distance from the bulb is not the reason for series connection.

activities.explanation: Right: an ammeter measures current only when it is connected in series.

activities.prompt: In circuit X, one coulomb of charge flows past a point every second. In circuit Y, two coulombs flow past a point in two seconds. Compare the currents.
options: X has the bigger current.
Y has the bigger current.
Both have the same current.
You cannot compare them at all.

This only counts the charge and forgets the time taken.
This only counts the charge and forgets the time taken.
You can compare them by looking at charge per second.

activities.explanation: Right: one coulomb per second is one ampere, and Y also gives one coulomb per second.

lessons.sceneCaption: Circuit diagrams of a simple circuit, comparing pictorial and schematic styles.

lessons.title: Electric Potential and Potential Difference

activities.prompt: Why does charge need a 'push' to move through a wire?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What Makes Charges Move?
activities.body: Water flows only when there is a pressure difference between the two ends of a tube. In the same way, charges do not flow in a copper wire by themselves. A battery can create a difference of potential. When it is joined to a circuit, this potential difference sets the charges in motion. The work done to move a unit charge between two points is called potential difference. It is measured in volts.
keyPoints: Charges do not flow in a wire by themselves.
A battery makes a potential difference that sets charges in motion.
Potential difference is work done to move a unit charge.
Its SI unit is the volt.
activities.explanation: Just as water needs a pressure difference to flow, charges need a potential difference to move.

activities.title: Light the bulb

tasks.then: Closing the switch completes the circuit, so current flows.
More cells for each bulb push more current through it.

activities.takeaway: Current flows only round a closed circuit; more cells push more current.
activities.explanation: Current flows only round a closed circuit; more cells push more current.

activities.prompt: A torch does not glow without batteries inside. Why does the battery make the charges move?
steps: Charges do not flow in a wire by themselves, so something must push them.
A battery makes a potential difference between its two ends, like a push.
When the battery is joined to the bulb, this difference sets the charges moving.
So the battery gives the push that makes the torch glow.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The SI unit of potential difference is the ______.
activities.hint: It starts with the letter v.
activities.explanation: Great! Potential difference is measured in volts.

activities.prompt: One volt means a certain amount of work moves a certain amount of charge. Which pair is correct?
options: 1 joule of work moves 1 coulomb
1 coulomb of work moves 1 joule
1 volt of work moves 1 joule
1 metre of work moves 1 coulomb
activities.explanation: Spot on! One volt is when 1 joule of work moves 1 coulomb of charge.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what it does.
pairs: Makes potential difference by chemical action
Can produce a difference of potential
activities.explanation: Nice matching! Each part has its own special job in a circuit.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order, from first to last.
items: Chemical action in the cell makes a potential difference across its terminals.
The cell is connected to a circuit element.
The potential difference sets the charges in motion.
The cell uses its stored chemical energy to keep the current going.
activities.explanation: Perfect order! The cell first makes a potential difference, then charges move, and chemical energy keeps the current going.

activities.prompt: A cell keeps a current flowing by using its stored chemical energy. What happens if this stored energy is used up?
options: The current can no longer be maintained
The current becomes stronger
The wire changes colour
The charges flow faster by themselves
activities.explanation: Good thinking! The cell needs its chemical energy to maintain the current. Without it, the current stops.

activities.prompt: One copper wire lies alone on a table. Nothing is joined to it. A second identical wire is joined to a battery. In which wire do charges move?
options: Only in the wire joined to the battery
Only in the wire lying alone
In both wires the same way
In neither wire at all

why.Only in the wire lying alone: Thinks copper alone can make charges flow, but charges need a push.
why.In both wires the same way: Thinks all wires behave the same, but only one has a potential difference.
why.In neither wire at all: Forgets that a battery can set charges in motion in a circuit.

activities.explanation: Right: the battery makes a potential difference, and that sets charges moving.

activities.prompt: A torch glows for many hours. Then it grows dim and stops. The battery is old. Why did the charges stop moving?
options: The battery used up its stored chemical energy
The bulb used up all its potential difference
The charges inside the wire got tired
The copper wire lost all its charges

why.The bulb used up all its potential diffe: Thinks the bulb stores potential difference, but the cell is the source.
why.The charges inside the wire got tired: Thinks charges get tired, but charges stop when the push is gone.
why.The copper wire lost all its charges: Thinks wires run out of charges, but charges are not used up.

activities.explanation: Right: the cell keeps current going by using its stored chemical energy.

activities.prompt: Meera wants to measure the potential difference across a bulb. She joins the voltmeter in the path of the current. What is her mistake?
options: The voltmeter should be joined across the bulb, in parallel
The voltmeter should be joined in the path, in series
The voltmeter should be joined to the battery only
The voltmeter should be joined outside the circuit

why.The voltmeter should be joined in the pa: Thinks the meter must sit in the current path, like a check point.
why.The voltmeter should be joined to the ba: Thinks only the battery has potential difference worth measuring.
why.The voltmeter should be joined outside t: Thinks a meter works without touching the part being measured.

activities.explanation: Right: a voltmeter measures potential difference and is connected in parallel.

activities.prompt: Water flows in a pipe only when one end has more pressure. Charges in a wire behave the same way. What makes charges flow in a wire?
options: A potential difference between two points of the wire
The wire being made of copper metal
The charges pushing each other from behind
The wire being long and thin

why.The wire being made of copper metal: Thinks the material alone causes flow, but a push is needed.
why.The charges pushing each other from behi: Thinks charges push each other, but the driving cause is the difference.
why.The wire being long and thin: Thinks the wire shape causes flow, not the potential difference.

activities.explanation: Right: like water pressure, potential difference sets charges in motion.

activities.prompt: Moving one coulomb between two points takes one joule of work. Moving two coulombs between the same two points takes two joules of work. What is the potential difference between the points?
options: One volt
Two volts
Half a volt
Zero volt

why.Two volts: Thinks more work means more volts, but the work grew with the charge.
why.Half a volt: Thinks doubling charge halves the value, which is backwards.
why.Zero volt: Thinks work was wasted, but work was done moving the charges.

activities.explanation: Right: one volt means one joule of work moves one coulomb.

activities.prompt: Ravi says charges flow in any copper wire by themselves. Sana joins a wire to a cell, and charges flow. Who is right, and why?
options: Sana is right; the cell made a potential difference that moved charges
Ravi is right; copper wires always move charges by themselves
Both are right; charges flow with or without a cell
Neither is right; charges never flow in any copper wire

why.Ravi is right; copper wires always move: Thinks copper alone causes flow, but charges do not flow by themselves.
why.Both are right; charges flow with or wit: Thinks flow happens anyway, but the cell was needed here.
why.Neither is right; charges never flow in: Thinks charges can never flow, but a cell can set them moving.

activities.explanation: Right: charges need a potential difference, and the cell made one.

lessons.sceneAlt: A circuit diagram of a primary cell battery showing the difference in cell potential and electrons flowing through a resistor.
lessons.sceneCaption: Diagram of a primary cell showing difference in cell potential, and flow of electrons through a resistor.

lessons.title: Circuit Diagram and Ohm's Law

activities.prompt: How do scientists draw circuits without drawing a single wire?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Circuits, Symbols and Ohm's Law
activities.body: An electric circuit has a cell or battery, a plug key, components and wires. We draw it using a schematic diagram, where each part gets its own symbol. Ohm studied how current depends on potential difference. He found that V is directly proportional to I when temperature stays the same. The ratio V/I is a constant called resistance.
keyPoints: A circuit has a cell or battery, plug key, components and wires.
Schematic diagrams use symbols for circuit components.
Ohm's law: V is directly proportional to I at constant temperature.
V/I is a constant called resistance.
activities.explanation: Circuits can be drawn with symbols, and Ohm's law links voltage and current.

activities.prompt: Why does a ceiling fan slow down when you slide its regulator?
steps: The regulator is a rheostat, so sliding it changes the resistance in the fan circuit.
Current is inversely proportional to resistance, so more resistance makes the current smaller.
A smaller current flows through the fan, so the fan gets less push and runs slower.
So the regulator slows the fan by raising resistance, which lowers the current.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Resistance Does
activities.body: Resistance is a conductor's property to resist the flow of charge. Think of it as a crowd blocking a doorway. A bigger resistance lets less current pass, so current is inversely proportional to resistance. A rheostat is a special component that changes the resistance in a circuit, letting you control the current.
keyPoints: Resistance resists the flow of charge.
Current through a resistor is inversely proportional to resistance.
A rheostat changes resistance in a circuit.
activities.explanation: More resistance means less current, and a rheostat lets you adjust it.

activities.prompt: You want to draw a circuit neatly on paper. What does a schematic diagram use?
options: Symbols for each component
A photo of each component
Long paragraphs of text
Coloured beads and glue
activities.explanation: A schematic diagram uses symbols for circuit components, so anyone can read the drawing.

activities.prompt: The SI unit of resistance is the ______.
activities.hint: It is named after the scientist who studied current and potential difference.
activities.explanation: The unit of resistance is the ohm, shown by the Greek letter Ω.

activities.prompt: Ohm's law says V is directly proportional to I when the temperature stays constant.
activities.explanation: Well done! At constant temperature, V grows in step with I. That is Ohm's law.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with what it means.
pairs: V is proportional to I at constant temperature
activities.explanation: Each idea has its own job in the lesson. Great matching!

activities.prompt: A wire has a potential difference of 1 V across it and a current of 1 A through it. What is its resistance?
options: 1 Ω
2 Ω
0 Ω
1 A
activities.explanation: When V is 1 V and I is 1 A, the resistance is 1 Ω. You remembered it well!

activities.prompt: Put Ohm's steps of discovery in order, from first to last.
items: Ohm studied current and potential difference
He found V is proportional to I at constant temperature
He saw that V/I is a constant for a metallic wire
This constant was named resistance
The ohm (Ω) became its SI unit
activities.explanation: Ohm studied first, then found the pattern, then the constant got its name and unit. Superb ordering!

activities.prompt: A rheostat can change the resistance in a circuit. Riya turns it so the resistance goes up. What happens to the current?
options: It becomes smaller.
It becomes bigger.
It stays the same.
It stops completely.

Wrong: this mixes up the link and thinks more resistance pushes more current.
Wrong: this thinks changing resistance has no effect on current.
Wrong: this thinks any rise in resistance cuts the current off fully.

activities.explanation: Right: current is inversely proportional to resistance, so more resistance gives less current.

activities.prompt: Two wires are joined to the same battery. Wire A lets a big current flow. Wire B lets a small current flow. What does wire B have more of?
options: It has more resistance.
It has more current.
It has more charge.
It has more voltage.

Wrong: this confuses current with resistance; wire B has less current.
Wrong: this thinks the wire itself makes charge, but charge flow is the current.
Wrong: this thinks the wire changes voltage, but both wires use the same battery.

activities.explanation: Right: with the same battery, a smaller current means the wire resists the flow more.

activities.prompt: Ohm's law holds at constant temperature. Meera changes V and measures I many times for a wire. What must she keep the same for a fair test?
options: The temperature of the wire.
The current in the wire.
The length of the battery.
The reading of the voltmeter.

Wrong: current is what she measures, so it cannot be fixed.
Wrong: the battery length is not part of the law she is testing.
Wrong: the voltmeter reading is V, which she is changing on purpose.

activities.explanation: Right: the law is stated only at constant temperature, so this must not change.

activities.prompt: A student says: 'I made the resistance double. So the current also doubled.' What is wrong with this claim?
options: Current becomes half when resistance doubles.
Current becomes double when resistance halves.
Current stays the same when resistance changes.
Current becomes zero when resistance doubles.

why.Current becomes double when resistance h: Wrong: this states the correct rule but does not point out the student's mistake.
why.Current stays the same when resistance c: Wrong: this thinks resistance has no effect on current at all.
why.Current becomes zero when resistance dou: Wrong: this thinks doubling resistance stops the flow completely.

activities.explanation: Right: current is inversely proportional to resistance, so doubling resistance halves the current.

activities.prompt: A student measures V and I for a wire many times. Each time, V divided by I gives the same number. What does this show?
options: The wire has a steady resistance.
The wire has no resistance at all.
The battery voltage keeps changing.
The current changes by itself.

Wrong: this thinks a constant ratio means zero, but a constant ratio is the resistance value.
Wrong: this blames the battery, but the changing V is what the student sets.
Wrong: the current changes because V changes, not on its own.

activities.explanation: Right: V divided by I is a constant for the wire, and this constant is resistance.

activities.prompt: A book shows a circuit using symbols for the cell, key and bulb. A student in another country reads the same diagram. Why can she understand it?
options: The same symbols are used for components.
She knows the language of the book.
Real parts look the same in all places.
Every circuit must be drawn as a picture.

Wrong: symbols are pictures, not words, so the book's language does not matter.
Wrong: real parts can look different, but their symbols stay the same.
why.Every circuit must be drawn as a picture: Wrong: circuits can be drawn in many ways; symbols are just the clear choice.

activities.explanation: Right: schematic diagrams use conventional symbols, so the same symbol means the same part everywhere.

lessons.sceneAlt: A simple circuit made with a 9-volt battery, wires, an LED and a resistor laid out for building.
lessons.sceneCaption: A simple circuit with a battery, wires, LED and resistor, showing the basic parts of an electric circuit.

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Resistance

activities.prompt: Why does the same battery push different currents through different wires?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What changes resistance?
activities.body: Electrons are not completely free to move inside a conductor. Their motion is slowed by resistance. Different materials resist flow differently, so different parts let different currents pass. A part with low resistance is a good conductor. A part with noticeable resistance is called a resistor. Resistance depends on the length of the wire, its area of cross-section, and the material it is made of.
keyPoints: Resistance slows the flow of electrons in a conductor.
A low-resistance part of a given size is a good conductor; one with noticeable resistance is a resistor.
Resistance depends on length, area of cross-section, and material.
activities.explanation: Think of resistance as how much a wire slows the electron traffic passing through it.

activities.prompt: Two wires carry current to a small bulb. One wire is long and thin. The other is short and thick. The bulb glows brighter with one of them. Which wire makes the bulb glow brighter, and why?
steps: The long thin wire makes electrons travel a longer path, so it slows them more.
The short thick wire gives electrons a wider path, so it slows them less.
Less slowing means less resistance, so more current can flow through the short thick wire.
More current makes the bulb glow brighter, so the short thick wire wins.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Resistivity: the material's own mark
activities.body: Every material has its own special value called resistivity. Resistivity is a constant characteristic property of the material. It does not change when you cut the wire shorter or make it thicker. But heat it, and things change: both resistance and resistivity vary with temperature. So the same wire can resist a little more on a hot day than a cool one.
keyPoints: Resistivity is a constant characteristic property of the material.
Resistivity does not depend on the wire's length or thickness.
Both resistance and resistivity change with temperature.
activities.explanation: Resistivity is like the material's fingerprint, but warming it up can still change it a bit.

activities.prompt: A conductor with appreciable resistance is called a ______.
activities.hint: It sounds like 'resistance'.
activities.explanation: Great! A resistor is a conductor that has noticeable resistance.

activities.prompt: Two wires are made of the same material and are the same length. One wire is thicker than the other. What happens?
options: The thicker wire has less resistance
The thicker wire has more resistance
Both wires have equal resistance
Neither wire lets current pass
activities.explanation: Nice thinking! Resistance is inversely proportional to area of cross-section, so a thicker wire resists less.

activities.prompt: Match each change with its effect on resistance.
activities.explanation: Superb! Length raises resistance, area lowers it, and the material sets the resistivity.

activities.prompt: Three wires are of the same material. Put them in order from MOST resistance to LEAST resistance.
items: Long and thin wire
Long and thick wire
Short and thick wire
activities.explanation: Brilliant! More length means more resistance, and more area means less resistance.

activities.prompt: A wire's resistance is directly proportional to its length. If you join two equal pieces of this wire end to end, what happens to the resistance?
options: It stays the same
It becomes half
It doubles
It becomes zero
activities.explanation: Well done! Doubling the length doubles the resistance, because resistance is directly proportional to length.
derived: doubling length doubles resistance: resistance is directly proportional to length

activities.prompt: A fan has a long thin wire. You swap it for a short thick wire of the same material. What happens to the current in the fan?
options: It becomes less, because short wires store current
It becomes more, because the new wire slows electrons less
It stays the same, because the material did not change
It becomes zero, because the wire is too thick

why.It becomes less, because short wires sto: Wires do not store current; shorter and thicker means less resistance, not less current.
why.It stays the same, because the material: Material matters, but length and area also change the resistance here.
why.It becomes zero, because the wire is too: A thick wire does not block current; it lets current flow more easily.

activities.explanation: Correct. Shorter length and bigger area both lower resistance, so more current flows.

activities.prompt: Riya says a thick wire always has less resistance than a thin wire. Her friend tests two wires of different materials. Why is Riya's claim not always right?
options: She forgot that the material of the wire also changes resistance
She forgot that current always chooses the thickest wire
She forgot that thick wires get longer when current flows
She forgot that resistance only depends on the length

why.She forgot that current always chooses t: Current does not pick wires by thickness; resistance decides how much flows.
why.She forgot that thick wires get longer w: Wires do not stretch just because current flows through them.
why.She forgot that resistance only depends: Length matters, but area and material matter as well.

activities.explanation: Correct. Resistance depends on material too, so a thick wire of another material can resist more.

activities.prompt: A student wants to test only how length changes resistance. She has wires of many sizes. Which wire pair should she use for a fair test?
options: Same material and same area, but different lengths
Different materials and different areas, same length
Same material, but one thin and one thick wire
Different lengths and different materials, same area

why.Different materials and different areas,: Two things change at once, so she cannot tell what caused the result.
why.Same material, but one thin and one thic: Area changes here, so the test does not check length alone.
why.Different lengths and different material: Material changes too, so the result mixes two causes.

activities.explanation: Correct. Changing only the length means any change in resistance comes from length alone.

activities.prompt: Two wires are exactly the same size. One is a good conductor with low resistance. The other is an insulator. What happens when the same push is applied to both?
options: The insulator passes more current, because it is smoother
Both pass the same current, because their size is the same
The conductor passes more current, because it resists less
The insulator passes more current, because it is stronger

why.The insulator passes more current, becau: Smoothness is not the reason; the insulator resists flow much more.
why.Both pass the same current, because thei: Same size does not mean same resistance; the material matters a lot.
why.The insulator passes more current, becau: Strength of the material does not decide how much current flows.

activities.explanation: Correct. Lower resistance slows electrons less, so more current flows.

lessons.title: Resistors in Series and Parallel

activities.prompt: Why do fairy lights all go dark when just one bulb fails?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Ways to Join Resistors
activities.body: Resistors can be joined in two main ways. Joined end to end, they are in series. Think of beads on one string. Joined between the same two points, they are in parallel. Think of rungs on a ladder. In series, the same current flows through every part. In parallel, the current splits and shares between the branches.
keyPoints: Resistors joined end to end are in series.
Resistors joined between two points are in parallel.
In series the current is the same everywhere; in parallel the current divides.
activities.explanation: Series is one path; parallel is many paths between the same two points.

activities.prompt: Your fairy lights are in series. One bulb burns out. Why do all the lights go dark?
steps: The bulbs are joined end to end, so they are in series.
In series, the same current must flow through every bulb, so each bulb depends on the others.
A burnt-out bulb has a broken path, so the current cannot flow anywhere in the circuit.
So one broken bulb stops the current, and all the lights go dark together.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Why Parallel Helps
activities.body: In a parallel circuit, the total current is the sum of the currents in each branch. The total resistance goes down when you add resistors in parallel. This is why parallel circuits are so useful. Each gadget gets its own path. If one gadget stops, the others keep working happily.
keyPoints: In parallel, total current equals the sum of the branch currents.
Total resistance in parallel decreases.
Each gadget in parallel has its own path for current.
activities.explanation: More paths means easier flow, so parallel lowers the total resistance.

activities.prompt: Three resistors are joined end to end in one line. How are they connected?
options: In parallel
In series
In a mixed way
Not connected
activities.explanation: Well done! End to end means series, like beads on one string.

activities.prompt: In a series circuit, the current is the ______ in every part of the circuit.
activities.hint: Think of one road with the same traffic all along it.
activities.explanation: Great! Series has only one path, so the same current flows everywhere.

activities.prompt: You join two resistors in series. How does the equivalent resistance compare with each single resistor?
options: It is smaller than each
It is equal to each
It is greater than each
It becomes zero
activities.explanation: Correct! In series the resistances add up, so the total is greater than any one of them.

activities.prompt: Match each circuit type with what happens in it.
pairs: Adds up to a bigger total
activities.explanation: Nice matching! Series shares the current equally; parallel shares it into branches.

activities.prompt: Put these events in order when one bulb fails in a series circuit.
items: Current flows through every bulb
One bulb stops working
The circuit breaks
None of the bulbs work
activities.explanation: Spot on! In series there is one path, so one failure breaks the whole circuit.

activities.prompt: Two resistors, each of 2 ohms, are joined in parallel. Their equivalent resistance is ______ ohm.
activities.hint: Add the reciprocals: one half plus one half, then flip it.
activities.explanation: Brilliant! Half plus half makes one whole, so the answer is 1 ohm. Parallel always lowers resistance.

activities.prompt: A string of old fairy lights is in series. One bulb breaks and the whole string goes dark. Your new lights are in parallel. One bulb breaks. What happens to the other bulbs?
options: All the other bulbs go dark too.
The other bulbs keep glowing brightly.
The other bulbs glow for a moment, then stop.
The other bulbs glow less brightly than before.

This treats parallel like series, where one break stops everything.
why.The other bulbs glow for a moment, then: There is no reason the others would stop after a delay.
why.The other bulbs glow less brightly than: The other bulbs have their own paths, so their current does not change.

activities.explanation: Right. In parallel each bulb has its own path, so one break does not stop the others.

activities.prompt: Two identical bulbs are in series with a battery. You connect a third identical bulb in parallel with the second bulb. What happens to the total resistance of the circuit?
options: It increases, because there are more bulbs now.
It stays the same, because the bulbs are identical.
It decreases, because parallel paths give more ways for current.
It becomes zero, because the extra bulb shorts the circuit.

why.It increases, because there are more bul: This counts bulbs instead of thinking about how they are connected.
why.It stays the same, because the bulbs are: Identical bulbs do not matter; how they are connected matters.
why.It becomes zero, because the extra bulb: A parallel bulb is still a resistor, so the resistance does not vanish.

activities.explanation: Right. Adding a parallel path decreases the total resistance.

activities.prompt: Two resistors are connected between the same two points. A student wants to find which connection makes the total resistance smaller. Which test is fair?
options: Compare the total resistance when they are in parallel with when they are in series.
Compare the series total with just one resistor alone in the circuit.
Compare the parallel total with the sum of both resistances added.
Compare the current in parallel with the current in one branch only.

why.Compare the series total with just one r: This compares different circuits, not the two ways of joining the same two resistors.
why.Compare the parallel total with the sum: The sum of resistances is the series total, so this does not test parallel against series.
why.Compare the current in parallel with the: One branch is not the total, so this compares a part with the whole.

activities.explanation: Right. Comparing the same two resistors in both connections shows which gives smaller total resistance.

activities.prompt: A classroom has many gadgets connected in parallel. A student claims the total resistance of the whole parallel circuit grows bigger as more gadgets are switched on. Is the student right?
options: Yes, because more gadgets mean more resistance added up.
Yes, because more gadgets make the current smaller.
No, because each new parallel path makes the total resistance smaller.
No, because gadgets in parallel have no resistance at all.

why.Yes, because more gadgets mean more resi: This adds resistances like series, but parallel works differently.
why.Yes, because more gadgets make the curre: More gadgets in parallel actually make the total current bigger.
why.No, because gadgets in parallel have no: Gadgets do have resistance; the paths just combine to lower the total.

activities.explanation: Right. Each new parallel path lets more current flow, so total resistance decreases.

lessons.sceneCaption: Simple conception of 3 bulbs connected in series versus parallel.

lessons.title: Heating Effect and Electric Power

activities.prompt: Why does your phone charger get warm when it's charging?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: When Current Makes Heat
activities.body: When current flows through a wire, the wire can get warm. In a purely resistive circuit, all the source energy turns into heat. This is called the heating effect of electric current. It is why a heater warms a room and an iron smooths your clothes. The heat made in time t is H = VIt. Electric power is measured in watts.
keyPoints: In a purely resistive circuit, source energy becomes heat.
This is the heating effect of electric current.
Heaters and irons use this effect.
Heat in time t is H = VIt.
Power is measured in watts.
activities.explanation: Electric current can do useful work by making heat.

activities.prompt: A fuse wire is very thin. The main wire in the circuit is thick. The same current flows through both. Why does only the fuse melt when the current gets too high?
steps: The fuse is in series with the device, so the same current flows through the fuse and the wire.
The fuse wire is thin, so it has more resistance than the thick main wire.
For the same current, more resistance makes more heat, so the fuse heats up much faster.
So the fuse gets hot enough to melt first and stops the current before the device is harmed.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: In a purely resistive circuit, what happens to the source energy?
options: It turns into heat
It turns into light
It disappears completely
It turns into sound
activities.explanation: In a purely resistive circuit, the energy is dissipated entirely as heat.

activities.prompt: What is the SI unit of electric power?
options: Volt
Watt
Ampere
Ohm
activities.explanation: The SI unit of electric power is the watt.

activities.prompt: Joule's law says the heat produced is H = ______.
activities.hint: It uses current, resistance and time.
activities.explanation: Joule's law gives H = I2Rt. It links heat to current, resistance and time.

activities.prompt: Match each item with what it does.
pairs: Uses heating effect to warm a room
Uses heating effect to press clothes
activities.explanation: Heaters and irons use the heating effect. A fuse keeps circuits safe.

activities.prompt: Why does a fuse protect a circuit?
options: It stops unduly high current
It makes the current stronger
It stores extra energy
It cools the wires down
activities.explanation: A fuse protects circuits by stopping unduly high current. That keeps the circuit safe.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to show how a fuse keeps a device safe.
items: Current flows through the circuit
The current becomes unduly high
The fuse stops the high current
The device stays safe
activities.explanation: The fuse sits in series, so when the current grows too high, it stops it and saves the device.

activities.prompt: Two wires carry the same current. One wire is thin. One wire is thick. The thin wire has more resistance. Which wire gets hotter?
options: The thin wire gets hotter
The thick wire gets hotter
Both wires get equally hot
Neither wire gets hot at all

why.The thick wire gets hotter: Thinks a thicker wire carries more, so it must heat more.
why.Both wires get equally hot: Thinks current alone decides heat and resistance does not matter.
why.Neither wire gets hot at all: Thinks wires never heat up when current flows.

activities.explanation: Right: for the same current, more resistance makes more heat.

activities.prompt: Ravi heats water with a coil of fixed resistance. He says: 'If I double the current, the heat doubles too.' What is wrong with his claim?
options: The heat actually becomes four times
The heat actually stays the same
The heat actually becomes half
The heat actually becomes two times

why.The heat actually stays the same: Thinks resistance changes when current changes.
why.The heat actually becomes half: Thinks more current somehow means less heat.
why.The heat actually becomes two times: Thinks heat grows in step with current, not with its square.

activities.explanation: Right: heat depends on the square of current, and two squared is four.

activities.prompt: Meera wants to test how current changes the heating of a coil. She wants a fair test. What must she keep the same?
options: Same resistance and same time
Same current and same time
Same current and same resistance
Different resistance and different time

why.Same current and same time: Keeps the thing she is testing fixed, so the test cannot work.
why.Same current and same resistance: Changes everything, so no fair comparison is possible.
why.Different resistance and different time: Changes two things at once, so she cannot tell what caused the heat.

activities.explanation: Right: only the current should change, so resistance and time must stay fixed.

activities.prompt: Too many appliances run on one socket. The current becomes too high. A fuse is in series with the circuit. What happens?
options: The fuse melts and stops the current
The fuse lets even more current pass
The appliances receive even more current
Nothing changes in the circuit

why.The fuse lets even more current pass: Thinks a fuse helps push more current through.
why.The appliances receive even more current: Thinks the fuse protects appliances by giving them more current.
why.Nothing changes in the circuit: Thinks a fuse sits there but never does anything.

activities.explanation: Right: the fuse heats up on high current and breaks the circuit.

lessons.sceneAlt: A comparison of a simple circuit drawn in pictorial style and the same circuit drawn in schematic style.
lessons.sceneCaption: Circuit diagrams of a simple circuit, comparing pictorial and schematic styles.
